preface.title: Preface: How to Use This Document

secs.t: Preface: How to Use This Document
secs.html:
This document is a single, sequenced path from 9th-grade mathematics to the research frontier of rocketry, hypersonic flight and advanced space propulsion. It is written from first principles: each result is derived from, or explicitly traced to, something established earlier. It is concise by design. Every definition, assumption and limit of validity is stated so that nothing is left to interpretation. Depth beyond the essential core is delegated to the canonical texts listed in Appendix K.

Honest scope statement. No single document can contain literally everything a field knows. What this document does contain is (1) the complete map of required knowledge, with nothing essential missing; (2) the essential core of every topic at the depth needed to use it correctly; and (3) a quiz after every chapter that tests both that chapter and its dependence on earlier ones. Mastery means you can derive each boxed result unaided, apply it to a new problem, and state when it fails.

Part Level Chapters What you gain
I Grades 9–12 1–7 Units, algebra, trigonometry, conics, Newtonian physics, chemistry, first rocket physics
II Undergraduate mathematics 8–14 Calculus, vector calculus, linear algebra, ODEs/PDEs, statistics, numerical methods
III Undergraduate engineering science 15–22 Dynamics, thermodynamics, combustion, fluids, heat transfer, solids, electromagnetism, control
IV Aerospace engineering core 23–35 Compressible flow, aerodynamics, rocket propulsion, astrodynamics, flight mechanics, structures, avionics, systems engineering
V Graduate (MS/PhD coursework) 36–50 Hypersonics, high-temperature and rarefied gas dynamics, heating, TPS, entry, scramjets, CFD, GNC, advanced combustion, plasma and electric propulsion, testing, MDO/UQ
VI Doctoral, postdoctoral and beyond 51–54 Beyond-chemical propulsion, research methodology, open problems, professional practice

Appendices provide notation (A), constants and planetary data (B), a mathematics reference (C), computed tables for the standard atmosphere (D), compressible flow (E), oblique shocks and cones (F), and rocket nozzles (G), propellant and material data (H), a year-by-year study roadmap with capstone projects (I), the quiz answer keys (J), an annotated bibliography (K), a glossary (L), three integrated worked case studies (M), a master formula sheet (N), and a safety, dual-use and learning-pathways register (O).

1. Read a section once for structure, then again for every assumption.
  2. Derive every boxed result on paper without looking. If you cannot, re-read the chapter it builds on.
  3. Quiz yourself at the end of the chapter, closed-book. Questions are tagged [C] concept, [N] numerical, and [I: Ch x] integrative (draws on earlier chapter x).
  4. Check against Appendix J. A wrong answer points to a specific prerequisite; go back to it.
  5. Build something: a short program, a calculation spreadsheet or (safely) hardware. Appendix I lists projects in order.

Proceed to the next chapter only when you score at least 80% and can explain each missed item.

SI units are used throughout; US customary conversions are in Appendix B. Vectors are bold (\mathbf{v}), unit vectors carry a hat (\widehat{\mathbf{n}}), and g_{0} = 9.80665\ m/s^{2} exactly. Subscripts: 0 or t = stagnation (total), \infty = freestream, * = sonic, c = chamber, e = exit (or boundary-layer edge, as stated), a = ambient, w = wall. Every symbol is defined where first used and collected in Appendix A.

The content follows openly published university curricula and the open literature. It deliberately omits energetic-material formulations and manufacturing procedures, and any weapon-specific design, targeting or intercept content. Hands-on work should use certified commercial motors under the National Association of Rocketry or Tripoli Rocketry Association safety codes and the applicable aviation regulations (Chapter 54). Rocketry is dual-use: Chapter 54 explains export-control law and professional responsibility, which every practitioner must know.

The rule applied throughout: the document teaches the open, university-level science and engineering principles, and leaves out material whose main value is enabling harm, or that the law permits only under supervision or authorization. Wherever a section touches such material, an orange Safety and scope flag box at the end of that section states the concern, explains the concepts that make it a concern, names anything deliberately omitted, and lists sanctioned ways to learn more. Flags use four categories:

  • Physical hazard: the activity or substance can injure or kill.
  • Legal: the activity requires licenses, permits or certifications.
  • Dual-use or export control: the knowledge enables weapons or is controlled by export law.
  • Omitted content: material left out of this document on purpose.

Appendix O collects every flag in one register and lists sanctioned learning pathways for every stage, from secondary school to professional practice.

parts.title: Foundations (Grades 9–12)
parts.html: Part I builds the toolkit every later chapter assumes: exact use of units, algebraic and trigonometric fluency, the geometry of orbits (conic sections), Newtonian mechanics, the chemistry of combustion, and the first physics of rockets. Nothing here is optional. Most errors made by graduate students trace back to a weakness in this part.

parts.title: Undergraduate Mathematics
parts.html: Mathematics is the language in which every later law is written. Part II covers the calculus of one and several variables, linear algebra, ordinary and partial differential equations, probability and statistics, and numerical methods. Each chapter is aimed at the specific uses that rocketry and hypersonics make of it.

parts.title: Undergraduate Engineering Science
parts.html: Part III turns mathematics into physics and engineering. Dynamics in rotating frames, the laws of thermodynamics, chemical equilibrium and kinetics, fluid mechanics, heat transfer, solid mechanics, electromagnetism and feedback control are the eight pillars on which every aerospace discipline stands.

parts.title: Aerospace Engineering Core
parts.html: Part IV is the professional core of aerospace engineering: how compressible gases flow through nozzles and around vehicles, how rocket engines and motors work and are designed, how spacecraft move under gravity, how launch vehicles fly and are steered, how structures survive, how avionics sense and communicate, and how all of it is organized into a reliable system.

parts.title: Graduate Level: Hypersonics and Advanced Topics
parts.html: Part V is the content of master’s and doctoral coursework in hypersonics, propulsion and guidance. It assumes everything before it. Hypersonic flight differs from supersonic flight in kind, not just degree: the gas stops behaving as a perfect gas, boundary layers interact with shocks and with chemistry, heating dominates design, and no ground facility can reproduce flight completely. These chapters give the theory, the models, the computational and experimental tools, and the design methods.

parts.title: Doctoral, Postdoctoral and Beyond
parts.html: The last part looks past chemical rockets and past the classroom. It covers the physical limits and the candidate technologies beyond chemical propulsion; how original research is actually done, written and funded; the open problems where new knowledge is most needed, with a concrete strategy for surpassing today’s leading programs; and the safety, ethical, legal and export-control responsibilities that come with this field.

chapters.title: Method, Units and Dimensional Analysis

secs.html:
A physical quantity is a number times a unit: p = 101\, 325\ Pa. The International System (SI) defines seven base units by fixing exact values of natural constants (2019 redefinition): the second (caesium hyperfine frequency), metre (speed of light c = 299\, 792\, 458 m/s), kilogram (Planck constant h), ampere (elementary charge e), kelvin (Boltzmann constant k_{B}), mole (Avogadro constant N_{A}), and candela. All other units are derived:

Quantity Unit In base units
Force newton (N) kg\, m\, s^{- 2}
Pressure, stress pascal (Pa) N\, m^{- 2} = kg\, m^{- 1}\, s^{- 2}
Energy, work, heat joule (J) N\, m = kg\, m^{2}\, s^{- 2}
Power watt (W) J\, s^{- 1}
Charge coulomb (C) A\, s
Voltage volt (V) W\, A^{- 1}

Prefixes: n (10^{- 9}), μ (10^{- 6}), m (10^{- 3}), k (10^{3}), M (10^{6}), G (10^{9}). Temperature in thermodynamic equations is always absolute (K); T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.

Every quantity has a dimension built from mass M, length L, time T, temperature \Theta (plus current and amount when needed). Write \lbrack F\rbrack = MLT^{- 2}.

Rule of homogeneity. Every additive term in a valid physical equation has the same dimension, and the argument of any transcendental function (\exp, \ln, \sin, …) is dimensionless. An equation that violates this is wrong, whatever its source.

Example: the rocket thrust equation F = \dot{m}v_{e} + \left( p_{e} - p_{a} \right)A_{e}. Term 1: (kg/s)(m/s) = kg\, m\, s^{- 2}. Term 2: \left( N/m^{2} \right)\left( m^{2} \right) = N. Consistent. A logarithm such as \ln\left( m_{0}/m_{f} \right) is legitimate because m_{0}/m_{f} is dimensionless; \ln\left( m_{0} \right) alone is not.

Multiply by factors equal to one: 1 = 0.3048\ m/1\ ft. Exact definitions: 1 ft = 0.3048 m; 1 lbm = 0.45359237 kg; 1 nautical mile = 1852 m; 1 in = 25.4 mm. Derived: 1 lbf = 4.448222 N; 1 psi = 6894.757 Pa; 1 slug = 14.5939 kg; 1 BTU = 1055.06 J; T(°R) = 1.8 T(K).

The pound-mass/pound-force system needs the constant g_{c} = 32.174\ lbm\, ft/\left( lbf\, s^{2} \right): F = ma/g_{c}. Specific impulse in seconds, I_{sp} = F/\left( \dot{m}g_{0} \right), has the same numerical value in SI and US units, which is why it is quoted in seconds.

Pitfalls. (1) Mass vs weight: weight is a force, W = mg. (2) Gauge vs absolute pressure: p_{abs} = p_{gauge} + p_{atm}; “psig” vs “psia”. (3) Degrees vs radians in calculators and code. (4) Celsius in gas laws. (5) Mixed units between teams: the Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 because one team’s software output impulse in pound-force seconds while the navigation software expected newton-seconds.

A measurement is x \pm u_{x}, where u_{x} is its uncertainty; the relative uncertainty is u_{x}/|x|. Report results to the precision the inputs justify. Before any detailed calculation, make an order-of-magnitude estimate: round inputs to one significant figure and powers of ten. After the calculation, apply four sanity checks: units, limiting cases (does the result behave correctly as a parameter goes to 0 or ∞?), symmetry, and magnitude against known values.

secs.t: Dimensional analysis and the Buckingham Π theorem
secs.html:
Buckingham Π theorem. If a physical relation involves n variables containing k independent dimensions, it can be rewritten as a relation among n - k independent dimensionless groups \Pi_{1},\ldots,\Pi_{n - k}.

Procedure: (1) list all relevant variables; (2) pick k repeating variables that together contain all dimensions and cannot themselves form a dimensionless group; (3) combine each remaining variable with powers of the repeating ones to make it dimensionless.

Example (drag): F = f(\rho,V,L,\mu,a), with n = 6, k = 3. Repeating variables \rho,V,L give

C_{D} = \frac{F}{\frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}L^{2}} = \phi\left( Re = \frac{\rho VL}{\mu},\; M = \frac{V}{a} \right).

This is why a wind-tunnel model gives flight-relevant data only if Re and M (and, later, other groups) match flight. Chapter 18 develops similarity fully; Chapter 49 shows why hypersonic testing cannot match all groups at once.

quiz.q: Which of these are SI base units: newton, kilogram, kelvin, joule, ampere, mole?
quiz.a: Kilogram, kelvin, ampere and mole are base units. The newton and the joule are derived.

quiz.q: Convert 1 psi to Pa, 1 lbf to N, and 10 000 ft to m.
An engine produces 1.8 MN of thrust. Express this in lbf.
quiz.a: 1.8 \times 10^{6}/4.448222 = 4.047 \times 10^{5} lbf.

quiz.q: Show that p = \rho gh and q = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2} are dimensionally consistent and give the SI unit of q.
quiz.a: \rho gh: \left( kg\, m^{- 3} \right)\left( m\, s^{- 2} \right)(m) = kg\, m^{- 1}s^{- 2} = Pa. \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}: \left( kg\, m^{- 3} \right)\left( m^{2}s^{- 2} \right) = Pa. Dynamic pressure is a pressure and is measured in Pa.

quiz.q: Assume a pendulum period obeys T_{p} = kL^{a}g^{b}. Find a and b by dimensional analysis.
quiz.a: T = L^{a}\left( LT^{- 2} \right)^{b}. Equating powers: L: a + b = 0; T: - 2b = 1. So b = - \frac{1}{2}, a = \frac{1}{2} and T_{p} = k\sqrt{L/g}; the full analysis of Chapter 15 gives k = 2\pi.

quiz.q: Compute the kinetic energy of a 1000 kg vehicle at orbital speed, 7.8 km/s. What mass of kerosene (43 MJ/kg) releases the same energy on burning? Comment.
quiz.a: E = \frac{1}{2}(1000)(7800)^{2} = 3.04 \times 10^{10} J, equal to the combustion energy of about 707 kg of kerosene. Orbital kinetic energy per kilogram (30 MJ/kg) is comparable to chemical energy per kilogram of fuel alone, and the oxidizer adds mass that releases no energy of its own. That is the root reason rockets are mostly propellant.

quiz.q: Convert I_{sp} = 300 s to effective exhaust velocity in m/s.
quiz.a: c = I_{sp}g_{0} = 300 \times 9.80665 = 2942 m/s.

quiz.q: One report gives a chamber pressure of 2000 psig; another gives 13.9 MPa. Are they consistent? Explain.
quiz.a: 2000\ psig + 14.696 = 2014.7 psia = 13.89 MPa absolute. They agree to three figures. Always state whether a pressure is gauge or absolute.

chapters.goalsHtml: use SI units exactly; convert between unit systems without error; check every equation dimensionally; reduce a physical problem to dimensionless groups.

chapters.title: Algebra, Functions, Exponentials and Logarithms

secs.html: A linear system in two unknowns, a_{1}x + b_{1}y = c_{1} and a_{2}x + b_{2}y = c_{2}, is solved by substitution or elimination. Geometrically each equation is a line. The system has one solution if the lines intersect, none if they are parallel, and infinitely many if they coincide. The determinant D = a_{1}b_{2} - a_{2}b_{1} decides which: a unique solution exists if and only if D \neq 0. Chapter 10 generalizes this to n unknowns as \mathbf{Ax} = \mathbf{b}.

ax^{2} + bx + c = 0\; \Rightarrow \; x = \frac{- b \pm \sqrt{b^{2} - 4ac}}{2a}.

The discriminant \Delta = b^{2} - 4ac gives two real roots (\Delta > 0), one repeated root (\Delta = 0) or a complex pair (\Delta < 0). The vertex lies at x = - b/(2a). Vertical motion under constant gravity, h(t) = v_{0}t - \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}, is quadratic: peak time t^{*} = v_{0}/g, peak height v_{0}^{2}/(2g), return time 2v_{0}/g.

A function f assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain. It has an inverse f^{- 1} only on an interval where it is one-to-one (strictly monotonic). Composition is written (f \circ g)(x) = f\left( g(x) \right). Graph transformations: f(x - h) + k shifts the graph right by h and up by k; af(bx) stretches it vertically by a and compresses it horizontally by b. A function is even if f( - x) = f(x) and odd if f( - x) = - f(x).

For a > 0: a^{x + y} = a^{x}a^{y}, \left( a^{x} \right)^{y} = a^{xy}, a^{0} = 1. The logarithm inverts the exponential: y = \log_{a}x \Leftrightarrow a^{y} = x. Its laws are \log(xy) = logx + logy, \log\left( x^{n} \right) = n\log x, and \log_{a}x = lnx/lna. The natural base is

e = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}\left( 1 + \frac{1}{n} \right)^{n} = 2.718281828\ldots,\quad\quad\ln x \equiv \log_{e}x.

Exponential decay: N(t) = N_{0}e^{- t/\tau}, with half-life \tau\ln 2. Isothermal atmosphere: \rho(h) = \rho_{0}e^{- h/H}, with scale height H = RT/g \approx 7–8.5 km on Earth (derived in Chapter 18).

Preview of the rocket equation. \Delta v = c\ln\left( m_{0}/m_{f} \right), equivalently m_{0}/m_{f} = e^{\Delta v/c}. The mass ratio grows exponentially with the velocity change demanded. This single fact shapes all of launch-vehicle design (Chapters 7 and 26).

secs.t: Power laws, scaling and log–log plots
secs.html: y = kx^{n} becomes \log y = logk + n\log x: a straight line of slope n on log–log axes. Fitting such a line to data reveals the exponent of an unknown law. Geometric scaling: if every length scales by s, areas scale by s^{2} and volumes by s^{3} (the square–cube law). A tank’s propellant capacity therefore grows faster than its wall area, which is one reason larger launch vehicles achieve better mass fractions. Aerodynamic drag scales as V^{2}, and heating rates (Chapter 41) as roughly V^{3}.

Multiplying an inequality by a negative number reverses it. |x - a| < \delta means a - \delta < x < a + \delta. Engineering uses ordering constantly: x \ll 1 means terms of order x^{2} may be neglected relative to terms of order x. Each such neglect is an assumption that must be stated and later checked.

Pitfalls. “log” means \log_{10} in most engineering tables but \ln in most programming languages. Take logarithms only of dimensionless ratios. \ln(a + b) \neq lna + lnb.

quiz.q: Solve 3x + 2y = 12, x - y = - 1.
quiz.a: From the second equation, x = y - 1. Substituting: 3y - 3 + 2y = 12, so y = 3 and x = 2.

quiz.q: A ball has height h(t) = 20t - 4.9t^{2} (SI units). Find its maximum height, the time it occurs and the landing time.
quiz.a: t^{*} = 20/9.8 = 2.04 s; h_{\max} = 20^{2}/(4 \times 4.9) = 20.4 m; landing at t = 40/9.8 = 4.08 s.

quiz.q: Solve 2^{x} = 10. Simplify \ln\left( e^{3} \right).
quiz.a: x = ln10/ln2 = 3.322; \ln\left( e^{3} \right) = 3.

quiz.q: A vehicle needs \Delta v = 9.4 km/s with c = 3.3 km/s. Find the required mass ratio m_{0}/m_{f} and the fraction of liftoff mass that is propellant.
quiz.a: m_{0}/m_{f} = e^{9.4/3.3} = 17.26. Propellant fraction = 1 - 1/17.26 = 0.942: 94.2% of liftoff mass would be propellant, leaving 5.8% for structure, engines and payload. A single stage cannot do this practically (Chapter 26).

quiz.q: For an isothermal atmosphere with H = 8.5 km, compute \rho(30\ km)/\rho_{0}.
quiz.a: e^{- 30/8.5} = 0.0293, about 3% of sea-level density.

quiz.q: How does y = 5x^{3} appear on log–log axes?
quiz.a: A straight line of slope 3 that crosses \log y = log5 at x = 1.

quiz.q: A spherical tank’s radius is doubled at the same wall thickness. By what factors do the propellant volume and the wall mass change?
quiz.a: Volume scales by 2^{3} = 8; wall area, and hence wall mass, by 2^{2} = 4. (Chapter 20 shows that a constant stress limit actually requires the wall thickness to scale with radius.)

quiz.q: Is \Delta v = c\ln\left( m_{0} \right) - c\ln\left( m_{f} \right) dimensionally acceptable? Explain.
quiz.a: Taken separately, each term is the logarithm of a dimensional quantity, which is meaningless. Their difference equals c\ln\left( m_{0}/m_{f} \right), which is valid, but write it that way.

chapters.goalsHtml: solve linear systems and quadratics; manipulate functions and inverses; use exponentials, logarithms and power laws fluently. These underlie the rocket equation, the atmosphere model and every scaling law in the document.

chapters.title: Geometry, Trigonometry and Vectors

secs.html:
Shape Area or surface Volume
Circle, radius r \pi r^{2} (circumference 2\pi r) —
Sphere 4\pi r^{2} \frac{4}{3}\pi r^{3}
Cylinder, length \ell 2\pi r\ell (side) \pi r^{2}\ell
Cone, height h, slant s \pi rs (side) \frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h
Ellipse, semi-axes a,b \pi ab —

Similar triangles have equal angles and proportional sides. Pythagoras: c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2} for a right triangle.

The radian is the angle subtending an arc equal to the radius: arc length s = r\theta (\theta in rad), 1\ rad = {57.29578}^{\circ}. Angular speed \omega = d\theta/dt gives tangential speed v = \omega r. All calculus formulas for trigonometric functions assume radians.

On the unit circle, a point at angle \theta has coordinates \left( \cos\theta,sin\theta \right); \tan\theta = sin\theta/cos\theta. Core identities:

\sin^{2}\theta + \cos^{2}\theta = 1,\quad\quad\sin(a \pm b) = sina\cos b \pm cosa\sin b,\quad\quad\cos(a \pm b) = cosa\cos b \mp \sin a\sin b,

\sin 2\theta = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta,\quad\quad\cos 2\theta = \cos^{2}\theta - \sin^{2}\theta = 1 - 2\sin^{2}\theta.

For small \theta (rad): \sin\theta \approx \theta, \tan\theta \approx \theta, \cos\theta \approx 1 - \theta^{2}/2. Inverse functions have restricted ranges: arcsin \in \lbrack - \pi/2,\pi/2\rbrack, arccos \in \lbrack 0,\pi\rbrack. Use the two-argument function atan2(y,x) to obtain the correct quadrant.

For any triangle with sides a,b,c opposite angles A,B,C:

\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} = \frac{c}{\sin C},\quad\quad c^{2} = a^{2} + b^{2} - 2ab\cos C.

The law of cosines reappears in velocity triangles, for example in the plane-change maneuvers of Chapter 29.

A vector has magnitude and direction: \mathbf{a} = a_{x}\widehat{\mathbf{i}} + a_{y}\widehat{\mathbf{j}} + a_{z}\widehat{\mathbf{k}}, with \left| \mathbf{a} \right| = \sqrt{a_{x}^{2} + a_{y}^{2} + a_{z}^{2}} and unit vector \widehat{\mathbf{a}} = \mathbf{a}/\left| \mathbf{a} \right|.

Dot product: \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = \left| \mathbf{a} \right|\left| \mathbf{b} \right|\cos\theta = a_{x}b_{x} + a_{y}b_{y} + a_{z}b_{z}; zero for perpendicular vectors. The projection of \mathbf{a} on \widehat{\mathbf{b}} is \mathbf{a} \cdot \widehat{\mathbf{b}}. Cross product: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \left( a_{y}b_{z} - a_{z}b_{y},\ a_{z}b_{x} - a_{x}b_{z},\ a_{x}b_{y} - a_{y}b_{x} \right), magnitude \left| \mathbf{a} \right|\left| \mathbf{b} \right|\sin\theta, direction by the right-hand rule, and \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = - \mathbf{b} \times \mathbf{a}.

Applications: work is \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{d}; torque is \mathbf{\tau} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{F}; angular momentum is \mathbf{h} = \mathbf{r} \times m\mathbf{v}. A thrust vector gimballed by angle \delta has an axial component F\cos\delta and a lateral (steering) component F\sin\delta.

Rotating a vector counterclockwise by \theta (an active rotation):

\begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & - \sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix}.

Expressing a fixed vector in a coordinate frame rotated by \theta (a passive rotation) uses the transpose. Confusing the two is the most common sign error in attitude work (Chapter 32).

On a sphere, the shortest path between two points is a great-circle arc. The central angle d between latitudes and longitudes \left( \phi_{1},\lambda_{1} \right) and \left( \phi_{2},\lambda_{2} \right) satisfies

\cos d = sin\phi_{1}\sin\phi_{2} + cos\phi_{1}\cos\phi_{2}\cos\left( \lambda_{2} - \lambda_{1} \right),

and the surface distance is Rd. Ground tracks and launch azimuths (Chapter 29) use this geometry.

Pitfalls. Using \arctan(y/x) instead of atan2(y,x) loses the quadrant. Small-angle formulas need radians. The order of factors in a cross product matters.

quiz.q: A propellant tank is a cylinder of radius 1.5 m and length 10 m with hemispherical end caps. Compute its volume.
Convert 30° to radians. Using R = 6371 km, find the surface distance spanned by 1° of a great circle.
quiz.a: 30^{\circ} = \pi/6 = 0.5236 rad. s = R\theta = 6371 \times \pi/180 = 111.2 km.

quiz.q: A 100 kN thrust is gimballed 5°. Find its axial and lateral components.
quiz.a: Axial: 100\cos 5^{\circ} = 99.62 kN. Lateral: 100\sin 5^{\circ} = 8.716 kN.

quiz.q: For \mathbf{a} = (3,4,0) and \mathbf{b} = (4, - 3,5), compute \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} and \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}. What does the dot product tell you?
quiz.a: \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = 12 - 12 + 0 = 0, so the vectors are perpendicular. \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \left( 4 \cdot 5 - 0,\ 0 - 3 \cdot 5,\ 3( - 3) - 4 \cdot 4 \right) = (20, - 15, - 25).

quiz.q: Two stations are 300 km and 400 km from a tracking site, separated by 60° as seen from the site. How far apart are the stations?
What is the relative error of \sin\theta \approx \theta at \theta = 10^{\circ}?
quiz.a: \theta = 0.17453 and \sin\theta = 0.17365, a relative error of 0.51%.

quiz.q: Rotate the vector (1,0) counterclockwise by 30°.
quiz.a: \left( \cos 30^{\circ},sin30^{\circ} \right) = (0.866,0.5).

quiz.q: A nose cone of base radius 0.5 m has a volume of 0.5 m³. Find its height.
quiz.a: h = 3V/\left( \pi r^{2} \right) = 1.5/(\pi \times 0.25) = 1.910 m.

chapters.goalsHtml: compute areas and volumes of vehicle shapes; master radians and trigonometric identities; resolve, add and multiply vectors; rotate coordinates.

chapters.title: Precalculus: Polar Coordinates, Conic Sections, Complex Numbers and Series

secs.html: A point is (r,\theta) with x = r\cos\theta, y = r\sin\theta, and conversely r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}, \theta = atan2(y,x). A curve r = f(\theta) is natural whenever motion is organized around a center, as orbits are around a planet.

A conic is the set of points whose distance to a focus equals e times the distance to a line (the directrix); e is the eccentricity. With the focus at the origin and \theta measured from the closest point:

Polar equation of a conic: r = \frac{p}{1 + e\cos\theta}, where p is the semi-latus rectum. e = 0: circle; 0 < e < 1: ellipse; e = 1: parabola; e > 1: hyperbola.

For the ellipse, with semi-major axis a and semi-minor axis b:

p = a\left( 1 - e^{2} \right),\quad b = a\sqrt{1 - e^{2}},\quad r_{\min} = a(1 - e),\quad r_{\max} = a(1 + e),\quad\frac{x^{2}}{a^{2}} + \frac{y^{2}}{b^{2}} = 1\text{ (centered form)}.

The foci lie at distance c = ae from the center. For a parabola, r_{\min} = p/2 and r \rightarrow \infty as \theta \rightarrow \pi. For a hyperbola, r \rightarrow \infty as \cos\theta \rightarrow - 1/e, so the asymptotes are at \theta_{\infty} = arccos( - 1/e). In orbital mechanics the hyperbola’s a is taken negative so that p = a\left( 1 - e^{2} \right) > 0 still holds.

A curve may be given as x(t),y(t). The ellipse in centered coordinates is x = a\cos E, y = b\sin E. The parameter E (the eccentric anomaly) is the key to computing time along an orbit (Kepler’s equation, Chapter 29).

z = x + iy with i^{2} = - 1. Modulus |z| = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}, argument \arg z = atan2(y,x), conjugate \bar{z} = x - iy, and z\bar{z} = |z|^{2}.

Euler’s formula: e^{i\theta} = cos\theta + i\sin\theta, so z = |z|e^{i\arg z}. Multiplying by e^{i\phi} rotates by \phi; multiplying moduli scales. De Moivre: \left( e^{i\theta} \right)^{n} = e^{in\theta}.

Oscillations are represented as phasors: x(t) = Re\{ Ae^{i\omega t}\}, where the complex amplitude A carries amplitude and phase. Complex numbers become indispensable in vibrations (Chapter 11), signals (Chapter 21), control (Chapter 22) and potential flow (Chapter 12).

A geometric series with ratio r has partial sum S_{n} = a\left( 1 - r^{n} \right)/(1 - r) and converges to a/(1 - r) when |r| < 1. Sigma notation: \sum_{k = 0}^{n}a_{k}. An infinite series converges only if its terms tend to zero (necessary but not sufficient: \sum 1/k diverges). Chapter 8 extends this to Taylor series.

secs.t: The binomial theorem and first-order approximations
secs.html:
(1 + x)^{n} = \sum_{k = 0}^{n}\binom{n}{k}x^{k},\quad\quad(1 + x)^{n} \approx 1 + nx + \frac{n(n - 1)}{2}x^{2}\quad\left( |x| \ll 1,\ \text{any real }n \right).

For example, \sqrt{1 + x} \approx 1 + x/2 and 1/(1 + x) \approx 1 - x. Linearized theories (small disturbances in Chapters 25 and 36, small perturbations of orbits in Chapter 30) all start here.

A derivation is a chain of implications A \Rightarrow B. The contrapositive (\neg B \Rightarrow \neg A) is equivalent; the converse (B \Rightarrow A) is not. Induction proves a statement for all integers n by proving it for n = 1 and showing that truth for n implies truth for n + 1. When reading any derivation, list its assumptions explicitly. The result is valid only where all of them hold.

quiz.q: An elliptical orbit has a = 7000 km and e = 0.1. Find r_{\min}, r_{\max}, p and b.
quiz.a: r_{\min} = 6300 km, r_{\max} = 7700 km, p = 7000(0.99) = 6930 km, b = 7000\sqrt{0.99} = 6964.9 km.

quiz.q: For the orbit of Question 1, find r at \theta = 90^{\circ}.
quiz.a: \cos 90^{\circ} = 0, so r = p = 6930 km. This is the geometric meaning of the semi-latus rectum.

quiz.q: Compute (3 + 4i)(1 - 2i), |3 + 4i| and e^{i\pi}.
quiz.a: (3 + 4i)(1 - 2i) = 3 - 6i + 4i - 8i^{2} = 11 - 2i; |3 + 4i| = 5; e^{i\pi} = cos\pi + i\sin\pi = - 1.

quiz.q: Sum 1 + \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{4} + \cdots to infinity, and \sum_{k = 0}^{9}{0.9}^{k}.
quiz.a: 1/\left( 1 - \frac{1}{2} \right) = 2. \left( 1 - {0.9}^{10} \right)/(1 - 0.9) = 6.513.

quiz.q: Estimate {1.02}^{10} with the first-order binomial approximation and compare with the exact value.
quiz.a: Approximation: 1 + 10(0.02) = 1.20. Exact: 1.21899. The error (1.6%) comes from the neglected x^{2} term, 45(0.02)^{2} = 0.018.

quiz.q: Classify the conics with e = 0,0.5,1,1.5.
quiz.a: Circle, ellipse, parabola, hyperbola.

quiz.q: A hyperbolic flyby has e = 1.5. Find the asymptote angle \theta_{\infty}.
quiz.a: \theta_{\infty} = arccos( - 1/1.5) = {131.8}^{\circ}.

quiz.q: Show that r = p/\left( 1 + e\cos\theta \right) with e = 0 is a circle, and give the circumference in terms of p.
quiz.a: With e = 0, r = p is constant: a circle of radius p and circumference 2\pi p.

chapters.goalsHtml: describe orbits as conic sections in polar form; compute with complex numbers and Euler’s formula; sum series and use binomial approximations. Conics return in Chapter 29 as the exact solutions of the two-body problem.

chapters.title: Physics I: Motion, Forces, Momentum, Energy and Gravitation

secs.html:
Velocity is the rate of change of position, and acceleration the rate of change of velocity (made precise with derivatives in Chapter 8). For constant acceleration a:

v = v_{0} + at,\quad\quad x = x_{0} + v_{0}t + \frac{1}{2}at^{2},\quad\quad v^{2} = v_{0}^{2} + 2a\left( x - x_{0} \right).

Projectile motion without drag separates into independent horizontal (constant velocity) and vertical (constant acceleration - g) motions. Launched at speed v_{0} and angle \theta, the range is v_{0}^{2}\sin 2\theta/g and the apex height is v_{0}^{2}\sin^{2}\theta/(2g). Relative velocity: \mathbf{v}_{A/C} = \mathbf{v}_{A/B} + \mathbf{v}_{B/C}.

1. A body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net force (this defines inertial frames).
  2. For a body of constant mass, \sum\mathbf{F} = m\mathbf{a}. More generally, for a fixed set of particles, \sum\mathbf{F} = d\mathbf{p}/dt with \mathbf{p} = m\mathbf{v}.
  3. Forces between two bodies are equal and opposite.

Method: isolate the body, draw every external force (a free-body diagram), choose axes, write \sum F = ma for each axis, and solve. Common forces: weight mg; normal force; friction f \leq \mu_{s}N (static) or f = \mu_{k}N (kinetic); aerodynamic drag D = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}C_{D}A opposite to the velocity; lift perpendicular to it. When drag balances weight, the falling body reaches terminal velocity V_{t} = \sqrt{2mg/\left( \rho C_{D}A \right)}.

Variable mass. Writing F = d(mv)/dt = m\, dv/dt + v\, dm/dt for a rocket alone is wrong: the rocket is not a fixed set of particles. The correct treatment follows the rocket together with the mass it ejects (Chapters 7 and 15).

The impulse \mathbf{J} = \int\mathbf{F}\, dt equals the change in momentum \Delta\mathbf{p}. If the net external force on a system is zero, its total momentum is conserved. This is the principle of the rocket: momentum given to the exhaust in one direction is matched by momentum given to the vehicle in the other.

Work W = \int\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{s}. Kinetic energy K = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}. Work–energy theorem: the net work on a body equals \Delta K. A force is conservative if its work is path-independent; then a potential energy U exists with \mathbf{F} = - \nabla U. Near the surface U = mgh; in general gravity has U = - \mu m/r. When only conservative forces act, K + U is constant. Power is P = dW/dt = \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{v}.
Uniform circular motion at speed v and radius r requires a center-directed (centripetal) acceleration a_{c} = v^{2}/r = \omega^{2}r, supplied by some real force: tension, friction, lift or gravity.

F = \frac{GMm}{r^{2}},\quad\quad\mu \equiv GM\ \left( \mu_{\oplus} = 398\, 600.4418\ km^{3}/s^{2} \right),\quad\quad g(r) = \frac{\mu}{r^{2}}.

Circular orbit: gravity supplies the centripetal force, \mu m/r^{2} = mv^{2}/r, so v_{c} = \sqrt{\mu/r} and the period is T = 2\pi r/v_{c}. Escape: setting K + U = 0 gives v_{esc} = \sqrt{2\mu/r} = \sqrt{2}\, v_{c}.

Astronauts in orbit are weightless because they are in continuous free fall, not because gravity is absent: at 400 km altitude, g is still about 89% of its surface value. Kepler’s laws are stated here and derived in Chapter 29: (1) orbits are ellipses with the central body at a focus; (2) the line to the planet sweeps equal areas in equal times; (3) T^{2} \propto a^{3}.

For rotation about a fixed axis: angular velocity \omega, angular acceleration \alpha, torque \tau = rF\sin\phi, moment of inertia I = \sum m_{i}r_{i}^{2}, and the rotational second law \tau = I\alpha. Angular momentum is L = I\omega and rotational kinetic energy is \frac{1}{2}I\omega^{2}. The center of mass is \mathbf{r}_{cm} = \sum m_{i}\mathbf{r}_{i}/\sum m_{i}; in uniform gravity it coincides with the center of gravity (CG). Chapter 15 generalizes all of this to three dimensions.

quiz.q: A car accelerates uniformly from 0 to 30 m/s in 6 s. Find its acceleration and distance traveled.
quiz.a: a = 30/6 = 5 m/s². x = \frac{1}{2}(5)\left( 6^{2} \right) = 90 m.

quiz.q: A projectile is launched at 100 m/s and 45° with no drag (g = 9.81 m/s²). Find its range and maximum height.
quiz.a: Range = 100^{2}\sin 90^{\circ}/9.81 = 1019 m. Height = 100^{2}(0.5)/(2 \times 9.81) = 254.8 m.

quiz.q: Find the circular orbit speed and period at 400 km altitude (R_{\oplus} = 6378 km).
quiz.a: r = 6778 km. v_{c} = \sqrt{398\, 600/6778} = 7.669 km/s. T = 2\pi(6778)/7.669 = 5553 s = 92.6 min.

quiz.q: Find the escape speed from Earth’s surface.
Compute g at 400 km altitude as a fraction of the surface value (use the mean radius 6371 km).
quiz.a: (6371/6771)^{2} = 0.885, so g = 8.68 m/s².

quiz.q: A 2 kN force acts for 3 s on a 50 kg body at rest. Find its final speed.
quiz.a: \Delta v = J/m = (2000)(3)/50 = 120 m/s.

quiz.q: Why is “weightless because there is no gravity in space” wrong?
quiz.a: Gravity at orbital altitudes is nearly as strong as at the surface. Occupants feel weightless because they and their vehicle fall together: no contact force acts between them.

quiz.q: The 5°-gimballed 100 kN thrust of Quiz 3 acts 8 m behind the vehicle’s CG. Find the pitching torque.
quiz.a: Lateral thrust = 8.716 kN. Torque = 8.716 \times 8 = 69.7 kN·m.

chapters.goalsHtml: solve kinematics problems; apply Newton’s laws with free-body diagrams; use momentum and energy conservation; compute orbital and escape speeds; understand torque and rotation.

chapters.title: Chemistry: Atoms, Moles, Stoichiometry, Gases and Reaction Energy

secs.html: An atom has Z protons, Z electrons and a mass number A (protons plus neutrons). Electrons occupy shells; the outermost (valence) electrons determine bonding. Bonds may be covalent (shared electrons), ionic (transferred) or metallic (delocalized). Bond dissociation energies set chemical energy scales: N≡N 945 kJ/mol, O=O 498 kJ/mol, H–H 436 kJ/mol. The very strong N₂ triple bond is why nitrogen is nearly inert and dissociates only at very high temperatures (Chapter 39).

N_{A} = 6.02214076 \times 10^{23}\ mol^{- 1} (exact). The molar mass \mathcal{M} (g/mol, numerically equal to kg/kmol) converts mass to amount: n = m\mathcal{/M}. Examples: H₂ 2.016, O₂ 31.999, H₂O 18.015, CO₂ 44.010, CH₄ 16.043.

A balanced equation conserves each element: 2\, H_{2} + O_{2} \rightarrow 2\, H_{2}O. The mixture ratio (oxidizer-to-fuel ratio by mass) is O/F = {\dot{m}}_{ox}/{\dot{m}}_{f}. Stoichiometric means exactly enough oxidizer to burn all the fuel to the most oxidized products. The equivalence ratio is \phi = (F/O)/(F/O)_{st}: \phi > 1 is fuel-rich and \phi < 1 fuel-lean. Stoichiometric O/F: H₂/O₂ 7.94; CH₄/O₂ 3.99; kerosene (≈ CH₂)/O₂ ≈ 3.4.

Ideal gas law: pV = nR_{u}T = mRT, i.e. p = \rho RT, with R_{u} = 8.314462618\ J/(mol\, K) and specific gas constant R = R_{u}\mathcal{/M} (air: 287.05 J/(kg·K)).

In a mixture, each species exerts a partial pressure p_{i} = X_{i}p, where X_{i} = n_{i}/n is the mole fraction (Dalton’s law). The mixture molar mass is \mathcal{M} = \sum X_{i}\mathcal{M}_{i} and mass fractions are Y_{i} = X_{i}\mathcal{M}_{i}\mathcal{/M}. The ideal-gas law fails near condensation and at very high density (Chapter 16).

Enthalpy H is the energy measure that accounts for flow work at constant pressure (Chapter 16). The standard enthalpy of formation \Delta h_{f}^{\circ} is the enthalpy change forming one mole of a species from its elements in their reference states at 298.15 K and 1 bar. By Hess’s law:

\Delta H_{rxn} = \sum_{\text{products}}^{}\nu_{i}\,\Delta h_{f,i}^{\circ} - \sum_{\text{reactants}}^{}\nu_{i}\,\Delta h_{f,i}^{\circ}.

Selected values (kJ/mol): H₂O(g) −241.83; H₂O(l) −285.83; CO₂ −393.52; CH₄ −74.87; NO +90.29; O +249.17; H +217.99; N +472.68; elements in reference state 0. Atoms have positive formation enthalpies: dissociating molecules absorbs energy, which is why dissociation lowers flame temperatures and stores energy in hypersonic shock layers. The lower heating value (LHV) assumes the product water is vapor; the higher (HHV) assumes liquid.

Reactions proceed through molecular collisions energetic enough to overcome an activation energy; rates therefore rise steeply with temperature. Catalysts lower the activation energy. Reversible reactions approach chemical equilibrium, where forward and reverse rates balance. Le Chatelier’s principle: a disturbed equilibrium shifts to oppose the disturbance. Raising the pressure favors the side with fewer gas moles, so high chamber pressure suppresses dissociation. Chapter 17 makes all of this quantitative.

Liquid oxidizers include liquid oxygen (LOX, cryogenic, 1141 kg/m³), nitrogen tetroxide (NTO, storable) and hydrogen peroxide. Liquid fuels include liquid hydrogen (LH₂, cryogenic, 70.8 kg/m³), kerosene (RP-1, ≈ 810 kg/m³), liquid methane (LCH₄, 423 kg/m³) and the hydrazine family. Hypergolic pairs (such as NTO with hydrazines) ignite on contact. Solid propellants hold oxidizer and fuel together in a solid matrix (Chapter 28). Selection trades performance against density, storability, toxicity, cost and safety; Chapters 26–28 quantify these trades.

Pitfalls. Confusing mass-based and mole-based ratios; mixing LHV with HHV; forgetting that \Delta h_{f}^{\circ} depends on phase (liquid or gas water).

Safety and scope flag · Physical hazard

Concern. Several propellants named here are dangerous to handle. Hydrazines and nitrogen tetroxide are acutely toxic (hydrazines are also suspected carcinogens); liquid oxygen makes ordinary materials burn violently; cryogens cause severe cold burns, and their boil-off gas can displace breathing air in a closed space.

Why it is flagged. These hazards are physical and chemical properties of the substances themselves. Knowing a propellant’s name and performance does not make it safe to handle, and none of these substances is suitable for home experiments.

Learn it safely. Read the substances’ Safety Data Sheets and the NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards (both public). Take accredited chemistry and chemical-engineering laboratory courses, which include hazardous-materials training. Handle real propellants only in an institutional or industrial setting under its safety program.

quiz.q: Balance the H₂–O₂ reaction to water and compute the stoichiometric O/F by mass.
quiz.a: 2\, H_{2} + O_{2} \rightarrow 2\, H_{2}O. O/F = 31.999/(2 \times 2.016) = 7.94.

quiz.q: Compute the stoichiometric O/F for CH₄ + 2 O₂ → CO₂ + 2 H₂O.
Dry air is 78.08% N₂, 20.95% O₂, 0.93% Ar and 0.04% CO₂ by mole. Compute its molar mass.
Compute the density of air at 101 325 Pa and 288.15 K.
Using \Delta h_{f}^{\circ}(H₂O, g) = −241.83 kJ/mol, find the heat released per kg of H₂ burned (LHV) and per kg of stoichiometric H₂ + O₂ mixture.
quiz.a: Per kg H₂: 241.83/2.016 = 120.0 MJ/kg. Per kg of mixture (18.015 g per mole of water): 241.83/18.015 = 13.4 MJ/kg.

quiz.q: What does \phi > 1 mean? Hydrogen–oxygen engines usually run at O/F \approx 5.5–6 rather than 7.94. Suggest why.
quiz.a: \phi > 1 is fuel-rich. Running fuel-rich lowers the mean molar mass of the products (excess H₂ is very light). Exhaust velocity scales as \sqrt{T\mathcal{/M}} (Chapter 26), so this outweighs the small temperature loss; it also lowers chamber temperature, easing cooling.

quiz.q: A gas of 2 mol H₂O and 1 mol H₂ is at 10 MPa. Find the partial pressure of H₂.
quiz.a: X_{H_{2}} = 1/3, so p_{H_{2}} = 3.33 MPa.

quiz.q: Compute R for a combustion product gas of molar mass 13 kg/kmol and check its units.
quiz.a: R = 8314.46/13 = 639.6 J/(kg·K). Units: J\, kmol^{- 1}K^{- 1}/\left( kg\, kmol^{- 1} \right) = J\, kg^{- 1}K^{- 1}.

chapters.goalsHtml: balance combustion reactions; compute mixture ratios, molar masses and partial pressures; use the ideal gas law; compute reaction enthalpies from formation enthalpies; reason qualitatively about rates and equilibrium.

chapters.title: Introduction to Rockets and Flight

secs.html: A rocket produces thrust by expelling mass that it carries, so it works in vacuum. Physically, the thrust is the net pressure force on the internal walls of the chamber and nozzle. Equivalently, it is the momentum flux of the exhaust leaving the vehicle. Air-breathing engines take their oxidizer from the atmosphere instead (Chapter 44).

Thrust: F = \dot{m}v_{e} + \left( p_{e} - p_{a} \right)A_{e}, where \dot{m} is the propellant mass flow, v_{e} the exhaust velocity, p_{e} the exit pressure, p_{a} the ambient pressure and A_{e} the nozzle exit area (derived in Chapter 26). Effective exhaust velocity: c = F/\dot{m}. Specific impulse: I_{sp} = F/\left( \dot{m}g_{0} \right) = c/g_{0}, in seconds. Total impulse: I_{t} = \int F\, dt.

secs.t: The rocket equation from first principles
secs.html:
Consider a rocket of mass m and velocity v with no external force. In time dt it ejects a propellant mass dm_{p} > 0 at velocity c relative to itself, i.e. at v - c in the fixed frame. Conserving the momentum of the whole system (rocket plus ejected mass):

mv = \left( m - dm_{p} \right)(v + dv) + dm_{p}\,(v - c)\; \Rightarrow \; m\, dv = c\, dm_{p}

after dropping the second-order product dm_{p}\, dv. Since the rocket’s mass changes by dm = - dm_{p}, dv = - c\, dm/m. Integrating from m_{0} to m_{f} at constant c:

Tsiolkovsky rocket equation: \Delta v = c\ln\frac{m_{0}}{m_{f}} = I_{sp}\, g_{0}\ln\frac{m_{0}}{m_{f}}. Assumptions: no external forces and constant c. m_{0}/m_{f} is the mass ratio.

With gravity and no drag, dv/dt = F/m - g. Integrating at constant c and g over a burn time t_{b} gives the burnout velocity v_{b} = c\ln\left( m_{0}/m_{f} \right) - gt_{b}. The term gt_{b} is the gravity loss: every second spent fighting gravity costs g of velocity. A higher thrust-to-weight ratio F/\left( m_{0}g_{0} \right) shortens the burn and reduces this loss, at the price of heavier engines. Chapter 31 treats real trajectories.

Pressure and density fall roughly exponentially with altitude (Chapter 18; table in Appendix D). By convention, space begins at the Kármán line, 100 km. Aerodynamic loads scale with the dynamic pressure q = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}: drag is D = qC_{D}A. For an ascending rocket, V rises while \rho falls, so q peaks at max-Q, typically 10–15 km altitude and 25–40 kPa for large launchers. The Mach number M = V/a (where a is the speed of sound) defines the flight regimes:

Regime Mach range Defining physics
Subsonic M < 0.8 No shocks; pressure signals propagate everywhere
Transonic 0.8–1.2 Mixed subsonic and supersonic regions; drag rise; buffet
Supersonic 1.2–5 Shocks and expansions; wave drag
Hypersonic \gtrsim 5 Strong shocks, thin shock layers, severe heating, high-temperature chemistry

The hypersonic boundary is a rule of thumb, not a sharp threshold. Chapter 38 gives the physical definition.

The aerodynamic forces act effectively at the center of pressure (CP). If the CG lies ahead of the CP, a disturbance in angle of attack creates a moment that rotates the nose back into the wind: the vehicle is statically stable. The distance from CG to CP divided by body diameter is the static margin in calibers; 1–2 calibers is typical for small rockets. Fins move the CP aft. Many large launch vehicles are aerodynamically unstable (CP ahead of CG) and are stabilized by active thrust-vector control (Chapters 22 and 32).

secs.t: Flight phases and the nature of orbit
secs.html: An orbital ascent runs: liftoff, vertical rise, pitch-over, gravity turn through max-Q, booster cutoff and staging, upper-stage burn, and orbit insertion. Reaching orbit is mainly about horizontal speed: about 7.8 km/s near Earth. Reaching 100 km altitude takes only about 1.4 km/s of ideal velocity, but the vehicle then falls back. A sounding rocket flies a vertical arc; an orbital launcher spends most of its energy accelerating sideways.

Hands-on rocketry must use certified commercial motors and follow the NAR or Tripoli safety codes, with the certification level required for each motor class. In the United States, amateur rocket operations fall under 14 CFR Part 101. Never attempt to make propellants. Use flight simulators (for example OpenRocket) to predict stability and apogee before flying.

Safety and scope flag · Physical hazard and legal

Concern. Rocket motors are energetic devices. Launches create fire, impact and debris hazards, and airspace use is regulated (14 CFR Part 101 in the United States).

Why it is flagged. Serious amateur-rocketry injuries are dominated by homemade motors and propellants, improvised igniters and unsafe launch practice, not by certified motors flown under club safety codes.

Omitted here. How to make motors, propellants or igniters.

Learn it safely. Join the National Association of Rocketry (NAR) or the Tripoli Rocketry Association (TRA) and fly at club launches run by a range safety officer. Progress through their certification levels; both offer youth or mentoring routes with age limits. Compete in student programs such as the American Rocketry Challenge (secondary school), NASA Student Launch, or the Spaceport America Cup (university). Simulate every design in OpenRocket before flight, and follow NFPA 1122 (model) and NFPA 1127 (high-power) rocketry codes.

quiz.q: An engine has \dot{m} = 250 kg/s and v_{e} = 3000 m/s with p_{e} = p_{a}. Find F and I_{sp}.
quiz.a: F = 250 \times 3000 = 750 kN. I_{sp} = 3000/9.80665 = 305.9 s.

quiz.q: A rocket with m_{0} = 50\, 000 kg, m_{f} = 15\, 000 kg and I_{sp} = 300 s fires in free space. Find \Delta v.
quiz.a: c = 2942 m/s. \Delta v = 2942\ln(50/15) = 3542 m/s.

quiz.q: Find the liftoff thrust-to-weight ratio for 750 kN of thrust and m_{0} = 50 t.
Find q at 10 km (\rho = 0.4135 kg/m³) and 500 m/s.
quiz.a: q = \frac{1}{2}(0.4135)\left( 500^{2} \right) = 51.7 kPa.

quiz.q: Explain why the CG must lie ahead of the CP for passive stability.
quiz.a: With the CG ahead of the CP, an angle-of-attack disturbance produces a normal force aft of the CG whose moment turns the nose back toward the velocity vector (restoring). With the CP ahead, the moment increases the disturbance.

quiz.q: For the rocket of Question 2 with \dot{m} = 250 kg/s, flying vertically without drag, find the burn time, gravity loss and burnout velocity.
quiz.a: t_{b} = 35\, 000/250 = 140 s. Gravity loss = 9.81 \times 140 = 1373 m/s. v_{b} = 3542 - 1373 = 2169 m/s.

quiz.q: Why does a constant-thrust rocket’s acceleration increase during the burn?
quiz.a: Acceleration = F/m - g and m decreases as propellant is consumed.

quiz.q: Why is reaching orbit mostly about horizontal speed rather than altitude?
quiz.a: An orbit is free fall in which the horizontal speed is high enough that the ground curves away as fast as the vehicle falls (v_{c} = \sqrt{\mu/r}). Altitude alone, without that speed, gives a suborbital arc.

chapters.goalsHtml: state the thrust equation and specific impulse; derive the rocket equation from momentum conservation; estimate gravity losses; compute dynamic pressure and drag; explain static stability; name the flight regimes and phases.

chapters.title: Single-Variable Calculus

secs.html: \lim_{x \rightarrow a}f(x) = L means that for every \varepsilon > 0 there is a \delta > 0 such that 0 < |x - a| < \delta implies \left| f(x) - L \right| < \varepsilon. f is continuous at a if \lim_{x \rightarrow a}f(x) = f(a). Limits at infinity and one-sided limits are defined analogously.

f'(x) = \frac{df}{dx} = \lim_{h \rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}: the instantaneous rate of change, or the slope of the tangent line. Differentiability implies continuity, but not conversely (|x| at 0).

Rules: linearity; product (uv)' = u'v + uv'; quotient (u/v)' = (u'v - uv')/v^{2}; chain \frac{d}{dx}f\left( g(x) \right) = f'\left( g(x) \right)\, g'(x). Basic derivatives: \left( x^{n} \right)' = nx^{n - 1}; \left( e^{x} \right)' = e^{x}; \left( \ln x \right)' = 1/x; \left( \sin x \right)' = cosx; \left( \cos x \right)' = - sinx; \left( \tan x \right)' = \sec^{2}x; \left( \arctan x \right)' = 1/\left( 1 + x^{2} \right); \left( a^{x} \right)' = a^{x}\ln a. Implicit differentiation differentiates both sides of F(x,y) = 0 treating y = y(x).

Kinematics: v = dx/dt, a = dv/dt. Optimization: interior extrema occur where f' = 0 (or f' is undefined); f'' > 0 indicates a minimum and f'' < 0 a maximum; always check the endpoints. Linearization: f(x + \Delta x) \approx f(x) + f'(x)\Delta x, the basis of sensitivity analysis and error propagation. Mean value theorem: if f is differentiable on (a,b) and continuous on \lbrack a,b\rbrack, then f'(\xi) = \left\lbrack f(b) - f(a) \right\rbrack/(b - a) for some \xi \in (a,b).

The definite integral is the limit of Riemann sums, \int_{a}^{b}f\, dx = \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty}\sum f\left( x_{i}^{*} \right)\Delta x.

Fundamental theorem of calculus. If F' = f, then \int_{a}^{b}f(x)\, dx = F(b) - F(a); and \frac{d}{dx}\int_{a}^{x}f(t)\, dt = f(x).

Techniques: substitution (u = g(x), du = g'dx); integration by parts \int u\, dv = uv - \int v\, du; partial fractions for rational functions; trigonometric substitution for \sqrt{a^{2} - x^{2}} and similar forms. Improper integrals take limits at infinite bounds or at singularities. Key antiderivatives: \int x^{n}dx = x^{n + 1}/(n + 1) for n \neq - 1; \int dx/x = ln|x|; \int e^{ax}dx = e^{ax}/a; \int lnx\, dx = x\ln x - x.

Area between curves; volumes of revolution (disks \pi\int r^{2}dx, shells 2\pi\int xf\, dx); arc length \int\sqrt{1 + f'^{2}}\, dx; work W = \int F\, dx; impulse \int F\, dt; average value \frac{1}{b - a}\int_{a}^{b}f\, dx; centroids and moments of inertia; the gravitational energy needed to reach infinity, \int_{R}^{\infty}\mu/r^{2}\, dr = \mu/R per unit mass.

f(x) = \sum_{n = 0}^{N}\frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x - a)^{n} + R_{N}, with remainder R_{N} = \frac{f^{(N + 1)}(\xi)}{(N + 1)!}(x - a)^{N + 1} for some \xi between a and x.

Standard expansions about 0: e^{x} = \sum x^{n}/n!; \sin x = x - x^{3}/3! + x^{5}/5! - \cdots; \cos x = 1 - x^{2}/2! + \cdots; \ln(1 + x) = x - x^{2}/2 + x^{3}/3 - \cdots for |x| < 1; (1 + x)^{\alpha} = 1 + \alpha x + \alpha(\alpha - 1)x^{2}/2 + \cdots; 1/(1 - x) = \sum x^{n}. The radius of convergence is the distance to the nearest singularity in the complex plane. Taylor series underlie linearized theories, numerical differencing (Chapter 14) and truncation-error analysis (Chapter 45).

secs.t: L’Hôpital’s rule and orders of magnitude
secs.html: For 0/0 or \infty/\infty forms, \lim f/g = limf'/g' when the latter exists. Big-O: f = O(g) as x \rightarrow a means |f| \leq C|g| near a. As x \rightarrow \infty, exponentials beat powers and powers beat logarithms.

A rocket of initial mass m_{0} burns at constant \dot{m} with exhaust velocity c in uniform gravity g, without drag. With m(t) = m_{0} - \dot{m}t:

\frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{c\dot{m}}{m_{0} - \dot{m}t} - g\; \Rightarrow \; v(t) = - c\ln(1 - kt) - gt,\quad\quad k \equiv \dot{m}/m_{0}.

Integrating again with U = 1 - kt:

h(t) = \frac{c}{k}\left( U\ln U - U + 1 \right) - \frac{1}{2}gt^{2}.

Check the limit: for small t, v \approx (ck - g)t, i.e. initial acceleration F/m_{0} - g, as expected.

quiz.q: Differentiate x^{2}\sin x.
quiz.a: 2x\sin x + x^{2}\cos x (product rule).

quiz.q: Evaluate \int_{0}^{\pi}\sin x\, dx.
quiz.a: \left\lbrack - \cos x \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi} = 1 + 1 = 2.

quiz.q: A closed cylindrical tank must hold 10 m³. Find the radius and height that minimize surface area.
quiz.a: Minimize S = 2\pi r^{2} + 2\pi rh with h = V/\left( \pi r^{2} \right): S = 2\pi r^{2} + 2V/r, so S' = 4\pi r - 2V/r^{2} = 0 gives r = (V/2\pi)^{1/3} = 1.168 m and h = 2r = 2.335 m. The optimal closed cylinder is as tall as it is wide.

quiz.q: Estimate e^{0.1} with four Taylor terms and compare with the exact value.
quiz.a: 1 + 0.1 + 0.005 + 0.000167 = 1.105167; exact 1.105171; error 4 \times 10^{- 6}, consistent with the next term {0.1}^{4}/24.

quiz.q: How much energy per kilogram is needed to lift a mass from Earth’s surface (R = 6378 km) to infinity?
quiz.a: \mu/R = 3.986 \times 10^{14}/6.378 \times 10^{6} = 62.5 MJ/kg.

quiz.q: Using §8.8 with m_{0} = 50 t, \dot{m} = 250 kg/s, c = 2942 m/s and g = 9.80665 m/s², find v and h at t = 100 s.
quiz.a: k = 0.005 s⁻¹ and U = 0.5. v = 2942\ln 2 - 980.7 = 1059 m/s. h = (2942/0.005)\left( 0.5\ln 0.5 - 0.5 + 1 \right) - 49\, 033 = 41.2 km.

quiz.q: Evaluate \lim_{x \rightarrow 0}\left( 1 - \cos x \right)/x^{2}.
quiz.a: Applying L’Hôpital twice gives \cos x/2 \rightarrow 1/2.

quiz.q: Why must the endpoints be checked in an optimization on a closed interval?
quiz.a: A function continuous on a closed interval attains its extrema either at interior critical points or at the endpoints; the derivative test finds only the former.

chapters.goalsHtml: differentiate and integrate fluently; optimize; linearize; expand functions in Taylor series with error bounds; integrate the equations of rocket flight exactly.

chapters.title: Multivariable and Vector Calculus

secs.t: Partial derivatives and the chain rule
secs.html: For f(x,y,z), \partial f/\partial x is the derivative with the other variables held fixed. Total differential: df = f_{x}dx + f_{y}dy + f_{z}dz. Chain rule: if x = x(t) and so on, df/dt = f_{x}\dot{x} + f_{y}\dot{y} + f_{z}\dot{z}. Mixed partials commute for smooth f (Clairaut’s theorem). Notation matters in thermodynamics, where (\partial h/\partial T)_{p} explicitly names the variable held constant.

abla f = \left( f_{x},f_{y},f_{z} ight) points in the direction of steepest increase and is normal to the level surfaces of f. The directional derivative is D_{\widehat{u}}f = abla f \cdot \widehat{\mathbf{u}}. Second-order Taylor expansion: f\left( \mathbf{x} + \Delta\mathbf{x} ight) \approx f + abla f \cdot \Delta\mathbf{x} + rac{1}{2}\Delta\mathbf{x}^{T}\mathbf{H}\Delta\mathbf{x}, where \mathbf{H} is the Hessian. A critical point is a minimum if \mathbf{H} is positive definite (Chapter 10).

Lagrange multipliers. To extremize f\left( \mathbf{x} ight) subject to g\left( \mathbf{x} ight) = 0, solve abla f = \lambda abla g together with g = 0. At the optimum the level surface of f is tangent to the constraint surface. Multiple constraints: abla f = \sum\lambda_{i} abla g_{i}.

Lagrange multipliers yield optimal rocket staging (Chapter 26) and, in function-space form, optimal control (Chapter 46).

\iint_{R}^{}f\, dA and \iiint_{V}^{}f\, dV are computed as iterated integrals (Fubini). A change of variables multiplies by the Jacobian determinant \left| \partial(x,y,z)/\partial(u,v,w) \right|: polar dA = r\, dr\, d\theta; cylindrical dV = r\, dr\, d\theta\, dz; spherical dV = r^{2}\sin\phi\, dr\, d\phi\, d\theta (\phi from the pole). Applications: mass \int\rho\, dV, center of mass, and moment of inertia I = \int r_{\bot}^{2}\, dm. For a solid sphere I = \frac{2}{5}MR^{2}; for a thin spherical shell \frac{2}{3}MR^{2}; for a solid cylinder about its axis \frac{1}{2}MR^{2}.

For a vector field \mathbf{F}: the divergence abla \cdot \mathbf{F} is the net outflow per unit volume (source density); the curl abla imes \mathbf{F} measures local rotation (for a velocity field, abla imes \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{\omega}, the vorticity, is twice the local angular velocity of a fluid element); the Laplacian abla^{2}f = abla \cdot abla f measures how f differs from its local average, and is the operator of diffusion. Formulas in cylindrical and spherical coordinates are in Appendix C.

The line integral \int_{C}^{}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r} gives work, or around a closed loop the circulation \Gamma. A field is conservative (path-independent, \mathbf{F} = \nabla\phi) if and only if \nabla \times \mathbf{F} = 0 on a simply connected domain. The surface integral \iint_{S}^{}\mathbf{F} \cdot \widehat{\mathbf{n}}\, dA is the flux through S.

Divergence (Gauss): \iiint_{V}^{}\nabla \cdot \mathbf{F}\, dV = ∯_{S}^{}\mathbf{F} \cdot \widehat{\mathbf{n}}\, dA. Stokes: \iint_{S}^{}\left( \nabla \times \mathbf{F} \right) \cdot \widehat{\mathbf{n}}\, dA = \oint_{C}^{}\mathbf{F} \cdot d\mathbf{r}. Reynolds transport theorem: \frac{d}{dt}\iiint_{V(t)}^{}f\, dV = \iiint_{V}^{}\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}dV + ∯_{S(t)}^{}f\,\left( \mathbf{u}_{b} \cdot \widehat{\mathbf{n}} \right)\, dA, where \mathbf{u}_{b} is the velocity of the boundary.

The transport theorem is the bridge from the laws of mechanics (stated for fixed collections of matter) to control volumes (fixed regions of space), the starting point of Chapter 18 and of the rocket thrust derivation in Chapter 26.

Repeated indices are summed (Einstein convention): \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} = a_{i}b_{i}. The Kronecker delta \delta_{ij} is 1 if i = j and 0 otherwise. The Levi-Civita symbol \varepsilon_{ijk} is + 1 for even permutations of 123, - 1 for odd permutations and 0 otherwise, so that \left( \mathbf{a} imes \mathbf{b} ight)_{i} = \varepsilon_{ijk}a_{j}b_{k} and \varepsilon_{ijk}\varepsilon_{imn} = \delta_{jm}\delta_{kn} - \delta_{jn}\delta_{km}. Identities used throughout:

abla \cdot \left( abla imes \mathbf{A} ight) = 0,\quad abla imes abla\phi = 0,\quad abla imes \left( abla imes \mathbf{A} ight) = abla\left( abla \cdot \mathbf{A} ight) - abla^{2}\mathbf{A},

\left( \mathbf{u} \cdot abla ight)\mathbf{u} = abla\left( rac{1}{2}\left| \mathbf{u} ight|^{2} ight) - \mathbf{u} imes \left( abla imes \mathbf{u} ight),\quad\quad abla \cdot \left( \phi\mathbf{A} ight) = \phi abla \cdot \mathbf{A} + \mathbf{A} \cdot abla\phi.

The fourth identity yields Bernoulli’s equation (Chapter 18) and Crocco’s theorem (Chapter 36).

quiz.q: For f = x^{2}y + e^{yz}, compute \nabla f at (1,1,0).
quiz.a: \nabla f = \left( 2xy,\ x^{2} + ze^{yz},\ ye^{yz} \right) = (2,1,1).

quiz.q: Compute \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} for \mathbf{v} = (x,y,z) and \nabla \times \mathbf{w} for \mathbf{w} = ( - y,x,0). Interpret.
quiz.a: \nabla \cdot \mathbf{v} = 3: a uniform source. \nabla \times \mathbf{w} = (0,0,2): rigid rotation at unit angular velocity, whose vorticity is twice the angular velocity.

quiz.q: Maximize xy subject to x + y = 10 using a Lagrange multiplier.
quiz.a: \nabla(xy) = \lambda\nabla(x + y) gives y = \lambda = x, so x = y = 5 and the maximum is 25.

quiz.q: Derive I = \frac{2}{5}MR^{2} for a uniform solid sphere about a diameter, then evaluate for M = 100 kg and R = 0.5 m.
quiz.a: Thin shells of radius r about a diameter contribute \frac{2}{3}r^{2}\, dm with dm = \rho 4\pi r^{2}dr. Then I = \int_{0}^{R}\frac{2}{3}r^{2}\rho 4\pi r^{2}dr = \frac{8\pi\rho R^{5}}{15} = \frac{2}{5}MR^{2}. Numerically I = 10 kg·m².

quiz.q: Use the divergence theorem to find the flux of \mathbf{F} = (x,y,z) through a sphere of radius 2.
quiz.a: \nabla \cdot \mathbf{F} = 3, so the flux is 3 \times \frac{4}{3}\pi(2)^{3} = 32\pi = 100.5.

quiz.q: Why does \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0 express incompressibility?
quiz.a: By the divergence theorem, \nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} is the net volume outflow per unit volume. If it is zero everywhere, no fluid element changes volume.

quiz.q: q = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2} with independent relative uncertainties of 2% in \rho and 1% in V. Use the total differential to find the relative uncertainty in q, combined in quadrature, and its worst case.
quiz.a: dq/q = d\rho/\rho + 2\, dV/V. In quadrature: \sqrt{{0.02}^{2} + (2 \times 0.01)^{2}} = 2.8\%. Worst case: 2 + 2 = 4\%.

quiz.q: Verify \nabla \times \nabla\phi = 0 for \phi = xyz.
quiz.a: \nabla\phi = (yz,xz,xy); curl x-component = \partial_{y}(xy) - \partial_{z}(xz) = x - x = 0, and similarly for the other components.

chapters.goalsHtml: use partial derivatives, gradients and Lagrange multipliers; integrate over areas and volumes in any coordinate system; master divergence, curl, the integral theorems, the Reynolds transport theorem and index notation. This is the mathematical core of fluid mechanics.

chapters.title: Linear Algebra

secs.html: A set of vectors is linearly independent if no nontrivial combination equals zero. A basis is an independent set that spans the space; its size is the dimension. An inner product \langle\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\rangle = \mathbf{x}^{T}\mathbf{y} defines the norm \parallel \mathbf{x} \parallel_{2} = \sqrt{\mathbf{x}^{T}\mathbf{x}} and orthogonality. Other norms: \parallel \mathbf{x} \parallel_{1} = \sum\left| x_{i} \right| and \parallel \mathbf{x} \parallel_{\infty} = max\left| x_{i} \right|.

\left( \mathbf{AB} \right)_{ij} = \sum_{k}^{}A_{ik}B_{kj}; in general \mathbf{AB} \neq \mathbf{BA}. \left( \mathbf{AB} \right)^{T} = \mathbf{B}^{T}\mathbf{A}^{T} and \left( \mathbf{AB} \right)^{- 1} = \mathbf{B}^{- 1}\mathbf{A}^{- 1}. The determinant is the signed volume scale factor of the map: \det\left( \mathbf{AB} \right) = det\mathbf{A}\det\mathbf{B}, and \mathbf{A} is invertible if and only if \det\mathbf{A} \neq 0. For a 2 \times 2 matrix, \begin{bmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{bmatrix}^{- 1} = \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{bmatrix} d & - b \\ - c & a \end{bmatrix}.

\mathbf{Ax} = \mathbf{b} is solved by Gaussian elimination, organized as the factorization \mathbf{PA} = \mathbf{LU} (cost \frac{2}{3}n^{3} operations). A solution exists if \mathbf{b} lies in the column space of \mathbf{A}, and it is unique if the null space is \{\mathbf{0}\}. Rank–nullity: rank\mathbf{A} + dimnull\mathbf{A} = n. Never form \mathbf{A}^{- 1} explicitly to solve a system.

For an overdetermined system (m > n equations), the least-squares solution minimizes \parallel \mathbf{Ax} - \mathbf{b} \parallel_{2} and satisfies the normal equations \mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{Ax} = \mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{b}. The residual is orthogonal to the column space. Numerically, solve through the QR factorization (Gram–Schmidt or Householder), \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{QR}, giving \mathbf{Rx} = \mathbf{Q}^{T}\mathbf{b}; forming \mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{A} squares the condition number. Weighted least squares, \mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{WAx} = \mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{Wb}, is the static ancestor of the Kalman filter (Chapter 46).

\mathbf{Av} = \lambda\mathbf{v}, with \lambda the roots of \det\left( \mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I} \right) = 0. If \mathbf{A} has n independent eigenvectors, \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{V\Lambda V}^{- 1}. Spectral theorem: a real symmetric matrix has real eigenvalues and orthonormal eigenvectors, \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{Q\Lambda Q}^{T}. It is positive definite (\mathbf{x}^{T}\mathbf{Ax} > 0 for all \mathbf{x} \neq 0) if and only if all \lambda > 0.

Eigenvectors of the inertia tensor are the principal axes of a body (Chapter 15). Eigenvalues of a system matrix determine stability (Chapter 11). Eigenvalues of stiffness and mass matrices give vibration frequencies (Chapter 33). Covariance matrices are symmetric positive semi-definite (Chapter 13).

Every matrix factors as \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{U\Sigma V}^{T}, with \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{V} orthogonal and \mathbf{\Sigma} diagonal with singular values \sigma_{1} \geq \sigma_{2} \geq \cdots \geq 0. The rank is the number of nonzero \sigma; the pseudo-inverse is \mathbf{A}^{+} = \mathbf{V\Sigma}^{+}\mathbf{U}^{T}; the 2-norm condition number is \kappa = \sigma_{\max}/\sigma_{\min}. Solving a system with \kappa = 10^{k} can lose about k significant digits. Truncated SVD underlies reduced-order modeling (proper orthogonal decomposition), a frontier tool for hypersonic multiphysics (Chapter 53).

A rotation matrix is orthogonal with determinant + 1: \mathbf{R}^{T}\mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I}, \mathbf{R}^{- 1} = \mathbf{R}^{T}. Elementary passive rotations (coordinate-frame rotations) by angle \theta:

\mathbf{R}_{3}(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta & 0 \\ - \sin\theta & \cos\theta & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix},\quad\mathbf{R}_{1}(\theta) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ 0 & - \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix},

and \mathbf{R}_{2} analogously, with the sines in the 1–3 positions and their signs reversed. Successive frame rotations multiply right to left: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{R}_{1}(\phi)\mathbf{R}_{2}(\theta)\mathbf{R}_{3}(\psi) for a 3-2-1 sequence. Every rotation has an eigenvalue 1, whose eigenvector is the rotation axis (Euler’s theorem, Chapter 32). The skew-symmetric matrix \left\lbrack \mathbf{a} \times \right\rbrack satisfies \left\lbrack \mathbf{a} \times \right\rbrack\mathbf{b} = \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}.

e^{\mathbf{A}t} = \sum_{k}^{}\left( \mathbf{A}t \right)^{k}/k! solves \dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{Ax}: \mathbf{x}(t) = e^{\mathbf{A}t}\mathbf{x}_{0}. If \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{V\Lambda V}^{- 1}, then e^{\mathbf{A}t} = \mathbf{V}e^{\mathbf{\Lambda}t}\mathbf{V}^{- 1}, so every solution is a combination of modes e^{\lambda_{i}t}\mathbf{v}_{i}. In discrete-time simulation and estimation, e^{\mathbf{A}\Delta t} is the state transition matrix.

quiz.q: Find \det\mathbf{A} and \mathbf{A}^{- 1} for \mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}.
quiz.a: det = 5; \mathbf{A}^{- 1} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & - 1 \\ - 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.

quiz.q: Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}.
quiz.a: \lambda = 1 with (1, - 1); \lambda = 3 with (1,1).

quiz.q: Fit y = a + bx by least squares to the points (0,1), (1,3), (2,4).
quiz.a: \bar{x} = 1, \bar{y} = 8/3, S_{xy} = 3, S_{xx} = 2. So b = 1.5 and a = \bar{y} - b\bar{x} = 1.167.

quiz.q: Apply an active 90° rotation about z to (1,0,0), and verify that the rotation matrix is orthogonal with determinant 1.
quiz.a: The active rotation \begin{bmatrix} 0 & - 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} maps (1,0,0) to (0,1,0). Its columns are orthonormal and its determinant is + 1.

quiz.q: A system has condition number 10^{8} and is solved in double precision (about 16 digits). How many digits of the solution can you trust?
quiz.a: About 16 - 8 = 8 significant digits.

quiz.q: A point mass of 2 kg sits at \mathbf{r} = (1,1,0) m. Using \mathbf{I} = m\left( r^{2}\mathbf{E} - \mathbf{rr}^{T} \right), where \mathbf{E} is the identity, compute its inertia tensor and principal moments.
quiz.a: r^{2} = 2, so \mathbf{I} = 2\begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 1 & 0 \\ - 1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & - 2 & 0 \\ - 2 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 \end{bmatrix} kg·m². Principal moments are 0, 4 and 4. The zero moment is about the axis through the mass, as it must be for a point mass.

quiz.q: Is \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} positive definite?
quiz.a: The eigenvalues are \left( 7 \pm \sqrt{17} \right)/2 = 5.56 and 1.44, both positive, so it is positive definite. Equivalently, the leading minors 4 and 8 are both positive.

quiz.q: Why should one avoid the normal equations for ill-conditioned least-squares problems?
quiz.a: \kappa\left( \mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{A} \right) = \kappa\left( \mathbf{A} \right)^{2}, so roughly twice as many digits are lost. QR or SVD works directly with \mathbf{A}.

chapters.goalsHtml: solve and analyze linear systems; use least squares; compute and interpret eigenvalues; use the SVD and condition numbers; manipulate rotation matrices and the matrix exponential. Linear algebra is the computational backbone of structures, control, estimation and CFD.

chapters.title: Ordinary Differential Equations and Laplace Transforms

secs.html: An ODE relates a function of one variable to its derivatives. Order is the highest derivative. It is linear if the unknown and its derivatives appear linearly. If \dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{f}\left( t,\mathbf{x} \right) with \mathbf{f} continuous and Lipschitz in \mathbf{x}, the initial-value problem has a unique solution (Picard–Lindelöf). Any nth-order ODE can be rewritten as n first-order equations.

Separable: dy/dx = g(x)h(y) \Rightarrow \int dy/h = \int g\, dx. Linear: y' + p(x)y = q(x); multiply by the integrating factor \mu = e^{\int p\, dx} to get (\mu y)' = \mu q. Examples: Newton cooling \dot{T} = - \left( T - T_{\infty} \right)/\tau gives T - T_{\infty} = \left( T_{0} - T_{\infty} \right)e^{- t/\tau}. A body falling with quadratic drag, m\dot{v} = mg - \frac{1}{2}\rho C_{D}Av^{2}, approaches V_{t} = \sqrt{2mg/\left( \rho C_{D}A \right)} as v = V_{t}\tanh\left( gt/V_{t} \right).

\ddot{x} + 2\zeta\omega_{n}\dot{x} + \omega_{n}^{2}x = f(t)/m describes every mass–spring–damper, every pendulum near equilibrium, and the short-period motion of a vehicle.

Characteristic roots: s = - \zeta\omega_{n} \pm \omega_{n}\sqrt{\zeta^{2} - 1}. Underdamped (\zeta < 1): x = e^{- \zeta\omega_{n}t}\left( A\cos\omega_{d}t + B\sin\omega_{d}t \right) with \omega_{d} = \omega_{n}\sqrt{1 - \zeta^{2}}. Critically damped (\zeta = 1): (A + Bt)e^{- \omega_{n}t}. Overdamped (\zeta > 1): two decaying exponentials. Under harmonic forcing at \omega, the steady amplitude ratio is \left\lbrack \left( 1 - r^{2} \right)^{2} + (2\zeta r)^{2} \right\rbrack^{- 1/2} with r = \omega/\omega_{n}, peaking near r = 1 at about 1/(2\zeta) (resonance).

The general solution is the homogeneous solution plus any particular solution (undetermined coefficients or variation of parameters).

Write \dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{Ax} + \mathbf{Bu}. The free response is \mathbf{x} = e^{\mathbf{A}t}\mathbf{x}_{0} (Chapter 10). The equilibrium is asymptotically stable if and only if every eigenvalue of \mathbf{A} has a negative real part. In two dimensions the phase portrait classifies equilibria: real eigenvalues of one sign give a node (stable if negative); real eigenvalues of opposite signs give a saddle (unstable); a complex pair gives a focus (spiral) whose stability follows the sign of the real part; purely imaginary eigenvalues give a center.

Equilibria satisfy \mathbf{f}\left( \mathbf{x}^{*} \right) = 0. Linearize with the Jacobian \mathbf{J} = \partial\mathbf{f}/\partial\mathbf{x} at \mathbf{x}^{*}. If no eigenvalue of \mathbf{J} has zero real part, the local behavior matches the linearization (Hartman–Grobman). Otherwise use a Lyapunov function V\left( \mathbf{x} \right) > 0 with \dot{V} \leq 0 to prove stability. Nonlinear systems can have limit cycles: isolated periodic orbits, as in combustion instability (Chapter 47) and aeroelastic flutter (Chapter 33).

\mathcal{L}\{ f\} = F(s) = \int_{0}^{\infty}f(t)e^{- st}dt. Key pairs: 1 \rightarrow 1/s; e^{- at} \rightarrow 1/(s + a); t^{n} \rightarrow n!/s^{n + 1}; \sin\omega t \rightarrow \omega/\left( s^{2} + \omega^{2} \right); \cos\omega t \rightarrow s/\left( s^{2} + \omega^{2} \right); \delta(t) \rightarrow 1. Properties: \mathcal{L}\{ f'\} = sF - f(0); \mathcal{L}\{ f''\} = s^{2}F - sf(0) - f'(0); delay f(t - T)u(t - T) \rightarrow e^{- sT}F; final value \lim_{t \rightarrow \infty}f = \lim_{s \rightarrow 0}sF(s), valid only if the limit exists (all poles of sF in the left half-plane).

Procedure: transform the ODE, solve algebraically for X(s), expand in partial fractions, and invert term by term. For zero initial conditions, X(s) = G(s)U(s), where G is the transfer function, the foundation of Chapter 22.

Conditions at two ends (for example y(0) = y(L) = 0) define a boundary-value problem. y'' + \lambda y = 0 with those conditions has nontrivial solutions only for \lambda_{n} = (n\pi/L)^{2}, with y_{n} = sin(n\pi x/L). The same structure gives column buckling loads (Chapter 20), vibration modes (Chapter 33), acoustic modes of combustion chambers (Chapter 27) and the separation-of-variables solutions of Chapter 12.

quiz.q: Solve y' = - 2y with y(0) = 5, and evaluate y(1).
quiz.a: y = 5e^{- 2t}, so y(1) = 0.677.

quiz.q: Find the terminal velocity for m = 80 kg, \rho = 1.225 kg/m³, C_{D} = 1.0 and A = 0.7 m².
For \ddot{x} + 4\dot{x} + 20x = 0, find \omega_{n}, \zeta, the roots and \omega_{d}.
quiz.a: \omega_{n} = \sqrt{20} = 4.472 rad/s; \zeta = 4/(2 \times 4.472) = 0.447; roots - 2 \pm 4i; \omega_{d} = 4 rad/s.

quiz.q: Find \mathcal{L}\{ e^{- at}\} and the inverse transform of 1/\left\lbrack s(s + 2) \right\rbrack.
quiz.a: 1/(s + a). 1/\left\lbrack s(s + 2) \right\rbrack = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack 1/s - 1/(s + 2) \right\rbrack, which inverts to \frac{1}{2}\left( 1 - e^{- 2t} \right).

quiz.q: Use the final value theorem on Y(s) = 5/\left\lbrack s\left( s^{2} + 3s + 2 \right) \right\rbrack.
quiz.a: The poles of sY are at - 1 and - 2 (stable), so y(\infty) = \lim_{s \rightarrow 0}5/\left( s^{2} + 3s + 2 \right) = 2.5.

quiz.q: Linearize the pendulum \ddot{\theta} + (g/L)\sin\theta = 0 about \theta = 0 and \theta = \pi, and classify each equilibrium.
quiz.a: About 0: \ddot{\theta} + (g/L)\theta = 0, eigenvalues \pm i\sqrt{g/L}, a center (any damping makes it stable). About \pi: with \theta = \pi + \epsilon, \ddot{\epsilon} - (g/L)\epsilon = 0, eigenvalues \pm \sqrt{g/L}, a saddle (unstable).

quiz.q: Classify the equilibrium of \dot{\mathbf{x}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ - 2 & - 3 \end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x}.
quiz.a: \det\left( \mathbf{A} - \lambda\mathbf{I} \right) = \lambda^{2} + 3\lambda + 2 = 0 gives \lambda = - 1, - 2: a stable node.

quiz.q: Why may the final value theorem not be applied to Y(s) = 1/\left( s^{2} + 1 \right)?
quiz.a: sY = s/\left( s^{2} + 1 \right) has poles at \pm i; y = sint oscillates forever and has no limit.

chapters.goalsHtml: solve first-order and linear second-order ODEs; characterize damping and resonance; write systems in state-space form and judge stability from eigenvalues; linearize nonlinear systems; solve initial-value problems with Laplace transforms.

chapters.title: Partial Differential Equations, Fourier Methods and Complex Variables

secs.html:
For Au_{xx} + 2Bu_{xy} + Cu_{yy} + \ldots = 0, the discriminant B^{2} - AC classifies the equation. (With the common form Au_{xx} + Bu_{xy} + Cu_{yy}, use B^{2} - 4AC.)

Type Discriminant Prototype Physics Data needed
Elliptic < 0 \nabla^{2}u = 0 Steady subsonic potential flow, steady conduction Boundary data on a closed boundary
Parabolic = 0 u_{t} = \alpha u_{xx} Diffusion, boundary layers Initial data plus boundary data
Hyperbolic > 0 u_{tt} = c^{2}u_{xx} Waves, supersonic flow Initial or upstream data, propagated along characteristics

Boundary conditions may be Dirichlet (value), Neumann (normal derivative) or Robin (a combination, such as convective heat transfer). A problem is well-posed if a solution exists, is unique and depends continuously on the data.

Why this matters. Steady supersonic flow is hyperbolic: information travels only downstream along Mach lines, so solutions can be marched. Subsonic flow is elliptic: every point influences every other, so the whole field is solved at once. Boundary layers are parabolic and march downstream. Numerical methods must respect these domains of dependence (Chapter 45).

secs.t: Separation of variables: the heat equation
secs.html:
u_{t} = \alpha u_{xx} on 0 < x < L with u(0,t) = u(L,t) = 0. Trying u = X(x)T(t) gives X'' + \lambda X = 0 and T' + \alpha\lambda T = 0. So \lambda_{n} = (n\pi/L)^{2} and

u = \sum_{n = 1}^{\infty}b_{n}\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}\, e^{- \alpha(n\pi/L)^{2}t},\quad\quad b_{n} = \frac{2}{L}\int_{0}^{L}u(x,0)\sin\frac{n\pi x}{L}dx.

High-wavenumber modes decay fastest: diffusion smooths.

A 2L-periodic function has f = \frac{a_{0}}{2} + \sum\left\lbrack a_{n}\cos(n\pi x/L) + b_{n}\sin(n\pi x/L) \right\rbrack, with coefficients given by orthogonality integrals. The Fourier transform \widehat{f}(\omega) = \int f(t)e^{- i\omega t}dt decomposes signals into frequencies. Parseval’s theorem: energy is the same in time and frequency. Convolution in time is multiplication in frequency. These tools are used for spectra of turbulence and combustion instability (Chapters 37 and 47), for vibration (Chapter 33) and in signal processing (Chapter 21).

u_{tt} = c^{2}u_{xx} has d’Alembert’s general solution u = F(x - ct) + G(x + ct): two shapes traveling at \pm c without change. The lines x \mp ct = \text{const} are the characteristics. Acoustics, structural waves and the linearized gas dynamics of Chapter 36 all follow this pattern.

Solutions of abla^{2}\phi = 0 (harmonic functions) attain their extrema on the boundary and equal their own average over any sphere. In incompressible irrotational flow, \mathbf{u} = abla\phi with abla^{2}\phi = 0 (Chapter 25).

f(z) = \phi + i\psi is analytic if it is differentiable in the complex sense, which requires the Cauchy–Riemann equations \phi_{x} = \psi_{y} and \phi_{y} = - \psi_{x}. Then both \phi and \psi are harmonic and their level curves are orthogonal. In 2-D flow, f is the complex potential: \phi is the velocity potential, \psi the stream function, and u - iv = df/dz. Elementary flows: uniform Uz; source \frac{m}{2\pi}\ln z; vortex - \frac{i\Gamma}{2\pi}\ln z; doublet \kappa/z. A conformal map \zeta = g(z) carries solutions to new geometries. The Joukowski map \zeta = z + c^{2}/z turns the flow around a cylinder into the flow around an airfoil (Chapter 25). The residue theorem evaluates contour integrals and yields Blasius’ force theorem.

Some PDEs collapse to ODEs in a combined variable. For a semi-infinite solid x > 0 initially at T_{i} whose surface jumps to T_{s} at t = 0, the variable \eta = x/\left( 2\sqrt{\alpha t} \right) gives

\frac{T - T_{s}}{T_{i} - T_{s}} = erf\eta; surface heat flux q_{s} = \frac{k\left( T_{s} - T_{i} \right)}{\sqrt{\pi\alpha t}}; penetration depth \sim \sqrt{\alpha t}. For a constant surface flux q instead: T_{s} - T_{i} = \frac{2q}{k}\sqrt{\frac{\alpha t}{\pi}}.

These solutions size short-duration heat-flux gauges (Chapter 49), thermal-protection insulation (Chapter 42) and transient chamber walls. The Blasius boundary layer (Chapter 37) is another similarity solution.
The response to a point source, G, lets one build any solution by superposition: u = \int G(x,\xi)f(\xi)\, d\xi. Boundary-element and panel methods for aerodynamics rest on this idea.

quiz.q: Classify u_{xx} + 4u_{xy} + 4u_{yy} = 0, the wave equation and Laplace’s equation.
quiz.a: B^{2} - 4AC = 16 - 16 = 0: parabolic. The wave equation is hyperbolic; Laplace’s equation is elliptic.

quiz.q: A semi-infinite steel-like solid (\alpha = 1.0 \times 10^{- 5} m²/s) initially at 300 K has its surface raised suddenly to 1000 K. Find the temperature 1 cm deep after 100 s.
quiz.a: \eta = 0.01/\left( 2\sqrt{10^{- 5} \times 100} \right) = 0.158 and erf(0.158) = 0.177. Then T = 1000 + (300 - 1000)(0.177) = 876 K.
