quiz.q: The square wave of amplitude 1 has Fourier series \frac{4}{\pi}\sum_{n\ odd}^{}\sin(nx)/n. What is the amplitude of the fundamental?
quiz.a: 4/\pi = 1.273, larger than the square wave’s own amplitude.

quiz.q: Show that u = x^{2} - y^{2} is harmonic and find its harmonic conjugate.
quiz.a: u_{xx} + u_{yy} = 2 - 2 = 0. Cauchy–Riemann gives v = 2xy; together u + iv = z^{2}.

quiz.q: An acoustic pulse travels along a tube at 340 m/s. How far does it move in 5 ms?
quiz.a: 340 \times 0.005 = 1.7 m.

quiz.q: Why can supersonic flow be marched in space while subsonic flow cannot?
quiz.a: Supersonic steady flow is hyperbolic: a point is influenced only by its upstream Mach cone, so the solution can be advanced downstream. Subsonic flow is elliptic: every point depends on the whole boundary.

quiz.q: Show that separating variables in the heat equation with X(0) = X(L) = 0 leads to \lambda_{n} = (n\pi/L)^{2}.
quiz.a: X'' + \lambda X = 0. For \lambda \leq 0 the boundary conditions force X \equiv 0. For \lambda > 0, X = A\sin\sqrt{\lambda}x + B\cos\sqrt{\lambda}x; X(0) = 0 gives B = 0 and X(L) = 0 gives \sqrt{\lambda}L = n\pi.

quiz.q: Show that \phi = Ux + \frac{m}{2\pi}\ln r satisfies Laplace’s equation away from the origin.
quiz.a: abla^{2}(Ux) = 0, and in 2-D polar coordinates abla^{2}\ln r = rac{1}{r} rac{d}{dr}\left( r \cdot rac{1}{r} ight) = 0 for r eq 0.

chapters.goalsHtml: classify PDEs and know which boundary data they need; solve the heat, wave and Laplace equations by separation of variables, Fourier series and similarity variables; use analytic functions and conformal maps for potential flow.

chapters.title: Probability, Statistics and Uncertainty

secs.html:
Axioms: 0 \leq P(A) \leq 1, P(\Omega) = 1, and probabilities of disjoint events add. Conditional probability: P\left( A|B \right) = P(A \cap B)/P(B). Events are independent if P(A \cap B) = P(A)P(B).

Bayes’ theorem: P\left( H|D \right) = \frac{P\left( D|H \right)P(H)}{P(D)}: posterior ∝ likelihood × prior. A rare condition detected by an imperfect test produces many false positives. This governs inspection, fault detection and all of estimation theory.

A continuous variable has a PDF p(x) and CDF F(x) = P(X \leq x). Mean \mu = E\lbrack X\rbrack = \int xp\, dx; variance \sigma^{2} = E\left\lbrack (X - \mu)^{2} \right\rbrack. Key distributions: uniform; normal N\left( \mu,\sigma^{2} \right), with 68.27%, 95.45% and 99.73% of probability within 1, 2 and 3σ; exponential p = \lambda e^{- \lambda t} (memoryless times to failure); Poisson (counts of rare events); binomial (successes in n trials); Weibull (material strength, wear-out); chi-square and Student t (sampling statistics).

Covariance cov(X,Y) = E\left\lbrack \left( X - \mu_{X} \right)\left( Y - \mu_{Y} \right) \right\rbrack; correlation \rho = cov/\left( \sigma_{X}\sigma_{Y} \right) \in \lbrack - 1,1\rbrack. A random vector has mean \mathbf{\mu} and covariance matrix \mathbf{P} = E\left\lbrack \left( \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{\mu} \right)\left( \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{\mu} \right)^{T} \right\rbrack, which is symmetric positive semi-definite. Its eigenvectors are the principal axes of the uncertainty ellipsoid, and the square roots of its eigenvalues are the standard deviations along them. Linear maps transform covariances as \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{Ax} \Rightarrow \mathbf{P}_{y} = \mathbf{AP}_{x}\mathbf{A}^{T}, the propagation step of the Kalman filter (Chapter 46).

Central limit theorem: the mean of n independent samples tends to a normal distribution with standard error \sigma/\sqrt{n}. With sample standard deviation s, a confidence interval for the mean is \bar{x} \pm t_{n - 1}s/\sqrt{n}. A p-value is the probability, assuming the null hypothesis, of data at least as extreme as observed. It is not the probability that the hypothesis is true. Significance is not importance, and repeated testing inflates false discoveries.

For y = f\left( x_{1},\ldots,x_{n} \right) with small independent uncertainties: u_{y}^{2} = \sum_{i}^{}\left( \frac{\partial f}{\partial x_{i}} \right)^{2}u_{x_{i}}^{2}. For products of powers, y = \prod x_{i}^{a_{i}}: \left( u_{y}/y \right)^{2} = \sum a_{i}^{2}\left( u_{x_{i}}/x_{i} \right)^{2}. With correlations, use u_{y}^{2} = \mathbf{J}\mathbf{P}_{x}\mathbf{J}^{T}.

Monte Carlo propagation: sample inputs from their distributions, evaluate f, and take statistics of the outputs. It is exact as samples → ∞, handles nonlinearity and needs no derivatives; its standard error falls as 1/\sqrt{N}. Uncertainty itself comes in two kinds: aleatory (inherent randomness, irreducible) and epistemic (lack of knowledge, reducible by data). They are treated differently in Chapter 50.

Least squares (Chapter 10) gives the best linear unbiased estimate when errors have zero mean, equal variance and no correlation. Inspect residuals for structure: a trend in the residuals means the model is wrong. R^{2} alone is not evidence of a good model.

For a constant failure rate \lambda, reliability is R(t) = e^{- \lambda t} and MTBF = 1/\lambda. Series system: R = \prod R_{i}. Parallel (redundant) system: R = 1 - \prod\left( 1 - R_{i} \right). k-of-n systems use binomial sums. Redundancy helps only against independent failures; common-cause failures defeat it (Chapter 35).

Treat unknown parameters as random. For a Gaussian prior N\left( {\widehat{x}}^{-},P^{-} \right) and a Gaussian measurement z = x + v with v \sim N(0,R), the posterior is Gaussian with \widehat{x} = {\widehat{x}}^{-} + K\left( z - {\widehat{x}}^{-} \right), K = P^{-}/\left( P^{-} + R \right) and P = (1 - K)P^{-}. This is the scalar Kalman update (Chapter 46).

quiz.q: A crack detector finds real cracks with 95% probability and gives false positives 2% of the time; 1% of parts are cracked. Given a positive result, what is the probability that the part is cracked?
quiz.a: P = \frac{0.95(0.01)}{0.95(0.01) + 0.02(0.99)} = 0.324. Two-thirds of positives are false.

quiz.q: For a normal variable, what fraction of outcomes lie within ±2σ and within ±3σ?
Three engines each have reliability 0.99 for a mission. Find the system reliability if all three are required, and if any two suffice.
quiz.a: All required: {0.99}^{3} = 0.9703. Two of three: R^{3} + 3R^{2}(1 - R) = 0.999702.

quiz.q: I_{sp} = F/\left( \dot{m}g_{0} \right), with 1σ uncertainties of 0.5% in F and 1.0% in \dot{m}. Find the relative uncertainty in I_{sp}.
Ten thrust measurements have s = 2 N. Find the standard error and the 95% confidence half-width (t_{9} = 2.262).
quiz.a: 2/\sqrt{10} = 0.632 N; half-width 2.262 \times 0.632 = 1.43 N.

quiz.q: Distinguish aleatory and epistemic uncertainty, with one rocketry example of each.
quiz.a: Aleatory: turbulent gust loads, or part-to-part scatter in material strength. Epistemic: an uncertain reaction-rate coefficient, or an unvalidated turbulence model (reducible by experiments).

quiz.q: A 2-D position covariance is \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 3 \end{bmatrix} m². Find the principal standard deviations.
quiz.a: Eigenvalues 5.56 and 1.44 m², giving standard deviations of 2.36 m and 1.20 m along the eigenvector directions.

quiz.q: A test of 30 trials shows p = 0.04 for a 1% performance gain. What does p mean, and what does it not mean?
quiz.a: If there were truly no gain, data this extreme would occur 4% of the time. It is not the probability that the gain is real, and says nothing about whether 1% matters.

chapters.goalsHtml: manipulate probabilities with Bayes’ theorem; use distributions, covariance and the multivariate Gaussian; build confidence intervals; propagate uncertainty analytically and by Monte Carlo; compute system reliability. These tools recur in testing, estimation, reliability and UQ.

chapters.title: Numerical Methods and Scientific Computing

secs.html: IEEE double precision stores about 16 significant digits; machine epsilon is \varepsilon_{m} = 2^{- 52} \approx 2.2 \times 10^{- 16}. Round-off error comes from representation; truncation error from approximating continuous mathematics. Catastrophic cancellation: subtracting nearly equal numbers loses relative precision (for example 1 - \cos x for small x; use 2\sin^{2}(x/2)). Reorder formulas to avoid it.

Bisection: guaranteed and linear (halves the bracket each step). Newton–Raphson: x_{k + 1} = x_{k} - f\left( x_{k} \right)/f'\left( x_{k} \right), quadratically convergent near a simple root (correct digits roughly double each step) but needs a good start. Secant: Newton with a finite-difference slope, order 1.618. Robust practice combines a bracket with Newton steps (Brent’s method). Kepler’s equation M = E - e\sin E (Chapter 29) is solved by Newton from E_{0} = M.

Polynomial interpolation through many equispaced points oscillates wildly (Runge’s phenomenon); use piecewise cubic splines or Chebyshev points. Fitting noisy data uses least squares, not interpolation.

Forward difference f' \approx \left\lbrack f(x + h) - f(x) \right\rbrack/h has truncation error O(h); the central difference \left\lbrack f(x + h) - f(x - h) \right\rbrack/(2h) has O\left( h^{2} \right). Round-off grows as \varepsilon_{m}/h, so the optimal step is about \sqrt{\varepsilon_{m}} for forward differences and \varepsilon_{m}^{1/3} for central. The complex step (Chapter 50) avoids this trade-off. Quadrature: trapezoid (O\left( h^{2} \right)), Simpson (O\left( h^{4} \right), exact for cubics), Gauss–Legendre (n points exact to degree 2n - 1).

For \dot{y} = f(t,y): explicit Euler y_{n + 1} = y_{n} + hf_{n} (first order); implicit (backward) Euler y_{n + 1} = y_{n} + hf_{n + 1}; classical RK4 (fourth order, four evaluations per step); adaptive embedded pairs (RK45) control the local error.

Stability. For \dot{y} = \lambda y, explicit Euler is stable only if |1 + h\lambda| \leq 1, i.e. h \leq 2/|\lambda| for real negative \lambda. A system is stiff when its eigenvalues span many orders of magnitude, so that stability, not accuracy, limits an explicit step. Stiff problems, such as chemical kinetics (Chapters 17 and 40), need implicit methods (backward differentiation formulas).

For long orbit propagation, symplectic integrators (for example leapfrog or Störmer–Verlet) preserve the Hamiltonian structure, so energy errors stay bounded instead of drifting.

Dense direct solvers cost O\left( n^{3} \right). Discretized PDEs give sparse matrices, solved with sparse direct methods or iteratively: Jacobi and Gauss–Seidel (simple, slow), conjugate gradients (symmetric positive definite), GMRES (general). Convergence depends on the condition number, so preconditioning is essential. Multigrid solvers reach O(n) work for elliptic problems.

Unconstrained: gradient descent; Newton’s method (uses the Hessian, quadratic convergence); quasi-Newton (BFGS builds a Hessian approximation). Constrained: penalty methods, sequential quadratic programming (SQP) and interior-point methods, with the Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions generalizing Lagrange multipliers to inequalities. Convex problems have a single global minimum and are solved reliably, which is exploited in real-time guidance (Chapter 46).

Use version control (git). Write unit tests. Verify code by showing that the error falls at the theoretical rate as the step size shrinks: if errors at steps h and h/2 are e_{1} and e_{2}, the observed order is p = \log_{2}\left( e_{1}/e_{2} \right). Make results reproducible with recorded inputs, versions and random seeds. Python (NumPy/SciPy) suits prototyping; C++, Fortran and Julia suit performance; MPI and GPUs bring parallel scale (Chapter 45).

quiz.q: Apply Newton’s method to x^{2} - 2 = 0 from x_{0} = 1 for three iterations.
quiz.a: x_{1} = 1.5, x_{2} = 1.416667, x_{3} = 1.414216 (\sqrt{2} = 1.414214). Note the doubling of correct digits.

quiz.q: Solve Kepler’s equation M = E - e\sin E for M = 1 rad and e = 0.5 to four decimals.
quiz.a: Newton from E_{0} = 1: E_{1} = 1.5765, E_{2} = 1.5002, E_{3} = 1.4987. So E = 1.4987 rad.

quiz.q: Approximate \int_{0}^{1}x^{3}dx with the trapezoid rule and with Simpson’s rule, using two intervals.
quiz.a: Trapezoid: 0.5\lbrack 0/2 + 0.125 + 1/2\rbrack = 0.3125. Simpson: \frac{0.5}{3}\left\lbrack 0 + 4(0.125) + 1 \right\rbrack = 0.25, exact because Simpson integrates cubics exactly.

quiz.q: What is the largest stable explicit Euler step for \dot{y} = - 1000y?
quiz.a: h \leq 2/1000 = 0.002.

quiz.q: A grid study gives errors of 1.0 \times 10^{- 3} and 2.5 \times 10^{- 4} at steps h and h/2. Find the observed order.
quiz.a: p = \log_{2}(4) = 2.

quiz.q: Why are symplectic integrators preferred for long-term orbit propagation?
quiz.a: They preserve the geometric (symplectic) structure of Hamiltonian dynamics, so energy and angular-momentum errors stay bounded over very long times instead of drifting secularly.

quiz.q: A system has eigenvalues - 1 and - 10^{6}. Is it stiff, and what follows for the choice of integrator?
quiz.a: Yes: the stiffness ratio is 10^{6}. An explicit method would need h < 2 \times 10^{- 6} for stability long after the fast mode has died out. Use an implicit method.

quiz.q: Why can a very small h make a forward-difference derivative less accurate?
quiz.a: Round-off error \sim \varepsilon_{m}|f|/h grows as h shrinks and eventually exceeds the falling truncation error \sim h|f''|/2.

chapters.goalsHtml: understand floating-point error; find roots; interpolate, differentiate and integrate numerically; integrate ODEs with control of accuracy and stability; solve large linear systems; optimize; write verifiable scientific software. Every later computational chapter depends on this one.

chapters.title: Classical and Rigid-Body Dynamics

secs.t: Reference frames and the transport theorem
secs.html:
Newton’s laws hold in inertial frames. Vehicles are described in body frames that rotate. If frame B rotates relative to inertial frame I with angular velocity \mathbf{\omega}, then for any vector \mathbf{A}:

Transport theorem: \left( \frac{d\mathbf{A}}{dt} \right)_{I} = \left( \frac{d\mathbf{A}}{dt} \right)_{B} + \mathbf{\omega} \times \mathbf{A}.

Applying the theorem twice to the position \mathbf{r} of a particle (frames sharing an origin):

\mathbf{a}_{I} = \mathbf{a}_{B} + 2\mathbf{\omega} \times \mathbf{v}_{B} + \mathbf{\omega} \times \left( \mathbf{\omega} \times \mathbf{r} \right) + \dot{\mathbf{\omega}} \times \mathbf{r}.

An observer in the rotating frame sees apparent forces: Coriolis - 2m\mathbf{\omega} \times \mathbf{v}_{B}, centrifugal - m\mathbf{\omega} \times \left( \mathbf{\omega} \times \mathbf{r} \right) and Euler - m\dot{\mathbf{\omega}} \times \mathbf{r}. Earth rotates at \omega_{\oplus} = 7.2921159 \times 10^{- 5} rad/s, giving the equatorial surface 465.1 m/s eastward. A site at latitude \phi moves at 465.1\cos\phi m/s, the free velocity gained by launching east. The centrifugal term makes effective gravity 9.780 m/s² at the equator and 9.832 m/s² at the poles. Coriolis deflection matters for long-duration atmospheric flight and for trajectory simulation in Earth-fixed coordinates (Chapter 31).

For any system, the total external force accelerates the center of mass: \mathbf{F}_{ext} = M\mathbf{a}_{cm}. The angular momentum about the center of mass, \mathbf{H}_{cm} = \sum\mathbf{r}_{i}' \times m_{i}\mathbf{v}_{i}' (primes relative to the CM), obeys {\dot{\mathbf{H}}}_{cm} = \mathbf{M}_{cm,ext}. Kinetic energy splits as T = \frac{1}{2}Mv_{cm}^{2} + \frac{1}{2}\sum m_{i}\left| \mathbf{v}_{i}' \right|^{2} (König’s theorem). Internal forces cancel in pairs and cannot change total momentum.

secs.t: Rigid-body kinematics and the inertia tensor
secs.html:
Points of a rigid body move as \mathbf{v}_{P} = \mathbf{v}_{O} + \mathbf{\omega} \times \mathbf{r}_{P/O}. The angular momentum about the CM is \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{I\omega}, with the inertia tensor

I_{ij} = \int\left( r^{2}\delta_{ij} - x_{i}x_{j} \right)dm,\quad\quad\text{e.g. }I_{xx} = \int\left( y^{2} + z^{2} \right)\, dm,\quad I_{xy} = - \int xy\, dm.

Parallel-axis theorem: about a point displaced by \mathbf{d} from the CM, \mathbf{I}_{O} = \mathbf{I}_{cm} + m\left( d^{2}\mathbf{E} - \mathbf{dd}^{T} \right). \mathbf{I} is symmetric positive semi-definite; its eigenvectors are the principal axes, where the products of inertia vanish. Rotational kinetic energy is T_{rot} = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{\omega}^{T}\mathbf{I\omega}.

Differentiating \mathbf{H} = \mathbf{I\omega} in body axes (where \mathbf{I} is constant) with the transport theorem gives \mathbf{I}\dot{\mathbf{\omega}} + \mathbf{\omega} \times \mathbf{I\omega} = \mathbf{M}. In principal axes:

I_{1}{\dot{\omega}}_{1} - \left( I_{2} - I_{3} \right)\omega_{2}\omega_{3} = M_{1}, \quad I_{2}{\dot{\omega}}_{2} - \left( I_{3} - I_{1} \right)\omega_{3}\omega_{1} = M_{2}, \quad I_{3}{\dot{\omega}}_{3} - \left( I_{1} - I_{2} \right)\omega_{1}\omega_{2} = M_{3}.

Torque-free axisymmetric body (I_{1} = I_{2}): \omega_{3} is constant, and the transverse angular velocity rotates in the body frame at \lambda = \left( I_{3} - I_{1} \right)\omega_{3}/I_{1}; the body nutates about the fixed \mathbf{H}. Stability of pure spin: for a rigid body, spin about the axis of maximum or minimum inertia is stable, while spin about the intermediate axis is unstable (the tennis-racket or Dzhanibekov effect). With internal energy dissipation, only the maximum-inertia axis is stable (Chapter 32).

Choose independent generalized coordinates q_{k} that satisfy all constraints automatically. With L = T - V:

Lagrange’s equations: \frac{d}{dt}\frac{\partial L}{\partial{\dot{q}}_{k}} - \frac{\partial L}{\partial q_{k}} = Q_{k}, where Q_{k} are generalized non-conservative forces obtained from virtual work, \delta W = \sum Q_{k}\delta q_{k}.

Example: a pendulum with T = \frac{1}{2}mL^{2}{\dot{\theta}}^{2} and V = - mgL\cos\theta gives \ddot{\theta} + (g/L)\sin\theta = 0, with small-angle period 2\pi\sqrt{L/g}. If L does not depend on some q_{k} (a cyclic coordinate), its momentum p_{k} = \partial L/\partial{\dot{q}}_{k} is conserved. Noether’s theorem: every continuous symmetry implies a conservation law (time invariance gives energy; rotational invariance gives angular momentum). The Hamiltonian \mathcal{H} = \sum p_{k}{\dot{q}}_{k} - L leads to Hamilton’s equations. Hamilton’s principle (stationary action) underlies finite elements (Chapter 33) and optimal control (Chapter 46).

Apply momentum conservation to a control volume that encloses the vehicle, with the exhaust crossing its boundary (Chapter 26). The result for translation is

m\frac{d\mathbf{v}}{dt} = \mathbf{F}_{thrust} + \mathbf{F}_{aero} + m\mathbf{g},\quad\quad\mathbf{F}_{thrust} = - \dot{m}\mathbf{c}_{rel} + \left( p_{e} - p_{a} \right)A_{e}{\widehat{\mathbf{n}}}_{e}.

Thrust thus behaves as an external force. For rotation, exhaust leaving with the vehicle’s angular velocity removes angular momentum. This produces jet damping, a small damping moment proportional to \dot{m} times the square of the distance from the CM to the nozzle exit. Internal relative motion (propellant slosh, gimballing engines) adds further terms that are modeled explicitly in launch-vehicle dynamics (Chapter 32).

quiz.q: Find Earth’s equatorial surface speed and the eastward speed at Cape Canaveral (28.5° N).
quiz.a: \omega_{\oplus}R = 7.2921 \times 10^{- 5} \times 6\, 378\, 137 = 465.1 m/s. At 28.5°: 465.1\cos{28.5}^{\circ} = 408.7 m/s.

quiz.q: Find the Coriolis acceleration magnitude for a body moving at 1000 m/s perpendicular to Earth’s axis.
quiz.a: 2\omega v = 2\left( 7.292 \times 10^{- 5} \right)(1000) = 0.146 m/s².

quiz.q: A uniform rod of 10 kg and 2 m length rotates about one end. Find its moment of inertia.
quiz.a: I = \frac{1}{3}mL^{2} = \frac{1}{3}(10)(4) = 13.3 kg·m².

quiz.q: A torque-free axisymmetric body has I_{1} = I_{2} = 100 kg·m², I_{3} = 50 kg·m² and spins at \omega_{3} = 10 rad/s. Find the body-frame rate \lambda of the transverse angular velocity.
quiz.a: \lambda = \left( I_{3} - I_{1} \right)\omega_{3}/I_{1} = (50 - 100)(10)/100 = - 5 rad/s. The negative sign means it rotates opposite to the spin for this prolate body.

quiz.q: Why is spin about the intermediate principal axis unstable?
quiz.a: Linearizing Euler’s equations about \omega_{2} = \Omega gives {\ddot{\omega}}_{1} = \frac{\left( I_{2} - I_{3} \right)\left( I_{1} - I_{2} \right)}{I_{1}I_{3}}\Omega^{2}\omega_{1}. The coefficient is positive (exponential growth) exactly when I_{2} lies between I_{1} and I_{3}.

quiz.q: Derive the pendulum equation by Lagrange’s method and give the small-angle period for L = 2 m.
quiz.a: L = \frac{1}{2}mL^{2}{\dot{\theta}}^{2} + mgL\cos\theta gives mL^{2}\ddot{\theta} + mgL\sin\theta = 0. Period = 2\pi\sqrt{2/9.807} = 2.84 s.

quiz.q: Find the principal moments of the inertia tensor of Quiz 10, Question 6, and explain the zero moment.
quiz.a: 0, 4 and 4 kg·m². All the mass lies on the axis through the mass point, so the moment about that axis is zero.

quiz.q: Why can the thrust of a rocket be treated as an external force on the vehicle, even though it originates inside?
quiz.a: Choosing a control volume that encloses the vehicle, the momentum flux and pressure at the exit plane appear as surface terms equivalent to a force on the vehicle (Chapter 26). The internal pressure distribution never needs to be known.

chapters.goalsHtml: differentiate vectors in rotating frames; apply Coriolis and centrifugal effects; compute inertia tensors and principal axes; use Euler’s equations; derive equations of motion with Lagrange’s method; treat variable-mass systems correctly.

chapters.title: Thermodynamics

secs.html: A closed system exchanges energy but not mass; a control volume exchanges both. Properties are intensive (independent of amount: T, p, specific volume v = 1/\rho) or extensive (V, U). The state postulate: the state of a simple compressible substance is fixed by two independent intensive properties. A quasi-static process passes through equilibrium states. The zeroth law (two bodies in equilibrium with a third are in equilibrium with each other) makes temperature measurable.

Closed system: dE = \delta Q - \delta W, where E includes internal, kinetic and potential energy, Q is heat added and W is work done by the system. Quasi-static boundary work is \delta W = p\, dV. Define the enthalpy h = u + pv. For a control volume in steady flow:

Steady-flow energy equation: \dot{Q} - {\dot{W}}_{s} = \dot{m}\left\lbrack \left( h_{2} + \frac{1}{2}V_{2}^{2} + gz_{2} \right) - \left( h_{1} + \frac{1}{2}V_{1}^{2} + gz_{1} \right) \right\rbrack. Stagnation enthalpy h_{0} = h + \frac{1}{2}V^{2} is conserved in adiabatic flow with no shaft work, even through shocks and friction. A nozzle therefore converts enthalpy into kinetic energy: V_{e} = \sqrt{2\left( h_{0} - h_{e} \right)}.

For an ideal gas, u and h depend on T alone: c_{v} = du/dT, c_{p} = dh/dT, c_{p} - c_{v} = R, \gamma = c_{p}/c_{v}, and so

c_{p} = \frac{\gamma R}{\gamma - 1},\quad\quad c_{v} = \frac{R}{\gamma - 1}.

A calorically perfect gas has constant c_{p}; a thermally perfect gas has c_{p}(T). Monatomic gases have \gamma = 5/3. Diatomic gases near room temperature have \gamma = 7/5, falling toward 9/7 as molecular vibration is excited above roughly 600–1000 K (Chapter 39). Rocket exhaust typically has \gamma \approx 1.15–1.25.

Isothermal: pv = \text{const}, W = RT\ln\left( v_{2}/v_{1} \right). Isobaric: Q = \Delta h. Isochoric: Q = \Delta u. Polytropic: pv^{n} = \text{const}.

Isentropic relations (calorically perfect ideal gas): \frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}} = \left( \frac{\rho_{2}}{\rho_{1}} \right)^{\gamma} = \left( \frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}} \right)^{\gamma/(\gamma - 1)}.

Statements: no cyclic device can convert heat from a single reservoir entirely into work (Kelvin–Planck), and heat does not flow spontaneously from cold to hot (Clausius). Entropy is defined by dS = \delta Q_{rev}/T; for any process dS \geq \delta Q/T, i.e. S_{gen} \geq 0. The Gibbs equation T\, ds = du + p\, dv = dh - v\, dp holds between any equilibrium states. For an ideal gas:

s_{2} - s_{1} = c_{p}\ln\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}} - R\ln\frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}.

An isentropic process is one that is both adiabatic and reversible. Sources of irreversibility: friction, heat transfer across finite temperature differences, mixing, unrestrained expansion, shock waves and chemical reaction away from equilibrium. The maximum efficiency between reservoirs at T_{H} and T_{L} is the Carnot value 1 - T_{L}/T_{H}. Since h_{0} is conserved across an adiabatic loss, T_{0} is unchanged while p_{0} falls: p_{02}/p_{01} = e^{- \Delta s/R}. Stagnation-pressure loss is the measure of irreversibility in gas dynamics.

Ideal Brayton (isentropic compression, constant-pressure heating, isentropic expansion): \eta = 1 - \pi_{c}^{- (\gamma - 1)/\gamma}, where \pi_{c} is the pressure ratio. Turbojets, ramjets and scramjets are Brayton cycles (Chapter 44). Humphrey (constant-volume heat addition) is more efficient at equal compression; this is the thermodynamic case for pressure-gain and detonation combustion (Chapter 47). A liquid rocket is an open cycle: propellants are pumped as liquids, which needs very little work because the pump work \int v\, dp is small when v is small; heat is added at high pressure in the chamber; and the gas expands in the nozzle. Pumping a liquid instead of compressing a gas is the thermodynamic reason rockets achieve high chamber pressures cheaply.

Phase diagrams show solid, liquid and vapor regions, the saturation curve and the critical point, above which liquid and gas are indistinguishable (supercritical). Critical points: O₂ 154.6 K, 5.04 MPa; H₂ 33.2 K, 1.30 MPa; CH₄ 190.6 K, 4.60 MPa; N₂ 126.2 K, 3.40 MPa; H₂O 647.1 K, 22.06 MPa. Modern engine chambers often operate above the propellants’ critical pressures, which changes injection physics (Chapter 47). The compressibility factor Z = pv/(RT) measures departure from ideality; cubic equations of state (van der Waals, Peng–Robinson) model it. The Clausius–Clapeyron relation dp_{sat}/dT = h_{fg}/\left( Tv_{fg} \right) \approx p\, h_{fg}/\left( RT^{2} \right) governs boiling, cryogenic tank pressurization and boil-off.

Safety and scope flag · Physical hazard

Concern. Cryogenic liquids expand about 700 to 860 times in volume when they vaporize. A sealed container of cryogen becomes a pressure bomb, and nitrogen or helium boil-off in an enclosed room can cause asphyxiation without warning, because the body does not sense low oxygen.

Why it is flagged. The same thermodynamics taught in this section (phase change, the Clausius–Clapeyron relation) is what makes these hazards real.

Learn it safely. University cryogenics and low-temperature laboratory courses; Compressed Gas Association (CGA) safety publications; institutional cryogen-handling training before using even liquid nitrogen in any laboratory.

Helmholtz a = u - Ts; Gibbs g = h - Ts. At fixed T and p, a system’s equilibrium state minimizes G, the principle behind chemical-equilibrium calculations (Chapter 17). Maxwell relations follow from the equality of mixed partial derivatives, for example (\partial s/\partial p)_{T} = - (\partial v/\partial T)_{p}. The chemical potential is \mu_{i} = \left( \partial G/\partial n_{i} \right)_{T,p,n_{j \neq i}}; for an ideal-gas species, \mu_{i} = \mu_{i}^{\circ}(T) + R_{u}T\ln\left( p_{i}/p^{\circ} \right).

quiz.q: Compute c_{p} and c_{v} for air (\gamma = 1.4, R = 287 J/(kg·K)).
quiz.a: c_{p} = 1.4(287)/0.4 = 1004.5 J/(kg·K); c_{v} = 717.5 J/(kg·K).

quiz.q: Air at 100 kPa and 300 K is compressed isentropically to 1 MPa. Find T_{2}.
Find the ideal Brayton efficiency at a pressure ratio of 30.
Air is heated at constant pressure from 300 K to 600 K. Find \Delta s.
quiz.a: \Delta s = c_{p}\ln 2 = 696 J/(kg·K).

quiz.q: Gas with c_{p} = 2000 J/(kg·K) expands adiabatically from rest at 3000 K to 1000 K. Find the velocity reached.
quiz.a: V = \sqrt{2c_{p}\Delta T} = \sqrt{2(2000)(2000)} = 2828 m/s, the essence of a rocket nozzle.

quiz.q: Using Carnot reasoning, explain why adding heat at higher pressure raises cycle efficiency.
quiz.a: Isentropic compression to a higher pressure raises the temperature at which heat is received, so the mean temperature of heat addition rises relative to that of heat rejection, raising the equivalent Carnot efficiency.

quiz.q: Find the density of gaseous hydrogen at 300 K and 1 atm, and compare it with liquid hydrogen (70.8 kg/m³).
quiz.a: \rho = p\mathcal{M}/\left( R_{u}T \right) = 101\, 325(0.002016)/(8.314 \times 300) = 0.082 kg/m³, about 860 times less dense than the liquid. Only liquid storage makes hydrogen practical.

quiz.q: Show that a shock wave in adiabatic flow leaves T_{0} unchanged but lowers p_{0}.
quiz.a: h_{0} is conserved in adiabatic, work-free flow, and for a perfect gas T_{0} = h_{0}/c_{p}. The shock generates entropy, and at fixed T_{0}, p_{02}/p_{01} = e^{- \Delta s/R} < 1.

chapters.goalsHtml: apply the first and second laws to closed systems and control volumes; use ideal-gas relations, including isentropic processes; analyze Brayton and related cycles; handle real fluids near their critical points; use Gibbs and Helmholtz functions. This chapter is the root of propulsion and gas dynamics.

chapters.title: Chemical Thermodynamics and Combustion

secs.html: Each species’ enthalpy combines chemical and sensible parts: h_{i}(T) = \Delta h_{f,i}^{\circ} + \int_{298.15}^{T}c_{p,i}\, dT. Property data are tabulated as NASA polynomials (7 or 9 coefficients per temperature range) giving c_{p}, h and s^{\circ}; the JANAF tables are the classic source.

At constant pressure with no heat loss and no work, the products’ absolute enthalpy equals the reactants’: \sum_{R}^{}n_{i}h_{i}\left( T_{in} \right) = \sum_{P}^{}n_{i}h_{i}\left( T_{ad} \right). Ignoring dissociation grossly overestimates T_{ad} for energetic propellants. At high temperature the products partly dissociate into H, O, OH and similar species, absorbing energy (their formation enthalpies are positive), so the true T_{ad} is found together with the equilibrium composition. Stoichiometric H₂/O₂ at 1 atm reaches about 3080 K; at rocket chamber pressures, about 3500–3600 K.

Gibbs minimization. At fixed T and p, the equilibrium composition minimizes G = \sum_{i}^{}n_{i}\mu_{i} subject to conservation of each element j: \sum_{i}^{}a_{ij}n_{i} = b_{j}. With Lagrange multipliers \lambda_{j}: \mu_{i} + \sum_{j}^{}\lambda_{j}a_{ij} = 0 for every species. This is the method of NASA’s CEA code. Single reaction \sum u_{i}A_{i} = 0: K_{p}(T) = \prod_{i}^{}\left( p_{i}/p^{\circ} ight)^{ u_{i}} = exp\left( - \Delta G^{\circ}/R_{u}T ight).

Because p_{i} = X_{i}p, K_{p} = \prod X_{i}^{ u_{i}}\left( p/p^{\circ} ight)^{\Delta u} with \Delta u = \sum u_{i}. For dissociation (\Delta u > 0), raising p lowers the dissociated fraction, quantifying Le Chatelier’s principle. The temperature dependence follows the van ’t Hoff equation, d\ln K_{p}/dT = \Delta H^{\circ}/\left( R_{u}T^{2} ight).

An elementary reaction \sum u_{i}'A_{i} ightleftharpoons \sum u_{i}''A_{i} proceeds at net rate k_{f}\prod\left\lbrack A_{i} ight brack^{ u_{i}'} - k_{b}\prod\left\lbrack A_{i} ight brack^{ u_{i}''} (law of mass action), with k_{b} = k_{f}/K_{c} by detailed balance. Rate coefficients follow the modified Arrhenius form

k = AT^{n}\exp\left( - rac{E_{a}}{R_{u}T} ight).

Third-body reactions (H + O_{2} + M ightarrow HO_{2} + M) depend on total density and can show pressure fall-off. Chain mechanisms have initiation, propagation, branching (the key H₂/O₂ step H + O_{2} ightarrow OH + O doubles the radicals) and termination. The competition between branching and termination sets the explosion limits and the ignition delay. Detailed mechanisms contain tens to thousands of reactions. They are stiff (Chapter 14) and are often reduced for CFD.

Premixed flames are self-propagating reaction–diffusion waves. Thermal theory gives the laminar flame speed S_{L} \sim \sqrt{\alpha\,\omega/\rho} and the thickness \delta \sim \alpha/S_{L}: about 0.4 m/s for methane–air and 2–3 m/s for hydrogen–air. Mixtures burn only between flammability limits. Non-premixed (diffusion) flames are controlled by mixing. In the fast-chemistry (Burke–Schumann) limit they sit at the stoichiometric surface of the mixture fraction Z (the local fraction of mass that came from the fuel stream), Z_{st} = 1/\left\lbrack 1 + (O/F)_{st} \right\rbrack. Excessive strain extinguishes them. Rocket injectors produce mostly non-premixed or partially premixed combustion.

A burning or evaporating droplet follows the d² law, d^{2} = d_{0}^{2} - Kt, with K of order 1 mm²/s, so its lifetime is d_{0}^{2}/K. Halving the droplet size quarters the lifetime. Atomization quality therefore sets the chamber length needed for complete combustion (Chapter 27).

A detonation is a shock wave sustained by the energy released just behind it. It travels supersonically relative to the reactants, typically 1.5–3 km/s in gases, and roughly doubles the pressure beyond what constant-volume combustion would give. A deflagration is subsonic and driven by diffusion. The Chapman–Jouguet (CJ) theory selects the detonation speed at which the products leave at their local sound speed. Accidental deflagration-to-detonation transition is a major hazard in propellant handling. Its controlled use powers rotating detonation engines (Chapter 47).

Safety and scope flag · Physical hazard and dual-use

Concern. Fuel vapors and hydrogen–air or hydrogen–oxygen mixtures can transition from burning to detonation inside pipes, tanks and rooms, producing pressures far beyond what those structures were designed for.

Why it is flagged. Detonation physics is also the science of explosives. This document teaches the wave physics needed for propulsion and safety (Chapman–Jouguet theory, ZND structure, cell size; Chapter 47).

Omitted here. Explosive compositions, initiation devices and charge design. They give weapons uplift, are tightly regulated, and are not needed to understand propulsion.

Learn it safely. Graduate combustion courses; university detonation-research laboratories operating under institutional safety review; the Combustion Institute’s journals and symposia; industrial process-safety and explosion-protection training (for example NFPA standards on explosion prevention).

Chapter 26 will show that the ideal exhaust velocity scales as \sqrt{T_{c}\mathcal{/M}}, where T_{c} is the chamber temperature and \mathcal{M} the product molar mass. Good propellants therefore release much energy per unit mass and form light products (H₂O, H₂ and CO rather than CO₂). Real choices also weigh density (smaller tanks), storability, ignition behavior, toxicity, cost and material compatibility.

quiz.q: Estimate T_{ad} for H₂ + ½O₂ → H₂O from 298 K, ignoring dissociation, with a mean c_{p} of 52 J/(mol·K) for H₂O. Compare with the equilibrium value of about 3080 K at 1 atm and explain the gap.
quiz.a: T \approx 298 + 241\, 830/52 = 4950 K. The equilibrium value is about 1900 K lower because dissociation into H, O, OH and H₂ absorbs a large part of the reaction energy.

quiz.q: A reaction has \Delta G^{\circ} = + 100 kJ/mol at 3000 K. Find K_{p}.
quiz.a: K_{p} = exp\left\lbrack - 100\, 000/(8.314 \times 3000) \right\rbrack = 0.0182.

quiz.q: With E_{a} = 150 kJ/mol, by what factor does k increase between 1000 K and 1500 K?
quiz.a: \exp\left\lbrack \frac{150\, 000}{8.314}\left( \frac{1}{1000} - \frac{1}{1500} \right) \right\rbrack = 409.

quiz.q: Find the lifetime of a 100 μm droplet with K = 1 mm²/s.
quiz.a: d_{0}^{2}/K = (0.1\ mm)^{2}/\left( 1\ mm^{2}/s \right) = 0.01 s = 10 ms.

quiz.q: Why does raising chamber pressure raise performance through its effect on dissociation?
quiz.a: Dissociation increases the number of moles. Higher pressure suppresses it (Le Chatelier), so more chemical energy appears as sensible heat, raising T_{c} and the energy available for expansion.

quiz.q: Compute Z_{st} for H₂/O₂.
Distinguish a detonation from a deflagration.
quiz.a: A detonation is a shock-coupled reaction front, supersonic relative to the reactants, with a large pressure rise. A deflagration is diffusion-driven, subsonic, and nearly isobaric.

quiz.q: For O₂ ⇌ 2O, show that K_{p} = \frac{4\alpha^{2}}{1 - \alpha^{2}}\frac{p}{p^{\circ}}, where \alpha is the fraction of O₂ dissociated.
quiz.a: Start with 1 mol O₂: 1 - \alpha mol O₂ and 2\alpha mol O, 1 + \alpha in total. X_{O} = 2\alpha/(1 + \alpha) and X_{O_{2}} = (1 - \alpha)/(1 + \alpha). K_{p} = X_{O}^{2}/X_{O_{2}} \cdot \left( p/p^{\circ} \right) = \frac{4\alpha^{2}}{(1 + \alpha)(1 - \alpha)}\frac{p}{p^{\circ}}.

chapters.goalsHtml: compute adiabatic flame temperatures; formulate chemical equilibrium by Gibbs minimization and equilibrium constants; use Arrhenius kinetics and mechanisms; distinguish premixed, diffusion and droplet combustion; recognize detonations; judge propellant quality from first principles.

chapters.title: Fluid Mechanics

secs.html:
A fluid is treated as a continuum when the molecular mean free path \lambda is much smaller than the flow scale L (Knudsen number Kn = \lambda/L \ll 1; Chapter 40 covers the alternative). A Newtonian fluid has shear stress proportional to strain rate: \tau = \mu\, du/dy, with dynamic viscosity \mu and kinematic viscosity \nu = \mu/\rho. Gas viscosity increases with temperature (molecules carry momentum farther); liquid viscosity decreases. For air, Sutherland’s law is

\mu = \frac{1.458 \times 10^{- 6}\, T^{3/2}}{T + 110.4}\ \ Pa\, s\quad\left( T\ \text{in K} \right).

Other properties: surface tension \sigma (atomization and capillarity) and bulk modulus K = \rho\,\partial p/\partial\rho (compressibility).

At rest, \nabla p = \rho\mathbf{g}; vertically, dp/dz = - \rho g. In a tank accelerating at a along its axis, the effective gravity is g + a, so the pressure at depth h below the liquid surface is p = p_{ullage} + \rho(g + a)h. This sets turbopump inlet conditions and structural loads (Chapters 27 and 33). Buoyancy equals the weight of displaced fluid (Archimedes).

Atmosphere from first principles. Combine dp/dz = - \rho g with p = \rho RT: dp/p = - g\, dz/(RT). Isothermal layer: p = p_{1}e^{- \left( z - z_{1} \right)/H} with scale height H = RT/g (about 7–8.5 km). Linear temperature layer T = T_{1} - L\left( z - z_{1} \right): p/p_{1} = \left( T/T_{1} \right)^{g/(RL)}. The 1976 U.S. Standard Atmosphere (Appendix D) stacks such layers.

The Eulerian description gives fields \mathbf{u}\left( \mathbf{x},t \right) at fixed points; the Lagrangian description follows particles. The rate of change following a particle is the material derivative D/Dt = \partial/\partial t + \mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla. Streamlines are everywhere tangent to \mathbf{u}; in steady flow they coincide with pathlines and streaklines. The velocity gradient splits into the strain-rate tensor S_{ij} = \frac{1}{2}\left( \partial_{j}u_{i} + \partial_{i}u_{j} \right) and rotation. Vorticity is \mathbf{\omega} = \nabla \times \mathbf{u}, and circulation \Gamma = \oint\mathbf{u} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = \iint\mathbf{\omega} \cdot \widehat{\mathbf{n}}\, dA. Kelvin’s theorem: in inviscid, barotropic flow with conservative body forces, the circulation around a material loop is constant. Flows that start irrotational stay irrotational until viscosity, baroclinic effects or curved shocks (Chapter 36) generate vorticity.

Applying the Reynolds transport theorem (Chapter 9) to a fixed control volume V with surface S:

Mass: \frac{d}{dt}\int_{V}^{}\rho\, dV + \oint_{S}^{}\rho\left( \mathbf{u} \cdot \widehat{\mathbf{n}} \right)\, dA = 0. Momentum: \frac{d}{dt}\int_{V}^{}\rho\mathbf{u}\, dV + \oint_{S}^{}\rho\mathbf{u}\left( \mathbf{u} \cdot \widehat{\mathbf{n}} \right)\, dA = \oint_{S}^{}\left( - p\widehat{\mathbf{n}} + \mathbf{\tau} \cdot \widehat{\mathbf{n}} \right)dA + \int_{V}^{}\rho\mathbf{g}\, dV + \mathbf{F}_{ext}. Energy: \frac{d}{dt}\int_{V}^{}\rho e_{0}\, dV + \oint_{S}^{}\rho h_{0}\left( \mathbf{u} \cdot \widehat{\mathbf{n}} \right)\, dA = \dot{Q} - {\dot{W}}_{s} + {\dot{W}}_{visc}, with e_{0} = e + \frac{1}{2}u^{2} and h_{0} = h + \frac{1}{2}u^{2}.

Control-volume analysis gives forces without knowing interior details: jet impingement, nozzle thrust (Chapter 26) and the drag of a body from a wake survey.

Integrating the momentum equation along a streamline for steady, inviscid, incompressible flow with no shaft work or heat addition gives p + \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2} + \rho gz = \text{const} along that streamline (and everywhere, if the flow is also irrotational). A Pitot-static probe then gives V = \sqrt{2\left( p_{0} - p \right)/\rho}.

When Bernoulli fails. Across streamlines in rotational flow; in viscous regions (boundary layers, wakes); through shocks; across pumps, turbines and heat addition; in unsteady flow (add \rho\,\partial\phi/\partial t); for M \gtrsim 0.3 (use the compressible form of Chapter 23). The popular “equal transit time” explanation of lift is false; lift follows from circulation (Chapter 25).

Shrinking the control volume to a point gives

rac{\partial ho}{\partial t} + abla \cdot \left( ho\mathbf{u} ight) = 0,\quad\quad ho rac{D\mathbf{u}}{Dt} = - abla p + abla \cdot \mathbf{ au} + ho\mathbf{g}.

For a Newtonian fluid with Stokes’ hypothesis, au_{ij} = \mu\left( \partial_{j}u_{i} + \partial_{i}u_{j} ight) - rac{2}{3}\mu\left( abla \cdot \mathbf{u} ight)\delta_{ij}. For constant ho and \mu, these become the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations:

abla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0,\quad\quad ho\left( rac{\partial\mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + \mathbf{u} \cdot abla\mathbf{u} ight) = - abla p + \mu abla^{2}\mathbf{u} + ho\mathbf{g}.

The energy equation in enthalpy form is ho\, Dh/Dt = Dp/Dt + abla \cdot (k abla T) + \Phi, where \Phi \geq 0 is viscous dissipation. Exact solutions: Couette flow (linear profile between sliding plates); Poiseuille flow (parabolic profile in a pipe or channel); Stokes’ first problem, a plate started impulsively, with u = U\, erfc\left\lbrack y/\left( 2\sqrt{ u t} ight) ight brack, showing that vorticity diffuses a distance \sim \sqrt{ u t}.

Nondimensionalizing the governing equations exposes the controlling groups: Reynolds Re = \rho VL/\mu (inertia/viscous); Mach M = V/a (compressibility); Froude Fr = V/\sqrt{gL} (inertia/gravity; free surfaces, slosh); Strouhal St = fL/V (unsteadiness); Prandtl \Pr = \mu c_{p}/k (momentum/thermal diffusion); Weber We = \rho V^{2}L/\sigma (inertia/surface tension; atomization); Knudsen Kn (rarefaction); Eckert Ec = V^{2}/\left( c_{p}\Delta T \right) (viscous heating). Complete similarity requires every relevant group to match between model and prototype. Usually only partial similarity is achievable, and choosing which groups to match is an engineering judgment (Chapter 49).

Laminar pipe flow (Hagen–Poiseuille): \Delta p = 128\mu LQ/\left( \pi D^{4} \right), valid for Re_{D} < 2300. In general, \Delta p = f\,(L/D)\,\frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2} (Darcy–Weisbach), with f = 64/Re (laminar). For turbulent flow the Haaland approximation to Colebrook gives

\frac{1}{\sqrt{f}} = - 1.8\log_{10}\left\lbrack \left( \frac{\varepsilon/D}{3.7} \right)^{1.11} + \frac{6.9}{Re_{D}} \right\rbrack,

where \varepsilon is wall roughness. Fittings add losses K\frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}. Noncircular passages, such as cooling channels, use the hydraulic diameter D_{h} = 4A/P.

At high Re, viscous effects are confined to thin layers near walls. Over a flat plate (zero pressure gradient):

Quantity Laminar (Blasius) Turbulent (power law)
Thickness \delta_{99}/x 5.0/\sqrt{Re_{x}} 0.37/Re_{x}^{1/5}
Local skin friction c_{f} 0.664/\sqrt{Re_{x}} 0.0592/Re_{x}^{1/5}
Average over length L, C_{F} 1.328/\sqrt{Re_{L}} 0.074/Re_{L}^{1/5}

Transition on a smooth flat plate in a quiet stream occurs at roughly Re_{x} \approx 5 \times 10^{5}, but it is highly sensitive to disturbances (Chapter 37). An adverse pressure gradient (dp/dx > 0) decelerates the near-wall fluid until the layer separates, producing form drag; streamlining delays separation. The sudden drag drop of spheres near Re \approx 3 \times 10^{5} (the drag crisis) occurs because a turbulent boundary layer resists separation better.

Turbulence is unsteady, three-dimensional, vortical, strongly diffusive and dissipative over a wide range of scales. Decompose u = \bar{u} + u'. Averaging the momentum equation produces the Reynolds stresses - \rho\overline{u_{i}'u_{j}'}, unknowns that must be modeled (the closure problem; Chapter 37). Energy cascades from large eddies (size L, velocity u, dissipation rate \varepsilon \sim u^{3}/L) to the Kolmogorov scales \eta = \left( \nu^{3}/\varepsilon \right)^{1/4} and \tau_{\eta} = (\nu/\varepsilon)^{1/2}, where viscosity converts kinetic energy to heat. Since L/\eta \sim Re^{3/4}, resolving all scales (direct numerical simulation) costs roughly Re^{3} operations.

quiz.q: A LOX column (\rho = 1141 kg/m³) 20 m tall accelerates axially at 4g. Find the pressure increase at its base, beyond the ullage pressure, due to inertia alone.
quiz.a: Using the inertial load alone, \Delta p = \rho ah = 1141(4 \times 9.807)(20) = 0.895 MPa. Including gravity (effective 5g at liftoff) would add 0.224 MPa. State which frame and acceleration you mean.

quiz.q: Using Sutherland’s law, find \mu at 223.25 K, then Re for V = 300 m/s, \rho = 0.4135 kg/m³ and L = 1 m.
Water (\mu = 10^{- 3} Pa·s) flows at 5 \times 10^{- 6} m³/s through a 5 mm tube 2 m long. Check that the flow is laminar and find \Delta p.
quiz.a: V = Q/A = 0.255 m/s and Re = 1000(0.255)(0.005)/10^{- 3} = 1273, which is laminar. \Delta p = 128\left( 10^{- 3} \right)(2)\left( 5 \times 10^{- 6} \right)/\left( \pi \times {0.005}^{4} \right) = 652 Pa.

quiz.q: For a laminar plate boundary layer at x = 1 m with Re_{x} = 10^{6}, find \delta_{99} and c_{f}.
quiz.a: \delta_{99} = 5.0(1)/1000 = 5 mm; c_{f} = 0.664/1000 = 6.64 \times 10^{- 4}.

quiz.q: How many dimensionless groups govern drag if F = f(\rho,V,L,\mu,a)? Name them.
quiz.a: Six variables minus three dimensions gives three groups: C_{D}, Re and M.

quiz.q: List four conditions under which Bernoulli’s equation may not be applied.
quiz.a: Viscous regions, flow through shocks, rotational flow across streamlines, shaft work or heat addition, unsteady flow (without the \partial\phi/\partial t term), and compressible flow above M \approx 0.3.

quiz.q: Derive the differential continuity equation from the integral form.
quiz.a: For a fixed volume, \int\partial\rho/\partial t\, dV + \oint\rho\mathbf{u} \cdot \widehat{\mathbf{n}}\, dA = 0. The divergence theorem converts the surface term to \int\nabla \cdot \left( \rho\mathbf{u} \right)\, dV. Since the volume is arbitrary, the integrand must vanish: \partial\rho/\partial t + \nabla \cdot \left( \rho\mathbf{u} \right) = 0.

quiz.q: Find the Kolmogorov length for air (\nu = 1.5 \times 10^{- 5} m²/s) with \varepsilon = 1000 m²/s³.
quiz.a: \eta = \left\lbrack \left( 1.5 \times 10^{- 5} \right)^{3}/1000 \right\rbrack^{1/4} = 4.3 \times 10^{- 5} m = 43 μm.

chapters.goalsHtml: apply statics (including the atmosphere and accelerating tanks); write and use the integral and differential conservation laws; know exactly when Bernoulli holds; use dimensional analysis for similarity; analyze pipe flow; describe boundary layers and turbulence quantitatively.

chapters.title: Heat Transfer

secs.html:
Heat flux is \mathbf{q} = - k abla T. Representative conductivities (W/(m·K)): copper alloys 300–400; aluminum 120–237; titanium alloys 7; nickel superalloys 11–25; carbon–carbon 5–50 (direction-dependent); silica reusable tile about 0.05; still air 0.026. Energy conservation gives the heat equation

ho c rac{\partial T}{\partial t} = abla \cdot (k abla T) + \dot{q}''',\quad\quad\alpha = rac{k}{ ho c}\ ext{(thermal diffusivity)}.

Plane wall: q = k\Delta T/L. Thermal resistances add like electrical ones: wall L/(kA); cylinder \ln\left( r_{2}/r_{1} \right)/(2\pi kL); convection 1/(hA); contact R''_{c}/A. Fins extend area; a uniform fin with an adiabatic tip has efficiency \eta_{f} = tanh(mL)/(mL) with m = \sqrt{hP/\left( kA_{c} \right)}.

The Biot number Bi = hL_{c}/k (L_{c} = V/A_{s}) compares internal to surface resistance. If Bi < 0.1, the body is nearly isothermal (lumped capacitance): T - T_{\infty} = \left( T_{0} - T_{\infty} \right)e^{- t/\tau} with \tau = \rho cV/\left( hA_{s} \right). Otherwise solve the heat equation. At early times (Fo = \alpha t/L^{2} \lesssim 0.1) every body behaves as a semi-infinite solid (Chapter 12); at later times use one-term series solutions.

Newton’s law q = h\left( T_{w} - T_{ref} \right) defines the heat-transfer coefficient h. At low speed T_{ref} is the free-stream temperature; at high speed it is the adiabatic wall temperature T_{aw} (Chapter 37), so that q = h\left( T_{aw} - T_{w} \right). Dimensionless forms: Nusselt Nu = hL/k; Prandtl \Pr = \nu/\alpha (air 0.71, water about 7, liquid metals about 0.01); Stanton St = h/\left( \rho uc_{p} \right) = Nu/\left( Re\,\Pr \right).

Configuration Correlation
Flat plate, laminar (local) Nu_{x} = 0.332\, Re_{x}^{1/2}Pr^{1/3}
Flat plate, turbulent (local) Nu_{x} = 0.0296\, Re_{x}^{4/5}Pr^{1/3}
Pipe, laminar, fully developed Nu_{D} = 3.66 (uniform T_{w}), 4.36 (uniform q)
Pipe, turbulent (Dittus–Boelter) Nu_{D} = 0.023\, Re_{D}^{0.8}Pr^{n}; n = 0.4 heating, 0.3 cooling the fluid

Momentum and heat are carried across a boundary layer by the same molecular and turbulent mixing. For \Pr = 1, St = c_{f}/2. More generally:

Chilton–Colburn analogy: St\, Pr^{2/3} = c_{f}/2. Heating can be predicted from skin friction and vice versa. This is the central link in aerothermodynamics (Chapter 41): wherever friction is high, heating is high.

The gas-side heat-transfer coefficient in chambers and nozzles is estimated by the Bartz correlation:

h_{g} = \frac{0.026}{D_{t}^{0.2}}\left( \frac{\mu^{0.2}c_{p}}{Pr^{0.6}} \right)_{0}\left( \frac{p_{c}}{c^{*}} \right)^{0.8}\left( \frac{D_{t}}{r_{c}} \right)^{0.1}\left( \frac{A_{t}}{A} \right)^{0.9}\sigma,

\sigma = \left\lbrack \frac{1}{2}\frac{T_{w}}{T_{c}}\left( 1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2}M^{2} \right) + \frac{1}{2} \right\rbrack^{- 0.68}\left\lbrack 1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2}M^{2} \right\rbrack^{- 0.12},

where D_{t} is the throat diameter, r_{c} the throat radius of curvature, c^{*} the characteristic velocity (Chapter 26), and subscript 0 denotes chamber stagnation properties. Because h_{g} \propto \left( p_{c}/c^{*} \right)^{0.8}\left( A_{t}/A \right)^{0.9}, i.e. roughly to the 0.8 power of the local mass flux, the heat flux peaks at the throat and rises nearly linearly with chamber pressure. This is the central challenge of high-pressure engines (Chapter 27).

A blackbody emits E_{b} = \sigma T^{4}, with \sigma = 5.670374 \times 10^{- 8} W/(m²·K⁴), with spectral peak at \lambda_{\max}T = 2897.8 μm·K (Wien). Real surfaces emit \varepsilon\sigma T^{4}. Kirchhoff’s law: spectral absorptivity equals spectral emissivity, and for a gray surface \alpha = \varepsilon. The view factor F_{ij} is the fraction of radiation leaving surface i that strikes j; reciprocity gives A_{i}F_{ij} = A_{j}F_{ji} and summation gives \sum_{j}^{}F_{ij} = 1. Two large parallel gray plates exchange q = \sigma\left( T_{1}^{4} - T_{2}^{4} \right)/\left( 1/\varepsilon_{1} + 1/\varepsilon_{2} - 1 \right).

Radiative equilibrium. If a surface rejects all incoming convective flux by radiation to cold surroundings (no conduction inward): q_{conv} = \varepsilon\sigma T_{w}^{4} \Rightarrow T_{w} = \left( q_{conv}/\varepsilon\sigma \right)^{1/4}. High emissivity lowers the wall temperature, the principle of radiatively cooled nozzle extensions and reusable thermal protection (Chapter 42).

Gases such as H₂O and CO₂ emit and absorb in bands, and soot radiates as a near-continuum. Chamber, plume and high-speed shock-layer radiation (Chapter 41) require participating-media methods.

As wall superheat rises, a liquid moves from natural convection through nucleate boiling (very high h) to the critical heat flux (CHF). Beyond CHF a vapor film insulates the wall (film boiling) and the wall temperature jumps, possibly to failure (“burnout”). Regenerative cooling with subcritical coolant must remain below CHF. Coolants above their critical pressure do not boil, but their properties vary sharply near the pseudo-critical temperature, which can cause heat-transfer deterioration.

With capacity rates C = \dot{m}c_{p}, the effectiveness–NTU method gives q = \varepsilon_{hx}C_{\min}\left( T_{h,in} - T_{c,in} \right), where \varepsilon_{hx} depends on NTU = UA/C_{\min}, C_{\min}/C_{\max} and the flow arrangement. Counterflow is the most effective arrangement. Regenerative cooling jackets and the precoolers of combined-cycle engines (Chapter 44) are heat exchangers.

quiz.q: Find the heat flux through a 5 cm insulating layer with k = 0.1 W/(m·K) and a 1000 K temperature difference.
quiz.a: q = 0.1(1000)/0.05 = 2 kW/m².

quiz.q: A 1 cm diameter aluminum sphere (\rho = 2700, c = 900, k = 237, SI units) is cooled with h = 50 W/(m²·K). Check the lumped approximation and find the time constant.
quiz.a: L_{c} = r/3 = 1.67 mm and Bi = 50(0.00167)/237 = 3.5 \times 10^{- 4} \ll 0.1, so lumping is valid. \tau = \rho cL_{c}/h = 2700(900)(0.00167)/50 = 81 s.

quiz.q: A surface with \varepsilon = 0.85 receives 100 kW/m² of convective heating and is in radiative equilibrium. Find T_{w}.
quiz.a: T_{w} = \left\lbrack 10^{5}/\left( 0.85 \times 5.670 \times 10^{- 8} \right) \right\rbrack^{1/4} = 1200 K.

quiz.q: Find the blackbody emissive power at 1500 K and the wavelength of peak emission at 3000 K.
quiz.a: E_{b} = 5.670 \times 10^{- 8}(1500)^{4} = 287 kW/m². \lambda_{\max} = 2897.8/3000 = 0.966 μm, in the near infrared.

quiz.q: Water in a tube has Re_{D} = 10^{5} and \Pr = 5 and is being heated. Estimate Nu_{D}.
State the Reynolds analogy and explain physically why it works.
quiz.a: St = c_{f}/2 for \Pr = 1, or St\, Pr^{2/3} = c_{f}/2 in general. The same molecular and turbulent mixing transports momentum and enthalpy, and for \Pr = 1 the governing boundary-layer equations are identical.

quiz.q: A wall with k = 20 W/(m·K) and \alpha = 5 \times 10^{- 6} m²/s receives a sudden constant flux of 1 MW/m². Find the surface temperature rise after 1 s.
quiz.a: \Delta T_{s} = (2q/k)\sqrt{\alpha t/\pi} = \left( 2 \times 10^{6}/20 \right)\sqrt{5 \times 10^{- 6}/\pi} = 126 K.

quiz.q: Why is operating beyond the critical heat flux dangerous for a regeneratively cooled chamber?
quiz.a: Beyond CHF a vapor film forms and the coolant-side heat-transfer coefficient collapses. The wall can no longer reject the hot-gas heat flux, its temperature rises rapidly, and the wall can melt or burn through within seconds.

chapters.goalsHtml: solve steady and transient conduction problems; use convection correlations and the Reynolds analogy; apply the Bartz correlation to rocket nozzles; compute radiative exchange and radiative-equilibrium temperatures; recognize boiling limits; size heat exchangers. These are the tools of engine cooling and thermal protection.

chapters.title: Solid Mechanics and Materials

secs.html: The traction on a surface with normal \widehat{\mathbf{n}} is \mathbf{t} = \mathbf{\sigma} \cdot \widehat{\mathbf{n}}, where the Cauchy stress tensor \mathbf{\sigma} is symmetric. Its eigenvalues are the principal stresses \sigma_{1} \geq \sigma_{2} \geq \sigma_{3}, acting on planes free of shear; the maximum shear stress is \left( \sigma_{1} - \sigma_{3} \right)/2. In 2-D, Mohr’s circle has center \left( \sigma_{x} + \sigma_{y} \right)/2 and radius \sqrt{\left\lbrack \left( \sigma_{x} - \sigma_{y} \right)/2 \right\rbrack^{2} + \tau_{xy}^{2}}. Equilibrium requires \partial\sigma_{ij}/\partial x_{j} + f_{i} = 0. For small displacements \mathbf{u}, the strain tensor is \varepsilon_{ij} = \frac{1}{2}\left( \partial_{j}u_{i} + \partial_{i}u_{j} \right).

Isotropic linear elasticity with thermal strain: \varepsilon_{ij} = rac{1 + u}{E}\sigma_{ij} - rac{ u}{E}\sigma_{kk}\delta_{ij} + \alpha\Delta T\,\delta_{ij}, with Young’s modulus E, Poisson’s ratio u, shear modulus G = E/\left\lbrack 2(1 + u) ight brack, bulk modulus K = E/\left\lbrack 3(1 - 2 u) ight brack and thermal expansion coefficient \alpha.

Composites are anisotropic: an orthotropic lamina needs nine constants (Chapter 33). Beyond yield, metals deform plastically; polymers and composite matrices are viscoelastic.

Axial: \sigma = P/A, elongation \delta = PL/(EA). Torsion of a circular shaft: \tau = Tr/J, twist \phi = TL/(GJ), with J = \pi d^{4}/32. Thin-walled closed sections carry a shear flow q = T/\left( 2A_{m} \right) (Bredt), where A_{m} is the area enclosed by the wall midline. Bending: \sigma = - My/I with I = bh^{3}/12 (rectangle), \pi d^{4}/64 (solid circle) or \pi r^{3}t (thin tube). Euler–Bernoulli beam: EI\, w⁗ = q(x); a cantilever with tip load P deflects PL^{3}/(3EI).

Thin-walled vessels (t/r < 0.1): cylinder hoop stress \sigma_{\theta} = pr/t, axial stress \sigma_{x} = pr/(2t); sphere \sigma = pr/(2t). Minimum mass: for a sphere sized to allowable stress \sigma_{a}, m = \frac{3}{2}pV\rho/\sigma_{a}. Tank mass scales with pV and inversely with the specific strength \sigma_{a}/\rho, independent of shape details.

This scaling governs propulsion architecture: pressure-fed stages need high tank pressures and therefore heavy tanks, while pump-fed stages keep tank pressures low (Chapter 27). Composite overwrapped pressure vessels (COPVs), with a thin metal liner wrapped in carbon fiber, store high-pressure helium efficiently but bring their own failure modes.

Safety and scope flag · Physical hazard

Concern. A pressurized vessel stores energy that is released explosively if it ruptures. A gas-filled vessel stores far more energy than a liquid-filled one at the same pressure; Chapter 54 gives the formula and a worked number.

Why it is flagged. Improvised pressure vessels and pneumatic (gas) proof tests have killed and injured experimenters, students included.

Learn it safely. Proof tests are done hydrostatically (with liquid), behind barriers, by trained staff. Study the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code and pressure-system safety courses offered by universities and professional bodies. Never pressurize an untested, modified or improvised container.

Slender compressed members fail by instability below their material strength. An Euler column has P_{cr} = \pi^{2}EI/(KL)^{2}, with effective-length factor K = 1 (pinned–pinned), 0.5 (fixed–fixed), 0.7 (fixed–pinned) or 2 (cantilever). A flat plate has \sigma_{cr} = k\pi^{2}E(t/b)^{2}/\left\lbrack 12\left( 1 - u^{2} ight) ight brack. A thin cylinder in axial compression has the classical value

\sigma_{cl} = rac{E}{\sqrt{3\left( 1 - u^{2} ight)}} rac{t}{R} \approx 0.605\, E rac{t}{R}\ ( u = 0.3),

but real shells buckle at a fraction of this because of geometric imperfections. Design therefore uses empirical knockdown factors (Chapter 33). Internal pressure stiffens thin shells, which is why lightweight tanks are often pressurized before carrying flight loads.

Ductile yielding: von Mises predicts yield when \sigma_{vm} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack \left( \sigma_{1} - \sigma_{2} \right)^{2} + \left( \sigma_{2} - \sigma_{3} \right)^{2} + \left( \sigma_{3} - \sigma_{1} \right)^{2} \right\rbrack} reaches \sigma_{y}; Tresca uses the maximum shear. Fracture mechanics: a crack of size a under stress \sigma has stress-intensity factor K_{I} = Y\sigma\sqrt{\pi a} (Y is a geometry factor of order 1), and fracture occurs when K_{I} = K_{IC} (fracture toughness), giving a critical crack size a_{c} = \left( K_{IC}/Y\sigma \right)^{2}/\pi. Pressure vessels are designed to leak before burst: a crack should penetrate the wall before reaching critical length. Fatigue: cyclic stress causes failure after N cycles described by S–N curves; mean stress reduces life (Goodman correction). Miner’s rule estimates cumulative damage as D = \sum n_{i}/N_{i}, with failure expected near D = 1. Crack growth follows the Paris law da/dN = C(\Delta K)^{m}. Creep: above roughly 0.4T_{m}, strain grows with time under constant load. The Larson–Miller parameter P = T\left( C + logt_{r} \right) collapses stress-rupture data.

A bar fully restrained against expansion develops \sigma = - E\alpha\Delta T; a plate restrained in two directions, \sigma = - E\alpha\Delta T/(1 - \nu). Through-thickness temperature gradients cause bending stresses even without external restraint. The thermal shock resistance R = \sigma_{f}(1 - \nu)/(E\alpha) ranks materials for sudden heating. Engineering remedies: allow free expansion (sliding joints, flexible standoffs), match expansion coefficients at joints, and grade material properties. These issues dominate hot structures and thermal protection (Chapter 42).

secs.t: Materials for rockets and hypersonic vehicles
secs.html:
Crystal structure governs ductility: face-centered cubic metals (Al, Ni, Cu) stay ductile at cryogenic temperatures; body-centered cubic refractory metals (W, Mo, Nb) have a ductile-to-brittle transition. Strength comes from solid solution, precipitates (Al alloys; the γ′ phase in nickel superalloys), fine grains and cold work.

Material (representative, room temperature) \mathbf{\rho} (kg/m³) \mathbf{E} (GPa) \mathbf{\sigma}_{\mathbf{y}} (MPa) Typical use
Al 2219-T87 2840 74 ≈ 395 Cryogenic tanks
Al–Li 2195-T8 2710 76 ≈ 550 Lightweight cryogenic tanks
Ti-6Al-4V 4430 114 ≈ 880 Pressure vessels, structures to ≈ 400 °C
Inconel 718 8190 200 ≈ 1100 Turbopumps, manifolds to ≈ 650 °C
Copper alloys (e.g. GRCop) ≈ 8800 ≈ 110 ≈ 200 Regeneratively cooled chamber liners
CFRP (quasi-isotropic) ≈ 1600 50–70 500–700 (ultimate) Interstages, fairings, COPVs

Values are representative only; design uses statistically based allowables (for example MMPDS). Special environments: hydrogen embrittlement degrades high-strength steels and some nickel alloys; oxygen compatibility matters because many metals ignite in high-pressure oxygen, which drives the choice of nickel alloys and coatings in oxygen-rich turbines; composites microcrack and leak at cryogenic temperatures. Ceramics are strong at high temperature but brittle, and their strength scatter follows Weibull statistics (Chapter 42).

Material indices (Ashby). Minimum mass for a given function: tie in tension, maximize \sigma/\rho; stiff beam, E^{1/2}/\rho; stiff panel, E^{1/3}/\rho; pressure vessel, \sigma/\rho. Plotting materials on log axes of the two properties turns selection into drawing a line of constant index.

quiz.q: A cylindrical tank of radius 1.5 m holds 0.3 MPa with allowable stress 300 MPa. Find the wall thickness required by hoop stress.
quiz.a: t = pr/\sigma = 0.3 \times 10^{6}(1.5)/300 \times 10^{6} = 1.5 mm (before safety factors and minimum-gauge limits).

quiz.q: Find the Euler buckling load of a pinned aluminum tube with E = 70 GPa, I = 1 \times 10^{- 6} m⁴ and L = 2 m.
quiz.a: P_{cr} = \pi^{2}\left( 70 \times 10^{9} \right)\left( 10^{- 6} \right)/2^{2} = 173 kN.

quiz.q: An Inconel bar (E = 200 GPa, \alpha = 13 \times 10^{- 6}/K) is fully restrained and heated 500 K. Find the thermal stress and comment.
quiz.a: \sigma = E\alpha\Delta T = 200 \times 10^{9}\left( 13 \times 10^{- 6} \right)(500) = 1.3 GPa, compressive, which exceeds yield. Hot structures must be designed to expand freely rather than to resist.

quiz.q: Find K_{I} for \sigma = 200 MPa and a crack with a = 2 mm (Y = 1). Is it safe for Ti-6Al-4V (K_{IC} \approx 55 MPa√m)?
quiz.a: K_{I} = 200\sqrt{\pi \times 0.002} = 15.9 MPa√m, well below 55, so it is safe against fracture. The critical crack size is a_{c} = (55/200)^{2}/\pi = 24 mm.

quiz.q: Find the von Mises stress for principal stresses 200, 100 and 0 MPa.
quiz.a: \sqrt{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack (100)^{2} + (100)^{2} + (200)^{2} \right\rbrack} = \sqrt{30\, 000} = 173 MPa.

quiz.q: A part sees 10^{4} cycles at a level where N = 10^{5} and 2 \times 10^{5} cycles where N = 10^{6}. Find the Miner damage.
Why is \sigma/\rho the right index for minimum-mass pressure vessels?
quiz.a: Wall mass is area × thickness × \rho, and thickness is proportional to pr/\sigma_{a}. Mass is therefore proportional to pV\rho/\sigma_{a}, and for fixed p and V it is minimized by maximizing \sigma_{a}/\rho.

quiz.q: Show that a pinned column satisfying EIw'' + Pw = 0 has nontrivial solutions only for P = n^{2}\pi^{2}EI/L^{2}.
quiz.a: With k^{2} = P/(EI), w = A\sin kx + B\cos kx. w(0) = 0 gives B = 0; w(L) = 0 with A \neq 0 requires \sin kL = 0, i.e. kL = n\pi.

chapters.goalsHtml: analyze stress and strain in three dimensions; apply Hooke’s law with thermal strain; size bars, beams, shafts and pressure vessels; predict buckling, yielding, fracture, fatigue and creep; select materials with performance indices.

chapters.title: Electromagnetism, Circuits and Signals

secs.html: Coulomb’s law: F = q_{1}q_{2}/\left( 4\pi\varepsilon_{0}r^{2} \right) with \varepsilon_{0} = 8.854 \times 10^{- 12} F/m. The field \mathbf{E} = \mathbf{F}/q derives from a potential, \mathbf{E} = - \nabla V. Gauss’s law: \oint\mathbf{E} \cdot d\mathbf{A} = Q_{enc}/\varepsilon_{0}. Capacitance is C = Q/V; a parallel-plate capacitor has C = \varepsilon A/d and stores energy \frac{1}{2}CV^{2}.

Current I = dQ/dt; Ohm’s law V = IR; power P = IV = I^{2}R. Kirchhoff’s laws: currents into a node sum to zero, and voltages around a loop sum to zero. An RC circuit has time constant \tau = RC and step response 1 - e^{- t/\tau}; an RL circuit has \tau = L/R. A series RLC circuit is a second-order system (Chapter 11) with \omega_{n} = 1/\sqrt{LC} and \zeta = (R/2)\sqrt{C/L}. In AC analysis, impedances are Z_{R} = R, Z_{C} = 1/(j\omega C) and Z_{L} = j\omega L (engineers write j for \sqrt{- 1}), so circuits are solved algebraically with phasors.

Lorentz force: \mathbf{F} = q\left( \mathbf{E} + \mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B} \right). A charge in a uniform field \mathbf{B} gyrates at the cyclotron frequency \omega_{c} = |q|B/m with radius r_{L} = mv_{\bot}/\left( |q|B \right). A wire experiences \mathbf{F} = I\mathbf{L} \times \mathbf{B}.

Ampère’s law: \oint\mathbf{B} \cdot d\mathbf{l} = \mu_{0}I_{enc}, with \mu_{0} = 4\pi \times 10^{- 7} H/m; a long solenoid has B = \mu_{0}nI. Faraday’s law: the induced EMF is - d\Phi_{B}/dt (Lenz’s law gives the sign). Electric motors drive actuators and electric turbopumps; generators and alternators supply vehicle power.

abla \cdot \mathbf{E} = rac{ ho_{q}}{\varepsilon_{0}},\quad abla \cdot \mathbf{B} = 0,\quad abla imes \mathbf{E} = - rac{\partial\mathbf{B}}{\partial t},\quad abla imes \mathbf{B} = \mu_{0}\mathbf{J} + \mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0} rac{\partial\mathbf{E}}{\partial t}.

In vacuum these give waves traveling at c = 1/\sqrt{\mu_{0}\varepsilon_{0}}, with wavelength \lambda = c/f. The Poynting vector \mathbf{S} = \mathbf{E} imes \mathbf{H} is the power flux. Waves cannot penetrate a plasma at frequencies below its plasma frequency, the cause of entry communication blackout (Chapter 48).

An antenna’s gain G concentrates radiated power in direction; its effective aperture is A_{e} = G\lambda^{2}/(4\pi), and a dish of diameter D has G = \eta(\pi D/\lambda)^{2}. Between isotropic antennas, power falls by the free-space path loss (4\pi d/\lambda)^{2}. Logarithmic units: dB = 10\log_{10}\left( P_{2}/P_{1} \right) = 20\log_{10}\left( V_{2}/V_{1} \right); dBW and dBm are referenced to 1 W and 1 mW. The effective isotropic radiated power is EIRP = P_{t}G_{t}. Link budgets add and subtract these decibel quantities (Chapter 34).

Diodes conduct one way; transistors (BJT, MOSFET) act as switches or amplifiers. Ideal op-amp rules (with negative feedback): no current enters the inputs and the two inputs sit at the same voltage. Hence an inverting amplifier has gain - R_{f}/R_{in} and a non-inverting one 1 + R_{f}/R_{g}. An N-bit analog-to-digital converter resolves 2^{N} levels; for a full-scale sine its ideal quantization-limited signal-to-noise ratio is 6.02N + 1.76 dB.

Sampling theorem. A band-limited signal is recoverable from samples taken at f_{s} > 2f_{\max}. A component at frequency f above f_{s}/2 appears falsely at the alias \left| f - kf_{s} \right| for the integer k that brings it into \left\lbrack 0,f_{s}/2 \right\rbrack. An analog anti-aliasing low-pass filter must precede the converter, because aliasing cannot be undone afterward.

A first-order RC low-pass filter has cutoff f_{c} = 1/(2\pi RC) and rolls off at 20 dB/decade. Digital filters are FIR (always stable, can have linear phase) or IIR (efficient, can be unstable). Thermal noise power in bandwidth B is kTB, which is −174 dBm/Hz at 290 K. Receiver quality is expressed by the noise figure, or the system noise temperature.

Lithium-ion cells store roughly 150–270 Wh/kg; multi-junction solar cells convert about 30% of sunlight (1361 W/m² at 1 AU). Power budgets sum loads by mode, including converter efficiencies, harness losses and margin. Electric-pump-fed engines (Chapter 27) and electric propulsion (Chapter 48) are limited by battery or array specific power.

Safety and scope flag · Physical hazard

Concern. Lithium-ion cells can enter thermal runaway, producing fire and toxic gas, when overcharged, short-circuited, crushed or overheated. Vehicle electrical systems and ground equipment can carry lethal voltages and currents.

Why it is flagged. Battery and electrical failures are a common cause of laboratory fires and of test-site incidents.

Learn it safely. University electronics laboratories and battery-safety training; manufacturers’ charge, discharge and temperature limits; protection circuits and fused wiring; electrical-safety training (lockout/tagout) before working on powered hardware.

A strain gauge changes resistance as \Delta R/R = GF \cdot \varepsilon (gauge factor about 2) and is read in a Wheatstone bridge. Thermocouples generate a Seebeck voltage (type K about 41 μV/K) and need cold-junction compensation. Resistance temperature detectors are accurate at moderate temperature. Pressure transducers may be piezoresistive (static and dynamic) or piezoelectric (dynamic only). Every measurement passes through a chain of sensor, signal conditioning (excitation, amplification, filtering), conversion, processing and recording. Each link contributes uncertainty (Chapter 13) and must be calibrated against traceable standards.

quiz.q: Find the cutoff frequency of an RC filter with R = 10 kΩ and C = 10 nF.
quiz.a: f_{c} = 1/\left\lbrack 2\pi\left( 10^{4} \right)\left( 10^{- 8} \right) \right\rbrack = 1592 Hz.

quiz.q: Find the thermal noise power at 290 K in a 1 MHz bandwidth, in W and dBm.
quiz.a: kTB = 1.381 \times 10^{- 23}(290)\left( 10^{6} \right) = 4.0 \times 10^{- 15} W = - 114.0 dBm.

quiz.q: Find the free-space path loss at 2.2 GHz over 1000 km.
quiz.a: \lambda = 0.1363 m. 20\log_{10}\left( 4\pi \times 10^{6}/0.1363 \right) = 159.3 dB.

quiz.q: Find the cyclotron frequency (in Hz) of an electron in a 0.02 T field.
quiz.a: f = eB/\left( 2\pi m_{e} \right) = 1.602 \times 10^{- 19}(0.02)/\left( 2\pi \times 9.109 \times 10^{- 31} \right) = 560 MHz.

quiz.q: A 300 Hz vibration is sampled at 400 Hz without filtering. At what frequency does it appear?
quiz.a: |300 - 400| = 100 Hz.

quiz.q: Why must the anti-aliasing filter be analog and placed before the ADC?
quiz.a: Once a signal is sampled, an alias is indistinguishable from a genuine low-frequency signal. Only an analog filter acting before sampling can remove the high-frequency content.

quiz.q: How long does an RC circuit take to reach 95% of a step input?
quiz.a: t = - \tau\ln(0.05) = 3.0\tau.

quiz.q: A 16-bit ADC: what is its ideal quantization-limited SNR?

chapters.goalsHtml: use Maxwell’s equations and the Lorentz force; analyze DC and AC circuits; reason in decibels; design sampling chains free of aliasing; understand antennas, path loss, noise and sensors. Prepares Chapters 34 (avionics) and 48 (plasma and electric propulsion).

chapters.title: Classical Feedback Control

secs.html: Feedback compares a measured output with the desired value and acts on the error. It reduces sensitivity to plant uncertainty, rejects disturbances, and can stabilize an unstable plant. The costs are injection of sensor noise and the possibility of making a stable plant unstable. With loop transfer function L = GC (plant G, controller C, unity feedback), the closed loop is T = L/(1 + L), the sensitivity is S = 1/(1 + L), and S + T = 1. Good tracking at low frequency needs |L| \gg 1 there; good noise rejection at high frequency needs |L| \ll 1 there.

G(s) = N(s)/D(s): zeros are roots of N and poles are roots of D. A linear time-invariant system is (bounded-input bounded-output) stable if and only if every pole has a negative real part. The Routh–Hurwitz array decides this from the coefficients of the characteristic polynomial without solving for the roots. For example, s^{3} + a_{2}s^{2} + a_{1}s + a_{0} is stable if and only if all coefficients are positive and a_{2}a_{1} > a_{0}.

For the canonical second-order system \omega_{n}^{2}/\left( s^{2} + 2\zeta\omega_{n}s + \omega_{n}^{2} \right):

Overshoot M_{p} = exp\left( - \pi\zeta/\sqrt{1 - \zeta^{2}} \right); 2% settling time t_{s} \approx 4/\left( \zeta\omega_{n} \right); rise time t_{r} \approx 1.8/\omega_{n}. Steady-state error to a step is zero if the loop contains at least one integrator (“type 1”). In general, use the final value theorem.

As a gain K in 1 + KG_{0}(s) = 0 rises from 0 to ∞, the closed-loop poles move from the open-loop poles to the open-loop zeros, or to infinity along asymptotes at angles (2k + 1)180^{\circ}/(n - m) centered at (\sum p - \sum z)/(n - m). Real-axis segments lie to the left of an odd number of real poles and zeros. The locus shows at a glance which gains are stable and how damping varies with gain.

L(j\omega) has a magnitude and a phase; Bode plots draw 20\log|L| and \angle L against \log\omega, with each pole contributing −20 dB/decade and up to −90°. Nyquist criterion: the number of unstable closed-loop poles is Z = N + P, where N is the number of clockwise encirclements of −1 by L(j\omega) and P the number of unstable open-loop poles.

Stability margins. Gain margin: the factor by which gain can rise before instability, read where the phase is −180°. Phase margin (PM): 180^{\circ} + \angle L at the crossover frequency where |L| = 1. For moderately damped loops, \zeta \approx PM/100^{\circ}. A pure time delay T multiplies L by e^{- sT}, adding phase lag \omega T with no change in gain. Delay therefore always erodes phase margin.

u = K_{p}e + K_{i}\int e\, dt + K_{d}\, de/dt. The proportional term sets stiffness, the integral term removes steady error, and the derivative term adds damping (phase lead). The derivative must be filtered, for example K_{d}s/\left( \tau_{f}s + 1 \right), to limit noise amplification. When the actuator saturates, the integrator keeps accumulating error (windup) and causes large overshoot; anti-windup clamps the integrator or back-calculates it from the saturated output.

A lead compensator (s/z + 1)/(s/p + 1) with p > z adds phase near crossover to improve the margins. A lag compensator raises low-frequency gain to reduce steady error. A notch filter suppresses a narrow band, such as a structural bending mode (Chapter 32).

With \dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{Ax} + \mathbf{Bu} and \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{Cx} + \mathbf{Du}, the transfer matrix is \mathbf{G}(s) = \mathbf{C}\left( s\mathbf{I} - \mathbf{A} \right)^{- 1}\mathbf{B} + \mathbf{D}. If the controllability matrix \left\lbrack \mathbf{B}\ \mathbf{AB}\ \cdots\ \mathbf{A}^{n - 1}\mathbf{B} \right\rbrack has full rank, state feedback \mathbf{u} = - \mathbf{Kx} can place the closed-loop eigenvalues anywhere. If the observability matrix \left\lbrack \mathbf{C};\ \mathbf{CA};\ \ldots \right\rbrack has full rank, an observer \dot{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}} = \mathbf{A}\widehat{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{Bu} + \mathbf{L}\left( \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{C}\widehat{\mathbf{x}} \right) can reconstruct the state. By the separation principle (for linear models) the two can be designed independently. Chapter 46 makes both optimal (LQR, Kalman filter).

Controllers run in discrete time with period T. A zero-order hold adds an effective delay of about T/2, plus any computation delay. The z-transform (z = e^{sT}) maps the stable left half-plane into the unit disk |z| < 1. Continuous designs are discretized, for example by Tustin’s substitution s \leftarrow (2/T)(z - 1)/(z + 1). Rule of thumb: sample at least 10–30 times the closed-loop bandwidth, and account for the delay in the phase margin.

secs.t: Example: stabilizing an unstable launch vehicle in pitch
secs.html:
A simplified rigid-body pitch model (no wind, small angles, angle of attack ≈ attitude error) is \ddot{\theta} = M_{\alpha}\theta + M_{\delta}\delta, where \delta is the engine gimbal angle. If the center of pressure is ahead of the CG, M_{\alpha} > 0 and the open-loop poles \pm \sqrt{M_{\alpha}} include an unstable one. With PD control \delta = - K_{p}\theta - K_{d}\dot{\theta}:

s^{2} + M_{\delta}K_{d}s + \left( M_{\delta}K_{p} - M_{\alpha} \right) = 0.

Stability requires M_{\delta}K_{p} > M_{\alpha}, a minimum gain. A maximum gain is set by actuator bandwidth, sensor noise, time delay and flexible bending modes. The design must fit between these limits at every flight condition, which is why gains are scheduled with dynamic pressure and why notch filters and slosh models appear in real autopilots (Chapter 32).

quiz.q: Find the percent overshoot for \zeta = 0.5.
quiz.a: \exp\left( - \pi \times 0.5/\sqrt{0.75} \right) = 0.163, i.e. 16.3%.

quiz.q: Find the 2% settling time for \zeta = 0.5 and \omega_{n} = 4 rad/s.
quiz.a: 4/(0.5 \times 4) = 2 s.

quiz.q: For what K > 0 is s^{3} + 2s^{2} + 3s + K stable?
quiz.a: Routh array: s^{3}: 1, 3; s^{2}: 2, K; s^{1}: (6 - K)/2; s^{0}: K. Stable for 0 < K < 6.

quiz.q: For \ddot{\theta} = 4\theta + 2\delta with PD control, choose K_{p} and K_{d} to give \omega_{n} = 4 rad/s and \zeta = 0.7.
quiz.a: s^{2} + 2K_{d}s + \left( 2K_{p} - 4 \right) = s^{2} + 2(0.7)(4)s + 16. So K_{d} = 2.8 and K_{p} = 10.

quiz.q: Find the gain crossover frequency and phase margin of L(s) = 10/\left\lbrack s(s + 1) \right\rbrack.
quiz.a: |L| = 1 when \omega\sqrt{\omega^{2} + 1} = 10, giving \omega_{c} = 3.08 rad/s. Phase = - 90^{\circ} - \arctan 3.08 = - 162^{\circ}, so PM = 18^{\circ}: poorly damped.

quiz.q: Why does time delay reduce phase margin but not gain?
quiz.a: e^{- j\omega T} has unit magnitude and phase - \omega T, so it rotates the Nyquist plot toward −1 without changing |L|.

quiz.q: Is \dot{\mathbf{x}} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 4 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\mathbf{x} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}u controllable? Is it open-loop stable?
quiz.a: \left\lbrack \mathbf{B}\ \mathbf{AB} \right\rbrack = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} has rank 2, so it is controllable. The eigenvalues are \pm 2, so it is open-loop unstable but stabilizable by feedback.

quiz.q: What is integrator windup and how is it prevented?
quiz.a: While the actuator is saturated, the integral of the error keeps growing. When the error reverses, the bloated integral causes large overshoot. Prevent it by clamping or conditionally freezing the integrator, or by back-calculating it from the saturated actuator output.

chapters.goalsHtml: model systems with transfer functions and state space; judge stability (Routh, root locus, Nyquist); meet time- and frequency-domain specifications; design PID and lead–lag compensators; place poles; implement digital controllers; stabilize an aerodynamically unstable vehicle.

chapters.title: Compressible Flow I: Isentropic Flow and Nozzles

secs.html:
