Consider a weak pressure wave moving at speed a into still gas. In the frame of the wave, gas enters at a and leaves at a + du with property changes dp and d\rho. Continuity gives a\, d\rho = - \rho\, du, and momentum gives dp = - \rho a\, du. Eliminating du gives a^{2} = dp/d\rho. The wave is infinitesimally weak and adiabatic, hence isentropic:

a^{2} = \left( \frac{\partial p}{\partial\rho} \right)_{s} = \frac{\gamma p}{\rho} = \gamma RT (ideal gas). Mach number M = V/a. Mach angle \mu = arcsin(1/M): in supersonic flow a small disturbance is felt only inside a downstream cone of half-angle \mu.

Air at 288 K: a = 340 m/s. Hydrogen at 300 K: about 1320 m/s. Rocket exhaust at 3500 K with \mathcal{M} = 13 kg/kmol and \gamma = 1.2: about 1640 m/s.

For adiabatic flow without work, h_{0} = h + V^{2}/2 is constant (Chapter 16). With h = c_{p}T and V^{2} = M^{2}\gamma RT:

\frac{T_{0}}{T} = 1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2}M^{2}, and for isentropic deceleration \frac{p_{0}}{p} = \left( \frac{T_{0}}{T} \right)^{\gamma/(\gamma - 1)}, \frac{\rho_{0}}{\rho} = \left( \frac{T_{0}}{T} \right)^{1/(\gamma - 1)}. Sonic state (M = 1): \frac{T^{*}}{T_{0}} = \frac{2}{\gamma + 1}, \frac{p^{*}}{p_{0}} = \left( \frac{2}{\gamma + 1} \right)^{\gamma/(\gamma - 1)} (0.8333 and 0.5283 for γ = 1.4). Maximum speed (expansion to 0 K): V_{\max} = \sqrt{2c_{p}T_{0}}.

T_{0} is constant in any adiabatic flow, even through shocks and friction, whereas p_{0} is constant only in isentropic flow. Expanding p_{0}/p for small M gives p_{0} - p = \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}\left( 1 + M^{2}/4 + \cdots \right). Below about M = 0.3, density changes are under 5% and incompressible analysis suffices.

secs.t: Quasi-one-dimensional flow and the area–velocity relation
secs.html:
Assume the area A(x) varies slowly and properties are uniform across each section. Then \rho VA = \text{const} and, for inviscid flow, dp = - \rho V\, dV. Logarithmic differentiation of continuity, combined with dp = a^{2}d\rho, gives:

Area–velocity relation: \frac{dA}{A} = \left( M^{2} - 1 \right)\frac{dV}{V}. Subsonic flow accelerates in a converging duct; supersonic flow accelerates in a diverging duct; M = 1 can occur only where dA = 0, at a throat. Hence the converging–diverging (de Laval) nozzle.

Relating any section to the (possibly fictitious) sonic area A^{*}:

\frac{A}{A^{*}} = \frac{1}{M}\left\lbrack \frac{2}{\gamma + 1}\left( 1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2}M^{2} \right) \right\rbrack^{\frac{\gamma + 1}{2(\gamma - 1)}}.

Every A/A^{*} > 1 has two solutions, one subsonic and one supersonic; which one occurs is set by the downstream conditions. Invert it numerically (Chapter 14) or with Appendix E.

\dot{m} = \frac{p_{0}A}{\sqrt{RT_{0}}}\sqrt{\gamma}\, M\left( 1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2}M^{2} \right)^{- \frac{\gamma + 1}{2(\gamma - 1)}}.

This is maximal at M = 1:

Choked flow: \dot{m} = \frac{\Gamma\, p_{0}A^{*}}{\sqrt{RT_{0}}}, with \Gamma = \sqrt{\gamma}\left( \frac{2}{\gamma + 1} \right)^{\frac{\gamma + 1}{2(\gamma - 1)}} (0.6847 for γ = 1.4; 0.6485 for γ = 1.2). Once the throat is sonic, mass flow depends only on upstream stagnation conditions and is independent of downstream pressure. It scales with p_{0} and 1/\sqrt{T_{0}}.

This is why rocket chamber pressure is proportional to mass flow (Chapter 26), and why choked orifices meter flow precisely.

For a fixed converging–diverging nozzle with reservoir pressure p_{0}, lowering the back pressure p_{b} produces this sequence:

  1. Fully subsonic flow, with the minimum pressure at the throat.
  2. Throat just sonic; subsonic flow downstream. The mass flow is now fixed.
  3. A normal shock stands in the diverging section, with subsonic flow after it. The shock moves toward the exit as p_{b} falls.
  4. The shock reaches the exit plane.
  5. Overexpanded: supersonic exit flow with p_{e} < p_{b}, adjusted by oblique shocks outside the nozzle.
  6. Design condition: p_{e} = p_{b} (ideally expanded).
  7. Underexpanded: p_{e} > p_{b}, adjusted by expansion fans outside.

Real overexpanded nozzles do not sustain cases 3–5 as ideal theory predicts: the boundary layer separates when the wall pressure falls to roughly p_{sep} \approx (0.25–0.4)p_{a} (Summerfield criterion, empirical). Separation causes asymmetric side loads during engine start at sea level and limits the area ratio of first-stage nozzles.

A supersonic tunnel accelerates gas through a first throat to the test-section Mach number and recovers pressure in a diffuser with a second throat. To start the tunnel, the starting normal shock must pass through the second throat. This requires A_{t2}/A_{t1} \geq p_{01}/p_{02}, the stagnation-pressure ratio across a normal shock at the test Mach number. The same physics governs the starting of supersonic inlets (Chapter 44).

These results assume a calorically perfect gas with constant \gamma. At high temperatures, vibrational excitation and dissociation change c_{p} and \gamma (Chapter 39), and a rocket nozzle’s flow may be frozen or in shifting chemical equilibrium (Chapter 26). In hypersonic blowdown tunnels the air must be heated before expansion so that it does not cool below its condensation temperature in the test section.

quiz.q: Find the speed of sound in air at 216.65 K.
Air at M = 2 has T = 216.65 K. Find T_{0} and p_{0}/p.
Find A/A^{*} for M = 3 (γ = 1.4).
quiz.a: A/A^{*} = 4.235.

quiz.q: A choked throat of 0.01 m² passes gas with p_{0} = 1 MPa, T_{0} = 3000 K, \gamma = 1.2 and R = 400 J/(kg·K). Find \dot{m}.
quiz.a: \dot{m} = 0.6485\left( 10^{6} \right)(0.01)/\sqrt{400 \times 3000} = 5.92 kg/s.

quiz.q: A nozzle has A_{e}/A_{t} = 10 (γ = 1.4). Find the supersonic exit Mach number and p_{e}/p_{0}.
quiz.a: Solving A/A^{*} = 10 on the supersonic branch: M_{e} = 3.92 and p_{e}/p_{0} = 0.0073.

quiz.q: Why can a purely converging nozzle never produce supersonic flow, however low the back pressure?
quiz.a: By the area–velocity relation, M = 1 is reached only at a minimum area, which for a converging nozzle is the exit. Once the exit is sonic, further lowering of p_{b} changes nothing upstream; the extra expansion happens outside the nozzle.

quiz.q: Show that stagnation pressure falls across any adiabatic irreversibility while T_{0} stays constant.
quiz.a: h_{0}, hence T_{0}, is conserved (adiabatic, no work). From the Gibbs equation at stagnation conditions, s_{2} - s_{1} = c_{p}\ln\left( T_{02}/T_{01} \right) - R\ln\left( p_{02}/p_{01} \right) = - R\ln\left( p_{02}/p_{01} \right). Since \Delta s > 0, p_{02} < p_{01}.

quiz.q: Find V_{\max} for air with T_{0} = 300 K.
quiz.a: \sqrt{2(1004.5)(300)} = 776 m/s.

chapters.goalsHtml: derive the speed of sound; use stagnation and sonic reference states; derive and apply the area–velocity and area–Mach relations; compute choked mass flow; predict nozzle behavior across back pressures. Tables for γ = 1.4 are in Appendix E; nozzle tables for low γ are in Appendix G.

chapters.title: Compressible Flow II: Shocks, Expansions and Duct Flows

secs.html:
Across a stationary normal shock (a thin, nonequilibrium region a few mean free paths thick), the conservation laws require

\rho_{1}u_{1} = \rho_{2}u_{2},\quad\quad p_{1} + \rho_{1}u_{1}^{2} = p_{2} + \rho_{2}u_{2}^{2},\quad\quad h_{1} + \frac{1}{2}u_{1}^{2} = h_{2} + \frac{1}{2}u_{2}^{2}.

For a calorically perfect gas, these give the Prandtl relation u_{1}u_{2} = a^{*2} and:

M_{2}^{2} = \frac{1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2}M_{1}^{2}}{\gamma M_{1}^{2} - \frac{\gamma - 1}{2}}, \quad\frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}} = 1 + \frac{2\gamma}{\gamma + 1}\left( M_{1}^{2} - 1 \right), \quad\frac{\rho_{2}}{\rho_{1}} = \frac{(\gamma + 1)M_{1}^{2}}{2 + (\gamma - 1)M_{1}^{2}}, \quad\frac{T_{2}}{T_{1}} = \frac{p_{2}/p_{1}}{\rho_{2}/\rho_{1}}. Stagnation pressure falls: p_{02}/p_{01} = e^{- \Delta s/R}.

The entropy change is positive only for M_{1} > 1, so only compression shocks exist. For weak shocks \Delta s \propto \left( M_{1}^{2} - 1 \right)^{3}: nearly isentropic. As M_{1} \rightarrow \infty, \rho_{2}/\rho_{1} \rightarrow (\gamma + 1)/(\gamma - 1) (6 for γ = 1.4) while p_{2}/p_{1} and T_{2}/T_{1} grow as M_{1}^{2}. This is the origin of extreme shock-layer temperatures at hypersonic speeds (Chapters 38–39). A Pitot probe in supersonic flow sits behind a normal shock, and the Rayleigh Pitot formula relates its reading to M_{1}:

\frac{p_{02}}{p_{1}} = \frac{\left\lbrack \frac{\gamma + 1}{2}M_{1}^{2} \right\rbrack^{\gamma/(\gamma - 1)}}{\left\lbrack \frac{2\gamma}{\gamma + 1}M_{1}^{2} - \frac{\gamma - 1}{\gamma + 1} \right\rbrack^{1/(\gamma - 1)}}.

A wedge of half-angle \theta in supersonic flow produces an attached oblique shock at angle \beta. The velocity component tangent to the shock is unchanged, so the normal-shock relations apply to the normal component M_{n1} = M_{1}\sin\beta. Then M_{2} = M_{n2}/sin(\beta - \theta), and

\tan\theta = 2\cot\beta\,\frac{M_{1}^{2}\sin^{2}\beta - 1}{M_{1}^{2}(\gamma + cos2\beta) + 2}.

For each M_{1} there is a maximum deflection \theta_{\max}. Below it, two solutions exist: the weak one (usually observed; M_{2} mostly supersonic) and the strong one (subsonic M_{2}). Above \theta_{\max} the shock detaches and stands ahead of the body as a curved bow shock, normal on the axis and weakening to a Mach wave far away (Appendix F tabulates β and θ_max).

An oblique shock striking a wall reflects so as to turn the flow back parallel to the wall. If the required turn exceeds \theta_{\max} for the post-shock Mach number, a Mach reflection forms, with a near-normal Mach stem. Shocks crossing each other, or shocks meeting expansion fans, are solved by matching pressure and flow direction across slip lines; the shock polar diagram organizes these solutions. Where a shock meets a boundary layer, it can cause separation (Chapter 37). Where a shock meets another shock near a surface, it can produce extreme local heating (Edney interactions, Chapter 41).

Supersonic flow turning around a convex corner expands isentropically through a fan of Mach waves. Each infinitesimal turn obeys d heta = \sqrt{M^{2} - 1}\, dV/V. Integrating gives the Prandtl–Meyer function:

u(M) = \sqrt{ rac{\gamma + 1}{\gamma - 1}}\arctan\sqrt{ rac{\gamma - 1}{\gamma + 1}\left( M^{2} - 1 ight)} - \arctan\sqrt{M^{2} - 1}, with a turn of heta giving u\left( M_{2} ight) = u\left( M_{1} ight) + heta. The maximum turning (expansion to vacuum) is u_{\max} = rac{\pi}{2}\left( \sqrt{ rac{\gamma + 1}{\gamma - 1}} - 1 ight) = {130.45}^{\circ} for γ = 1.4.

Combining exact oblique shocks (compression corners) with Prandtl–Meyer expansions (expansion corners) gives exact inviscid 2-D solutions for sharp-edged shapes, provided no wave reflections reach the surface. Applied to a flat plate at incidence \alpha, the lower surface is compressed by a shock turning the flow by \alpha, and the upper surface expands through \alpha. Lift and wave drag follow from integrating the surface pressures. Chapter 25 compares this exact result with linear (Ackeret) theory.

secs.t: Fanno flow: friction in a constant-area duct
secs.html:
Adiabatic flow with wall friction in a constant-area duct conserves h_{0} and \rho u while entropy rises. Friction always drives the Mach number toward 1: subsonic flow accelerates and supersonic flow decelerates. The duct length that brings Mach M to sonic is

\frac{4\bar{f}L^{*}}{D} = \frac{1 - M^{2}}{\gamma M^{2}} + \frac{\gamma + 1}{2\gamma}\ln\frac{(\gamma + 1)M^{2}}{2 + (\gamma - 1)M^{2}},

with \bar{f} the mean Fanning friction factor. A longer duct chokes, and the upstream flow must adjust: subsonic flow reduces its mass flow; supersonic flow forms a shock.

secs.t: Rayleigh flow: heat addition in a constant-area duct
secs.html:
Frictionless constant-area flow with heat addition q changes the stagnation temperature, q = c_{p}\left( T_{02} - T_{01} \right). Heating also drives M toward 1: it decelerates supersonic flow (raising p and T) and accelerates subsonic flow (lowering p).

\frac{T_{0}}{T_{0}^{*}} = \frac{(\gamma + 1)M^{2}\left\lbrack 2 + (\gamma - 1)M^{2} \right\rbrack}{\left( 1 + \gamma M^{2} \right)^{2}}. Thermal choking: the most heat a constant-area duct can accept raises T_{0} to T_{0}^{*}. Adding more forces the upstream flow to change: in a supersonic combustor, a shock system (or unstart) results. Scramjet combustors therefore diverge in area (Chapter 44).

In subsonic Rayleigh flow the static temperature peaks at M = 1/\sqrt{\gamma}, before choking: heating there lowers T while raising T_{0}.

Steady, irrotational, 2-D supersonic flow is hyperbolic (Chapter 12). Its characteristics are the Mach lines, at angles heta \pm \mu to the flow. Along them the Riemann invariants are constant: heta + u = K_{-} along C_{-} lines and heta - u = K_{+} along C_{+} lines. Unit processes (interior point, wall point, symmetry point) march the solution through a network of characteristics. A minimum-length nozzle expands the flow at a sharp throat corner of angle u_{e}/2 and cancels all waves on the contoured wall to deliver uniform exit flow. Rocket bell nozzles are designed with characteristics plus an optimization of the thrust for a given length (the Rao method).

quiz.q: For a normal shock at M_{1} = 3 (γ = 1.4), find M_{2}, p_{2}/p_{1}, T_{2}/T_{1} and p_{02}/p_{01}.
quiz.a: M_{2} = 0.475, p_{2}/p_{1} = 10.33, T_{2}/T_{1} = 2.679, p_{02}/p_{01} = 0.328.

quiz.q: Find β, M_{2} and p_{2}/p_{1} for M_{1} = 3 over a 15° wedge (weak solution).
quiz.a: \beta = {32.2}^{\circ}, M_{2} = 2.25, p_{2}/p_{1} = 2.82 (and p_{02}/p_{01} = 0.895, a far smaller loss than the normal shock’s).

quiz.q: Flow at M = 2 expands around a 10° corner. Find M_{2}.
quiz.a: \nu(2) = {26.38}^{\circ}, so \nu_{2} = {36.38}^{\circ} and M_{2} = 2.38.

quiz.q: Find \theta_{\max} at M = 3.
quiz.a: \theta_{\max} = {34.07}^{\circ}, at \beta = {65.2}^{\circ}.

quiz.q: A constant-area combustor receives air at M = 2.5 with T_{01} = 1500 K. What is the largest stagnation temperature reachable before thermal choking?
quiz.a: T_{0}/T_{0}^{*}(2.5) = 0.7101, so T_{0}^{*} = 1500/0.7101 = 2112 K: only about 610 K of heating before choking.

quiz.q: Why can an expansion shock not exist?
quiz.a: It would decrease entropy in an adiabatic flow, violating the second law.

quiz.q: A Pitot probe in a M = 2 stream reads p_{02}. Find p_{02}/p_{1}, and explain why p_{0} = p\left( 1 + 0.2M^{2} \right)^{3.5} would be wrong here.
quiz.a: p_{02}/p_{1} = 5.64. The probe measures the stagnation pressure behind the normal shock that stands in front of it. The isentropic formula gives p_{01}/p_{1} = 7.82, which no probe can measure directly.

quiz.q: Find 4\bar{f}L^{*}/D for M = 0.5 and M = 2.
quiz.a: 1.069 and 0.305. Supersonic duct flow chokes in far shorter lengths.

chapters.goalsHtml: derive and apply normal- and oblique-shock relations; use the θ–β–M relation; compute Prandtl–Meyer expansions and shock-expansion solutions; analyze duct flow with friction (Fanno) and heat addition (Rayleigh), including thermal choking; understand the method of characteristics.

chapters.title: Aerodynamics: Subsonic to Supersonic

secs.html: The resultant aerodynamic force splits into lift L (perpendicular to the free stream) and drag D (parallel to it), or, in body axes, normal force N and axial force A. Coefficients: C_{L} = L/\left( q_{\infty}S \right), C_{D} = D/\left( q_{\infty}S \right), C_{m} = M/\left( q_{\infty}S\bar{c} \right), with reference area S and length \bar{c} (always state which). The center of pressure is where the resultant acts and moves with angle of attack. The aerodynamic center is the point about which C_{m} does not vary with \alpha: the quarter chord in thin-airfoil theory and roughly mid-chord in supersonic flow.

secs.t: Potential flow and the origin of lift
secs.html:
For incompressible irrotational flow, \mathbf{u} = \nabla\phi with \nabla^{2}\phi = 0 (Chapter 12), so elementary solutions superpose. A uniform stream plus a doublet gives flow past a cylinder. Adding a vortex of circulation \Gamma creates lift:

Kutta–Joukowski theorem: lift per unit span L' = \rho_{\infty}V_{\infty}\Gamma. Kutta condition: at a sharp trailing edge, the flow leaves smoothly. This physical condition, enforced by viscosity, fixes the circulation. Inviscid potential flow predicts zero drag (d’Alembert’s paradox): real drag comes from viscosity, waves and trailing vortices.

Representing the camber line by a vortex sheet and enforcing flow tangency gives, for small \alpha:

c_{l} = 2\pi\left( \alpha - \alpha_{L = 0} \right),\quad\quad c_{m,c/4} = \text{const}\ \left( \text{zero for a symmetric section} \right).

The lift-curve slope is 2\pi per radian (about 0.11 per degree). Real airfoils stall when the boundary layer separates, typically at \alpha around 12–16°.

Trailing vortices induce downwash that tilts the local lift backward, creating induced drag. Prandtl’s lifting-line theory gives

C_{D,i} = \frac{C_{L}^{2}}{\pi e\, AR},\quad\quad a = \frac{a_{0}}{1 + a_{0}/(\pi e\, AR)},

with aspect ratio AR = b^{2}/S and span efficiency e \leq 1 (e = 1 for an elliptical lift distribution). The drag polar C_{D} = C_{D0} + kC_{L}^{2} gives a maximum lift-to-drag ratio (L/D)_{\max} = 1/\left( 2\sqrt{C_{D0}k} \right) at C_{L} = \sqrt{C_{D0}/k}, where induced drag equals parasite drag.

Linearizing the compressible potential equation gives \left( 1 - M_{\infty}^{2} \right)\phi_{xx} + \phi_{yy} = 0. Stretching coordinates reduces it to Laplace’s equation, which yields the Prandtl–Glauert rule C_{p} = C_{p0}/\sqrt{1 - M_{\infty}^{2}} (more accurate corrections: Kármán–Tsien, Laitone). The critical Mach number is the free-stream value at which the flow first reaches M = 1 somewhere on the body. Above it, shocks form and drag rises sharply at the drag-divergence Mach number. Supercritical airfoils flatten the upper surface to weaken these shocks. Sweep \Lambda reduces the effective normal Mach number to M_{\infty}\cos\Lambda, delaying both phenomena.

Linearized supersonic theory (Ackeret) gives the surface pressure directly from the local flow inclination \theta:

C_{p} = \frac{2\theta}{\sqrt{M_{\infty}^{2} - 1}}, so for a flat plate c_{l} = \frac{4\alpha}{\sqrt{M_{\infty}^{2} - 1}} and the wave drag is c_{d,w} = \frac{4\alpha^{2}}{\sqrt{M_{\infty}^{2} - 1}}. Thickness adds c_{d,w,t} = \frac{4}{\sqrt{M_{\infty}^{2} - 1}}\overline{\left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)^{2}}, averaged over both surfaces. The aerodynamic center moves to mid-chord.

Wave drag, which is absent in subsonic flow, makes thin sections and slender bodies mandatory at supersonic speed. The linear theory fails as M_{\infty} \rightarrow 1 (transonic flow) and at high M_{\infty}\theta (hypersonic flow, Chapter 38).

secs.t: Supersonic bodies and the area rule
secs.html: Slender-body theory gives a normal-force slope of C_{N\alpha} = 2 per radian for a pointed body of revolution (based on base area), independent of Mach number. Zero-lift wave drag depends on how the cross-sectional area S(x) is distributed along the length. The Sears–Haack body minimizes it for a given length and volume. The area rule (Whitcomb) states that near Mach 1 the wave drag of a whole configuration approximates that of a body of revolution with the same area distribution, so aircraft fuselages are “waisted” where the wings attach.

A launcher’s aerodynamics are summarized by the axial-force coefficient C_{A}(M) (peaking near Mach 1–1.2), the normal-force slope C_{N\alpha}(M), and the CP location. Noses and flares contribute most of the normal force; long cylinders contribute little at small α. Base drag at the aft end depends on plume interactions. The Barrowman method, a sum of component contributions, gives quick CP estimates for slender rockets. Transonic flow causes buffet and shock oscillation over shoulders and protuberances. Products of dynamic pressure and angle of attack (q\alpha, in kPa·deg) are the standard measure of aerodynamic bending load (Chapter 31).

A vehicle is statically stable in pitch if C_{m\alpha} < 0 about its CG, i.e. the CP of the incremental lift lies behind the CG. The static margin is the distance between them divided by a reference length (calibers for rockets, chord for aircraft). Trim requires C_{m} = 0 at the flight condition, achieved by control surfaces or engine gimballing. More stability means more control power is needed to maneuver. An unstable vehicle needs active control (Chapters 22 and 32).

For steady level cruise, L = W and T = D. The Breguet range equation follows from integrating dR = V\, dt with fuel flow {\dot{m}}_{f}g_{0} = T/I_{sp}:

R = V\, I_{sp}\,\frac{L}{D}\ln\frac{W_{i}}{W_{f}},

with I_{sp} in seconds defined on fuel flow. The product V\, I_{sp}\,(L/D) is the figure of merit that hypersonic cruise vehicles must maximize (Chapter 43).

quiz.q: Find c_{l} for a symmetric thin airfoil at \alpha = 4^{\circ}.
Find the induced drag coefficient for C_{L} = 0.5, AR = 8 and e = 0.85.
quiz.a: 0.25/(\pi \times 8 \times 0.85) = 0.0117.

quiz.q: A low-speed measurement gives C_{p0} = - 0.4. Estimate C_{p} at M_{\infty} = 0.7.
Find c_{l}, c_{d,w} and L/D for a flat plate at 3° and Mach 2 by linear theory.
quiz.a: c_{l} = 4(0.05236)/\sqrt{3} = 0.121; c_{d,w} = 4(0.05236)^{2}/\sqrt{3} = 0.00633; L/D = 1/\alpha = 19.1 (inviscid).

quiz.q: Find (L/D)_{\max} for C_{D0} = 0.02 and k = 0.05.
quiz.a: 1/\left( 2\sqrt{0.001} \right) = 15.8.

quiz.q: Explain how sweep delays drag divergence.
quiz.a: Only the velocity component normal to the leading edge, M_{\infty}\cos\Lambda, governs the chordwise pressure field and shock formation. Sweep lowers it, so local supersonic regions and shocks appear at a higher free-stream Mach number.

quiz.q: Compare the Ackeret C_{p} on the compression side of a plate at 3°, Mach 2, with the exact oblique-shock value.
quiz.a: Ackeret: 2(0.05236)/1.732 = 0.0605. Oblique shock (\beta = {32.5}^{\circ}): p_{2}/p_{1} = 1.181, so C_{p} = \left( p_{2}/p_{1} - 1 \right)/\left( 0.7M^{2} \right) = 0.0646. Linear theory is 6% low: second-order effects matter even at small angles.

quiz.q: A 10 m rocket of 1 m diameter has its CG at 6.0 m and CP at 7.0 m from the nose. Find the static margin and say whether it is stable.
quiz.a: Margin = (7.0 - 6.0)/1.0 = 1.0 caliber, with the CP aft of the CG: stable.

chapters.goalsHtml: define aerodynamic coefficients and centers; use potential flow and the Kutta–Joukowski theorem; apply thin-airfoil and lifting-line theory; correct for compressibility; compute supersonic lift and wave drag; estimate launch-vehicle normal force and static margin.

chapters.title: Rocket Propulsion Fundamentals

secs.html:
Draw a control volume around the vehicle, cutting the jet at the nozzle exit plane, and work in the vehicle’s frame at steady state. Outside the vehicle, ambient pressure p_{a} acts everywhere except over the exit area, where the jet’s pressure p_{e} acts instead. The momentum balance (Chapter 18) along the axis gives:

F = \dot{m}u_{e} + \left( p_{e} - p_{a} \right)A_{e}, assuming uniform, axial exit flow. Effective exhaust velocity c = F/\dot{m} = u_{e} + \left( p_{e} - p_{a} \right)A_{e}/\dot{m}. Specific impulse I_{sp} = c/g_{0}. Vacuum thrust (p_{a} = 0) is the largest; sea-level thrust is smaller by p_{a}A_{e}.

Assumptions: homogeneous perfect gas of fixed composition; adiabatic, frictionless, steady flow; negligible chamber velocity; one-dimensional axial exit. Then the steady-flow energy equation gives u_{e} = \sqrt{2c_{p}\left( T_{c} - T_{e} \right)}, and with isentropic expansion:

u_{e} = \sqrt{\frac{2\gamma}{\gamma - 1}\frac{R_{u}T_{c}}{\mathcal{M}}\left\lbrack 1 - \left( \frac{p_{e}}{p_{c}} \right)^{(\gamma - 1)/\gamma} \right\rbrack}. Exhaust velocity rises with \sqrt{T_{c}\mathcal{/M}} and with the expansion pressure ratio, approaching \sqrt{2\gamma R_{u}T_{c}/\left\lbrack (\gamma - 1)\mathcal{M} \right\rbrack} for infinite expansion.

Separate the chamber (combustion quality) from the nozzle (expansion quality):

c^{*} \equiv \frac{p_{c}A_{t}}{\dot{m}} = \frac{\sqrt{\gamma RT_{c}}}{\gamma\sqrt{\left( \frac{2}{\gamma + 1} \right)^{(\gamma + 1)/(\gamma - 1)}}},\quad\quad C_{F} \equiv \frac{F}{p_{c}A_{t}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\gamma^{2}}{\gamma - 1}\left( \frac{2}{\gamma + 1} \right)^{\frac{\gamma + 1}{\gamma - 1}}\left\lbrack 1 - \left( \frac{p_{e}}{p_{c}} \right)^{\frac{\gamma - 1}{\gamma}} \right\rbrack} + \frac{p_{e} - p_{a}}{p_{c}}\frac{A_{e}}{A_{t}},

with c = c^{*}C_{F}. c^{*} depends only on propellant thermochemistry (T_{c}, \mathcal{M}, \gamma); measured c^{*} divided by theoretical c^{*} is the combustion efficiency (typically 0.95–0.99). C_{F} depends only on \gamma, the area ratio \varepsilon = A_{e}/A_{t} (which fixes p_{e}/p_{c} through the area–Mach relation) and p_{a}/p_{c}. Its vacuum, infinite-expansion limit is about 2.25 for γ = 1.2. Chamber pressure therefore follows directly from mass flow: p_{c} = \dot{m}c^{*}/A_{t}.

At fixed chamber conditions, dF/dA_{e} = \left( p_{e} - p_{a} \right), so thrust at a given altitude is maximized when p_{e} = p_{a} (optimum expansion). A fixed nozzle is therefore ideal at one altitude only. First stages compromise between sea level (where large \varepsilon separates) and altitude; upper stages use very large \varepsilon. Altitude-compensating concepts include aerospikes, dual-bell nozzles and extendible nozzle skirts. Real nozzles lose performance through:

  • Divergence: a conical nozzle of half-angle \alpha has momentum efficiency \lambda = (1 + cos\alpha)/2 (0.983 at 15°). Contoured “bell” nozzles (Rao) recover most of this in shorter lengths.
  • Boundary layers: about 0.5–1.5% of thrust.
  • Chemical kinetics: recombination may freeze during rapid expansion (§26.5).
  • Two-phase flow: condensed particles (for example aluminum oxide in solid motors) lag the gas in velocity and temperature.
  • Nonuniform mixture from injector maldistribution.

Overall, delivered I_{sp} is typically 92–98% of ideal.

As gas expands and cools, dissociated species recombine and release chemical energy. The shifting-equilibrium assumption (instantaneous recombination) gives the upper bound on I_{sp}; frozen flow (composition fixed at the chamber or throat) gives the lower bound, typically a few percent less. Reality lies between, and finite-rate kinetics calculations locate it. Codes such as NASA CEA compute equilibrium chamber composition by Gibbs minimization (Chapter 17) and both expansion limits.

secs.t: The rocket equation and mass fractions
secs.html:
Define the structural coefficient \varepsilon_{s} = m_{s}/\left( m_{s} + m_{p} \right) (dry structure and engines over stage mass excluding payload) and the payload ratio \pi = m_{pl}/m_{0}. A single stage’s mass ratio is

\frac{m_{0}}{m_{f}} = \frac{1}{\varepsilon_{s} + \left( 1 - \varepsilon_{s} \right)\pi}.

The single-stage limit. Even with zero payload, \Delta v_{\max} = c\ln\left( 1/\varepsilon_{s} \right). With c = 2942 m/s and \varepsilon_{s} = 0.10 this is 6.8 km/s, less than the about 9.4 km/s needed for low Earth orbit. Reaching orbit with a single stage requires very low \varepsilon_{s} and high I_{sp} simultaneously. Staging discards dead mass so that later stages accelerate only what remains.

Total \Delta v = \sum c_{i}\ln n_{i}, where n_{i} is the mass ratio of stage i. Maximizing the overall payload ratio \prod\pi_{i} for a given total Δv with a Lagrange multiplier \eta (Chapter 9) gives

n_{i} = \frac{c_{i}\eta - 1}{c_{i}\varepsilon_{i}\eta},\quad\quad\text{with }\eta\text{ chosen so that }\sum c_{i}\ln n_{i} = \Delta v.

For identical stages this reduces to an equal Δv split. Returns diminish beyond three or four stages, while cost and failure modes grow. Parallel staging (boosters around a core) adds thrust at liftoff, and cross-feed propellant transfer between stages is a further refinement.

\Delta v_{required} = v_{orbit} + \Delta v_{gravity} + \Delta v_{drag} + \Delta v_{steering} - \Delta v_{rotation}.

Typical LEO values: orbital speed 7.7–7.8 km/s; gravity loss 1.0–1.5 km/s (Chapter 31); drag loss 0.1–0.3 km/s; steering loss 0.05–0.2 km/s; Earth rotation credit up to 0.465 km/s (eastward from the equator). The total is about 9.3–10 km/s, with each term depending on the trajectory and thrust-to-weight ratio.

A stage limited by tank volume rather than mass favors dense propellants. The bulk density at mixture ratio r = O/F is \rho_{b} = (1 + r)/\left( r/\rho_{o} + 1/\rho_{f} \right). Density-specific impulse \rho_{b}I_{sp} is a useful first-stage figure of merit.

Combination (typical \mathbf{O}\mathbf{/}\mathbf{F}) Vacuum \mathbf{I}_{\mathbf{sp}}, representative engines (s) Bulk density (kg/m³)
LOX/LH₂ (5.5–6) 450–465 ≈ 360
LOX/CH₄ (3.3–3.8) 350–380 ≈ 830
LOX/RP-1 (2.3–2.7) 310–350 ≈ 1020
NTO/MMH (≈ 2) 310–330 ≈ 1190
Composite solid (Al/AP/polymer) 265–295 ≈ 1750–1800

Values depend on chamber pressure, mixture ratio and area ratio. Hydrogen’s high I_{sp} comes with very large, cold, insulated tanks; that is why many vehicles use dense propellants in the first stage and hydrogen above. Cost, reusability (soot from kerosene versus clean methane), storability and operations also drive the choice.

quiz.q: An ideal engine has p_{c} = 10 MPa, T_{c} = 3500 K, \mathcal{M} = 13 kg/kmol, \gamma = 1.2 and \varepsilon = 40. Find p_{e}, u_{e}, c^{*}, C_{F,vac} and I_{sp,vac}.
quiz.a: \varepsilon = 40 gives M_{e} = 4.24 and p_{e}/p_{c} = 0.00209, so p_{e} = 20.9 kPa. R = 639.6 J/(kg·K). u_{e} = 4154 m/s; c^{*} = 2307 m/s; C_{F,vac} = 1.884; I_{sp,vac} = c^{*}C_{F}/g_{0} = 443 s.

quiz.q: Find the same engine’s sea-level C_{F} and I_{sp}, and check for flow separation.
quiz.a: C_{F,SL} = 1.884 - (0.101325/10)(40) = 1.479, so I_{sp,SL} = 348 s. But p_{e}/p_{a} = 0.21 is below the Summerfield range (0.25–0.4), so this vacuum-optimized nozzle would separate at sea level. It is an upper-stage nozzle.

quiz.q: A two-stage vehicle has identical stages (I_{sp} = 300 s, \varepsilon_{s} = 0.1), a 1000 kg payload and a total Δv of 9 km/s split equally. Find the liftoff mass. Can a single such stage do the job?
quiz.a: Each stage: n = e^{4500/2942} = 4.616 and \pi = (1/n - 0.1)/0.9 = 0.1296. Overall \pi^{2} = 0.0168, so m_{0} = 1000/0.0168 = 59.5 t. A single stage needs n = e^{9000/2942} = 21.3, i.e. 1/n = 0.047 < \varepsilon_{s}: impossible at any payload.

quiz.q: Find the divergence efficiency of a 15° conical nozzle.
quiz.a: \lambda = \left( 1 + cos15^{\circ} \right)/2 = 0.983.

quiz.q: Prove that thrust at fixed chamber conditions is maximized when p_{e} = p_{a}.
quiz.a: F = \dot{m}u_{e} + \left( p_{e} - p_{a} \right)A_{e}. Quasi-1-D momentum gives \dot{m}\, du_{e} = - A_{e}\, dp_{e}, and d\left( p_{e}A_{e} \right) = p_{e}\, dA_{e} + A_{e}\, dp_{e}. So dF = \left( p_{e} - p_{a} \right)\, dA_{e}, which vanishes at p_{e} = p_{a}. The second derivative shows this is a maximum.

quiz.q: Show that c^{*} depends only on chamber thermochemistry and not on the nozzle.
quiz.a: c^{*} = p_{c}A_{t}/\dot{m} and the choked-flow relation gives \dot{m} = \Gamma p_{c}A_{t}/\sqrt{RT_{c}}. Hence c^{*} = \sqrt{RT_{c}}/\Gamma(\gamma), which depends only on R (that is, \mathcal{M}), T_{c} and \gamma.

quiz.q: A vertical ascent has liftoff T/W = 1.3, I_{sp} = 300 s and burns to mass ratio 4. Estimate the burn time and an upper bound on the gravity loss.
quiz.a: t_{b} = I_{sp}(1 - 1/n)/(T/W) = 300(0.75)/1.3 = 173 s, so the vertical gravity loss is at most g_{0}t_{b} = 1.70 km/s. Real trajectories turn toward horizontal and lose less.

quiz.q: Compute the bulk densities of LOX/RP-1 at O/F = 2.56 and LOX/LH₂ at O/F = 6, and their density-impulse ratio using 340 s and 450 s.
quiz.a: LOX/RP-1: \rho_{b} = 3.56/(2.56/1141 + 1/810) = 1024 kg/m³. LOX/LH₂: 7/(6/1141 + 1/70.85) = 361 kg/m³. Density impulse: 340(1024) = 3.48 \times 10^{5} versus 450(361) = 1.63 \times 10^{5} s·kg/m³. Kerosene stores more than twice the impulse per unit tank volume.

chapters.goalsHtml: derive the thrust equation; compute exhaust velocity, c^{*}, C_{F} and I_{sp} for an ideal rocket; quantify nozzle losses and expansion effects; size single- and multi-stage vehicles; build a Δv budget; choose propellants using both I_{sp} and density.

chapters.title: Liquid Rocket Engines

secs.html: A liquid rocket engine comprises propellant tanks with a pressurization system (helium, or autogenous: vaporized propellant), a feed system (pressure-fed or pump-fed), valves and lines, an injector, a thrust chamber (combustion chamber and nozzle) with its cooling system, an igniter, controls, and usually a gimbal for thrust-vector control.

Propellant Normal boiling point (K) Density (kg/m³) Notes
LOX 90.2 1141 Cryogenic; strong oxidizer; materials must be oxygen-compatible
LH₂ 20.3 70.8 Deep cryogen; very low density; embrittles some metals
LCH₄ 111.7 423 Cryogenic; clean-burning; good regenerative coolant
RP-1 (kerosene) ≈ 450 (range) ≈ 810 Storable; dense; can coke in hot cooling channels
NTO (N₂O₄) 294 1440 Storable; toxic; hypergolic with hydrazines
MMH 361 874 Storable; toxic; hypergolic with NTO
Hydrazine (N₂H₄) 387 1004 Storable; toxic; also used as a monopropellant

Cryogens boil off and need insulation, chilldown before engine start, and careful pressurization. Subcooling (“densifying”) cryogens below their boiling point raises density and loads more propellant. Hypergolic pairs ignite reliably on contact but are highly toxic and require specialized handling.

Safety and scope flag · Physical hazard

Concern. Liquid-engine testing combines toxic or cryogenic propellants, high pressure and ignition. Failures include hard starts (accumulated propellant igniting at once), oxygen-fed fires and combustion instability that can destroy hardware within milliseconds (§27.8–27.11).

Why it is flagged. These failure modes are why engine tests are run remotely from hardened test stands with written procedures, clear zones and emergency plans.

Omitted here. Detailed injector, igniter and test-stand construction guidance.

Learn it safely. University liquid-rocket student teams and research laboratories operating under faculty supervision and institutional safety review; industry internships and co-ops; professional short courses (for example AIAA continuing-education courses on liquid rocket propulsion); Sutton and Biblarz and Huzel and Huang for the open engineering principles (Appendix K).

Pressure-fed: tank pressure must exceed p_{c} plus injector, line and cooling-jacket losses. It is simple and reliable but limits p_{c} to roughly 1–3 MPa and makes the tanks heavy, since tank mass scales with pV (Chapter 20). It is used on upper stages and spacecraft. Pump-fed: turbopumps raise the pressure, so tanks stay at a few bar. The turbine’s drive gas defines the cycle:

Cycle Turbine drive Exhaust of turbine Character
Gas generator (open) Small fraction of propellant burned off-ratio Dumped overboard Simple; Isp penalty of order 1–3%
Staged combustion (closed) Preburner burns one propellant with a little of the other Injected into main chamber Highest p_{c} (20–30 MPa) and Isp; very high pump pressures; oxidizer-rich, fuel-rich or full-flow variants
Expander (closed or bleed) Fuel heated in the cooling jacket Into chamber (or dumped, bleed) Clean and benign; thrust limited by available heat
Electric pump Battery-powered motors None Simple; battery mass limits burn time and size
Tap-off Hot gas tapped from chamber Dumped Few components; demanding turbine environment

Power balance. Pump power: P_{p} = \dot{m}\,\Delta p/\left( \rho\eta_{p} \right). Turbine power: P_{t} = {\dot{m}}_{t}c_{p}T_{in}\eta_{t}\left\lbrack 1 - \left( p_{out}/p_{in} \right)^{(\gamma - 1)/\gamma} \right\rbrack. The cycle closes when P_{t} = \sum P_{p} plus bearing and seal losses. Low-density liquid hydrogen needs about 16 times the pump power of LOX per unit mass for the same pressure rise. In closed cycles, the preburner must exceed p_{c} by the turbine pressure ratio, so pump discharge pressures reach 1.5–2 times p_{c}.

The expander cycle’s limit is geometric. Heat pickup scales with chamber surface area (\propto L^{2}) while the required pump power scales with flow (\propto L^{3}), so pure expander engines are limited to moderate thrust.

Pump head H = \Delta p/(\rho g). Euler’s turbomachinery equation gives the specific work as w = U_{2}c_{\theta 2} - U_{1}c_{\theta 1} (blade speed times swirl velocity), so the head per stage is limited by tip speed and therefore by material strength. The dimensionless specific speed N_{s} = \omega\sqrt{Q}/(gH)^{3/4} selects the pump type: radial (low N_{s}), mixed or axial (high N_{s}). Hydrogen pumps need enormous head and therefore very high tip speeds or several stages.

Cavitation: if the local pressure falls below the vapor pressure, vapor bubbles form and collapse, eroding blades and cutting head. The net positive suction head available, NPSH_{a} = \left( p_{in} - p_{v} \right)/(\rho g) + V^{2}/(2g), must exceed the pump’s requirement. Axial inducers ahead of the main impeller tolerate some cavitation, letting tanks run at low pressure (which saves tank mass). Turbines are impulse types (pressure drop in the nozzles, suited to high pressure ratios) or reaction types. Bearings, dynamic seals (with an inert purge separating oxidizer from fuel) and rotordynamics (critical speeds, whirl) are frequent sources of development failures.

An injector meters, atomizes, mixes and distributes propellants, and provides stable combustion and a wall environment the chamber can survive. Each orifice obeys \dot{m} = C_{d}A\sqrt{2\rho\Delta p}. An injector pressure drop of about 15–30% of p_{c} isolates the feed system from chamber pressure oscillations. Element types:

  • Impinging jets (unlike doublets, like doublets, triplets): common with storables and kerosene.
  • Shear coaxial: a central LOX post with an annulus of high-velocity gaseous hydrogen; mixing relies on the velocity ratio.
  • Swirl coaxial: used widely in oxidizer-rich staged-combustion engines.
  • Pintle: a single central element that throttles deeply and resists instability.

Peripheral elements often run fuel-rich (film cooling) to protect the chamber wall.

The throat area follows from A_{t} = \dot{m}c^{*}/p_{c}. The characteristic length L^{*} = V_{c}/A_{t} measures the volume available for vaporization, mixing and reaction. The residence time is t_{s} = \rho_{c}V_{c}/\dot{m} = L^{*}c^{*}/\left( RT_{c} \right), typically a few milliseconds. Typical L^{*} is of order 0.8–1.3 m, depending on propellants and injector quality. The contraction ratio A_{c}/A_{t} is about 2–5: larger ratios lower the chamber Mach number and the associated stagnation-pressure loss but add mass and wetted area.

Heat flux peaks just upstream of the throat (Bartz, Chapter 19) and rises roughly linearly with p_{c}. It reaches tens of MW/m² and exceeds 100 MW/m² in the highest-pressure engines. Methods:

  • Regenerative: propellant (usually fuel) flows through channels in the wall before injection. Copper-alloy liners with milled channels, closed out by electroformed nickel or a brazed jacket, keep the hot wall below about 800 K. The cyclic hot-wall compressive yielding causes low-cycle thermal fatigue (“doghousing”), the life limiter of reusable chambers. Hydrocarbon coolants can coke; supercritical coolants show property spikes (Chapter 19).
  • Film and transpiration: coolant injected along or through the wall forms a protective layer, at some cost in Isp.
  • Ablative: silica- or carbon-phenolic liners char and erode. They are cheap and simple, but limited in duration and throat-erosion tolerance.
  • Radiative: high-temperature walls (niobium alloys, rhenium/iridium, carbon–carbon, C/SiC) reject heat by radiation (Chapter 19). Used for nozzle extensions and small thrusters.

Oscillations are classified by frequency and mechanism. Low frequency (chugging): coupling between chamber pressure and feed-system flow, cured by higher injector Δp or feed-line accumulators. Intermediate (buzz): feed-system acoustics or entropy waves. High frequency (screech): coupling between chamber acoustic modes and combustion. It is the most destructive, able to destroy an injector face within milliseconds.

Chamber acoustic modes (closed cylinder of radius R and length L): f = \frac{a}{2}\sqrt{\left( \frac{\alpha_{mn}}{\pi R} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{q}{L} \right)^{2}}, with \alpha_{10} = 1.8412 (first tangential), \alpha_{20} = 3.0542 (second tangential), \alpha_{01} = 3.8317 (first radial). Rayleigh criterion: oscillations grow if heat-release fluctuations are in phase with pressure fluctuations, \oint p'q'\, dt > 0, by more than the acoustic losses.

Remedies include injector redesign (changing the combustion response time), injector-face baffles that block transverse modes, acoustic cavities or Helmholtz resonators that absorb energy, and higher injector Δp. Stability is demonstrated by bomb tests: small charges perturb the chamber, and the decay of the disturbance is measured. The F-1 engine of the Saturn V needed a long campaign of such full-scale tests before it was declared stable. Chapter 47 develops the theory.

Ignition sources: spark torches or augmented spark igniters (common for LOX/LH₂); pyrophoric slugs (triethylaluminum–triethylborane for LOX/kerosene); pyrotechnic igniters; hypergolic contact. Start sequences chill down cryogenic pumps, lead with one propellant to avoid hard starts (accumulated unburned mixture igniting at once), and bootstrap the turbopump. Throttling is limited by injector Δp, which falls as {\dot{m}}^{2} and with it stability margin; by pump stall; and by turbine matching. Pintle and variable-area injectors extend the range. Restart requires repeatable ignition and settled propellants (ullage settling burns in weightlessness).

Engine design balances the cycle (pressures, temperatures, flows), mass (thrust-to-weight ranges from about 50 to over 150), reliability, cost and, increasingly, reusability: turbine life, oxygen-compatibility margins, inspection access and chamber fatigue life. Development proceeds through component tests (injector, preburner, turbopump), engine hot-fire tests, and qualification beyond flight conditions.

Ullage pressure must satisfy the pumps’ suction requirement (NPSH) and stabilize thin tank walls (Chapter 33). It is supplied by stored helium (often chilled and warmed through heat exchangers) or autogenously, by vaporized propellant tapped from the engine (gaseous oxygen, hydrogen or methane). For a helium bottle expanding adiabatically from p_{0} to a final p_{f} while expelling propellant volume V_{t} at tank pressure p_{t}, the required pressurant mass is

m_{g} = \frac{p_{t}V_{t}}{RT_{0}} \cdot \frac{\gamma}{1 - p_{f}/p_{0}} (adiabatic bottle); replace γ by 1 for an isothermal bottle. Heat transfer and condensation in cryogenic tanks (ullage collapse) increase the real requirement, which is measured in tests.

In weightlessness, propellant must be positioned over the outlet before an engine start, either by a small settling burn or by propellant management devices (surface-tension vanes, screens and sponges, or bladders and diaphragms for storables). Feed lines bring their own hazards: geysering in vertical cryogenic lines, the need to chill down pumps and lines before start, vortexing at tank outlets (cured by anti-vortex baffles), slosh (damped by baffles, Chapter 32) and water hammer. Suddenly stopping a liquid column raises its pressure by \Delta p = \rho a\Delta u (Joukowsky); for liquid oxygen (a \approx 900 m/s) stopped from 10 m/s, that is about 10 MPa.

quiz.q: Find the pump power to raise 500 kg/s of LOX by 20 MPa at 75% efficiency.
quiz.a: P = 500\left( 20 \times 10^{6} \right)/(1141 \times 0.75) = 11.7 MW.

quiz.q: Find the pump head for a 20 MPa rise in LOX and in LH₂, and comment.
quiz.a: LOX: H = 20 \times 10^{6}/(1141 \times 9.807) = 1787 m. LH₂ (\rho = 70.8): 28 800 m. Hydrogen needs 16 times the head, hence high tip speeds and multiple stages.

quiz.q: Size one LOX injector orifice for 1 kg/s at Δp = 2 MPa with C_{d} = 0.7.
quiz.a: A = \dot{m}/\left( C_{d}\sqrt{2\rho\Delta p} \right) = 1/\left( 0.7\sqrt{2 \times 1141 \times 2 \times 10^{6}} \right) = 2.11 \times 10^{- 5} m², so d = 5.2 mm.

quiz.q: A chamber has L^{*} = 1 m and A_{t} = 0.01 m². Find its volume.
quiz.a: V_{c} = L^{*}A_{t} = 0.01 m³.

quiz.q: Find the first-tangential frequency of a 0.4 m diameter chamber with a = 1200 m/s.
quiz.a: f = 1.8412(1200)/(\pi \times 0.4) = 1758 Hz.

quiz.q: Why does staged combustion reach higher p_{c} and I_{sp} than the gas-generator cycle, and what does it cost?
quiz.a: All turbine drive gas passes through the main chamber, so nothing is dumped and the engine can afford the large turbine power needed for very high pump pressures. The costs are extreme preburner and pump discharge pressures, hot-gas compatibility problems (especially oxygen-rich gas) and complex start transients.

quiz.q: Why does wall heat flux peak near the throat?
quiz.a: Bartz gives h \propto (\rho V)^{0.8} roughly, and the mass flux per unit area \rho V = \dot{m}/A is greatest at the minimum area.

quiz.q: Compare tank wall mass for a pressure-fed stage at 3 MPa with a pump-fed stage at 0.3 MPa, for the same propellant volume.
quiz.a: Wall mass scales with pV/\sigma, so the pressure-fed tanks are 10 times heavier (before minimum-gauge effects). This is why pump-fed systems dominate large stages.

quiz.q: Find the helium mass needed to expel 10 m³ of propellant at 0.3 MPa from a bottle at 300 K blown down from 30 MPa to 1 MPa, for an adiabatic and an isothermal bottle (R = 2077 J/(kg·K), γ = 5/3).
quiz.a: p_{t}V_{t}/\left( RT_{0} \right) = 0.3 \times 10^{6}(10)/(2077 \times 300) = 4.81 kg. Adiabatic: 4.81(5/3)/(1 - 1/30) = 8.3 kg. Isothermal: 4.81/(1 - 1/30) = 5.0 kg. The adiabatic bottle cools as it empties, so it holds back more of its gas.

chapters.goalsHtml: explain engine architectures and power cycles and their trade-offs; size pumps, turbines and injectors from first principles; size chambers; design cooling; diagnose combustion instability; understand ignition, transients and throttling.

chapters.title: Solid, Hybrid and Other Chemical Propulsion

secs.html: A solid motor consists of a case (steel, titanium or filament-wound composite), internal insulation and liner, a cast propellant grain, a nozzle (graphite or carbon–carbon throat with an ablative exit cone) and an igniter. Strengths: storable, mechanically simple, high thrust and high density. Weaknesses: lower Isp than liquids, generally no shutdown or throttling once ignited, sensitivity to grain defects (cracks, voids, debonds), and explosive-hazard handling requirements.

Double-base propellants are homogeneous gels of energetic polymers. Composite propellants are a heterogeneous mixture of crystalline oxidizer particles (commonly ammonium perchlorate) in a rubbery polymer binder, often with powdered aluminum as additional fuel. Composites have densities of about 1.75–1.85 g/cm³ and vacuum Isp of about 265–295 s in large motors. Their mechanical behavior is viscoelastic, sensitive to temperature and to aging. Aluminum combustion produces condensed oxide particles, which cause two-phase flow losses (Chapter 26), and perchlorate exhaust contains HCl.

Safety and scope flag · Omitted content (physical hazard, legal and dual-use)

Concern. Solid propellants are energetic materials. They can ignite or detonate from impact, friction, static electricity or heat, and they are the core technology of missile propulsion.

Why it is flagged. Three reasons apply together. (1) Physical hazard: mixing, casting and machining accidents are a classic cause of fatalities in propellant work. (2) Legal: manufacture, storage and transport of energetic materials are regulated in most countries. (3) Dual-use: propellant constituents, production equipment and production technology are controlled internationally (Missile Technology Control Regime Annex) and nationally (ITAR and EAR in the United States). What this chapter does give (burning-rate laws, internal ballistics, stability, grain geometry, performance) is standard university material and is sufficient to analyze motors.

Omitted here. Propellant formulations and ingredient proportions; mixing, casting and curing procedures; igniter compositions; motor-manufacturing methods.

Learn it safely. Fly certified commercial motors through NAR or TRA. Certified adult TRA members may join TRA’s research program, which permits experimental motors under its own safety code and applicable law. University energetic-materials and propulsion laboratories; employment and formal training at licensed propellant and motor manufacturers.

The grain surface recedes normal to itself at the burning rate, empirically

\dot{r} = a\, p_{c}^{\, n}\quad\text{(Saint-Robert/Vieille law)},

with pressure exponent n typically 0.2–0.5 for composites. The coefficient a depends on the initial grain temperature through the temperature sensitivity \sigma_{p} = \left( \partial ln\dot{r}/\partial T_{i} \right)_{p}, typically 0.1–0.3% per K. High gas speeds along the port surface increase the rate (erosive burning), important near the aft end of long ports at ignition.

Mass conservation in the chamber: gas generated equals gas stored plus gas discharged through the choked nozzle,

\rho_{p}\dot{r}A_{b} = \frac{d\left( \rho_{g}V_{c} \right)}{dt} + \frac{p_{c}A_{t}}{c^{*}}.

At quasi-steady state, with K_{n} \equiv A_{b}/A_{t}:

Equilibrium chamber pressure: p_{c} = \left( \rho_{p}\, a\, c^{*}K_{n} \right)^{1/(1 - n)}. Stability: if p_{c} rises slightly, generation (\propto p_{c}^{n}) grows less than discharge (\propto p_{c}) only if n < 1. Hence n < 1 is required for stable operation. Sensitivity: \frac{\delta p_{c}}{p_{c}} = \frac{1}{1 - n}\frac{\delta K_{n}}{K_{n}} and \frac{\delta p_{c}}{p_{c}} = \frac{\sigma_{p}\,\delta T_{i}}{1 - n}. Low n makes motors less sensitive to defects and temperature.

Thrust is F = C_{F}p_{c}A_{t} (Chapter 26), so the thrust–time curve follows the evolution of A_{b} and of the throat area (which grows by erosion and lowers p_{c}).

The burning surface moves inward in parallel layers, so A_{b} is a function of the web distance burned. An internally burning cylinder is progressive (rising A_{b}); an externally burning rod is regressive; star, wagon-wheel and slotted shapes can be made neutral. An end-burner gives long, low-thrust burns. Design measures are the web fraction, the volumetric loading (propellant volume over case volume) and the sliver (propellant left unburned at the end). The grain must also survive structurally: thermal shrinkage after cure, pressurization strain, acceleration and storage aging. Launch boosters shape the thrust curve deliberately, reducing thrust through the max-Q region (Chapter 31).

secs.t: Nozzles and thrust-vector control for solids
secs.html: Steering uses a movable nozzle on a flexible bearing (laminated elastomer and metal shims), secondary fluid injection into the nozzle, or jet tabs and vanes. Ablative and graphite materials in the throat must limit erosion, since throat growth lowers pressure and thrust over the burn.

A hybrid burns a liquid or gaseous oxidizer over a solid fuel grain. The flame is a diffusion flame standing in the boundary layer above the fuel, and heat transferred to the surface vaporizes the fuel. Regression follows \dot{r} = aG_{ox}^{n}, where G_{ox} = {\dot{m}}_{ox}/A_{port} (classical theory: \dot{r} \propto G^{0.8}x^{- 0.2}, reduced by the “blocking” effect of fuel vapor).

Mixture-ratio shift. For one circular port of radius R and length L, {\dot{m}}_{f} = \rho_{f}\dot{r}(2\pi RL) \propto R^{1 - 2n} at constant oxidizer flow. For n > 1/2, fuel flow falls as the port opens and O/F rises during the burn; at n = 1/2 it stays constant.

Hybrids offer safety (the fuel is inert), throttling, restart and low cost. Their weaknesses are low regression rates (needing long grains or many ports), mixture-ratio shift, incomplete combustion and slivers. Liquefying fuels such as paraffin form a melt layer whose instability entrains droplets, raising regression rates several-fold; this remains an active research area.

Safety and scope flag · Physical hazard

Concern. Nitrous oxide, a common hybrid oxidizer, can decompose explosively when heated, contaminated or exposed to an ignition source in tanks and lines. In 2007 a nitrous oxide tank explosion during a cold-flow test in Mojave, California, killed three workers. Concentrated hydrogen peroxide decomposes violently on contact with contaminants.

Why it is flagged. Hybrids are “safer than solids” because their fuel grain is inert (§28.7); their oxidizer systems remain hazardous.

Learn it safely. Student hybrid programs with documented design and safety reviews; oxidizer-handling guidance from industrial gas suppliers and the Compressed Gas Association; faculty-supervised test facilities.

Hydrazine decomposes over an iridium-on-alumina catalyst: 3N_{2}H_{4} \rightarrow 4NH_{3} + N_{2} (exothermic), followed by partial endothermic dissociation of ammonia, 4NH_{3} \rightarrow 2N_{2} + 6H_{2}. More ammonia dissociation lowers both temperature and molar mass; catalyst-bed design sets the balance. Vacuum Isp is about 220–235 s. Green monopropellants based on hydroxylammonium nitrate (such as AF-M315E/ASCENT, flown in 2019) or ammonium dinitramide (such as LMP-103S, flown in 2010) offer roughly 10% more Isp, higher density and much lower toxicity, but need hotter catalyst beds. High-test hydrogen peroxide gives about 160–180 s.

Safety and scope flag · Physical hazard

Concern. Hydrazine is toxic by inhalation and skin contact and is a suspected carcinogen. Concentrated hydrogen peroxide is a strong oxidizer. Catalyst beds and exhaust are hot and toxic. Spacecraft are fueled by specialists in protective suits.

Why it is flagged. Toxicity is the main reason for the shift to the “green” monopropellants described in this section.

Learn it safely. Professional propellant-handling training at launch sites and spacecraft manufacturers; NIOSH and OSHA exposure data; NASA and ESA public literature on green propulsion.

secs.t: Bipropellant spacecraft thrusters and cold gas
secs.html: Pressure-fed, radiation-cooled NTO/MMH thrusters from newtons to kilonewtons deliver 300–325 s and can pulse in milliseconds. The minimum impulse bit sets attitude-control precision. Cold-gas thrusters expand stored gas without combustion. For complete expansion, I_{sp} = \sqrt{2\gamma RT_{0}/(\gamma - 1)}/g_{0}, about 80 s for nitrogen at 300 K (65–73 s in practice). They are simple, clean and precise but low-performing.

System Vacuum \mathbf{I}_{\mathbf{sp}} (s) Throttle and restart Storability Main strengths Main limits

Storable bipropellant 300–340 Yes Years Reliable restart Toxicity, lower Isp

Hybrid 250–320 Yes Long Safety, throttling Regression rate, O/F shift

Cold gas 50–75 Pulsed Years Cleanliness, precision Very low Isp

quiz.q: A motor has \rho_{p} = 1750 kg/m³, \dot{r} = 5\ mm/s \times \left( p_{c}/1\ MPa \right)^{0.35}, c^{*} = 1550 m/s and K_{n} = 200. Find p_{c}.
quiz.a: \rho_{p}\dot{r}A_{b} = p_{c}A_{t}/c^{*} with p_{c} in MPa as P: 10^{6}P = 1750(1550)(200)\left( 5 \times 10^{- 3} \right)P^{0.35}, so P^{0.65} = 2.7125 and p_{c} = 4.64 MPa.

quiz.q: By what percentage does p_{c} change if A_{b} rises 10%?
A hybrid has \dot{r} = 3.0 \times 10^{- 5}G_{ox}^{0.6} (SI units). Find \dot{r} at G_{ox} = 200 kg/(m²·s), and say how O/F evolves in a single circular port.
quiz.a: \dot{r} = 3.0 \times 10^{- 5}(200)^{0.6} = 7.2 \times 10^{- 4} m/s = 0.72 mm/s. With n = 0.6 > 0.5, fuel flow \propto R^{- 0.2} falls as the port grows, so O/F rises during the burn.

quiz.q: A 1000 kg spacecraft burns 50 kg of hydrazine at 230 s. Find Δv.
quiz.a: \Delta v = 230(9.807)\ln(1000/950) = 116 m/s.

quiz.q: Why must n < 1 for a stable solid motor?
quiz.a: A pressure rise must reduce the net mass accumulation. Generation scales as p^{n} and discharge as p, so only for n < 1 does discharge outgrow generation and restore equilibrium.

quiz.q: For the motor of Question 1 with A_{t} = 0.005 m² and C_{F} = 1.6, find the thrust.
quiz.a: F = C_{F}p_{c}A_{t} = 1.6\left( 4.64 \times 10^{6} \right)(0.005) = 37.1 kN.

quiz.q: Why are hybrids considered safer than solids?
quiz.a: The oxidizer and fuel are stored separately and in different phases. The fuel grain alone cannot burn, so cracks and voids do not cause the pressure runaway they can in solids, and the motor can be shut down by closing the oxidizer valve.

quiz.q: Find the ideal (fully expanded) cold-gas Isp for nitrogen at 300 K (\gamma = 1.4, R = 296.8 J/(kg·K)).

chapters.goalsHtml: compute solid-motor equilibrium pressure and its stability and sensitivity; relate grain geometry to the thrust profile; analyze hybrid regression and mixture-ratio shift; understand monopropellant, bipropellant spacecraft and cold-gas systems; compare all chemical options. (Propellant formulation and manufacture are deliberately outside the scope of this document.)

chapters.title: Orbital Mechanics I: The Two-Body Problem and Maneuvers

secs.html:
For two point (or spherically symmetric) masses with no other forces, the relative position \mathbf{r} of body 2 with respect to body 1 obeys

\ddot{\mathbf{r}} = - \frac{\mu}{r^{3}}\mathbf{r},\quad\quad\mu = G\left( m_{1} + m_{2} \right) \approx Gm_{1}\ \ \left( m_{2} \ll m_{1} \right).

Angular momentum \mathbf{h} = \mathbf{r} \times \mathbf{v} is constant, so the motion is planar and sweeps area at the rate h/2 (Kepler’s second law). Energy \varepsilon = \frac{v^{2}}{2} - \frac{\mu}{r} is constant. Eccentricity vector \mathbf{e} = \frac{\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{h}}{\mu} - \frac{\mathbf{r}}{r} is constant, points to periapsis, and has magnitude e.

Dotting \mathbf{e} with \mathbf{r} gives re\cos u = h^{2}/\mu - r, i.e.

r = rac{h^{2}/\mu}{1 + e\cos u},\quad\quad p = rac{h^{2}}{\mu},

a conic with the attracting body at a focus (Kepler’s first law; geometry in Chapter 4), where u is the true anomaly. For closed orbits \varepsilon = - \mu/(2a), giving the energy equation:

Vis-viva: v^{2} = \mu\left( rac{2}{r} - rac{1}{a} ight). Circular: v_{c} = \sqrt{\mu/r}. Parabolic (escape): v = \sqrt{2\mu/r}. Hyperbolic: a < 0 and v_{\infty}^{2} = - \mu/a.

Kepler’s third law: T = 2\pi\sqrt{a^{3}/\mu}, with mean motion n = \sqrt{\mu/a^{3}}. Velocity components: radial v_{r} = (\mu/h)e\sin u and transverse v_{ heta} = (\mu/h)\left( 1 + e\cos u ight). The flight-path angle (above the local horizontal) satisfies an\gamma = e\sin u/\left( 1 + e\cos u ight), and is zero at periapsis and apoapsis.

Introduce the eccentric anomaly E (Chapter 4): r = a\left( 1 - e\cos E \right) and \tan(\nu/2) = \sqrt{(1 + e)/(1 - e)}\tan(E/2). Then:

Kepler’s equation: M = E - e\sin E = n\left( t - t_{p} \right), with mean anomaly M and periapsis time t_{p}. Finding the time from position is explicit. Finding the position at a given time requires solving for E (Newton’s method from E_{0} = M, Chapter 14). For hyperbolas, M_{h} = e\sinh F - F.

Universal-variable formulations handle every conic with one set of equations, which is valuable in software.

The Earth-centered inertial (ECI) frame has z along the rotation axis and x toward the vernal equinox (J2000 epoch). The perifocal frame (PQW) has P toward periapsis and W along \mathbf{h}. The six classical elements are: semi-major axis a, eccentricity e, inclination i, right ascension of the ascending node \Omega, argument of periapsis \omega, and true anomaly u (or M at an epoch). From a state \left( \mathbf{r},\mathbf{v} ight): compute \mathbf{h}, the node vector \mathbf{n} = \widehat{\mathbf{z}} imes \mathbf{h} and \mathbf{e}. Then i = arccos\left( h_{z}/h ight); \Omega is the angle from \widehat{\mathbf{x}} to \mathbf{n}; \omega is the angle from \mathbf{n} to \mathbf{e}; u is the angle from \mathbf{e} to \mathbf{r}. Resolve each quadrant with signs: n_{y} for \Omega, e_{z} for \omega, and \mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v} for u. The rotation from perifocal to ECI is \mathbf{R}_{3}( - \Omega)\mathbf{R}_{1}( - i)\mathbf{R}_{3}( - \omega). For circular or equatorial orbits \omega or \Omega is undefined; use the argument of latitude u = \omega + u, the true longitude, or equinoctial elements.

A burn short compared with the orbital period changes velocity instantaneously by \Delta\mathbf{v}; propellant follows from the rocket equation.

  • Hohmann transfer between coplanar circular orbits r_{1} < r_{2}: an ellipse with a_{t} = \left( r_{1} + r_{2} \right)/2, tangent to both. \Delta v_{1} = \sqrt{\mu\left( 2/r_{1} - 1/a_{t} \right)} - \sqrt{\mu/r_{1}}, \Delta v_{2} = \sqrt{\mu/r_{2}} - \sqrt{\mu\left( 2/r_{2} - 1/a_{t} \right)}, and the transfer time is \pi\sqrt{a_{t}^{3}/\mu}. It is the optimal two-impulse transfer.
  • Bi-elliptic transfer: three impulses through an intermediate apoapsis. It beats Hohmann for r_{2}/r_{1} > 15.58 (for any intermediate radius); between 11.94 and 15.58 it depends on that radius; and it is slower.
  • Plane change at speed v: \Delta v = 2v\sin(\Delta i/2). Do it where v is smallest (apoapsis, high altitude), and combine it with other burns: rotating one vector into another costs \Delta v = \sqrt{v_{1}^{2} + v_{2}^{2} - 2v_{1}v_{2}\cos\Delta i} (law of cosines, Chapter 3).
  • Phasing: a temporary orbit of different period lets a spacecraft catch up with, or wait for, a target in the same orbit.

Oberth effect. The energy change from a small burn is \Delta\varepsilon \approx v\,\Delta v. Burns deep in a gravity well, at high speed, change orbital energy most per unit Δv. This is why departure burns are made at periapsis of a low parking orbit.

The hyperbolic excess speed v_{\infty} satisfies v_{\infty}^{2} = v^{2} - 2\mu/r, and the characteristic energy is C_{3} = v_{\infty}^{2}. Departing from a circular parking orbit of radius r costs \Delta v = \sqrt{v_{\infty}^{2} + 2\mu/r} - \sqrt{\mu/r}. The hyperbola bends the trajectory through \delta = 2\arcsin(1/e) (Chapter 30).

Spherical trigonometry (Chapter 3) relates inclination i, site latitude \phi and launch azimuth A_{z} (measured from north): \cos i = cos\phi\sin A_{z}. The minimum inclination reachable directly is therefore |\phi|, by launching due east. Lower inclinations require a costly plane change. The orbital plane passes over a site twice per day, defining launch windows for a given target plane (Chapter 31 adds Earth rotation). A circular orbit’s ground track shifts west each revolution by about 360^{\circ} \times T/(23.93\ h).

Geostationary orbit: r = 42\, 164 km, i = 0, period one sidereal day (86 164 s). Geosynchronous transfer orbit (GTO): perigee near LEO altitude, apogee at GEO radius. Molniya: 12 h period at the critical inclination 63.4°, so its apogee does not drift (Chapter 30). Sun-synchronous orbits (Chapter 30). Medium Earth orbit carries the navigation constellations (about 20 000 km altitude).

quiz.q: Compute a Hohmann transfer from a 300 km circular LEO (r = 6678 km) to GEO (r = 42\, 164 km): both Δv’s, the total, and the transfer time.
quiz.a: v_{1} = 7.726 km/s and the transfer perigee speed is 10.152 km/s, so \Delta v_{1} = 2.426 km/s. Transfer apogee speed 1.608 km/s and v_{GEO} = 3.075 km/s, so \Delta v_{2} = 1.467 km/s. Total 3.893 km/s. Transfer time 5.28 h.

quiz.q: Starting at Cape Canaveral’s inclination (28.5°), combine the GEO circularization with the plane change to 0°. Compare with doing them separately.
quiz.a: Combined: \sqrt{{1.608}^{2} + {3.075}^{2} - 2(1.608)(3.075)\cos{28.5}^{\circ}} = 1.830 km/s. Separately: 1.467 + 2(3.075)\sin{14.25}^{\circ} = 2.981 km/s. Combining saves 1.15 km/s.

quiz.q: Find the period of an orbit with a = 7000 km.
A spacecraft at r = 8000 km moves horizontally at 8 km/s. Find a, e and r_{a}.
quiz.a: \varepsilon = 32 - 49.825 = - 17.83 km²/s², so a = 11\, 181 km. The burn point is periapsis (horizontal and faster than circular), so e = 1 - 8000/11\, 181 = 0.284 and r_{a} = 14\, 362 km.

quiz.q: Find the Δv to depart a 300 km circular orbit with C_{3} = 10 km²/s².
What launch azimuth from latitude 28.5° reaches i = {51.6}^{\circ} (non-rotating Earth)?
quiz.a: \sin A_{z} = cos{51.6}^{\circ}/cos{28.5}^{\circ} = 0.7068, so A_{z} = {45.0}^{\circ} (northeast).

quiz.q: For e = 0.2 and a = 10\, 000 km, find the time from periapsis to \nu = 90^{\circ}.
quiz.a: E = 2\arctan\left( \sqrt{0.8/1.2}\tan 45^{\circ} \right) = 1.3694 rad, M = E - 0.2\sin E = 1.1735 rad, n = 6.313 \times 10^{- 4} rad/s, so t = 1859 s.

quiz.q: Why are plane changes cheapest at apoapsis?
quiz.a: The cost 2v\sin(\Delta i/2) is proportional to the speed at the burn, which is lowest at apoapsis.

chapters.goalsHtml: derive the conic orbit and its constants; use vis-viva, Kepler’s laws and Kepler’s equation; convert between state vectors and orbital elements; plan Hohmann, bi-elliptic, plane-change and escape maneuvers; relate launch site, azimuth and inclination.

chapters.title: Astrodynamics II: Perturbations, Interplanetary Transfer, Relative Motion and the Three-Body Problem

secs.html:
Cowell’s method integrates \ddot{\mathbf{r}} = - \mu\mathbf{r}/r^{3} + \mathbf{a}_{p} numerically, which is simple and general. Encke’s method integrates only the deviation from a reference conic. Variation of parameters tracks how the osculating elements drift. With perturbing acceleration components F_{R} (radial), F_{S} (along-track) and F_{W} (normal), and argument of latitude u = \omega + \nu, the Gauss equations include:

\frac{da}{dt} = \frac{2a^{2}}{h}\left( e\sin\nu\, F_{R} + \frac{p}{r}F_{S} \right),\quad\quad\frac{di}{dt} = \frac{r\cos u}{h}F_{W},\quad\quad\frac{d\Omega}{dt} = \frac{r\sin u}{h\sin i}F_{W}.

They show directly that along-track thrust changes a and normal thrust changes the plane.

The potential is U = \frac{\mu}{r}\left\lbrack 1 - \sum_{n \geq 2}^{}J_{n}\left( \frac{R}{r} \right)^{n}P_{n}\left( \sin\phi \right) + \text{tesseral terms} \right\rbrack, with J_{2} = 1.08263 \times 10^{- 3} for the equatorial bulge. Averaged over an orbit, J₂ produces secular drifts:

\dot{\Omega} = - \frac{3}{2}nJ_{2}\left( \frac{R}{p} \right)^{2}\cos i, \quad\quad\dot{\omega} = \frac{3}{4}nJ_{2}\left( \frac{R}{p} \right)^{2}\left( 5\cos^{2}i - 1 \right). The node regresses for prograde orbits. Apsides freeze at the critical inclination 63.43° (Molniya orbits). Sun-synchronous: choose i so that \dot{\Omega} = + {0.9856}^{\circ}/day, which requires a slightly retrograde inclination (96–100° in LEO). The orbit plane then keeps a fixed orientation to the Sun.

\mathbf{a}_{D} = - \frac{1}{2\beta}\rho v_{rel}^{2}{\widehat{\mathbf{v}}}_{rel}, with ballistic coefficient \beta = m/\left( C_{D}A \right) (free-molecular C_{D} \approx 2.0–2.2, Chapter 40). For a near-circular orbit, energy loss gives da/dt = - \rho\sqrt{\mu a}/\beta. Drag lowers the orbit and, paradoxically, raises the speed. Thermospheric density varies by an order of magnitude with solar activity (F10.7 index) and geomagnetic storms. Reentry-time predictions therefore carry uncertainties of order ±10–20% of the remaining lifetime.

The perturbation from a third body is the difference between its pull on the satellite and on the central body. Luni-solar perturbations drive GEO inclination growth of roughly 0.75–0.95° per year, which station-keeping must remove. Solar radiation pressure gives a = P_{\odot}C_{R}A/m, with P_{\odot} = 4.56 \times 10^{- 6} N/m² at 1 AU and reflectivity coefficient C_{R} between 1 and 2. It dominates for high area-to-mass objects and requires eclipse modeling.

Given two position vectors and a time of flight, find the connecting conic (and \mathbf{v}_{1}, \mathbf{v}_{2}). Lambert’s theorem: the transfer time depends only on a, r_{1} + r_{2} and the chord c. For zero revolutions and a specified direction the solution is unique; multi-revolution solutions come in pairs. Robust solvers (universal variables, Gooding, Izzo) iterate on one variable. Repeating Lambert solutions over grids of departure and arrival dates produces porkchop plots of C_{3} and arrival v_{\infty}, the starting point of mission design.

Inside a planet’s sphere of influence, r_{SOI} = a_{p}\left( m_{p}/M_{\odot} \right)^{2/5} (about 925 000 km for Earth), treat the motion as planet-centered; outside, as Sun-centered. Patch the two at the boundary, where the planet-relative v_{\infty} connects them. The Earth–Mars Hohmann transfer requires v_{\infty} \approx 2.94 km/s at departure and 2.65 km/s at arrival and takes about 259 days. Opportunities recur every synodic period 1/\left| 1/T_{1} - 1/T_{2} \right|, about 780 days for Mars. Arrival may use propulsive capture, aerocapture or aerobraking.

Gravity assist. In the planet’s frame a flyby only rotates \mathbf{v}_{\infty}, by \delta = 2\arcsin\left\lbrack 1/\left( 1 + r_{p}v_{\infty}^{2}/\mu_{p} \right) \right\rbrack, without changing its magnitude. In the Sun’s frame, adding the planet’s velocity converts that rotation into a heliocentric speed change of up to 2v_{\infty}\sin(\delta/2), at no propellant cost. Momentum is borrowed from the planet’s orbit.

In a frame rotating with a target in a circular orbit of mean motion n (x radial outward, y along-track, z cross-track), the linearized relative motion obeys the Clohessy–Wiltshire (Hill) equations:

\ddot{x} - 3n^{2}x - 2n\dot{y} = a_{x},\quad\quad\ddot{y} + 2n\dot{x} = a_{y},\quad\quad\ddot{z} + n^{2}z = a_{z}.

Consequences that defy intuition: a chaser below the target drifts ahead by 3\pi|x| per orbit; thrusting forward raises the orbit and makes the chaser fall behind. Cross-track motion is a simple oscillation. Rendezvous planning uses the closed-form solutions to compute two-impulse transfers, approaches along the velocity vector (V-bar) or radius vector (R-bar), and passively safe relative orbits.

Two primaries in circular orbit about their barycenter, plus a massless third body, viewed in the rotating frame with mass parameter \mu = m_{2}/\left( m_{1} + m_{2} \right). The Jacobi constant C = 2U^{*} - v^{2}, with U^{*} = \frac{1}{2}\left( x^{2} + y^{2} \right) + (1 - \mu)/r_{1} + \mu/r_{2}, is conserved. Surfaces of zero velocity bound the accessible regions. There are five equilibria: the collinear points L1–L3 (unstable, but with families of periodic halo and Lyapunov orbits) and the triangular points L4 and L5 (stable for \mu < 0.0385). The stable and unstable invariant manifolds of periodic orbits form low-energy transfer pathways, used by Genesis and by ballistic lunar transfers. Near-rectilinear halo orbits about the Moon support lunar-orbit operations.

Measurements (range, range-rate, angles, GNSS pseudoranges) are related to the state through models. Initial orbit determination uses three position vectors (Gibbs) or three angle sets (Gauss, Laplace). Batch least squares (differential correction) linearizes the residuals about a reference trajectory using the state-transition matrix and solves the normal equations (Chapters 10 and 13). Sequential estimation uses an extended Kalman filter (Chapter 46). Realistic covariance underlies conjunction assessment, the computation of collision probability between space objects.

With continuous small acceleration the orbit spirals. For a circle-to-circle transfer with plane change \Delta i (rad) at constant acceleration with optimal steering, Edelbaum’s approximation gives

\Delta v = \sqrt{v_{0}^{2} - 2v_{0}v_{1}\cos\left( \frac{\pi}{2}\Delta i \right) + v_{1}^{2}}.

Low-thrust Δv exceeds impulsive Δv because thrust is spent away from the most efficient points, but the high I_{sp} of electric propulsion (Chapter 48) more than compensates.

quiz.q: Find the sun-synchronous inclination for a 700 km circular orbit.
quiz.a: a = 7078 km and n = 1.0602 \times 10^{- 3} rad/s. Required \dot{\Omega} = 1.991 \times 10^{- 7} rad/s, so \cos i = - \dot{\Omega}/\left\lbrack 1.5nJ_{2}(R/a)^{2} \right\rbrack = - 0.1424 and i = {98.2}^{\circ}.

quiz.q: Compute the heliocentric Hohmann transfer from Earth (1 AU) to Mars (1.5237 AU): departure and arrival v_{\infty} and the transfer time.
quiz.a: Earth’s orbital speed 29.785 km/s; transfer perihelion speed 32.729 km/s, so v_{\infty,dep} = 2.94 km/s. At arrival, v_{\infty} = 2.65 km/s. Transfer time = \pi\sqrt{a_{t}^{3}/\mu_{\odot}} = 259 days.

quiz.q: Find the Δv to inject from a 300 km circular parking orbit with v_{\infty} = 2.94 km/s.
A spacecraft passes Venus (\mu = 324\, 859 km³/s², R = 6051.8 km) at 300 km altitude with v_{\infty} = 5 km/s. Find the turn angle.
quiz.a: e = 1 + 6351.8(25)/324\, 859 = 1.489, so \delta = 2\arcsin(1/1.489) = {84.4}^{\circ}.

quiz.q: For a target at 400 km altitude, find n and the along-track drift per orbit of a chaser 1 km below it.
quiz.a: n = \sqrt{\mu/6778^{3}} = 1.131 \times 10^{- 3} rad/s (period 5553 s). Drift = 3\pi(1\ km) = 9.4 km per orbit, ahead of the target.

quiz.q: What does the Jacobi constant tell a mission designer?
quiz.a: It is an energy-like integral in the rotating frame. Its value determines which regions (zero-velocity boundaries) are reachable, for example whether a spacecraft can pass through the L1 gateway to the secondary body.

quiz.q: A satellite at 400 km has \beta = 100 kg/m² and \rho = 3 \times 10^{- 12} kg/m³. Find the drag acceleration and the decay rate in meters per day.
quiz.a: a_{D} = \frac{1}{2}\left( 3 \times 10^{- 12} \right)(7669)^{2}/100 = 8.8 \times 10^{- 7} m/s². da/dt = - \rho\sqrt{\mu a}/\beta = - 1.56 \times 10^{- 3} m/s = - 135 m/day.

quiz.q: Use Edelbaum’s formula for a low-thrust transfer from a 7000 km circular orbit to GEO with a 28.5° plane change, and compare with the impulsive Hohmann-plus-plane-change value.
quiz.a: With v_{0} = 7.546 km/s and v_{1} = 3.075 km/s: \Delta v = 5.78 km/s, versus 4.15 km/s for a Hohmann transfer from the same 7000 km orbit with the plane change combined into the apogee burn. The low-thrust penalty is about 1.6 km/s, but at I_{sp} \sim 1800 s the propellant fraction is far smaller (Chapter 48).

chapters.goalsHtml: model and exploit perturbations (J₂, drag, third bodies, solar radiation pressure); solve Lambert’s problem; design patched-conic interplanetary transfers and gravity assists; plan rendezvous with the Clohessy–Wiltshire equations; use the circular restricted three-body problem; understand orbit determination and low-thrust transfers.

chapters.title: Launch-Vehicle Flight Mechanics and Trajectory Design

secs.html:
For a point mass in a vertical plane over a spherical, non-rotating Earth, let \gamma be the flight-path angle above the local horizontal and \alpha the angle of attack (thrust along the body axis):

\dot{V} = \frac{T\cos\alpha - D}{m} - g\sin\gamma, \quad V\dot{\gamma} = \frac{T\sin\alpha + L}{m} - \left( g - \frac{V^{2}}{r} \right)\cos\gamma, \quad\dot{h} = V\sin\gamma, \quad\dot{x} = V\cos\gamma\frac{R_{\oplus}}{r}, \quad\dot{m} = - {\dot{m}}_{p}, with g = \mu/r^{2}.

The term V^{2}/r is the centrifugal relief that eventually makes horizontal flight self-sustaining (orbit). Earth rotation adds Coriolis and centripetal terms. Engineering simulations are three-degree-of-freedom (point mass, attitude assumed) or six-degree-of-freedom (with rotational dynamics and control, Chapter 32).

Use the standard atmosphere (Appendix D) for design and measured or statistical profiles for operations. Upper-level winds and wind shear dominate aerodynamic loads. On launch day, balloon or radar wind measurements feed load assessments, and launch-commit criteria can stop a countdown.

1. Vertical rise to clear the tower.
  2. Pitch-over: a small “kick” angle at low speed starts the turn.
  3. Gravity turn: fly at \alpha \approx 0 so that thrust follows the velocity. Gravity then rotates the velocity toward horizontal by itself (V\dot{\gamma} = - \left( g - V^{2}/r \right)\cos\gamma), and lateral aerodynamic loads stay small.
  4. Max-Q: many vehicles throttle down (a “bucket”) to cap q near 30–35 kPa.
  5. Staging at high altitude and low q; the fairing is jettisoned once free-molecular heating falls below a threshold (a common criterion is about 1.1 kW/m²).
  6. Guided upper-stage steering in vacuum: for a flat Earth with no atmosphere, the minimum-time steering law is the linear tangent law \tan\theta = a - bt (Chapter 46). Closed-loop guidance solves for its parameters in flight.
  7. Insertion, either directly or via a coast to apogee followed by a circularization burn.

Rearranging the \dot{V} equation and integrating over the burn:

\Delta v_{ideal} = c\ln\frac{m_{0}}{m_{f}} = \int\frac{T}{m}dt = \Delta V + \int g\sin\gamma\, dt + \int\frac{D}{m}dt + \int\frac{T}{m}\left( 1 - \cos\alpha \right)\, dt.

The terms on the right are the velocity gain, the gravity loss, the drag loss and the steering loss. Typical values to LEO: gravity 1.0–1.5 km/s, drag 0.1–0.3 km/s, steering 0.05–0.2 km/s. Higher thrust-to-weight reduces gravity loss but raises drag loss (higher q low down) and engine mass. First-stage liftoff T/W is typically 1.2–1.5, and upper stages often run at T/W below 1, since by then \gamma is small and gravity loss accrues slowly.

Bending loads scale with the normal force, which is proportional to q\alpha (Chapter 25). A crosswind w produces \alpha \approx w/V, so wind shear near max-Q is the critical case. Load relief steers partially into the wind, using accelerometer or angle-of-attack feedback to reduce \alpha at the cost of trajectory dispersion. Every vehicle carries a q\alpha (and q\beta) limit derived from its structural allowables (Chapter 33).

Trajectory design maximizes payload (or minimizes propellant) subject to: maximum q; aerodynamic heating limits; acceleration (about 4–6g for crews and sensitive payloads); stage drop zones; ground-track and range-safety corridors; and terminal insertion conditions. Early designs parameterize the pitch program and optimize the parameters. Rigorous designs solve an optimal-control problem (Chapter 46).

Thrust, Isp, mass, aerodynamic coefficients, winds and density are uncertain. Monte Carlo simulation (Chapter 13) gives the distribution of insertion errors and propellant consumption. A flight performance reserve of propellant is carried so that the 3σ (or 99.7%) case still reaches orbit.

Propulsive return of a first stage requires a boostback burn to reverse horizontal velocity (for a return to the launch site), an entry burn to reduce velocity and heating through the dense atmosphere, aerodynamic steering (for example grid fins), and a landing burn. If the minimum-throttle thrust exceeds the stage’s empty weight, it cannot hover, so ignition must be timed so that velocity reaches zero exactly at touchdown. The propellant reserved for recovery reduces payload, more for return to the launch site than for downrange landing.

During flight, the instantaneous impact point (where the vehicle would land if thrust stopped now) is tracked continuously. A flight termination system, increasingly autonomous, ends thrust if the vehicle leaves its safety corridor. In the United States, FAA launch licensing (14 CFR Part 450) caps public risk. A typical criterion is an expected casualty of at most 10^{- 4} per launch. Launch sites are chosen for over-water downrange corridors and favorable latitudes.

Safety and scope flag · Legal and dual-use (scope note)

Concern. Flight termination systems use pyrotechnic or explosive devices, and launch and reentry operations require licenses.

Why it is flagged. Ordnance is regulated explosive technology, and destruct-system design is safety-critical work done only under the authority of a launch range or licensing agency.

Omitted here. Flight-termination ordnance and destruct-system design.
