Learn it safely. The Range Commanders Council’s public flight-termination-system standard (RCC 319); FAA Part 450 guidance documents and advisory circulars; range-safety training through launch-site operators and government ranges; professional employment in range safety.

quiz.q: Find the dynamic pressure at 12 km (\rho = 0.3119 kg/m³) and 450 m/s.
quiz.a: q = \frac{1}{2}(0.3119)\left( 450^{2} \right) = 31.6 kPa.

quiz.q: Over a 150 s first-stage burn the average \sin\gamma is 0.6 and g = 9.7 m/s². Estimate the gravity loss.
quiz.a: \Delta v_{g} \approx 0.6(9.7)(150) = 873 m/s.

quiz.q: Find the steering loss for a constant 5° angle of attack with average T/m = 20 m/s² over 100 s.
quiz.a: 20(100)\left( 1 - \cos 5^{\circ} \right) = 7.6 m/s: modest angles cost little.

quiz.q: A stage falls vertically at 250 m/s. With constant thrust giving T/W = 3 (ignore drag and mass change), find the landing-burn duration and ignition altitude.
quiz.a: Net deceleration (3 - 1)g = 19.6 m/s², so t = 250/19.6 = 12.7 s and the ignition altitude is V^{2}/(2a) = 1.59 km.

quiz.q: Why fly a gravity turn through the atmosphere?
quiz.a: At \alpha \approx 0 the normal force, and with it bending load and steering loss, is minimal, while gravity performs the turn at no cost.

quiz.q: Launching from 28.5° latitude at azimuth 45°, how much of Earth’s rotational velocity (408.7 m/s eastward) helps along the trajectory?
quiz.a: 408.7\sin 45^{\circ} = 289 m/s (non-rotating approximation).

quiz.q: Build a LEO Δv budget: orbital speed 7.73 km/s, gravity loss 1.2, drag 0.15, steering 0.1, rotation credit 0.4 km/s.
Why can raising liftoff T/W fail to increase payload?
quiz.a: Higher T/W means heavier engines and structure (lower mass fraction), higher drag loss and higher max-Q loads. Gravity-loss savings eventually fail to pay for these.

chapters.goalsHtml: write and integrate the ascent equations of motion; explain each ascent phase; decompose Δv losses exactly; manage aerodynamic loads; design and disperse trajectories; understand booster recovery and range safety.

chapters.title: Attitude Dynamics and Control

secs.html:
Representation Parameters Singularities Notes
Direction-cosine matrix \mathbf{C} 9 (6 constraints) None Composes by multiplication
Euler angles (e.g. 3-2-1: yaw ψ, pitch θ, roll φ) 3 At θ = ±90° (“gimbal lock”) Intuitive; 12 possible sequences
Euler axis and angle \left( \widehat{\mathbf{e}},\Phi \right) 4 Axis undefined at Φ = 0 Euler’s theorem: every rotation is about one axis
Quaternion \mathbf{q} = \left\lbrack \cos\frac{\Phi}{2},\ \widehat{\mathbf{e}}\sin\frac{\Phi}{2} \right\rbrack 4 (unit norm) None (but \mathbf{q} and - \mathbf{q} are the same attitude) Standard in flight software
Modified Rodrigues parameters \widehat{\mathbf{e}}\tan\frac{\Phi}{4} 3 At Φ = 360° (switch to the shadow set) Minimal; good for estimation

The DCM from Euler axis and angle is \mathbf{C} = cos\Phi\,\mathbf{I} + \left( 1 - \cos\Phi \right)\widehat{\mathbf{e}}{\widehat{\mathbf{e}}}^{T} - \sin\Phi\left\lbrack \widehat{\mathbf{e}} \times \right\rbrack. Kinematics: for the DCM mapping inertial to body components with body rates \mathbf{\omega}, \dot{\mathbf{C}} = - \left\lbrack \mathbf{\omega} \times \right\rbrack\mathbf{C}. For quaternions (scalar first, Hamilton product), \dot{\mathbf{q}} = \frac{1}{2}\mathbf{q} \otimes \left\lbrack 0,\ \mathbf{\omega} \right\rbrack. For 3-2-1 Euler angles with body rates (p,q,r):

\dot{\phi} = p + \left( q\sin\phi + r\cos\phi \right)\tan\theta,\quad\quad\dot{\theta} = q\cos\phi - r\sin\phi,\quad\quad\dot{\psi} = \frac{q\sin\phi + r\cos\phi}{\cos\theta},

which blow up at \theta = \pm 90^{\circ}.

Conventions. Quaternion conventions differ (scalar first or last; Hamilton or JPL/Shuster product order), and DCMs may be active or passive. Interface errors between conventions have caused real mission anomalies. State the convention in every document and code module, and test with known rotations.

Euler’s equations (Chapter 15) govern rotation. Spin stabilization exploits gyroscopic stiffness. With internal energy dissipation (flexing antennas, fuel slosh), only spin about the major axis is stable. Explorer 1 (1958), an elongated body spun about its long (minor) axis, went into a flat spin within hours. Dual-spin spacecraft carry a despun platform; their stability depends on where dissipation occurs. Nutation dampers remove residual coning.

• Gravity gradient: \mathbf{T}_{gg} = \frac{3\mu}{r^{3}}\widehat{\mathbf{r}} \times \left( \mathbf{I}\widehat{\mathbf{r}} \right) in body components. Its magnitude in one axis is \frac{3\mu}{2r^{3}}\left| I_{z} - I_{y} \right|\sin 2\theta. It can also be used for passive stabilization.
  • Aerodynamic: drag acting at a center of pressure offset from the center of mass; dominant below about 500 km.
  • Solar radiation pressure: also acting through a CP–CM offset; dominant at high altitude.
  • Magnetic: residual dipole \mathbf{m} crossed with the geomagnetic field \mathbf{B}.
  • Internal: moving parts, propellant slosh and thruster misalignment.

Thrusters (RCS) give large torques but have a minimum impulse bit and consume propellant. Reaction wheels exchange momentum with the body (body torque = - {\dot{\mathbf{h}}}_{w}), are smooth and precise, and saturate under secular disturbances; they are then desaturated with thrusters or magnetorquers. Control moment gyros tilt constant-speed rotors and produce large torques, \mathbf{\tau} = \dot{\mathbf{\delta}} \times \mathbf{h}, but have geometric singularities that steering laws must avoid. Magnetorquers produce \mathbf{m} \times \mathbf{B}, so they cannot torque about \mathbf{B} at any instant. Launch vehicles use gimballed engines (hydraulic or electromechanical actuators), aerodynamic fins or grid fins, differential throttling, and roll thrusters.

Gyroscopes (ring-laser, fiber-optic, hemispherical-resonator, MEMS) measure rates and are integrated between absolute fixes. Star trackers give arcsecond-class absolute attitude at a few hertz. Sun sensors range from coarse to fine. Magnetometers give degree-level attitude in LEO. Horizon sensors measure Earth’s limb. Multi-antenna GNSS can measure attitude directly. Error models are covered in Chapter 34.

TRIAD builds two orthonormal triads from two measured vectors (for example Sun and magnetic field) and their reference directions. Wahba’s problem finds the rotation \mathbf{A} minimizing \sum w_{i}\left| \mathbf{b}_{i} - \mathbf{A}\mathbf{r}_{i} \right|^{2} and is solved optimally by Davenport’s q-method (an eigenvalue problem), QUEST or the SVD (Chapter 10). In flight, gyro-propagated attitude is corrected by vector measurements in a multiplicative extended Kalman filter that estimates a small error quaternion and the gyro biases (Chapter 46).

A standard spacecraft law is quaternion feedback with gyroscopic compensation:

\mathbf{u} = - K_{p}\, sign\left( q_{e0} \right)\,\mathbf{q}_{e,v} - K_{d}\mathbf{\omega}_{e} + \mathbf{\omega} \times \mathbf{I\omega},

where \mathbf{q}_{e} is the error quaternion. The sign term makes the vehicle take the shorter rotation and avoids “unwinding” a full turn. Large slews rotate about the eigenaxis with rate limits. The time-optimal rest-to-rest single-axis slew with torque limit \tau_{\max} is bang-bang, with t = 2\sqrt{\theta/\alpha} where \alpha = \tau_{\max}/I. Thruster-only systems use deadbands and switching lines in the phase plane and settle into limit cycles whose amplitude is set by the minimum impulse bit.

The design model combines unstable rigid-body aerodynamics (Chapter 22), gimbal-actuator dynamics, flexible bending modes, propellant slosh and sensor dynamics. Bending: long launchers have first bending modes at a few hertz. The local slope of each mode shape at the gyro location determines whether that mode is gain-stabilized (attenuated with notch or low-pass filters) or phase-stabilized (kept in phase so that control adds damping). Slosh: the first lateral mode of liquid in a cylindrical tank of radius R and fill depth h has frequency \omega^{2} = \left( 1.841\, g_{ax}/R \right)\tanh(1.841h/R), where g_{ax} is the axial acceleration. It is modeled as a pendulum or spring-mass and damped with baffles. Gains are scheduled with dynamic pressure, mass and Mach number. Robustness is verified by stability margins at each flight condition and by Monte Carlo simulation.

quiz.q: Write the quaternion for a 90° rotation about z.
quiz.a: \mathbf{q} = \left\lbrack \cos 45^{\circ},0,0,sin45^{\circ} \right\rbrack = \lbrack 0.7071,0,0,0.7071\rbrack.

quiz.q: Estimate the maximum gravity-gradient torque for \left| I_{z} - I_{y} \right| = 100 kg·m² at 400 km altitude.
quiz.a: \frac{3\mu}{2r^{3}}\Delta I = \frac{3\left( 3.986 \times 10^{14} \right)}{2\left( 6.778 \times 10^{6} \right)^{3}}(100) = 1.9 \times 10^{- 4} N·m, at θ = 45°.

quiz.q: A secular torque of 10^{- 4} N·m acts for one 5553 s orbit. How much wheel momentum storage is needed?
quiz.a: h = \tau t = 10^{- 4}(5553) = 0.56 N·m·s per orbit, before desaturation.

quiz.q: Find the rest-to-rest bang-bang slew time for 90° with \tau_{\max} = 0.1 N·m and I = 100 kg·m².
quiz.a: \alpha = 10^{- 3} rad/s² and t = 2\sqrt{(\pi/2)/10^{- 3}} = 79 s.

quiz.q: Explain the Explorer 1 failure using the energy-sink argument.
quiz.a: At fixed angular momentum H, the rotational kinetic energy is H^{2}/(2I). Dissipation lowers the energy, which drives the spin toward the axis of maximum I. Spin about the minimum-inertia axis is therefore unstable with any energy loss, which the flexible antennas provided.

quiz.q: At q = 30 kPa, S = 10 m², C_{N\alpha} = 2.5 /rad and \alpha = 3^{\circ}, the CP lies 8 m ahead of the CG. A 2 MN engine acts 20 m behind the CG. Find the gimbal angle needed to trim.
quiz.a: N = qSC_{N\alpha}\alpha = 30\, 000(10)(2.5)(0.05236) = 39.3 kN and M = 39.3(8) = 314 kN·m. Then \delta = arcsin\left\lbrack 314\, 000/\left( 2 \times 10^{6} \times 20 \right) \right\rbrack = {0.45}^{\circ}.

quiz.q: Where are 3-2-1 Euler angles singular, and why does flight software prefer quaternions?
quiz.a: At pitch \theta = \pm 90^{\circ} the first and third rotation axes align, so yaw and roll become indistinguishable and the rate equations divide by \cos\theta = 0. Quaternions are singularity-free, need no trigonometric functions to propagate, and are easily renormalized.

quiz.q: Find the first slosh frequency for a tank of R = 2 m and h = 4 m at 2g axial acceleration.
quiz.a: \omega^{2} = (1.841 \times 2 \times 9.807/2)\tanh(3.682) = 18.05, so \omega = 4.25 rad/s and f = 0.68 Hz.

chapters.goalsHtml: represent attitude with DCMs, Euler angles and quaternions and know their singularities; model disturbance torques; size reaction wheels and thrusters; determine attitude from vector measurements; design attitude controllers; handle launch-vehicle flexibility and slosh.

chapters.title: Aerospace Structures and Loads

secs.html:
Limit load is the largest load expected in service; ultimate load is limit load times the factor of safety (FS), typically 1.25 for uncrewed and 1.4 for crewed structures, with separate yield factors of 1.0–1.25. The margin of safety is

MS = \frac{\text{allowable}}{FS \times \text{applied}} - 1 \geq 0.

Structures not verified by test carry higher “no-test” factors. Fracture control ensures that undetected flaws cannot grow to failure within the service life (Chapter 20).

Sources: quasi-static accelerations (thrust, maneuvers, typically 4–6g axial and 1–2g lateral at payload interfaces); internal pressure (ullage plus hydrostatic head, Chapter 18); aerodynamic loads (q\alpha, Chapter 31); transients (ignition, shutdown, staging); sine and random vibration; acoustics (liftoff and transonic flight); pyrotechnic shock; and thermal loads. For a thin cylinder of radius R under axial force P and bending moment M, the worst compressive line load is N = P/(2\pi R) + M/\left( \pi R^{2} \right). This is the line load of an equivalent axial load P_{eq} = P + 2M/R. Internal pressure relieves compression and stabilizes thin tanks (pressure stabilization).

Options include monocoque shells; semi-monocoque skin–stringer–frame construction; integrally machined isogrid or orthogrid panels; honeycomb sandwich, whose bending stiffness per unit width is about E_{f}t_{f}h^{2}/2 for thin face sheets of thickness t_{f} separated by h; and composite overwrapped structures. Thin-walled beams carry shear as shear flow, and closed cells carry torsion efficiently (Chapter 20).

Unstiffened cylinders in axial compression buckle far below the classical value \sigma_{cl} = Et/\left( R\sqrt{3\left( 1 - \nu^{2} \right)} \right) because they are highly sensitive to geometric imperfections. The classic design rule (NASA SP-8007) multiplies \sigma_{cl} by the empirical knockdown factor

\gamma = 1 - 0.901\left( 1 - e^{- \phi} \right),\quad\quad\phi = \frac{1}{16}\sqrt{\frac{R}{t}}.

Internal pressure raises the allowable. Stiffened shells must be checked for local skin, panel and general instability modes. Recent work derives less conservative knockdown factors from measured imperfections and high-fidelity nonlinear analysis validated by test.

A unidirectional lamina is orthotropic, described by E_{1}, E_{2}, G_{12} and \nu_{12}. In plane stress its reduced stiffness matrix \mathbf{Q} is rotated to each ply angle. Classical lamination theory relates resultant forces \mathbf{N} and moments \mathbf{M} to midplane strains \mathbf{\varepsilon}^{0} and curvatures \mathbf{\kappa}:

\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{N} \\ \mathbf{M} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{B} \\ \mathbf{B} & \mathbf{D} \end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{\varepsilon}^{0} \\ \mathbf{\kappa} \end{bmatrix}.

Symmetric layups have \mathbf{B} = 0 (no stretch–bend coupling); balanced layups avoid extension–shear coupling; \lbrack 0/ \pm 45/90\rbrack_{s} is quasi-isotropic in-plane. Failure criteria include maximum stress or strain, Tsai–Wu (interactive) and Hashin (separate fiber and matrix modes). Design must also account for impact damage (compression after impact), hot/wet environmental knockdowns, joints and residual thermal stresses. Composite cryogenic tanks must resist matrix microcracking that opens leak paths.

A single-degree-of-freedom system has \omega_{n} = \sqrt{k/m} and a resonant amplification Q = 1/(2\zeta). Multi-degree-of-freedom systems obey \mathbf{M}\ddot{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{C}\dot{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{Kx} = \mathbf{F}. Their modes come from \left( \mathbf{K} - \omega^{2}\mathbf{M} \right)\mathbf{\phi} = 0, and responses are built by modal superposition with 1–3% modal damping typical. Random vibration is specified as an acceleration spectral density (g²/Hz). The RMS acceleration is \sqrt{\int ASD\, df}, and for a single-degree-of-freedom system:

Miles’ equation: G_{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{\pi}{2}f_{n}Q\, ASD\left( f_{n} \right)}. Design to about 3G_{rms} peaks.

Acoustic levels (dB re 20 μPa) excite large panels, analyzed with finite elements at low frequency and statistical energy analysis at high frequency. Pyroshock is specified by a shock response spectrum. Coupled loads analysis combines launcher and payload models through the flight transients. Launch vehicles therefore impose minimum payload frequencies (typically tens of hertz axially and somewhat lower laterally) to avoid dynamic coupling.

Static aeroelasticity: wing torsional divergence and control reversal. Flutter: a dynamic instability in which aerodynamic forces couple two structural modes (bending and torsion) and extract energy from the flow. Panel flutter of thin skins in supersonic flow is analyzed with piston theory, p - p_{\infty} = \rho_{\infty}a_{\infty}\left( \partial w/\partial t + U_{\infty}\partial w/\partial x \right). POGO is a longitudinal instability: a structural mode modulates the pump inlet pressure, which modulates propellant flow and thrust, which drives the mode. It caused severe vibration on Saturn V flights (Apollo 6; the Apollo 13 second-stage center engine). The cure is to detune the feed system, typically with gas-charged accumulators in the propellant lines.

Structures see thermal stresses and thermal buckling, mismatched expansion at joints, and large cryogenic contraction (aluminum shrinks about 0.4% from room temperature to 20 K). Hot hypersonic structures couple heating, deformation and flow (aerothermoelasticity): deformation changes the flow, which changes heating, which changes stiffness (Chapters 42 and 53).

Starting from the principle of virtual work (Chapter 15), interpolate displacements within elements by shape functions. Each element contributes a stiffness matrix; for an axial bar, \mathbf{k}_{e} = (EA/L)\begin{bmatrix} 1 & - 1 \\ - 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. Assemble the global system \mathbf{Ku} = \mathbf{F}, apply boundary conditions, solve, and recover strains and stresses. Element families include bars, beams, shells and solids. Accuracy improves by mesh refinement (h) or higher-order elements (p). Common pitfalls: stress singularities at sharp corners or point loads, poor element shapes, wrong boundary conditions and inconsistent units. Always check results against hand calculations and validate the model by test. Linear buckling eigenvalues overpredict shell strength; use nonlinear analysis with imperfections.

secs.t: Mass estimation and the test program
secs.html: Early mass comes from structural-efficiency indices and historical data, with maturity-based growth allowances. The test program comprises development tests; qualification (static tests to ultimate, sometimes to failure; modal survey; vibration, acoustic and shock at qualification levels above flight); acceptance of every flight article at flight-like levels to screen workmanship; and proof testing of pressure vessels, which also screens flaws for fracture control.

Large aluminum–lithium tanks are joined by friction stir welding, a solid-state process that avoids the porosity and hot cracking of fusion welds. Domes are spin-formed, and integral stiffening is machined or chemically milled. Composite structures use automated fiber placement and, increasingly, out-of-autoclave cures. Additive manufacturing (laser powder-bed fusion of nickel and copper alloys; directed-energy deposition for large nozzles) consolidates injectors, chambers and turbomachinery parts into fewer pieces. Each process needs qualification, because porosity, surface roughness and residual stress change fatigue life and heat transfer; hot isostatic pressing and machining are common remedies. Nondestructive evaluation (radiography and CT, ultrasonics, eddy current, penetrant; thermography and shearography for composites) must reliably find flaws smaller than the critical sizes set by fracture control (Chapter 20). Quality systems add process control, material traceability, first-article inspection, configuration management and foreign-object-debris control.

quiz.q: Find the margin of safety for an allowable of 450 MPa, an applied stress of 300 MPa and FS = 1.4.
quiz.a: MS = 450/(1.4 \times 300) - 1 = 0.071 (positive, so acceptable).

quiz.q: A 2 m radius cylinder carries 1 MN of compression and a 2 MN·m bending moment. Find P_{eq} and the peak compressive line load.
quiz.a: P_{eq} = 1 + 2(2)/2 = 3 MN. Line load = 3 \times 10^{6}/(2\pi \times 2) = 239 kN/m.

quiz.q: Use Miles’ equation for f_{n} = 100 Hz, Q = 10 and ASD = 0.04 g²/Hz.
quiz.a: G_{rms} = \sqrt{(\pi/2)(100)(10)(0.04)} = 7.9 g, so design to roughly 24g peaks.

quiz.q: Find the SP-8007 knockdown factor for R/t = 400.
quiz.a: \phi = 20/16 = 1.25, so \gamma = 1 - 0.901\left( 1 - e^{- 1.25} \right) = 0.357.

quiz.q: Find the classical and knocked-down buckling stresses of an aluminum cylinder (E = 70 GPa, \nu = 0.33, R/t = 400).
quiz.a: \sigma_{cl} = 70\, 000(1/400)/\sqrt{3(1 - 0.109)} = 107 MPa. Knocked down: 0.357 \times 107 = 38.2 MPa.

quiz.q: Explain POGO and its standard remedy.
quiz.a: A closed loop: a structural longitudinal mode changes the pump inlet pressure, which changes propellant flow and thrust, which reinforces the mode. Remedy: accumulators (gas-charged volumes) in the feed lines shift the feed-system resonance away from the structural mode.

quiz.q: Find the natural frequency of a 25 kg component on a mount of stiffness 10^{7} N/m.
quiz.a: f_{n} = \frac{1}{2\pi}\sqrt{10^{7}/25} = 101 Hz.

quiz.q: Why is a linear buckling eigenvalue analysis unconservative for thin cylinders?
quiz.a: Thin shells are extremely imperfection-sensitive: small geometric deviations trigger buckling far below the perfect-shell eigenvalue. Only nonlinear analysis with realistic imperfections, or empirical knockdown, captures this.

quiz.q: Why are friction-stir welds preferred for Al–Li tanks, and why do additively manufactured engine parts need their own qualification?
quiz.a: Friction stir welding joins the metal below its melting point, so it avoids the solidification defects (porosity, hot cracking) and property loss of fusion welds in Al–Li alloys. Additive parts have process-specific porosity, roughness, anisotropy and residual stress that change fatigue strength and heat transfer, so the allowables must be established for the qualified process itself.

chapters.goalsHtml: apply factors and margins of safety; derive launch loads; design thin-walled and stiffened shells against buckling; analyze composite laminates; predict vibration, random, acoustic and shock responses; recognize aeroelastic and POGO instabilities; use the finite element method correctly; plan a structural test program.

chapters.title: Avionics, Navigation, Communications and Flight Software

secs.html: A typical vehicle carries redundant flight computers, an inertial measurement unit (IMU), GNSS receivers, telemetry transmitters and command receivers, power distribution and batteries, actuator controllers, and an independent flight termination system. Data buses include MIL-STD-1553B (1 Mbit/s, deterministic, dual-redundant), SpaceWire, CAN and Ethernet variants (including time-triggered Ethernet). Harness mass and electromagnetic compatibility are significant design drivers.

A gyro measures \widetilde{\mathbf{\omega}} = \left( \mathbf{I} + \mathbf{S} + \mathbf{M} \right)\mathbf{\omega} + \mathbf{b} + \mathbf{n}: scale factor, misalignment, bias and noise (accelerometers analogously). Key specifications are bias stability, angle random walk (gyro white noise, °/√h) and velocity random walk (accelerometer white noise). The Allan variance versus averaging time separates the noise types: slope −1/2 indicates white noise, a flat floor indicates bias instability, and slope +1/2 indicates rate random walk. Bias stability spans from about 0.01°/h (navigation grade) to 1–10°/h (tactical) and 10°/h or worse (consumer MEMS).

The IMU is fixed to the body. Integrate attitude from the gyros (quaternions with coning compensation, Chapter 32); rotate the measured specific force to the navigation frame; add a gravity model; then integrate to velocity and position.

Error growth. An uncorrected accelerometer bias b gives a position error of about \frac{1}{2}bt^{2} at short times. A gyro bias \varepsilon tilts the platform and gives about \frac{1}{6}g\varepsilon t^{3}. Over longer times, horizontal errors oscillate at the Schuler period 2\pi\sqrt{R/g} = 84.4 min instead of growing without bound. The vertical channel is unstable and needs external aiding (altimeter or GNSS).

A pseudorange is \rho = \left| \mathbf{r}_{sat} - \mathbf{r} \right| + c\,\delta t_{r} + \text{errors}. With four or more satellites, least squares (Chapter 10) solves for position and receiver clock offset. The covariance is \sigma^{2}\left( \mathbf{G}^{T}\mathbf{G} \right)^{- 1}, where \mathbf{G} is the geometry matrix; its trace terms define the dilution of precision (PDOP, GDOP). Error sources are ionospheric and tropospheric delay, multipath, and satellite clock and ephemeris errors. Carrier-phase processing reaches centimeters. GNSS is usable well above its own constellation by tracking signal sidelobes. GNSS/INS integration may be loosely coupled (position fixes), tightly coupled (pseudoranges) or ultra-tightly coupled (inside the tracking loops), each implemented as a Kalman filter (Chapter 46).

Safety and scope flag · Export control (scope note)

Concern. High-performance inertial sensors, GNSS receivers able to operate at high speed and altitude, and certain navigation algorithms and data are export-controlled because they enable missile guidance.

Why it is flagged. Even sharing controlled technical data with a foreign person can count as an export (Chapter 54). The principles in this chapter are openly taught; specific controlled hardware and data are not.

Omitted here. Specifications and designs of controlled navigation hardware and software.

Learn it safely. University navigation courses and the open textbooks in Appendix K (Groves; Titterton and Weston); the Institute of Navigation (ION) and its conferences; work with controlled hardware at employers with export-compliance programs.

Link equation (decibels): \frac{E_{b}}{N_{0}} = EIRP - L_{fs} - L_{other} + \frac{G}{T} + 228.6 - 10\log_{10}R_{b}, where 228.6 dB is - 10\log_{10}k and R_{b} is the bit rate. The margin is achieved minus required E_{b}/N_{0}; 3 dB or more is typical.

Required E_{b}/N_{0} depends on modulation and coding: uncoded BPSK needs about 9.6 dB for a bit error rate of 10^{- 5}, while modern LDPC and turbo codes need a few dB. Shannon’s limit, C = B\log_{2}(1 + S/N), implies E_{b}/N_{0} \geq - 1.6 dB. Bands: S (2–4 GHz), X (8–12 GHz), Ka (26–40 GHz). Antenna beamwidth is roughly 70\lambda/D degrees, so high gain needs pointing. Telemetry formats follow CCSDS standards. Tracking uses range and Doppler from ground networks and relay satellites.

Flight software runs on a real-time operating system with deterministic scheduling. Under rate-monotonic priority (faster tasks get higher priority), n periodic tasks are guaranteed schedulable if CPU utilization stays below n\left( 2^{1/n} - 1 \right), about 69% for large n. Mode logic is written as explicit state machines. Fault detection, isolation and recovery (FDIR) uses watchdog timers and safe modes. Redundancy may be dual (detects a fault), triple with voting (masks one fault), or Byzantine-tolerant (3f + 1 units for f arbitrary faults).

Common-mode failure. Identical redundant units running identical software fail together. On Ariane 5’s first flight (1996), both inertial reference units ran reused software that hit the same unprotected numeric overflow, because the new trajectory produced values the old vehicle never had. Requirements must be re-validated whenever software is reused.

Assurance standards (NASA NPR 7150.2; DO-178C, which requires MC/DC structural coverage at its highest level) define unit, integration and hardware-in-the-loop testing, static analysis, configuration control and, increasingly, formal methods.

Effects include total ionizing dose (krad(Si)) and displacement damage, which degrade parts gradually, and single-event effects: upsets (bit flips), latch-up (potentially destructive; requires current limiting and power cycling), transients and functional interrupts. The radiation comes from the trapped belts (including the South Atlantic Anomaly), solar particle events and galactic cosmic rays. Mitigation: radiation-hardened parts, error-detecting-and-correcting memory with scrubbing, triple modular redundancy in FPGAs, shielding, and latch-up protection. Screened commercial parts serve short or low-orbit missions.

Plasma around an entering vehicle blocks radio frequencies below the plasma frequency (Chapter 48), so navigation through blackout relies on inertial sensors alone. RF windows (silica-based composites, silicon nitride) must survive heating. Antennas are placed where electron density is lowest, often in the wake. Electronics must be thermally isolated and survive intense boundary-layer-induced vibration.

quiz.q: Find E_{b}/N_{0} for EIRP = 40 dBW, path loss 200 dB, other losses 3 dB, G/T = 20 dB/K and R_{b} = 1 Mbit/s.
Find the gain of a 1 m dish at 8.4 GHz with 60% efficiency.
quiz.a: \lambda = 0.0357 m and G = 0.6(\pi/0.0357)^{2} = 4650, i.e. 36.7 dBi.

quiz.q: Find the Shannon capacity for B = 1 MHz and S/N = 15.
quiz.a: C = 10^{6}\log_{2}(16) = 4 Mbit/s.

quiz.q: An uncorrected gyro bias of 1°/h acts for 10 minutes. Find the attitude error.
quiz.a: 1^{\circ}/h \times (1/6)\ h = {0.17}^{\circ}.

quiz.q: An uncorrected 1 mg accelerometer bias acts for 60 s. Find the position error.
quiz.a: \frac{1}{2}\left( 9.807 \times 10^{- 3} \right)\left( 60^{2} \right) = 17.7 m.

quiz.q: What faults can triple modular redundancy not mask?
quiz.a: Common-mode faults (identical design or software errors, shared power or environment) and faults that corrupt the voter itself.

quiz.q: A receiver has a noise floor of −114 dBm and receives −100 dBm. Find the SNR.
quiz.a: - 100 - ( - 114) = 14 dB.

quiz.q: Compute the Schuler period.
quiz.a: 2\pi\sqrt{6.371 \times 10^{6}/9.807} = 5064 s = 84.4 min.

chapters.goalsHtml: describe avionics architectures and data buses; model inertial-sensor errors; mechanize strapdown navigation and understand its error growth; position with GNSS and DOP; close a communication link budget; design dependable real-time flight software; mitigate radiation effects; account for the special conditions of entry and hypersonic flight.

chapters.title: Systems Engineering, Reliability and Safety

secs.html: Systems engineering ensures that the integrated system meets the stakeholders’ needs throughout its life. NASA’s phases: Pre-A (concept studies), A (concept and technology development), B (preliminary design), C (final design and fabrication), D (assembly, integration, test and launch), E (operations), F (closeout). Major reviews gate progress: Mission Concept, System Requirements, System Definition, Preliminary Design (PDR), Critical Design (CDR), System Integration, Test Readiness, Operational Readiness and Flight Readiness. The V-model pairs each level of decomposition on the way down with a level of integration and verification on the way up.

Requirements form a hierarchy (mission, system, subsystem, component) and are written as “shall” statements. Each must be necessary, unambiguous, verifiable, feasible, singular and traceable to a parent need, with a verification method assigned. Interfaces are defined in interface control documents. Unresolved values (TBD/TBR) are tracked and burned down. Uncontrolled requirement growth is a leading cause of cost overruns.

Decompose functions, map them to physical elements and capture interactions (N² diagrams, or SysML models in model-based systems engineering, Chapter 50). A trade study defines alternatives, figures of merit, weights and scores. Always test the sensitivity of the answer to the weights, discard dominated options, and record the rationale for the decision.

Budgets cover mass, power, Δv and propellant, link, pointing, data, thermal and cost. Mass-growth allowances shrink as maturity rises, from roughly 20–30% at concept to a few percent at CDR. Define margin explicitly: “25% margin” may mean 25% of the current best estimate or 25% of the allowable, and confusing the two has caused real problems.

Failure rates follow a bathtub curve: infant mortality (screened by burn-in and acceptance testing), a useful life with constant \lambda, then wear-out. Analysis tools:

  • FMEA/FMECA (bottom-up): for each failure mode of each part, record its effect, severity, likelihood and detectability.
  • Fault tree analysis (top-down): the undesired top event decomposes through AND/OR gates down to basic events. For independent rare events, P\left( \text{OR} \right) \approx \sum P_{i} and P\left( \text{AND} \right) = \prod P_{i}; minimal cut sets identify the critical combinations.
  • Probabilistic risk assessment combines event trees and fault trees into quantitative risk.

Common-cause failures defeat redundancy and are modeled explicitly (for example with a β-factor). Single-point failures need special justification. Demonstrated reliability from a few flights is statistically weak; estimate it with Bayesian methods (Chapter 13).

Verification asks “did we build it right?” (does it meet its requirements?); validation asks “did we build the right thing?” (does it meet the need?). Methods are test, analysis with validated models, inspection and demonstration. Prefer test for critical functions: “test like you fly, fly like you test.” Qualification demonstrates design margin, acceptance screens workmanship, and protoflight combines the two on flight hardware. The environmental campaign covers vibration, acoustics, shock, thermal vacuum and EMI/EMC, followed by end-to-end system tests. Every anomaly is investigated to root cause and closed.

TRL Meaning
1–2 Basic principles observed; concept formulated
3 Analytical or experimental proof of concept
4 Component validated in the laboratory
5 Component validated in a relevant environment
6 System or subsystem prototype demonstrated in a relevant environment
7 Prototype demonstrated in the operational (space) environment
8 Actual system completed and flight qualified
9 Actual system flight proven in operation

Risk is scored as likelihood × consequence (for example on a 5 × 5 matrix) and reduced by planned mitigation with a “burn-down” schedule. Immature technology (below TRL 6 at PDR) is the classic root of cost and schedule overruns.

secs.t: Safety engineering and the lessons of failure
secs.html:
Hazard analysis proceeds from a preliminary hazard list through system hazard analyses. Controls follow a hierarchy: eliminate the hazard; design for minimum hazard; add safety devices; add warnings; rely on procedures and training last. Crewed systems typically require two-fault tolerance against catastrophic hazards.

Event Year Lesson
Apollo 1 fire 1967 Pure oxygen at high pressure, flammable materials and an inward-opening hatch: test hazards are flight hazards
Challenger 1986 O-ring erosion had been seen and gradually accepted (normalization of deviance); cold-temperature data and engineering concerns were overridden
Ariane 5, flight 501 1996 Reused software in a new flight envelope; unhandled overflow in redundant units
Mars Climate Orbiter 1999 Units mismatch across an interface
Mars Polar Lander 1999 Likely spurious touchdown signal from leg deployment shut the engine down early
Columbia 2003 Foam strike damaged the wing leading edge; organizational culture discounted the risk
Genesis 2004 Deceleration sensors installed in the wrong orientation; parachute did not deploy

Parametric cost models relate cost to mass, complexity and heritage. Learning curves: the cost of the nth unit is T_{1}n^{\log_{2}LC}; with a 90% learning curve, each doubling of quantity cuts unit cost by 10%. Schedules are managed through the critical path; earned-value metrics (cost and schedule performance indices) track progress. Reusability changes the economics through refurbishment cost and flight rate.

quiz.q: Top event = A OR (B AND C), with independent probabilities 10^{- 3}, 10^{- 2} and 2 \times 10^{- 2}. Find P\left( \text{top} \right).
quiz.a: 10^{- 3} + \left( 10^{- 2} \right)\left( 2 \times 10^{- 2} \right) - \left( 10^{- 3} \right)\left( 2 \times 10^{- 4} \right) = 1.20 \times 10^{- 3}.

quiz.q: With a 90% learning curve, what does the 8th unit cost relative to the first?
A component has an MTBF of 10 000 h. Find its reliability over a 1000 h mission.
The current best estimate of mass is 800 kg and the allowable is 1000 kg. State the margin both ways.
quiz.a: 200 kg is 25% of the current best estimate, or 20% of the allowable. Always state the basis.

quiz.q: Explain “normalization of deviance” using Challenger.
quiz.a: Repeated O-ring erosion without failure was gradually reinterpreted as acceptable, so the boundary of acceptable risk drifted until a cold launch exceeded the real margin.

quiz.q: With a uniform prior, a vehicle has 20 successes in 20 flights. Find the posterior mean failure probability (Laplace’s rule).
quiz.a: (0 + 1)/(20 + 2) = 0.045: twenty clean flights still leave a several-percent failure estimate.

quiz.q: What is wrong with the requirement “The system shall be lightweight”? Rewrite it.
quiz.a: “Lightweight” is not verifiable. Better: “The dry mass of the system shall not exceed 1200 kg, verified by measurement.”

quiz.q: Distinguish verification from validation for a heat-shield design.
quiz.a: Verification: the shield meets its specified heat-flux and heat-load capability and bondline temperature limit, shown by arc-jet test and analysis. Validation: the specification itself was right, i.e. the shield protects the vehicle on the real entry, confirmed by flight data or a representative end-to-end test.

chapters.goalsHtml: run a project through its life-cycle phases and reviews; write verifiable requirements; conduct trade studies; manage budgets and margins; perform FMEA and fault-tree analysis; plan verification and validation; assess technology readiness and risk; learn from the major accidents; estimate cost.

chapters.title: Advanced Gas Dynamics: Governing Equations, Characteristics, Unsteady Waves and Similarity

secs.t: The governing equations in conservation form
secs.html:
With conserved variables \mathbf{U} = \left\lbrack \rho,\ \rho\mathbf{u},\ \rho E \right\rbrack^{T}, total energy E = e + \frac{1}{2}\left| \mathbf{u} \right|^{2} and total enthalpy H = E + p/\rho:

\frac{\partial\mathbf{U}}{\partial t} + \nabla \cdot \left( \mathbf{F}_{inv} - \mathbf{F}_{vis} \right) = \mathbf{S}, with \mathbf{F}_{inv} = \left\lbrack \rho\mathbf{u},\ \rho\mathbf{uu} + p\mathbf{I},\ \rho H\mathbf{u} \right\rbrack and \mathbf{F}_{vis} = \left\lbrack 0,\ \mathbf{\tau},\ \mathbf{\tau} \cdot \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{q} \right\rbrack, closed by \mathbf{\tau} (Newtonian, Chapter 18), \mathbf{q} = - k\nabla T (plus species diffusion in mixtures) and an equation of state. Dropping the viscous terms gives the Euler equations.

The conservation form matters. Its weak (integral) solutions automatically satisfy the Rankine–Hugoniot jump conditions across shocks, so numerical schemes built on it capture shocks at the correct speed and strength (Chapter 45).

Combining the momentum equation with the Gibbs relation gives Crocco’s theorem, for steady inviscid flow without body forces:

T abla s = abla h_{0} - \mathbf{u} imes \mathbf{\omega}.

Behind a curved shock in a uniform free stream (h_{0} uniform), different streamlines cross the shock at different angles and gain different entropy. The resulting entropy gradients require vorticity. This is the origin of the entropy layer over blunt hypersonic bodies (Chapter 38). The vorticity transport equation,

rac{D\mathbf{\omega}}{Dt} = \left( \mathbf{\omega} \cdot abla ight)\mathbf{u} - \mathbf{\omega}\left( abla \cdot \mathbf{u} ight) + rac{ abla ho imes abla p}{ ho^{2}} + u abla^{2}\mathbf{\omega},

shows the stretching, dilatation, baroclinic (misaligned density and pressure gradients) and diffusion mechanisms. The baroclinic term is how shocks crossing density interfaces generate mixing (Richtmyer–Meshkov instability), which is relevant to scramjet mixing and shock-tube test gas.

secs.t: One-dimensional unsteady flow and Riemann invariants
secs.html:
The 1-D isentropic Euler equations are hyperbolic with characteristic speeds u and u \pm a.

Riemann invariants: J_{\pm} = u \pm \frac{2a}{\gamma - 1} are constant along the characteristics dx/dt = u \pm a. In a simple wave, one invariant is uniform everywhere. A gas at rest with sound speed a_{0} can expand at most to the escape speed u_{\max} = 2a_{0}/(\gamma - 1) (expansion into vacuum).

Compression characteristics converge and steepen into shocks, the mechanism of shock formation. Expansion characteristics diverge into fans. In a centered rarefaction moving into gas at rest, u varies linearly with x/t.

A shock moving at speed W into gas at rest is a stationary shock with M_{1} = M_{s} = W/a_{1} in its own frame. The gas behind it moves at

u_{p} = \frac{2a_{1}}{\gamma + 1}\left( M_{s} - \frac{1}{M_{s}} \right).

This is the piston problem: a piston pushed impulsively at u_{p} drives a shock at M_{s}. Shocks reflect from closed ends, bringing the gas to rest at still higher pressure and temperature.

A diaphragm separates high-pressure driver gas (state 4) from low-pressure driven test gas (state 1). When it bursts, a shock runs into the test gas, an expansion fan runs into the driver, and a contact surface separates the two. Matching pressure and velocity across the contact gives the shock-tube equation:

\frac{p_{4}}{p_{1}} = \frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}}\left\lbrack 1 - \frac{\left( \gamma_{4} - 1 \right)\left( a_{1}/a_{4} \right)\left( p_{2}/p_{1} - 1 \right)}{\sqrt{2\gamma_{1}\left\lbrack 2\gamma_{1} + \left( \gamma_{1} + 1 \right)\left( p_{2}/p_{1} - 1 \right) \right\rbrack}} \right\rbrack^{- 2\gamma_{4}/\left( \gamma_{4} - 1 \right)}.

Strong shocks need a high driver sound speed a_{4}: light, hot gases such as helium or hydrogen, heated or combustion-driven drivers, or free-piston compression (Stalker tubes). Test time is limited by the arrival of the contact surface and of reflected waves. In tailored-interface operation the reflected shock passes through the contact without generating new waves, extending test time. The reflected-shock tunnel expands the stagnant, high-enthalpy gas behind the reflected shock (state 5) through a nozzle. This is the workhorse facility of high-enthalpy research (Chapter 49).

The method of characteristics (Chapter 24) extends to rotational and nonequilibrium flows with modified compatibility relations. Shock fitting tracks shocks as sharp boundaries with exact jump conditions; it is accurate but complex in topology. It contrasts with the shock capturing used by most CFD (Chapter 45).

Writing \mathbf{u} = U_{\infty}\widehat{\mathbf{x}} + \nabla\phi with small perturbations gives the linearized potential equation \left( 1 - M_{\infty}^{2} \right)\phi_{xx} + \phi_{yy} + \phi_{zz} = 0: elliptic for subsonic and hyperbolic for supersonic flow (Chapters 12 and 25). Near M_{\infty} = 1 the neglected nonlinear term is essential. The transonic small-disturbance equation

\left\lbrack 1 - M_{\infty}^{2} - (\gamma + 1)M_{\infty}^{2}\frac{\phi_{x}}{U_{\infty}} \right\rbrack\phi_{xx} + \phi_{yy} = 0

is of mixed type and captures embedded shocks. Linear theory also fails at high Mach number, because perturbations are no longer small compared with the free-stream sound speed.

For a slender body of thickness ratio \tau at M_{\infty} \gg 1, the streamwise velocity perturbation is O\left( \tau^{2}U_{\infty} \right) while the transverse one is O\left( \tau U_{\infty} \right). The governing equations then depend on M_{\infty} and \tau only through their product:

Hypersonic similarity parameter K = M_{\infty}\tau. Affine slender bodies with the same K and \gamma have the same p/p_{\infty} distribution, and C_{p}/\tau^{2} is a function of K alone. Equivalence principle (Hayes): steady hypersonic flow past a slender body is equivalent to unsteady flow in each cross-flow plane, driven by the body acting as an expanding piston. This leads to blast-wave theory (Chapter 38).

Example: a wedge with \tau = 0.1 at M = 10 and one with \tau = 0.05 at M = 20 (both K = 1) have exact pressure ratios of 3.47 and 3.47.

At high temperature the caloric equation e = c_{v}T and \gamma = \text{const} fail. The thermodynamic state needs h\left( T,p,\text{composition} \right), and acoustic waves propagate at the frozen sound speed or the equilibrium sound speed (lower), depending on whether chemistry keeps pace with the wave. Chapters 39 and 40 build this physics.

quiz.q: Gas at rest has a = 340 m/s (\gamma = 1.4). A piston withdraws at 100 m/s. Find the sound speed in the expanded gas next to the piston, and the maximum possible escape speed.
quiz.a: J_{+} is constant from the undisturbed gas: 0 + 2(340)/0.4 = u + 2a/0.4. With u = - 100 m/s, a = 340 - 0.2(100) = 320 m/s. Maximum escape speed = 2(340)/0.4 = 1700 m/s.

quiz.q: A shock with M_{s} = 2 moves into air at 300 K. Find p_{2}/p_{1}, T_{2}/T_{1} and the gas velocity behind it.
quiz.a: p_{2}/p_{1} = 4.50 and T_{2}/T_{1} = 1.688. a_{1} = 347.2 m/s, so u_{p} = (2 \times 347.2/2.4)(2 - 0.5) = 434 m/s.

quiz.q: What diaphragm pressure ratio p_{4}/p_{1} produces M_{s} = 2 with a helium driver at 300 K (a_{4} = 1019 m/s)? Compare with an air driver at 300 K.
quiz.a: Helium: p_{4}/p_{1} = 9.7. Air: p_{4}/p_{1} = 33.7. The light driver is about 3.5 times more effective.

quiz.q: Verify hypersonic similarity: find p_{2}/p_{1} for a wedge with \tan\theta = 0.1 at M = 10 and with \tan\theta = 0.05 at M = 20.
quiz.a: \theta = {5.71}^{\circ} at M = 10 gives p_{2}/p_{1} = 3.47; \theta = {2.86}^{\circ} at M = 20 gives 3.47. Equal, as similarity (K = 1) predicts.

quiz.q: Use Crocco’s theorem to explain why the flow behind a curved bow shock is rotational.
quiz.a: h_{0} is uniform, so T abla s = - \mathbf{u} imes \mathbf{\omega}. A curved shock gives different entropy jumps on different streamlines, so abla s eq 0 and therefore \mathbf{\omega} eq 0.

quiz.q: Explain, using domains of dependence, why a supersonic disturbance cannot propagate upstream.
quiz.a: Signals travel at u \pm a. When u > a both families move downstream, so a point is influenced only by its upstream Mach cone and can influence only the downstream cone.

quiz.q: A piston is pushed impulsively into still air at 434 m/s. What shock Mach number results (air at 300 K)?
quiz.a: From Question 2, u_{p} = 434 m/s corresponds to M_{s} = 2.

quiz.q: Why must shock-capturing schemes be written in conservation form?
quiz.a: Non-conservative forms admit discontinuous solutions with wrong jump conditions. Only the conservation form guarantees that converged weak solutions satisfy Rankine–Hugoniot (Lax–Wendroff theorem).

chapters.goalsHtml: write the compressible Navier–Stokes equations in conservation form; use Crocco’s theorem; solve 1-D unsteady problems with Riemann invariants; analyze moving shocks and shock tubes; understand linearized, transonic and hypersonic small-disturbance theories and the hypersonic similarity parameter.

chapters.title: Viscous Flow: Boundary Layers, Turbulence and Transition

secs.html:
In a layer of thickness \delta \sim L\, Re^{- 1/2}, an order-of-magnitude analysis of Navier–Stokes leaves (2-D, steady, incompressible)

uu_{x} + vu_{y} = - \frac{1}{\rho}p_{x} + \nu u_{yy},\quad\quad p_{y} = 0,\quad\quad u_{x} + v_{y} = 0.

The pressure is impressed by the outer inviscid flow, and the equations are parabolic: they march downstream. Integral thicknesses: displacement \delta^{*} = \int_{0}^{\infty}\left( 1 - \frac{\rho u}{\rho_{e}u_{e}} \right)dy; momentum \theta = \int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\rho u}{\rho_{e}u_{e}}\left( 1 - \frac{u}{u_{e}} \right)dy; shape factor H = \delta^{*}/\theta (2.59 for Blasius, about 1.3–1.4 turbulent, rising toward separation). The von Kármán momentum integral holds for any boundary layer:

\frac{d\theta}{dx} + (2 + H)\frac{\theta}{u_{e}}\frac{du_{e}}{dx} = \frac{c_{f}}{2}.

With \eta = y\sqrt{U/(\nu x)} and stream function \psi = \sqrt{\nu Ux}f(\eta), the flat-plate (Blasius) problem becomes f''' + \frac{1}{2}ff'' = 0, with f(0) = f'(0) = 0 and f'(\infty) = 1, giving the results of Chapter 18. Falkner–Skan solutions treat u_{e} \propto x^{m}; the case m = 1 is the stagnation-point flow used in heating theory (Chapter 41).

secs.t: Compressible boundary layers and aerodynamic heating
secs.html:
Viscous dissipation heats the layer. An insulated wall reaches the adiabatic wall (recovery) temperature:

T_{aw} = T_{e}\left( 1 + r\frac{\gamma - 1}{2}M_{e}^{2} \right), with recovery factor r \approx Pr^{1/2} (laminar, 0.84 for air) or Pr^{1/3} (turbulent, 0.89). Heat flux to a wall at T_{w}: q_{w} = St\,\rho_{e}u_{e}c_{p}\left( T_{aw} - T_{w} \right), with St from the Reynolds analogy (Chapter 19). Reference temperature method (Eckert, as given by Anderson for γ = 1.4): evaluate incompressible c_{f} and St formulas with properties at T^{*} = T_{e}\left\lbrack 1 + 0.032M_{e}^{2} + 0.58\left( T_{w}/T_{e} - 1 \right) \right\rbrack.

For \Pr = 1 and zero pressure gradient, temperature and velocity are linked by the Crocco–Busemann relation. In the general (Walz) form:

\frac{T}{T_{e}} = \frac{T_{w}}{T_{e}} + \frac{T_{aw} - T_{w}}{T_{e}}\frac{u}{u_{e}} - r\frac{\gamma - 1}{2}M_{e}^{2}\left( \frac{u}{u_{e}} \right)^{2}.

Hypersonic vehicles usually have cold walls (T_{w} \ll T_{aw}): the dense near-wall gas thins the boundary layer and raises the heat flux. Compressibility transformations (Howarth–Dorodnitsyn for laminar flow; Van Driest II for turbulent skin friction) map compressible layers to incompressible ones.

Compressible turbulence is averaged with density weighting (Favre averaging, \widetilde{u} = \overline{\rho u}/\bar{\rho}), producing Reynolds stresses - \bar{\rho}\widetilde{u_{i}''u_{j}''} and turbulent heat fluxes. Morkovin’s hypothesis: for moderate Mach numbers (M_{e} \lesssim 5), compressibility affects wall turbulence mainly through mean property variations. The law of the wall, with u^{+} = u/u_{\tau}, y^{+} = yu_{\tau}/\nu_{w} and u_{\tau} = \sqrt{\tau_{w}/\rho_{w}}:

u^{+} = y^{+}\ \left( y^{+} < 5 \right),\quad\quad u^{+} = \frac{1}{\kappa}\ln y^{+} + B\ \left( y^{+} \gtrsim 30 \right),\quad\quad\kappa = 0.41,\ B \approx 5.0.

For compressible flow it holds in Van Driest-transformed velocity, u_{VD}^{+} = \int_{0}^{u^{+}}\sqrt{\rho/\rho_{w}}\, du^{+}.

Approach Examples Strengths Weaknesses in hypersonics
Algebraic eddy viscosity Baldwin–Lomax, Cebeci–Smith Cheap No history effects; poor in separation
One-equation Spalart–Allmaras Robust; aerospace standard for attached flow Separation and heat flux in interactions
Two-equation k–ε, Wilcox k–ω, Menter SST Broad applicability Shock-unsteadiness, compressibility and heat-transfer errors
Reynolds-stress SSG/LRR Anisotropy, curvature Cost, robustness
LES / hybrid RANS–LES Dynamic Smagorinsky; DES/DDES/IDDES Resolve large eddies and unsteadiness Cost; near-wall modeling; inflow generation
DNS — No model Cost grows as roughly Re^{37/14}

Heat transfer additionally requires a turbulent Prandtl number (Pr_{t} \approx 0.85–0.9), itself a source of uncertainty. Grid-point estimates for a boundary layer (Choi and Moin): wall-resolved LES \sim Re_{L}^{13/7}, wall-modeled LES \sim Re_{L}, DNS \sim Re_{L}^{37/14}. RANS models typically mispredict peak heating and separation length in shock–boundary-layer interactions by tens of percent, an open problem (Chapter 53).

Transition decides whether a vehicle sees laminar or turbulent heating, a factor of three to eight (Chapter 41). Linear stability theory superposes normal modes \widehat{q}(y)\exp\left\lbrack i(\alpha x + \beta z - \omega t) \right\rbrack on the laminar profile. Incompressible flow obeys the Orr–Sommerfeld equation. Rayleigh’s criterion: inviscid instability requires an inflection point in u(y); for compressible flow, a generalized inflection point where (\rho u')' = 0 (Lees–Lin).

Instability mechanisms at high speed. First mode: vortical, most unstable as oblique waves at supersonic speeds; stabilized by wall cooling. Mack second mode: acoustic waves trapped between the wall and the relative sonic line; dominant for M_{e} \gtrsim 4; wavelength about twice the boundary-layer thickness, so f \approx u_{e}/(2\delta) (often 100 kHz–1 MHz); destabilized by wall cooling. Crossflow: swept or three-dimensional flows such as cones at incidence. Görtler: concave curvature. Attachment-line contamination: swept leading edges. Entropy-layer instabilities: blunt bodies.

Receptivity is how external disturbances (free-stream acoustic noise, vorticity, roughness, particles) seed the instabilities. Transient (non-modal) growth can bypass modal paths. The e^N method integrates linear growth rates to an amplification N = ln\left( A/A_{0} \right) and correlates transition with a critical N. Values of about 9–10 suit quiet, flight-like environments; conventional noisy wind tunnels give much lower values. Quiet tunnels (for example the Boeing/AFOSR Mach-6 Quiet Tunnel at Purdue) keep their walls laminar to reproduce flight-like noise levels. Parabolized stability equations add non-parallel and nonlinear effects. Isolated roughness trips transition when the roughness Reynolds number Re_{kk} = \rho_{k}u_{k}k/\mu_{k} exceeds a critical value of order hundreds. RANS-compatible transition models (amplification-factor transport, γ–Re_θ) are calibrated, not predictive, outside their data.

The pressure rise needed to separate a boundary layer depends mainly on the conditions at the start of the interaction, not on what caused it (free interaction, Chapman). A compression ramp or impinging shock above a critical strength separates the layer. A separation bubble forms with a λ-shock structure, and heating peaks at reattachment, roughly scaling as q_{pk}/q_{0} \approx \left( p_{pk}/p_{0} \right)^{0.8\text{–}0.85} for turbulent flow. Turbulent interactions also show low-frequency unsteadiness that loads structures. SWBLI governs control-surface heating, inlet behavior (Chapter 44) and much of the remaining uncertainty in vehicle design.

At high M_{\infty} and low Re, the thick, hot boundary layer displaces the outer flow enough to raise the surface pressure. The governing parameter is

\bar{\chi} = M_{\infty}^{3}\sqrt{\frac{C}{Re_{x}}},\quad\quad C = \frac{\rho_{w}\mu_{w}}{\rho_{\infty}\mu_{\infty}}\ \text{(Chapman–Rubesin)}.

For an insulated flat plate (γ = 1.4): weak interaction (\bar{\chi} \lesssim 3), p/p_{\infty} \approx 1 + 0.31\bar{\chi} + 0.05{\bar{\chi}}^{2}; strong interaction (\bar{\chi} \gtrsim 3), p/p_{\infty} \approx 0.514\bar{\chi} + 0.759. The rarefaction parameter \bar{V} = M_{\infty}\sqrt{C/Re_{x}} governs skin friction and heating corrections. Very near the leading edge, the shock and boundary layer merge, and the flow becomes rarefied (Chapter 40).

quiz.q: A turbulent boundary layer has M_{e} = 6, T_{e} = 220 K and \Pr = 0.71. Find T_{aw} and compare with T_{0}.
quiz.a: r = {0.71}^{1/3} = 0.892. T_{aw} = 220(1 + 0.892 \times 0.2 \times 36) = 1633 K, versus T_{0} = 220(8.2) = 1804 K. Recovery is about 90% of the stagnation temperature rise.

quiz.q: Estimate the second-mode frequency for u_{e} = 1000 m/s and \delta = 5 mm.
quiz.a: f \approx 1000/(2 \times 0.005) = 100 kHz.

quiz.q: Find \bar{\chi} and p/p_{\infty} for M_{\infty} = 10, Re_{x} = 10^{6} and C = 1.
quiz.a: \bar{\chi} = 1000/\sqrt{10^{6}} = 1 (weak), so p/p_{\infty} \approx 1 + 0.31 + 0.05 = 1.36.

quiz.q: Find u^{+} at y^{+} = 100.
For a flat plate at Re_{x} = 10^{7} (x = 1 m), estimate the first-cell height giving y^{+} = 1, using c_{f} = 0.0592Re_{x}^{- 0.2}.
quiz.a: c_{f} = 2.36 \times 10^{- 3}, so u_{\tau} = U\sqrt{c_{f}/2} = 0.0343U. Then \Delta y = \nu/u_{\tau} = x/\left( Re_{x} \times 0.0343 \right) = 2.9 μm.

quiz.q: Why does cooling the wall stabilize the first mode but destabilize the second mode?
quiz.a: The first mode is a vortical instability tied to the generalized inflection point, which cooling removes. The second mode is acoustic, trapped in the region between the wall and the relative sonic line; cooling raises near-wall density and enlarges that region, amplifying it.

quiz.q: Write the wall heat flux in terms of c_{f} using the Reynolds analogy, and state when it fails.
quiz.a: q_{w} = \frac{c_{f}}{2}Pr^{- 2/3}\rho_{e}u_{e}c_{p}\left( T_{aw} - T_{w} \right). It fails in separated flow (where c_{f} \rightarrow 0 but heating persists), in strong pressure gradients, in reacting flows with diffusion, and in non-equilibrium turbulence.

quiz.q: What is the e^N method, and why must N be calibrated to the disturbance environment?
quiz.a: Transition is assumed when the integrated linear amplification N of the most-amplified disturbance reaches a critical value. That value depends on the initial disturbance amplitude, which is set by receptivity to the environment, so it differs between noisy tunnels, quiet tunnels and flight.

chapters.goalsHtml: derive and solve boundary-layer equations, including compressible ones; compute recovery temperatures and heating with reference-temperature methods; master the law of the wall and turbulence-model families; explain modal transition mechanisms at high speed (including the Mack mode) and e^N prediction; analyze shock–boundary-layer interaction and hypersonic viscous interaction.

chapters.title: Hypersonic Aerodynamics: Inviscid Theory

secs.html:
Hypersonic flow is defined not by a Mach number but by five phenomena that become important together, roughly above Mach 5:

  1. Thin shock layers: the shock lies close to the body, and at low Reynolds number it merges with the boundary layer.
  2. Entropy layers: curved shocks around blunt noses create layers of strong entropy gradient and vorticity that wash over the downstream body (Chapter 36).
  3. Viscous interaction: thick, hot boundary layers displace the outer flow (Chapter 37).
  4. High-temperature effects: vibrational excitation, dissociation, ionization, chemical nonequilibrium and radiation (Chapters 39–41).
  5. Low-density effects: slip and rarefaction at high altitude (Chapter 40).

As M_{\infty} \rightarrow \infty the oblique-shock relations simplify:

\frac{p_{2}}{p_{\infty}} \rightarrow \frac{2\gamma}{\gamma + 1}M_{\infty}^{2}\sin^{2}\beta, \quad\frac{\rho_{2}}{\rho_{\infty}} \rightarrow \frac{\gamma + 1}{\gamma - 1}, \quad C_{p} \rightarrow \frac{4}{\gamma + 1}\sin^{2}\beta. For a thin wedge with M_{\infty}\theta \gg 1: \beta \approx \frac{\gamma + 1}{2}\theta, so the shock lies only 20% beyond the surface for γ = 1.4. In general, C_{p}/\tau^{2} = \frac{\gamma + 1}{2} + \sqrt{\left( \frac{\gamma + 1}{2} \right)^{2} + \frac{4}{K^{2}}} with K = M_{\infty}\tau (hypersonic small-disturbance wedge result).

Newton modeled the flow as particles that lose their normal momentum on striking the surface, giving C_{p} = 2\sin^{2}\theta, where \theta is the angle between the free stream and the local surface. The theory becomes exact as M_{\infty} \rightarrow \infty and \gamma \rightarrow 1, when the shock layer becomes infinitely thin. Modified Newtonian (Lees) replaces 2 with the stagnation value behind a normal shock:

C_{p} = C_{p,\max}\sin^{2}\theta,\quad\quad C_{p,\max} = \frac{p_{02} - p_{\infty}}{q_{\infty}} \rightarrow 1.839\ \left( \gamma = 1.4,\ M_{\infty} \rightarrow \infty \right).

Surfaces hidden from the flow (“shadow”) get C_{p} \approx 0. The Newton–Busemann correction subtracts centrifugal effects on curved surfaces. Classic results, with C_{p,\max} = 2:

  • Flat plate at angle of attack \alpha: C_{N} = 2\sin^{2}\alpha, C_{L} = 2\sin^{2}\alpha\cos\alpha, C_{D} = 2\sin^{3}\alpha, L/D = cot\alpha. Lift is maximal at \alpha = {54.7}^{\circ}.
  • Sphere: C_{D} = 1 on the frontal area (about 0.92 with modified Newtonian).
  • Cone of half-angle \theta_{c} at zero incidence: C_{D} = 2\sin^{2}\theta_{c}, with the normal-force center of pressure at two-thirds of the length from the apex.

Newtonian theory is best for blunt, high-inclination surfaces and poor for slender shapes at moderate K, where tangent-wedge and tangent-cone methods are better.

Engineering codes assign each panel a pressure from its local inclination: the tangent-wedge method (2-D, exact oblique-shock pressure at the local angle), the tangent-cone method (axisymmetric, conical-flow pressure, Appendix F), shock-expansion theory, or modified Newtonian on blunt regions. These methods give forces and moments in milliseconds and remain essential for conceptual design, trajectory optimization and early database generation, alongside CFD.

As M_{\infty} \rightarrow \infty (for a calorically perfect gas), p/p_{\infty} grows as M_{\infty}^{2}, but the coefficients C_{p}, C_{L}, C_{D} and the shock shape approach limits independent of M_{\infty} (Oswatitsch). This is visible above about Mach 10 for blunt bodies. It justifies extrapolating coefficients measured at Mach 6–10, but only for the perfect-gas part of the problem: real-gas effects break the independence (Chapter 43).

A strong explosion of energy E in a gas of density \rho_{\infty} drives a self-similar shock, R(t) \propto \left( E/\rho_{\infty} \right)^{1/(j + 3)}t^{2/(j + 3)}, with j = 0 (planar), 1 (cylindrical) or 2 (spherical). By the equivalence principle (Chapter 36), the nose drag of a blunt-nosed slender body acts as the “explosion” in each cross-flow plane. For γ = 1.4:

Body Induced surface pressure Shock shape
Blunt flat plate (planar blast) p/p_{\infty} = 0.121M_{\infty}^{2}C_{D}^{2/3}(x/d)^{- 2/3} y/d = 0.774C_{D}^{1/3}(x/d)^{2/3}
Blunt cylinder (cylindrical blast) p/p_{\infty} = 0.067M_{\infty}^{2}C_{D}^{1/2}(x/d)^{- 1} r/d = 0.795C_{D}^{1/4}(x/d)^{1/2}

These hold where the induced pressure greatly exceeds p_{\infty}, a few diameters downstream of the nose. They explain why nose bluntness raises pressure, and therefore drag and heating, far downstream.

secs.t: Blunt bodies, standoff and entropy layers
secs.html:
Behind the near-normal part of a bow shock the flow is subsonic, so the blunt-body problem is elliptic there and was historically hard. Today it is solved by time-marching CFD. Billig’s correlations give the standoff distance \Delta and the shock curvature R_{c} at the axis:

\text{sphere: }\frac{\Delta}{R} = 0.143e^{3.24/M_{\infty}^{2}},\ \frac{R_{c}}{R} = 1.143e^{0.54/\left( M_{\infty} - 1 \right)^{1.2}};\quad\quad\text{cylinder: }\frac{\Delta}{R} = 0.386e^{4.67/M_{\infty}^{2}},\ \frac{R_{c}}{R} = 1.386e^{1.8/\left( M_{\infty} - 1 \right)^{0.75}},

with a hyperbolic shock shape x = R + \Delta - R_{c}\cot^{2}\beta\left\lbrack \sqrt{1 + y^{2}\tan^{2}\beta/R_{c}^{2}} - 1 \right\rbrack, where \beta is the asymptotic shock angle (the free-stream Mach angle). In dissociating gas the density ratio across the shock rises, and for spheres \Delta/R \approx 0.78\,\rho_{\infty}/\rho_{2}: the shock layer thins. The entropy layer generated by the nose is swallowed by the growing boundary layer over a distance that depends on bluntness and Reynolds number. Nose bluntness delays transition, up to a point beyond which transition “reverses” and moves forward again, an active research topic.

secs.t: Hypersonic configurations and the L/D barrier
secs.html:
Configuration Hypersonic L/D Character
Ballistic sphere or sphere-cone ≈ 0 Maximum drag, no control
Capsule with CG offset 0.25–0.4 Trimmed at incidence; bank-angle steering
Slender cone or biconic 1–2.5 Low drag; higher heating at nose
Lifting body / winged orbiter 1–2 Cross-range; complex heating
Waverider 3–6+ Shock attached along leading edges; high L/D; low volume

Küchemann’s empirical “L/D barrier” for conventional shapes is (L/D)_{\max} \approx 4\left( M_{\infty} + 3 \right)/M_{\infty}. Skin friction becomes a large share of drag, so viscous effects limit what inviscid design can promise. Volume efficiency, measured by Küchemann’s \tau = V/S_{plan}^{3/2}, competes with L/D.

Capsules trim at an angle of attack set by a lateral CG offset, flying at modest L/D with static stability provided by the CG lying ahead of the aerodynamic center. Slender bodies gain stability from flares or fins. Real-gas effects shift pressure distributions and hence trim. The Shuttle’s first flight needed about twice the predicted body-flap deflection for this reason (Chapter 43).

quiz.q: Find C_{p,\max} at M_{\infty} = 10 (γ = 1.4) and compare with the M_{\infty} \rightarrow \infty limit.
quiz.a: p_{02}/p_{\infty} = 129.2 at M = 10, giving C_{p,\max} = 1.832; the limit is 1.839.

quiz.q: Find Newtonian C_{L}, C_{D} and L/D for a flat plate at \alpha = 10^{\circ}.
quiz.a: C_{L} = 2\sin^{2}\alpha\cos\alpha = 0.0594; C_{D} = 2\sin^{3}\alpha = 0.0105; L/D = cot10^{\circ} = 5.67 (inviscid).

quiz.q: Find Küchemann’s L/D barrier at M_{\infty} = 6.
quiz.a: 4(9)/6 = 6.0.

quiz.q: Estimate the shock standoff of a sphere of radius 0.5 m at M_{\infty} = 6.
quiz.a: \Delta/R = 0.143e^{0.09} = 0.156, so \Delta = 7.8 cm.

quiz.q: Estimate β for a 10° wedge in the hypersonic limit, and compare with the exact value at M = 20.
quiz.a: Limit: 1.2 \times 10^{\circ} = 12^{\circ}. Exact at M = 20: {12.7}^{\circ}. The limit is approached only when M\theta \gg 1; here M\theta = 3.5.

quiz.q: Explain Mach-number independence physically, and when it fails.
quiz.a: At very high M, the shock angle and post-shock flow pattern depend on M_{\infty}\sin\beta only through terms that vanish as M_{\infty}^{- 2}, so the coefficients freeze. It fails when real-gas effects (dissociation, lower effective γ) or viscous and rarefied effects change with M and altitude.

quiz.q: For a 10° wedge at M = 8, compare the exact oblique-shock C_{p} with Newtonian and modified Newtonian values, and explain the difference.
quiz.a: Exact (\beta = {15.5}^{\circ}): C_{p} = 0.093. Newtonian 2\sin^{2}\theta: 0.060. Modified: 0.055. At K = M\tau = 1.4 the shock layer is not thin and the flow is not Newtonian. For wedges, the tangent-wedge method is exact.

quiz.q: Find the blast-wave pressure ratio on a blunt cylinder at M_{\infty} = 20, C_{D} = 1, x/d = 5.

chapters.goalsHtml: state what makes flow hypersonic; use the hypersonic shock limits; apply Newtonian and modified Newtonian theory, tangent-wedge and tangent-cone methods; use Mach-number independence, similarity and blast-wave theory; estimate shock standoff and shape; reason about hypersonic configurations, L/D and trim.

chapters.title: High-Temperature Gas Dynamics: Statistical Thermodynamics and Chemical Equilibrium

secs.html: Behind a normal shock at Mach 25 (orbital entry, T_{\infty} \approx 220 K), perfect-gas theory predicts about 27 000 K. The real equilibrium temperature is only about 6000–7000 K, because the energy goes into molecular vibration, dissociation and ionization rather than into translational motion. These processes absorb energy, change the molar mass and \gamma, increase the density behind shocks, alter heating and radiation, and, when they lag the flow, create nonequilibrium (Chapter 40).

The energy of a molecule is the sum of translational, rotational, vibrational and electronic parts. Classical equipartition gives \frac{1}{2}kT per quadratic energy term: translation \frac{3}{2}kT, rotation of a linear molecule kT (fully excited above a few kelvin; characteristic rotational temperatures N₂ 2.88 K, O₂ 2.08 K). Vibration is quantized: \varepsilon_{v} = \left( v + \frac{1}{2} \right)h\nu, with characteristic temperature \theta_{v} = h\nu/k (N₂ 3393 K, O₂ 2274 K, NO 2740 K).

Harmonic-oscillator vibrational energy per unit mass: e_{vib} = \frac{R\theta_{v}}{e^{\theta_{v}/T} - 1}, approaching RT (two quadratic terms) for T \gg \theta_{v}. Its heat capacity is c_{v,vib}/R = \frac{\left( \theta_{v}/T \right)^{2}e^{\theta_{v}/T}}{\left( e^{\theta_{v}/T} - 1 \right)^{2}}. A diatomic gas goes from c_{v} = \frac{5}{2}R (\gamma = 1.4) toward \frac{7}{2}R (\gamma = 9/7 \approx 1.29) as vibration is excited.

Electronic excitation matters for atoms with low-lying levels (atomic oxygen) and for radiation.

In equilibrium, the populations of energy states follow the Boltzmann distribution N_{j}/N = g_{j}e^{- \varepsilon_{j}/kT}/Q, with degeneracy g_{j} and partition function Q = \sum_{j}^{}g_{j}e^{- \varepsilon_{j}/kT}. For independent modes, Q = Q_{tr}Q_{rot}Q_{vib}Q_{el}, with

Q_{tr} = \left( \frac{2\pi mkT}{h^{2}} \right)^{3/2}V,\quad\quad Q_{rot} = \frac{T}{\sigma\theta_{r}},\quad\quad Q_{vib} = \frac{1}{1 - e^{- \theta_{v}/T}},\quad\quad Q_{el} = \sum_{i}^{}g_{i}e^{- \theta_{el,i}/T}.

Here \sigma is the symmetry number (2 for homonuclear, 1 for heteronuclear molecules), and energies are measured from the ground vibrational level. All thermodynamic properties follow from Q: for example e = RT^{2}(\partial lnQ/\partial T)_{V} per unit mass.

For dissociation A_{2} \rightleftharpoons 2A, statistical mechanics gives

K_{c} = \frac{n_{A}^{2}}{n_{A_{2}}} = \frac{\left( Q_{A}/V \right)^{2}}{Q_{A_{2}}/V}e^{- D_{0}/kT},\quad\quad K_{p} = K_{c}kT,

where D_{0} is the dissociation energy from the ground vibrational state. Worked example: for O₂ ⇌ 2O at 3000 K, with D_{0} = 5.116 eV, \theta_{r} = 2.08 K, \theta_{v} = 2274 K and the electronic levels of O and O₂, this gives K_{p} \approx 0.013 atm, in agreement with the JANAF tables. The Saha equation plays the same role for ionization:

\frac{n_{e}n_{i}}{n_{n}} = \left( \frac{2\pi m_{e}kT}{h^{2}} \right)^{3/2}\frac{2Q_{i}}{Q_{n}}e^{- I/kT}.

At 1 atm, O₂ dissociation begins near 2500 K and is nearly complete by about 4000 K. N₂ dissociation begins near 4000 K and is nearly complete by about 9000 K. NO forms at intermediate temperatures (a few percent). Ionization becomes significant above about 9000 K. Lower pressure shifts all thresholds downward (Le Chatelier). Standard models are 5-species (N₂, O₂, NO, N, O), 7-species (adding NO⁺ and e⁻) and 11-species (adding N₂⁺, O₂⁺, N⁺ and O⁺). Equilibrium properties are presented as h(p,T), Mollier charts or curve fits. The effective ratio \gamma_{eff} = h/e falls to about 1.1–1.2 in dissociating air.

Solve iteratively. Guess \varepsilon = \rho_{1}/\rho_{2} (start near 0.1). From the conservation laws,

p_{2} = p_{1} + \rho_{1}u_{1}^{2}(1 - \varepsilon),\quad\quad h_{2} = h_{1} + \frac{1}{2}u_{1}^{2}\left( 1 - \varepsilon^{2} \right).

Then find \rho_{2}\left( p_{2},h_{2} \right) from equilibrium properties, update \varepsilon, and repeat to convergence. Compared with perfect-gas results, T_{2} is far lower, \rho_{2}/\rho_{1} reaches 10–20, and p_{2} changes only slightly, because p_{2} \approx \rho_{1}u_{1}^{2}(1 - \varepsilon) is insensitive to \varepsilon when \varepsilon is small. That is why Newtonian pressure estimates survive real-gas effects while temperature and heating estimates do not.

Kinetic theory (Chapman–Enskog) gives the viscosity of a pure gas as \mu = \frac{5}{16}\frac{\sqrt{\pi mkT}}{\pi\sigma^{2}\Omega^{(2,2)*}}, with collision integrals \Omega^{*} computed from intermolecular potentials. Mixtures use Wilke or Gupta–Yos mixing rules. Thermal conductivity includes internal-mode contributions (Eucken correction) and, in reacting gas, a reactive conductivity: atoms diffuse toward cooler regions and release recombination energy there. Species diffusion follows the Stefan–Maxwell relations, often simplified to Fick’s law with an effective Lewis number of about 1.4 for air atoms. Diffusion of atoms to a catalytic wall is a major heat-transfer path (Chapter 41).

To compute rocket performance: (1) find the chamber equilibrium at p_{c} and the reactant enthalpy by Gibbs minimization (Chapter 17); (2) expand isentropically to p_{e}, either recomputing the equilibrium at each pressure (shifting) or holding the composition fixed (frozen); (3) obtain u_{e} = \sqrt{2\left( h_{c} - h_{e} \right)}. Shifting expansion recovers recombination energy, so its Isp is higher. Real nozzles freeze partway, roughly where the expansion rate outruns the recombination rate (Bray’s criterion), which places the result between the two limits.

High-temperature gases emit through bound–bound transitions (atomic N and O lines; molecular bands such as N₂⁺ first negative, NO β and γ, and CN violet in CO₂ atmospheres), bound–free and free–free transitions. A gas may be optically thin (emission escapes) or thick (self-absorbing). Shock-layer radiation becomes a major heating component for Earth entry above about 10 km/s (Chapter 41).

quiz.q: Compute the perfect-gas temperature behind a normal shock at M = 25 with T_{1} = 220 K. Why is it unphysical?
quiz.a: T_{2}/T_{1} = 122.5, so T_{2} \approx 26\, 900 K. Long before that temperature, energy flows into vibration, dissociation and ionization; the real equilibrium value is about a quarter of this.

quiz.q: For N₂ at 3000 K (\theta_{v} = 3390 K), compute e_{vib}/\left( R\theta_{v} \right), e_{vib} in kJ/kg (R = 296.8 J/(kg·K)) and c_{v,vib}/R.
quiz.a: \theta_{v}/T = 1.13. e_{vib}/\left( R\theta_{v} \right) = 1/\left( e^{1.13} - 1 \right) = 0.477; e_{vib} = 0.477(296.8)(3390) = 480 kJ/kg; c_{v,vib}/R = 0.900. Vibration is nearly fully excited at 3000 K.

quiz.q: What fraction of N₂ molecules occupy v = 1 relative to v = 0 at 3000 K?
With K_{p} = 0.013 atm for O₂ ⇌ 2O at 3000 K, find the dissociated fraction \alpha at 1 atm and at 0.01 atm, using K_{p} = 4\alpha^{2}p/\left( 1 - \alpha^{2} \right) (Quiz 17).
quiz.a: \alpha = \sqrt{K_{p}/\left( 4p + K_{p} \right)}: 0.057 at 1 atm and 0.50 at 0.01 atm. Low pressure strongly promotes dissociation.

quiz.q: Why does dissociation thin the shock layer?
quiz.a: Dissociation absorbs energy at nearly fixed pressure, which lowers the temperature and raises the density behind the shock. Mass conservation then requires a thinner layer to carry the same flow.

quiz.q: Why does shifting equilibrium give higher Isp than frozen flow?
quiz.a: During shifting expansion, atoms recombine and release chemical energy that adds to the jet’s kinetic energy. Frozen flow carries that energy out unconverted.

quiz.q: Equilibrium air at some state has h = 2.0 \times 10^{7} J/kg and e = 1.6 \times 10^{7} J/kg. Find \gamma_{eff}.
quiz.a: \gamma_{eff} = h/e = 1.25.

quiz.q: Why does the vibrational energy per unit mass approach RT rather than \frac{1}{2}RT at high temperature?
quiz.a: A harmonic oscillator has two quadratic energy terms (kinetic and potential), each contributing \frac{1}{2}kT when fully excited, i.e. kT per molecule or RT per unit mass.

chapters.goalsHtml: explain why high-temperature effects dominate hypersonic flows; compute energy-mode contributions and partition functions; derive equilibrium constants from statistical mechanics; describe equilibrium air composition; solve equilibrium normal shocks; estimate high-temperature transport properties; compute equilibrium and frozen nozzle expansions.

chapters.title: Thermochemical Nonequilibrium and Rarefied Gas Dynamics

secs.t: Time scales and the Damköhler number
secs.html:
Da = \frac{\tau_{flow}}{\tau_{chem}} (with \tau_{flow} = L/V). Da \gg 1: chemistry keeps pace (local equilibrium). Da \ll 1: composition is frozen. Da \sim 1: nonequilibrium, needing finite-rate models. The same test applies to vibrational relaxation with \tau_{vib}.

Binary scaling. Dissociation proceeds by two-body collisions, so the extent of reaction over a body depends on \rho_{\infty}L. A subscale model at the same velocity and the same \rho_{\infty}L reproduces nonequilibrium dissociation. Recombination is a three-body process (\propto \rho^{2}) and breaks binary scaling. No single facility condition reproduces both (Chapter 49).

Molecular speeds in equilibrium follow the Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution, f\left( \mathbf{c} \right) = n\left( \frac{m}{2\pi kT} \right)^{3/2}\exp\left( - \frac{mc^{2}}{2kT} \right), with mean speed \bar{c} = \sqrt{8kT/(\pi m)}. For hard spheres of diameter d, the mean free path is

\lambda = \frac{kT}{\sqrt{2}\pi d^{2}p} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}n\pi d^{2}},

about 68 nm in sea-level air and about 0.14 m at 100 km. The collision frequency is \bar{c}/\lambda. Elementary kinetic theory gives \mu \approx \frac{1}{2}\rho\bar{c}\lambda; Chapman–Enskog theory (Chapter 39) gives accurate values.

The Landau–Teller equation relaxes vibrational energy toward its equilibrium value at the translational temperature: de_{v}/dt = \left\lbrack e_{v}^{*}(T) - e_{v} \right\rbrack/\tau_{v}. The relaxation time follows the Millikan–White correlation,

p\tau_{MW} = exp\left\lbrack A\left( T^{- 1/3} - 0.015\,{\widetilde{\mu}}^{1/4} \right) - 18.42 \right\rbrack\ \ (atm \cdot s),\quad\quad A = 1.16 \times 10^{- 3}{\widetilde{\mu}}^{1/2}\theta_{v}^{4/3},

where \widetilde{\mu} is the collision pair’s reduced mass in atomic mass units. At very high temperature, Millikan–White gives unphysically short times. Park adds a collision-limited term \tau_{P} = 1/\left( n\sigma_{v}\bar{c} \right) with \sigma_{v} = 3 \times 10^{- 21}(50\, 000/T)^{2} m², and uses \tau_{v} = \tau_{MW} + \tau_{P}.

Each species obeys a continuity equation with diffusion and a chemical source, \partial\left( \rho Y_{i} \right)/\partial t + \nabla \cdot \left( \rho Y_{i}\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{J}_{i} \right) = {\dot{\omega}}_{i}. The source is built from law-of-mass-action rates (Chapter 17). Air mechanisms (for example Park’s) include dissociation of N₂, O₂ and NO by every collision partner; the Zeldovich exchange reactions N₂ + O ⇌ NO + N and NO + O ⇌ O₂ + N; and, at higher speeds, associative ionization N + O ⇌ NO⁺ + e⁻, the first source of electrons. High-temperature rate coefficients are uncertain by factors of 2 to 10, a leading source of uncertainty in heating and radiation predictions.

When vibration lags translation, a single temperature cannot describe the gas. Park’s two-temperature model carries T (translation and rotation) and T_{v} (vibration, electrons and electronic excitation). Dissociation rates are evaluated at a controlling temperature T_{a} = T^{q}T_{v}^{1 - q} (commonly q = 0.5, i.e. \sqrt{TT_{v}}), because molecules dissociate preferentially from high vibrational levels. Coupled vibration–dissociation models (such as Treanor–Marrone) account for the vibrational energy removed by dissociation. Ionized flows add an electron temperature T_{e}. The source terms couple through Landau–Teller exchange, chemistry–vibration terms and electron–vibration terms.

Behind a strong shock, translation equilibrates within a few collisions, giving a frozen jump with γ ≈ 1.4 and a very high translational temperature. Vibration and dissociation then absorb energy over the relaxation zone: T falls, T_{v} rises, and both approach equilibrium. Radiation from this zone can overshoot the equilibrium value. In rapidly expanding nozzles, recombination and vibrational de-excitation freeze. The free streams of arc jets and reflected-shock tunnels are therefore partly dissociated and vibrationally excited, which complicates simulation of flight (Chapter 49). Nonequilibrium also changes heating (through wall catalysis, Chapter 41), aerodynamic moments (Chapter 43) and scramjet ignition (Chapter 44).

Quantum chemistry provides potential energy surfaces for molecular collisions. Quasi-classical trajectory (QCT) calculations on those surfaces give state-specific rates, and direct molecular simulation tracks ensembles of collisions directly. Master equations with coarse-grained energy bins evolve non-Boltzmann distributions. These methods have shown that dissociation proceeds through a quasi-steady, depleted high-vibrational population, and they are steadily replacing empirical rates. This is an active research frontier (Chapter 53).

Regime Knudsen number \mathbf{Kn}\mathbf{=}\mathbf{\lambda}\mathbf{/}\mathbf{L} Model
Continuum < 0.001 Navier–Stokes with no-slip walls
Slip 0.001–0.1 Navier–Stokes with velocity-slip and temperature-jump walls
Transitional 0.1–10 Boltzmann equation; DSMC
Free molecular > 10 Collisionless kinetic theory

A local Knudsen number based on gradient length scales, Kn_{GLL} = (\lambda/Q)| abla Q|, detects continuum breakdown inside shocks, boundary layers and wakes even when the global Kn is small. The Boltzmann equation, \partial f/\partial t + \mathbf{c} \cdot abla f + \mathbf{F} \cdot abla_{c}f = (\partial f/\partial t)_{coll}, governs the velocity distribution f. The BGK model approximates collisions as relaxation toward a Maxwellian, and the Chapman–Enskog expansion recovers Navier–Stokes at first order in Kn.
