Maxwell’s slip condition is u_{s} = rac{2 - \sigma}{\sigma}\lambda\left( rac{\partial u}{\partial y} ight)_{w}, where \sigma is the tangential momentum accommodation coefficient, with an analogous temperature jump.

DSMC (Bird) represents the gas by simulated particles, each standing for many molecules. Each time step it (1) moves particles ballistically; (2) applies surface interactions (diffuse or specular reflection with accommodation); (3) sorts particles into cells; (4) selects collision pairs statistically (no-time-counter scheme) with cross-sections from variable-hard-sphere or variable-soft-sphere models fitted to viscosity, exchanging internal energy by the Larsen–Borgnakke method and reacting by chemistry models; (5) samples macroscopic properties. Validity requires a time step below the mean collision time, cells smaller than about \lambda/3, and enough particles per cell. Results carry statistical noise that falls as 1/\sqrt{N}. Hybrid CFD–DSMC methods couple the two across breakdown surfaces.

Without collisions, surface forces follow from the flux of incoming molecules and the reflection law. High-speed satellites with diffuse reflection have C_{D} \approx 2.0–2.2, the value used in orbital decay (Chapter 30). The speed ratio is S = V/\sqrt{2RT}. For S \gg 1, the heat flux is q \approx \alpha \cdot \frac{1}{2}\rho_{\infty}V_{\infty}^{3}, where \alpha is the energy accommodation coefficient (0.8–1). This sets the fairing-jettison criterion (Chapter 31). Bridging functions interpolate coefficients between the free-molecular and continuum limits.

quiz.q: Find the hard-sphere mean free path at 100 km (T = 195 K, p = 0.032 Pa, d = 3.7 \times 10^{- 10} m) and Kn for a 1 m capsule.
quiz.a: \lambda = 1.381 \times 10^{- 23}(195)/\left\lbrack \sqrt{2}\pi\left( 3.7 \times 10^{- 10} \right)^{2}(0.032) \right\rbrack = 0.14 m. Kn = 0.14: transitional, so continuum methods are questionable.

quiz.q: Gas flows at 5000 m/s over a 0.5 m body. Find Da for \tau_{chem} = 10^{- 6} s and for 10^{- 2} s, and classify each.
quiz.a: \tau_{flow} = 0.5/5000 = 10^{- 4} s. Da = 100 (near equilibrium) and Da = 0.01 (frozen).

quiz.q: A 1/10-scale model is tested at flight velocity. What density preserves binary scaling?
quiz.a: The model density must be 10 times the flight density, at the same velocity.

quiz.q: Find the mean molecular speed of N₂ at 300 K.
quiz.a: \bar{c} = \sqrt{8\left( 1.381 \times 10^{- 23} \right)(300)/\left\lbrack \pi(28.01)\left( 1.661 \times 10^{- 27} \right) \right\rbrack} = 476 m/s.

quiz.q: Estimate the free-molecular heat flux at 150 km (\rho = 2.07 \times 10^{- 9} kg/m³) at 7.8 km/s with \alpha = 1.
quiz.a: q = \frac{1}{2}\left( 2.07 \times 10^{- 9} \right)(7800)^{3} = 491 W/m².

quiz.q: Why does the translational temperature behind a strong shock overshoot its equilibrium value?
quiz.a: Translation equilibrates within a few collisions, while vibration and dissociation need hundreds to thousands. Immediately behind the shock, all the energy is in translation and rotation (a frozen jump with γ ≈ 1.4). As the slow modes absorb energy, T falls toward the equilibrium value.

quiz.q: With Landau–Teller relaxation and constant \tau_{v} = 10^{- 5} s, how long does e_{v} take to close 95% of the gap to equilibrium?
quiz.a: 1 - e^{- t/\tau} = 0.95 gives t = 3\tau = 3 \times 10^{- 5} s.

quiz.q: Use Millikan–White to estimate p\tau for N₂–N₂ at 5000 K (\widetilde{\mu} = 14, \theta_{v} = 3390 K).
quiz.a: A = 1.16 \times 10^{- 3}\sqrt{14}(3390)^{4/3} = 221. p\tau = exp\left\lbrack 221(0.0585 - 0.0290) - 18.42 \right\rbrack = 6.7 \times 10^{- 6} atm·s, i.e. about 7 μs at 1 atm.

chapters.goalsHtml: judge equilibrium versus nonequilibrium with the Damköhler number; use kinetic theory for mean free path and transport; model vibrational relaxation (Landau–Teller, Millikan–White, Park) and finite-rate air chemistry with multi-temperature models; recognize nonequilibrium phenomena in flight and in facilities; classify rarefaction by Knudsen number; understand the Boltzmann equation, DSMC and free-molecular aerodynamics.

chapters.title: Aerothermodynamics: Prediction of Aerodynamic Heating

secs.html:
At a vehicle surface,

q_{conv} + q_{chem} + \alpha_{r}q_{rad,in} = \varepsilon\sigma T_{w}^{4} + q_{cond} + q_{abl},

where the left side is incoming convective, chemical (catalytic recombination) and absorbed radiative flux. The right side is re-radiation, conduction into the structure and energy absorbed by ablation (Chapter 42). This balance is the boundary condition linking aerothermodynamics to thermal protection.

For an equilibrium laminar boundary layer at an axisymmetric stagnation point, Fay and Riddell (1958) obtained:

q_{w} = 0.763\, Pr^{- 0.6}\left( \rho_{e}\mu_{e} \right)^{0.4}\left( \rho_{w}\mu_{w} \right)^{0.1}\sqrt{\left( \frac{du_{e}}{dx} \right)_{s}}\,\left( h_{0e} - h_{w} \right)\left\lbrack 1 + \left( Le^{0.52} - 1 \right)\frac{h_{D}}{h_{0e}} \right\rbrack, where h_{D} is the dissociation enthalpy at the boundary-layer edge (use Le^{0.63} for a frozen boundary layer on a fully catalytic wall; replace 0.763 by 0.570 for a 2-D cylinder). Newtonian velocity gradient: \left( \frac{du_{e}}{dx} \right)_{s} = \frac{1}{R_{n}}\sqrt{\frac{2\left( p_{e} - p_{\infty} \right)}{\rho_{e}}}.

Because p_{e} \approx \rho_{\infty}V_{\infty}^{2}, the result collapses to the engineering form

q_{s} = k\sqrt{\frac{\rho_{\infty}}{R_{n}}}V_{\infty}^{3}\quad\text{(Sutton–Graves)},\quad\quad k = 1.7415 \times 10^{- 4}\ kg^{1/2}/m\ \text{(Earth air)},\quad 1.9027 \times 10^{- 4}\ \text{(Mars)},

in W/m². Two scalings drive vehicle design: heating rises as V^{3}, and it falls as R_{n}^{- 1/2}. Allen and Eggers’ insight (1953) was that a blunt body dissipates most of the entry energy into the shock-heated air rather than into the vehicle, which made ballistic entry survivable.

secs.t: Heating away from the stagnation point
secs.html: Over blunt bodies, Lees’ laminar theory gives the heating distribution in terms of the local pressure and the integrated running length. On a hemisphere, heating falls off around the body roughly as the local pressure does. On sharp cones and wedges, use the reference-temperature method (Chapter 37) with the Mangler transformation: laminar heating on a cone is \sqrt{3} times that on a flat plate at the same edge conditions (about 1.1–1.2 times for turbulent flow). Turbulent heating scales roughly as \rho^{0.8}V^{3}x^{- 0.2} and is 3–8 times the laminar value at the same location. Transition location is therefore often the largest single uncertainty in thermal-protection sizing.

At orbital speeds a large fraction of the boundary-layer edge enthalpy is chemical, stored in dissociated atoms. If the boundary layer is frozen (low density), atoms reach the wall intact, and the heat released depends on whether the surface catalyzes their recombination. The catalytic efficiency \gamma_{w} runs from 0 (non-catalytic) to 1 (fully catalytic). Non-catalytic surfaces, such as the Shuttle’s reaction-cured glass coating, can cut heating substantially relative to fully catalytic metals. A sudden change from a low-catalytic to a high-catalytic material produces a local catalytic overshoot in heating. Measured \gamma_{w} depends on temperature, pressure and surface state, and remains uncertain.

Shock-layer radiation (Chapter 39) grows steeply with velocity, roughly as V^{8} to V^{15}, and is important for Earth entry above about 10 km/s. It is significant for lunar return (11 km/s), dominant for faster returns, and overwhelming for giant-planet entries such as the Galileo probe at about 47 km/s. Radiative heating increases with nose radius (more radiating gas), while convective heating decreases, so an optimum nose radius exists. Correlations take the form q_{r} = CR_{n}^{a}\rho_{\infty}^{b}f(V) (Tauber–Sutton). Nonequilibrium overshoot, vacuum-ultraviolet emission and absorption by ablation products (“radiation blockage”) complicate prediction.

When an oblique shock (from a forebody, wing or inlet ramp) strikes a bow shock near a surface, Edney’s six interaction types result. In the Type IV interaction, a supersonic jet forms between shear layers and impinges on the surface, producing a very narrow heating peak of 10 to 30 times the undisturbed stagnation value. In 1967 the X-15A-2 suffered severe local burn-through when the shock from a dummy ramjet hung beneath the aircraft interacted with its pylon. Cowl lips, wing and fin leading edges and struts must be designed to avoid or survive Type III and IV interactions. Sweeping a leading edge by \Lambda reduces stagnation-line heating roughly as \cos^{n}\Lambda with n \approx 1–1.5.

Gaps and steps between tiles, protruding gap fillers (which can trip transition), cavities (heating concentrated on the downstream lip), protuberances, hinge lines and control-surface interactions (shock–boundary-layer interaction, Chapter 37), corner vortices and base flows with plume interaction all create local heating peaks. They are often designed with empirical amplification factors validated by test.

Reliable heat flux requires: a wall-normal spacing with cell Reynolds number Re_{cell} = \rho_{w}a_{w}\Delta y/\mu_{w} of order 1; grids aligned with the bow shock, to avoid spurious entropy and heating errors (including the “carbuncle”, Chapter 45); low-dissipation schemes near walls; appropriate thermochemical and catalytic boundary conditions; and turbulence and transition models. Validated predictions typically carry uncertainties of ±10–20% for laminar flow and considerably more for turbulent and interaction regions. Design margins and uncertainty quantification (Chapter 50) account for this. Fast engineering methods remain essential for coupling heating to trajectories.

secs.t: Peak heat flux versus heat load
secs.html: The peak heat flux q_{max} sets surface temperature and therefore material selection. The integrated heat load Q = \int q\, dt sets how much material is needed (ablator thickness or insulation depth). Steep entries give high q_{\max} and low Q; shallow or lifting entries give low q_{\max} and high Q. Trajectory and thermal-protection design must be optimized together (Chapter 43).

quiz.q: Use Sutton–Graves to find the stagnation heating for V = 7.5 km/s, \rho_{\infty} = 3 \times 10^{- 4} kg/m³ and R_{n} = 1 m.
How does this change if R_{n} = 0.01 m (a sharp leading edge)?
quiz.a: q \propto R_{n}^{- 1/2}, so it rises 10 times, to 12.7 MW/m². Sharp leading edges need high-conductivity materials, heat pipes or active cooling (Chapter 42).

quiz.q: Find the radiative-equilibrium wall temperature for Question 1 with \varepsilon = 0.85.
quiz.a: T_{w} = \left\lbrack 1.27 \times 10^{6}/\left( 0.85 \times 5.670 \times 10^{- 8} \right) \right\rbrack^{1/4} = 2270 K.

quiz.q: A heating pulse is q(t) = q_{\max}e^{- \left( t - t_{0} \right)^{2}/\tau^{2}} with q_{\max} = 1 MW/m² and \tau = 60 s. Find the heat load.
quiz.a: Q = q_{\max}\sqrt{\pi}\tau = 10^{6}(1.7725)(60) = 1.06 \times 10^{8} J/m² = 106 MJ/m².

quiz.q: Why does a large nose radius reduce convective heating but raise radiative heating?
quiz.a: Convective heating scales as R_{n}^{- 1/2} because the stagnation velocity gradient falls as the nose blunts. Radiative heating scales with the volume of hot, radiating gas in the shock layer, which grows with standoff distance and hence with R_{n}.

quiz.q: Why does transition matter so much for thermal-protection mass?
quiz.a: Turbulent heating is 3–8 times laminar, and heat load integrates it over time. A transition onset earlier in the trajectory, or farther forward on the body, multiplies the required ablator or insulation thickness.

quiz.q: Explain the catalytic-wall effect and why it depends on boundary-layer chemistry being frozen.
quiz.a: When the boundary layer is frozen, atoms do not recombine in the gas and carry their dissociation energy to the wall. A catalytic surface makes them recombine there and release that energy; a non-catalytic surface does not, so it receives less heat. In an equilibrium boundary layer, recombination occurs in the gas anyway and wall catalysis matters less.

quiz.q: A Type IV interaction amplifies 1.27 MW/m² by 10. What is the local flux, and what does it imply for design?
quiz.a: 12.7 MW/m², far beyond the steady capability of passive reusable materials. The geometry must avoid the interaction, or the region must be actively cooled or made ablative.

chapters.goalsHtml: write the surface energy balance; compute stagnation-point heating with Fay–Riddell and Sutton–Graves; estimate heating away from the stagnation point; quantify catalytic and radiative heating; recognize shock–shock interaction heating; set up CFD for reliable heating; distinguish peak heat flux from heat load.

chapters.title: Thermal Protection Systems and Extreme-Environment Materials

secs.html:
Class Mechanism Examples
Passive: heat sink Absorbs heat in its mass Early nose cones (copper, beryllium)
Passive: hot structure Structure runs hot and re-radiates C/C or CMC control surfaces
Passive: insulated structure High-emissivity, low-conductivity insulation over cool structure Shuttle tiles and blankets
Semi-passive: ablator Absorbs heat by pyrolysis, blowing and surface reactions; consumed PICA, Avcoat, carbon-phenolic
Semi-passive: heat pipe Spreads heat from a hot stagnation zone by phase change Liquid-metal leading-edge concepts
Active Coolant carries heat away (transpiration, film, convective) Fuel-cooled scramjet walls

Selection follows peak heat flux (material temperature limits), total heat load (thickness and mass), pressure and shear (mechanical erosion), reusability, mass and cost.

Safety and scope flag · Physical hazard

Concern. Beryllium, used in early heat-sink nose cones, is highly toxic as dust and can cause chronic beryllium disease. Carbon and ceramic fibers and dusts are respiratory hazards, and phenolic and epoxy resins and their solvents need chemical-hygiene controls.

Why it is flagged. Machining, sanding or burning thermal-protection and composite materials releases these hazards.

Learn it safely. University materials-laboratory courses; OSHA and NIOSH guidance; institutional chemical-hygiene and respiratory-protection programs.

The Space Shuttle used silica-fiber tiles (LI-900: 144 kg/m³, coated with high-emissivity, low-catalycity reaction-cured glass) for surfaces up to about 1260 °C; flexible insulation blankets for cooler areas; and reinforced carbon–carbon (RCC) for the nose cap and wing leading edges, up to about 1650 °C. Later toughened systems (TUFI, TUFROC) improved impact resistance, and metallic TPS (superalloy honeycomb panels) offers robustness at lower temperatures. Reusable insulators are brittle and susceptible to impact damage; Columbia was lost when foam debris breached an RCC leading-edge panel. They also need gap and step control, waterproofing and inspection.

Heated in depth, a charring ablator has three zones: virgin material; a pyrolysis zone, where the resin decomposes endothermically and releases gas; and a porous carbon char. The pyrolysis gases absorb heat as they percolate outward (transpiration) and then blow into the boundary layer, thickening it and reducing convective heating (blockage). At the surface, char recedes by oxidation (diffusion-limited at high temperature), sublimation (above about 3800 K for carbon) and mechanical removal (spallation, shear).

Blowing correction (film theory): \frac{C_{H}}{C_{H0}} = \frac{\ln(1 + 2\lambda B')}{2\lambda B'}, with B' = {\dot{m}}_{w}/\left( \rho_{e}u_{e}C_{H} \right), \lambda \approx 0.5 (laminar) or 0.4 (turbulent). Surface energy balance for an ablator: \rho_{e}u_{e}C_{H}\left( h_{r} - h_{w} \right) + {\dot{m}}_{c}h_{c} + {\dot{m}}_{g}h_{g} - \left( {\dot{m}}_{c} + {\dot{m}}_{g} \right)h_{w} + \alpha q_{rad} - \varepsilon\sigma T_{w}^{4} - q_{cond} = 0, where {\dot{m}}_{c} and {\dot{m}}_{g} are the char and pyrolysis-gas mass fluxes. Surface thermochemistry is tabulated as B'_{c}\left( B'_{g},T_{w},p \right) from equilibrium calculations.

For first sizing, the effective heat of ablation Q^{*} = q/\dot{m} converts a heat load into recession mass. Detailed design uses material-response codes (classically CMA and FIAT; the open-source PATO) coupled to the aerothermal environment.

Material Density (g/cm³) Heritage Character
Carbon-phenolic ≈ 1.4 Pioneer Venus, Galileo Extreme heat flux and pressure; heavy
PICA (phenolic-impregnated carbon ablator) ≈ 0.25 Stardust, Mars Science Laboratory Low density, high heat flux; brittle; tiled
Avcoat (epoxy-novolac in honeycomb) ≈ 0.5 Apollo, Orion Moderate heat flux; monolithic or block forms
SLA-561V (silicone-based) ≈ 0.26 Viking, Mars Pathfinder Low heat flux (Mars)
3-D woven (e.g. HEEET) ≈ 0.5–1.4 (dual layer) NASA development Tailorable for extreme entries

Stardust’s PICA heat shield survived a 12.9 km/s Earth return in 2006, the fastest Earth entry of any human-made object. The Galileo probe entered Jupiter at about 47 km/s, and its carbon-phenolic shield lost a large fraction of its mass to ablation.

• Nickel and cobalt superalloys: oxidation-resistant to about 1000 °C, but dense.
  • Refractory metals: niobium (C-103, with silicide coatings, to about 1370 °C), molybdenum, tantalum, tungsten. Strong when hot but oxidize catastrophically without coatings.
  • Carbon–carbon: retains strength above 2000 °C in inert gas, but oxidizes above about 450 °C and needs SiC conversion coatings and glass-forming sealants.
  • SiC-based CMCs (C/SiC, SiC/SiC): form protective silica scale (passive oxidation) to about 1500–1650 °C. At low oxygen partial pressure and high temperature, SiC instead forms volatile SiO (active oxidation) and recedes rapidly.
  • Ultra-high-temperature ceramics (ZrB₂, HfB₂ with SiC): melt above 3000 °C; form oxide scales plus borosilicate glass; candidates for sharp leading edges beyond 2000 °C. Their weaknesses are B₂O₃ evaporation, brittleness and thermal-shock sensitivity.
  • Oxide CMCs (alumina-based): immune to oxidation to roughly 1000–1200 °C.

Emissivity and catalycity are as important as strength, since they control the surface energy balance (Chapter 41).

Solve 1-D transient conduction (Chapter 19) through the layered stack (outer TPS, bond, structure) with the surface energy balance as the boundary condition. Size the thickness so that the bondline stays below its limit, for example about 177 °C (350 °F) for aluminum structure, or the adhesive’s limit. Include heat soak: bondline temperature often peaks after heating ends. A first estimate of the required depth is the thermal penetration depth \sqrt{\alpha t}. Margins cover heating uncertainty (±20–30%), material property scatter, recession uncertainty and manufacturing tolerances.

secs.t: Sharp leading edges and active cooling
secs.html:
Because q \propto R_{n}^{- 1/2}, small radii (for low drag and high L/D) mean severe heating. Options:

  • High-conductivity materials (UHTCs, C/C with high-conductivity fibers) conduct heat aft to cooler, radiating surfaces.
  • Heat pipes with a liquid-metal working fluid (sodium or lithium) in a refractory envelope evaporate at the hot tip and condense aft, making the edge nearly isothermal. Start-up from a frozen state is the main difficulty.
  • Transpiration cooling through porous walls is very effective but risks clogging and coolant mass.
  • Film and regenerative (fuel) cooling are used for scramjet combustors (Chapter 44).

RF-transparent windows (silica composites, silicon nitride) must keep stable dielectric properties when hot. Optical windows need thermal-shock resistance. Control surfaces need hot seals. Gaps must be filled and expansion accommodated without tripping transition (Chapter 41).

Arc jets test material response at realistic heat flux and enthalpy for minutes, but at lower pressure and shear than flight and with a nonequilibrium free stream (Chapter 49). Lasers and quartz lamps provide radiant heating without chemistry. Flight instrumentation (such as the MEDLI sensor suites on Mars entries) measures in-depth temperatures, pressures and recession. Nondestructive evaluation (CT, ultrasound, thermography) screens manufacturing defects.

quiz.q: A copper heat-sink nose (c = 385 J/(kg·K)) must absorb 50 MJ/m² with a 700 K allowable temperature rise. Find its areal mass.
quiz.a: m'' = Q/(c\Delta T) = 5 \times 10^{7}/(385 \times 700) = 186 kg/m², which is why heat sinks were abandoned for high-heat-load entries.

quiz.q: Evaluate the laminar blowing correction for B' = 1 and B' = 3.
quiz.a: \ln(1 + 1)/1 = 0.69 and \ln(1 + 3)/3 = 0.46: blowing cuts convective heating by 31% and 54%.

quiz.q: An ablator has Q^{*} = 30 MJ/kg and must absorb a 300 MJ/m² heat load by ablation. Find the mass loss per unit area.
quiz.a: 300/30 = 10 kg/m², plus insulation thickness to protect the bondline.

quiz.q: Find the radiative-equilibrium temperature of C/C (\varepsilon = 0.85) under 0.5 MW/m².
quiz.a: T = \left\lbrack 5 \times 10^{5}/\left( 0.85 \times 5.670 \times 10^{- 8} \right) \right\rbrack^{1/4} = 1795 K (about 1520 °C), within coated C/C capability for limited duration.

quiz.q: Estimate the thermal penetration depth into tile insulation (\alpha = 3.5 \times 10^{- 7} m²/s) during a 1500 s entry.
quiz.a: \sqrt{3.5 \times 10^{- 7} \times 1500} = 2.3 cm, so a few centimeters of insulation is the right order.

quiz.q: Distinguish passive and active oxidation of SiC and the conditions for each.
quiz.a: Passive oxidation (high oxygen partial pressure) grows a protective SiO₂ scale, slowing further attack. Active oxidation (low oxygen partial pressure, high temperature) produces gaseous SiO, so no protective scale forms and the material recedes rapidly.

quiz.q: Why must reusable insulating tiles combine low conductivity with high emissivity?
quiz.a: High emissivity rejects most of the incoming heat by radiation at a tolerable surface temperature (radiative equilibrium). Low conductivity limits the fraction that reaches the structure during the entry.

quiz.q: Suggest a TPS class for (a) a LEO-return capsule at 7.8 km/s, (b) a lunar-return capsule at 11 km/s, (c) a reusable vehicle cruising at Mach 6 for 30 minutes.
quiz.a: 1. A reusable insulator or a light ablator such as PICA-class. (b) A higher-heat-flux ablator (Avcoat or PICA-class), since radiative heating is now significant. (c) Hot structures and CMCs with reusable insulation, actively cooled leading edges and inlets, and fuel-cooled engine walls, because the heat load is long-duration and reuse is required.

chapters.goalsHtml: classify TPS concepts and select one by heat flux, heat load and reusability; explain ablation physics, the blowing correction and the ablating surface energy balance; know the major ablators, reusable insulators, CMCs, UHTCs and refractory metals and their failure modes; size TPS to bondline limits; design sharp leading edges; plan TPS testing.

chapters.title: Atmospheric Entry and Hypersonic Flight Mechanics

secs.html:
For planar entry over a non-rotating planet, with flight-path angle \gamma (negative descending) and bank angle \sigma (which tilts the lift vector):

\dot{V} = - \frac{D}{m} - g\sin\gamma,\quad\quad V\dot{\gamma} = \frac{L}{m}\cos\sigma - \left( g - \frac{V^{2}}{r} \right)\cos\gamma,\quad\quad\dot{h} = V\sin\gamma.

The vehicle is characterized by its ballistic coefficient \beta = m/\left( C_{D}A \right) and its lift-to-drag ratio L/D. Analytical work uses the exponential atmosphere \rho = \rho_{0}e^{- h/H} (Earth: \rho_{0} = 1.225 kg/m³, H \approx 7–8 km).

Neglect gravity relative to drag and hold \gamma constant. With dV/dt = - \rho V^{2}/(2\beta) and dh = V\sin\gamma\, dt:

V = V_{E}\exp\left( - \frac{\rho H}{2\beta\sin|\gamma|} \right). Peak deceleration a_{\max} = \frac{V_{E}^{2}\sin|\gamma|}{2eH} occurs at V = V_{E}e^{- 1/2} = 0.607V_{E} and altitude h = H\ln\frac{\rho_{0}H}{\beta\sin|\gamma|}; its value is independent of β. Peak stagnation heating (q \propto \sqrt{\rho}V^{3}) occurs at V = V_{E}e^{- 1/6} = 0.846V_{E}. Heat load Q = kV_{E}^{2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi\beta H}{R_{n}\sin|\gamma|}} (using the Sutton–Graves constant k).

Steep entries bring high deceleration and high peak heating but a smaller heat load. Heavy (high-β) vehicles decelerate lower in the atmosphere, where denser air raises the heating. Peak deceleration is independent of β because a heavier body simply reaches the same velocity-loss profile deeper, where the density is proportionally higher.

In equilibrium glide (\gamma \approx 0, \dot{\gamma} \approx 0), lift balances weight minus centrifugal relief: \frac{1}{2}\rho V^{2}C_{L}S/m = g\left( 1 - V^{2}/gr \right). Then

- \frac{dV}{dt} = \frac{g\left( 1 - V^{2}/gr \right)}{L/D},\quad\quad s = \frac{r}{2}\frac{L}{D}\ln\frac{1}{1 - V_{E}^{2}/(gr)}.

Deceleration is about g/(L/D): gentle (about 1.5g for the Shuttle). Peak heating is lower, but the long duration raises the heat load. Bank-angle modulation controls downrange, and bank reversals control crossrange (Chapter 46). The Shuttle’s crossrange requirement of about 2000 km drove its delta-wing design and hypersonic L/D of roughly 1–1.3.

secs.t: Skip entry and the entry corridor
secs.html: A lifting vehicle can rise out of the atmosphere after a first dip and re-enter later (skip entry), extending range for precise landing after lunar return. A lunar-return skip trajectory was demonstrated by the Chang’e 5-T1 test vehicle in 2014. The entry corridor lies between an overshoot boundary (too shallow: insufficient capture, skip-out) and an undershoot boundary (too steep: deceleration or heating limits exceeded). Its width grows with L/D and sets the delivery accuracy that navigation must achieve.

Capsules use large, blunt heat shields and trim at incidence through a CG offset (L/D about 0.25–0.4), steering by rolling the lift vector. Mars aeroshells use 60–70° sphere-cones.

  • Mars: the atmosphere is about 1% of Earth’s surface pressure, so landers remain supersonic at low altitude. Supersonic parachutes (deployed near Mach 2) limit landed mass to about a tonne with traditional systems. Responses include the sky crane (Curiosity, Perseverance), supersonic retropropulsion (demonstrated in Earth’s upper atmosphere by returning boosters) and inflatable decelerators (LOFTID flight test, 2022).
  • Venus: dense, hot atmosphere; high entry heating.
  • Titan: thick atmosphere and low gravity make descent easy; Huygens landed in 2005.
  • Giant planets: extreme velocities and radiative heating (Galileo).
  • Earth return from deep space at 12–13 km/s: Stardust, Hayabusa, OSIRIS-REx.

The Breguet range (Chapter 25), R = V\, I_{sp}(L/D)\ln\left( W_{i}/W_{f} \right), ranks cruise vehicles by the product V\, I_{sp}\,(L/D). A subsonic airliner (V \approx 250 m/s, I_{sp} \approx 6000 s on fuel, L/D \approx 17) achieves about 2.6 \times 10^{7} m. A Mach 5–6 hydrocarbon-scramjet cruiser (V \approx 1500–1800 m/s, I_{sp} \approx 1000–1500 s, L/D \approx 4–5) reaches only about (0.6–1.4) \times 10^{7} m. High speed is bought with range efficiency. Air-breathing vehicles also fly a constrained corridor of dynamic pressure (about 25–100 kPa) for engine operability and structural load (Chapter 44).

A waverider is designed backward from a known shock flow field: the flow behind a planar oblique shock (Nonweiler’s caret wing, 1959), a conical shock (cone-derived), or a family of local conical flows (osculating cones). Its leading edges lie on the shock, so the high-pressure flow is contained beneath the vehicle and does not spill around the edges, giving high L/D at the design condition. Off-design performance, viscous drag, leading-edge blunting for heating and limited internal volume all reduce the ideal benefit. Integrating the forebody with a scramjet inlet is a natural extension (Chapter 44).

Safety and scope flag · Dual-use (scope note)

Concern. The flight mechanics of hypersonic gliding and cruise (§43.3, §43.6, §43.7) also underlie hypersonic weapons.

Why it is flagged. Weapon-specific material gives direct weapons uplift, is generally classified or controlled under ITAR and the MTCR, and is not needed for civil space, research or transport vehicles. The physics in this chapter is the same openly published physics used for capsules, orbiters and research aircraft.

Omitted here. Trajectory shaping to evade defenses, maneuvering re-entry-vehicle design, warhead or payload integration, targeting, and weapon accuracy budgets.

Learn it safely. Open textbooks (Vinh, Busemann and Culp; Regan and Anandakrishnan; Appendix K) and university entry-flight-mechanics courses; NASA’s public technical reports. Weapon-specific work is done only inside authorized government and industry programs with clearances and export authorization. The policy and arms-control dimensions are studied through public academic and policy literature.

Flap effectiveness at hypersonic speeds is limited by separation and shock–boundary-layer interaction at large deflections. Reaction-control jets provide control at high altitude, where dynamic pressure is low. On the Shuttle’s first flight (1981), real-gas effects (lower effective γ) altered the pressure distribution on the expanding aft lower surface and produced an unpredicted nose-up pitching moment. Trim needed a body-flap deflection of about 16° instead of the predicted 7.5°. Cold wind tunnels (γ = 1.4) had missed it. Low-γ test gases (such as CF₄) and real-gas CFD now address such effects (Chapter 49).

secs.t: Six-degree-of-freedom flight dynamics and dynamic modes
secs.html:
In body axes with velocity components (u,v,w) and rates (p,q,r), the translational equations are m\left( \dot{u} + qw - rv \right) = X - mg\sin\theta and its analogs, and the rotational equations are Euler’s (Chapter 15) with aerodynamic moments L, M, N. Aerodynamic forces and moments are expanded about a trim condition in stability derivatives such as C_{m\alpha}, C_{mq}, C_{n\beta}, C_{l\beta}, C_{lp} and C_{nr}, plus control derivatives. For a symmetric vehicle, the linearized equations split into longitudinal and lateral-directional sets.

Longitudinal modes. Short period: a fast, usually well-damped oscillation in angle of attack and pitch rate, with \omega_{sp}^{2} \approx - M_{\alpha} + Z_{\alpha}M_{q}/V (dimensional derivatives). Phugoid: a slow exchange of kinetic and potential energy at nearly constant α; Lanchester’s approximation gives \omega_{ph} \approx \sqrt{2}\, g/V and \zeta_{ph} \approx 1/\left\lbrack \sqrt{2}(L/D) \right\rbrack. Lateral-directional modes. Roll subsidence (time constant - 1/L_{p}), Dutch roll (coupled yaw–roll oscillation set mainly by C_{n\beta} and C_{nr}) and the slow spiral mode.

Hypersonic flight changes the balance. Aerodynamic damping scales with \rho V, so at high altitude every mode is lightly damped and reaction-control jets or stability augmentation must supply damping. At the high angles of attack of entry, directional departure is judged by the dynamic directional-stability parameter C_{n\beta,dyn} = C_{n\beta}\cos\alpha - \left( I_{z}/I_{x} \right)C_{l\beta}\sin\alpha, which must be positive. Ailerons can produce adverse yaw that reverses the roll response, so the Shuttle relied on yaw jets until dynamic pressure grew. Air-breathing hypersonic vehicles often have an unstable short period and a non-minimum-phase response to elevator (Chapter 46).

secs.t: Energy-state methods for ascent and cruise
secs.html: Define the energy height E_{s} = h + V^{2}/(2g) and the specific excess power P_{s} = dE_{s}/dt = (T - D)V/W. Minimum-time climbs fly, at each energy level, the speed–altitude combination that maximizes P_{s} (Rutowski’s energy-state approximation, formalized by Bryson). Minimum-fuel climbs maximize P_{s}/{\dot{m}}_{f}. Air-breathing hypersonic ascent usually follows a near-constant dynamic-pressure path (about 25–100 kPa) that balances engine operability against structural and heating limits, then transitions to rocket power or zooms (trading kinetic for potential energy) at the top of the corridor.

quiz.q: A ballistic body enters at 7.5 km/s and γ = −5°, with H = 7.2 km. Find a_{\max} (in g) and the velocity at which it occurs.
quiz.a: a_{\max} = (7500)^{2}\sin 5^{\circ}/(2e \times 7200) = 125 m/s² = 12.8g, at V = 0.607(7500) = 4550 m/s.

quiz.q: For \beta = 300 kg/m² and \rho_{0} = 1.225 kg/m³, find the altitude of peak deceleration.
quiz.a: h = 7200\ln\left\lbrack 1.225 \times 7200/\left( 300\sin 5^{\circ} \right) \right\rbrack = 41.9 km.

quiz.q: In equilibrium glide at 6 km/s with L/D = 1 (g = 9.5 m/s², r = 6471 km), find the deceleration.
quiz.a: 9.5\left( 1 - 3.6 \times 10^{7}/\left( 9.5 \times 6.471 \times 10^{6} \right) \right)/1 = 3.94 m/s² (0.40g).

quiz.q: Find the equilibrium-glide range from 7.0 km/s with L/D = 2 (same g and r).
quiz.a: s = (6471/2)(2)\ln\left\lbrack 1/\left( 1 - 4.9 \times 10^{7}/6.147 \times 10^{7} \right) \right\rbrack = 10\, 300 km.

quiz.q: Find the Breguet range for V = 1800 m/s, I_{sp} = 1200 s, L/D = 4 and W_{i}/W_{f} = 1.5.
quiz.a: R = 1800(1200)(4)\ln 1.5 = 3.50 \times 10^{6} m = 3500 km.

quiz.q: Why is peak deceleration in ballistic entry independent of β?
quiz.a: The deceleration \rho V^{2}/(2\beta) peaks where \rho = \beta\sin|\gamma|/H. Substituting gives V_{E}^{2}\sin|\gamma|/(2eH), in which β cancels. A heavier body reaches the same peak, only lower in the atmosphere.

quiz.q: Show that peak stagnation heating in ballistic entry occurs at V = V_{E}e^{- 1/6}.
quiz.a: q \propto \rho^{1/2}V^{3} with V = V_{E}e^{- \rho H/\left( 2\beta\sin|\gamma| \right)}. Setting d\ln q/d\rho = \frac{1}{2\rho} - \frac{3H}{2\beta\sin|\gamma|} = 0 gives \rho = \beta\sin|\gamma|/(3H), hence V = V_{E}e^{- 1/6}.

quiz.q: What caused the Shuttle’s hypersonic pitching-moment anomaly, and what does it teach?
quiz.a: Real-gas effects lowered the effective γ, changing the pressure on the expanding aft lower surface and producing a nose-up moment that perfect-gas tunnel data had not shown. Ground tests that match Mach and Reynolds numbers can still miss real-gas physics; such effects must be simulated or computed explicitly.

quiz.q: Estimate the phugoid period at V = 1800 m/s, and its damping ratio for L/D = 4.
quiz.a: \omega_{ph} = \sqrt{2}(9.807)/1800 = 7.7 \times 10^{- 3} rad/s, a period of 815 s (about 14 minutes). \zeta_{ph} = 1/\left( \sqrt{2} \times 4 \right) = 0.18. The mode is slow and lightly damped, so it is handled by guidance and autopilot outer loops.

chapters.goalsHtml: derive Allen–Eggers ballistic entry results; analyze equilibrium-glide entry and its range; understand skip entry, entry corridors and capsule design; compare planetary entries; evaluate hypersonic cruise with the Breguet equation; explain waveriders; recognize real-gas effects on stability and trim.

chapters.title: Air-Breathing Hypersonic Propulsion: Ramjets, Scramjets and Combined Cycles

secs.html: An air-breathing engine carries only fuel, so its fuel-specific impulse far exceeds a rocket’s. Hydrogen scramjets reach roughly 1000–4000 s (falling with Mach number), against about 450 s for the best rockets. The price is low thrust per unit frontal area and per unit engine weight, operation only within an atmospheric corridor (dynamic pressure about 25–100 kPa), and tight integration of engine and airframe.

Uninstalled thrust: F = {\dot{m}}_{a}\left\lbrack (1 + f)u_{e} - u_{0} \right\rbrack + \left( p_{e} - p_{0} \right)A_{e}, with fuel–air ratio f. Specific thrust is F/{\dot{m}}_{a}; fuel-specific impulse I_{sp} = F/\left( {\dot{m}}_{f}g_{0} \right); thrust-specific fuel consumption {\dot{m}}_{f}/F.

Efficiencies: thermal \eta_{th} = (rate of kinetic-energy gain of the flow)/(fuel energy rate); propulsive \eta_{p} = Fu_{0}/(rate of kinetic-energy gain) \approx 2/\left( 1 + u_{e}/u_{0} \right); overall \eta_{o} = \eta_{th}\eta_{p} = \frac{Fu_{0}}{{\dot{m}}_{f}h_{PR}}. Hence I_{sp} = \frac{\eta_{o}h_{PR}}{g_{0}u_{0}}: at fixed overall efficiency, Isp falls inversely with flight speed.

Isentropic ram compression to near-zero velocity (T_{t0} = T_{0}\tau_{r}, \tau_{r} = 1 + \frac{\gamma - 1}{2}M_{0}^{2}), constant-pressure heat addition to T_{t4}, and isentropic expansion to p_{0} give M_{e} = M_{0} and T_{e}/T_{0} = T_{t4}/T_{t0}, hence:

\frac{F}{{\dot{m}}_{a}} = a_{0}M_{0}\left( \sqrt{\frac{T_{t4}}{T_{t0}}} - 1 \right)\ (f \ll 1),\quad\quad\eta_{th} = 1 - \frac{1}{\tau_{r}}.

Ramjets work from about Mach 2 (enough ram compression) to about Mach 5–6. At higher speed, T_{t0} approaches material and dissociation limits, and the total-pressure loss of the terminal normal shock in a real inlet grows rapidly.

At Mach 7, T_{t} \approx 2500 K. Decelerating the air to subsonic speed would raise its static temperature close to that value, near the onset of dissociation. Fuel added there would mostly dissociate products rather than raise temperature (Chapter 39), so thrust would collapse. Pressures and structural loads would also be extreme, and the normal-shock loss severe. Keeping the combustor flow supersonic (roughly Mach 2–3.5 at the combustor entrance for flight at Mach 6–10) holds static temperature and pressure within bounds. The price is a residence time of about a millisecond, in which fuel must mix and burn.

Inlet and forebody. The vehicle forebody and inlet ramps compress the air through a sequence of oblique shocks, ideally converging on the cowl lip at the design point (shock-on-lip). Compression is measured by the temperature ratio \psi = T_{3}/T_{0} and the kinetic-energy efficiency \eta_{KE} (the fraction of the kinetic energy that would be recovered by isentropic re-expansion to p_{0}). Off-design operation causes spillage and loss of mass capture. Boundary layers on the long forebody are thick and may be tripped deliberately so that they resist separation in the inlet.

Starting and unstart. An internal-contraction inlet starts only if the normal shock that forms on start-up can pass through the throat. The Kantrowitz limit is A_{t}/A_{1} \geq \left( A^{*}/A \right)|_{M_{2}}, where M_{2} is the Mach number behind a normal shock at the entrance Mach number M_{1}. Unstart is the sudden expulsion of the shock system ahead of the inlet, caused by excessive combustor back pressure (thermal choking), low Mach number or attitude excursions. It collapses thrust, produces violent transient loads and must be avoided or recovered by control.

Isolator. A nearly constant-area duct between inlet and combustor contains a pre-combustion shock train, which lets the combustor raise its pressure without unstarting the inlet. The Waltrup–Billig correlation estimates the length needed for a pressure rise p_{2}/p_{1} with incoming Mach M_{u}, momentum thickness \theta and duct diameter D: \frac{L\left( M_{u}^{2} - 1 \right)Re_{\theta}^{1/4}}{\sqrt{\theta D}} = 50\left( \frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}} - 1 \right) + 170\left( \frac{p_{2}}{p_{1}} - 1 \right)^{2}, typically 8–12 duct heights.

Combustor. Fuel enters by wall-normal jets (penetration governed by the jet-to-cross-flow momentum-flux ratio J = \left( \rho u^{2} \right)_{j}/\left( \rho u^{2} \right)_{\infty}), by ramps or struts that generate streamwise vorticity, or by combinations. Wall cavities provide recirculation zones for flame holding; pilots or plasma assist ignition. Heat release is limited by thermal choking (Chapter 24), so combustors diverge in area. In dual-mode operation, below about Mach 5–6, the shock train and heat release create a thermal throat with locally subsonic combustion (ramjet mode); above that, combustion is supersonic (scramjet mode). Hydrogen ignites quickly and is an excellent coolant but has very low density. Hydrocarbons (such as JP-7) are dense and storable but ignite slowly. Endothermic cracking of hydrocarbon fuels in cooling passages increases their heat-sink capacity.

Nozzle. A single-expansion ramp nozzle uses the vehicle afterbody as one wall, expanding the flow externally beyond the cowl. Recombination may freeze (Chapter 39), and the nozzle’s force and moment couple strongly to vehicle trim.

Heiser and Pratt’s method uses the stream thrust function S_{a} = u + p/(\rho u) = u\left( 1 + RT/u^{2} \right), which turns the momentum equation of each component into a simple balance. The analysis steps are: (1) freestream (station 0) to combustor entrance (station 3) with specified \psi and efficiency; (2) combustion (constant-pressure or constant-area idealization) with fuel enthalpy h_{PR}, combustion efficiency, wall friction and fuel momentum; (3) expansion to the exit with a nozzle efficiency; (4) thrust from the difference of exit and entrance stream thrusts.

Net thrust is a small difference of large numbers. Inlet drag and nozzle thrust are each many times the net thrust at high Mach. A 1% error in a component efficiency can change net thrust by 10% or more, and the margin shrinks as Mach number rises. Bookkeeping of forces between “engine” and “airframe” must be explicit and consistent.

No single air-breathing cycle runs from takeoff to orbit.

  • Turbine-based (TBCC): a turbojet to about Mach 3–4, then a ramjet or scramjet; mode transition and inlet/nozzle sharing are the main challenges.
  • Rocket-based (RBCC): an embedded rocket acts as an ejector at low speed, then the duct runs as a ramjet and scramjet, then as a rocket again in vacuum.
  • Air-turborocket, liquid-air cycle (heavy) and precooled engines, in which a precooler drops inlet air from about 1000 °C to cryogenic temperatures in milliseconds. The SABRE precooler concept was ground-tested at Mach 5-equivalent temperatures.

The forebody is the compression system and the afterbody is the nozzle, so aerodynamics and propulsion cannot be separated. Fuel volume (especially hydrogen) drives vehicle size. The fuel’s heat-sink capacity must exceed the vehicle’s integrated heat load. The operability envelope (angle of attack, dynamic pressure) constrains trajectories. Inlet behavior, thrust and pitching moment couple with elastic deformation, a stiff challenge for control (Chapter 46).

Publicly documented research flights: HyShot II (2002), the first measured supersonic combustion in flight; NASA’s X-43A (2004), hydrogen-fueled, reaching Mach 6.8 and then Mach 9.7 for about 10 s of powered flight each; the X-51A (2013), hydrocarbon-fueled, sustaining about 210 s of scramjet operation near Mach 5.1; and the US–Australian HIFiRE program (2009–2018) on transition and scramjet physics. Flight remains the only complete validation (Chapter 49).

Safety and scope flag · Dual-use and export control (scope note)

Concern. Scramjet and combined-cycle engine technology is used in hypersonic cruise missiles as well as in research and access-to-space vehicles. Hydrogen and high-pressure fuel systems also carry the physical hazards flagged in Chapters 27 and 54.

Why it is flagged. Detailed engine designs and test data are export-controlled (ITAR, EAR, MTCR) and give meaningful weapons uplift. The cycle analysis in this chapter is standard textbook material.

Omitted here. Engine-specific designs and dimensions, performance databases and test data beyond published summaries, and fuel or thermal-management designs for specific vehicles.

Learn it safely. University hypersonic-propulsion courses and fundamental-research programs; Heiser and Pratt, Curran and Murthy, and Segal (Appendix K); NASA’s public technical reports and AIAA publications. Detailed engine work is done inside export-compliant organizations.
Pulse-detonation, rotating-detonation and oblique-detonation-wave engines seek pressure gain and shorter combustors by burning in detonation waves (Chapter 47).

quiz.q: Find the ideal-ramjet thermal efficiency at M_{0} = 3.
quiz.a: 1 - 1/(1 + 0.2 \times 9) = 0.643.

quiz.q: At M_{0} = 7 with T_{0} = 230 K, find T_{t}, and the static temperature if the air is slowed only to M = 2.5.
quiz.a: T_{t} = 230(1 + 0.2 \times 49) = 2484 K. At M = 2.5, T = 2484/2.25 = 1104 K.

quiz.q: Find the ideal-ramjet specific thrust at M_{0} = 3, T_{0} = 220 K and T_{t4} = 2200 K.
quiz.a: a_{0} = 297.3 m/s and T_{t0} = 616 K, so F/\dot{m} = 297.3(3)\left( \sqrt{2200/616} - 1 \right) = 794 N·s/kg.

quiz.q: Air enters a constant-area combustor at M = 2.5 with T_{t} = 2484 K (flight at Mach 7). Find the maximum T_{t} before thermal choking, and the corresponding hydrogen fuel–air and equivalence ratios (c_{p} = 1200 J/(kg·K), h_{PR} = 120 MJ/kg, f_{st} = 0.0292).
quiz.a: T_{t}^{*} = 2484/0.7101 = 3498 K, a rise of 1014 K. f = c_{p}\Delta T_{t}/h_{PR} = 0.0101, so \phi \approx 0.35. A constant-area combustor chokes well short of stoichiometric fueling, which is why combustors diverge.

quiz.q: An engine gives 10 kN at u_{0} = 2000 m/s while burning 0.5 kg/s of hydrogen. Find \eta_{o} and I_{sp}.
quiz.a: \eta_{o} = \left( 10^{4} \right)(2000)/\left( 0.5 \times 1.2 \times 10^{8} \right) = 0.333. I_{sp} = 10^{4}/(0.5 \times 9.807) = 2039 s.

quiz.q: What does an isolator do, and why does a dual-mode scramjet need one?
quiz.a: The isolator holds the shock train that raises pressure from inlet to combustor. It keeps combustor back-pressure from reaching and unstarting the inlet, and it lets the engine move between ramjet and scramjet modes.

quiz.q: Find the Kantrowitz minimum throat-to-entrance area ratio for M_{1} = 4 (γ = 1.4).
quiz.a: M_{2} = 0.435 behind the normal shock, and \left( A^{*}/A \right)|_{M_{2}} = 0.672. So A_{t}/A_{1} \geq 0.672: at most about 1.49:1 internal contraction for self-starting.

quiz.q: Why does dissociation in the combustor reduce thrust, and when is the energy recovered?
quiz.a: Energy stored in dissociated species does not raise temperature or pressure in the combustor. It is recovered only if the species recombine in the nozzle before the flow freezes; finite-rate recombination leaves part unrecovered.

chapters.goalsHtml: define air-breathing performance measures and efficiencies; analyze the ideal ramjet; explain why scramjets are needed above about Mach 5–6; understand inlets (including starting and unstart), isolators, combustors, thermal choking and nozzles; perform stream-thrust cycle analysis; compare combined cycles; learn from the flight-research record.

chapters.title: Computational Fluid Dynamics for High-Speed Flows

secs.html: Finite differences approximate derivatives at points. Finite volumes integrate the conservation laws over cells, so conservation holds exactly in discrete form; most aerospace codes use them. Finite elements and discontinuous Galerkin methods use weak forms with local polynomials (DG offers high order on unstructured grids). A scheme must be consistent (truncation error → 0 as the grid is refined) and stable (errors stay bounded). By the Lax equivalence theorem, for well-posed linear problems, consistency plus stability is equivalent to convergence. The modified equation reveals what a scheme really solves. First-order upwinding of u_{t} + au_{x} = 0 actually solves u_{t} + au_{x} = \nu_{num}u_{xx} with numerical viscosity \nu_{num} = \frac{a\Delta x}{2}(1 - CFL). Central schemes instead show dispersive errors, which appear as oscillations near discontinuities.

secs.t: Model problems and the CFL condition
secs.html: CFL condition: the numerical domain of dependence must contain the physical one, so explicit schemes need CFL = \left( |u| + a \right)\Delta t/\Delta x \leq C_{\max} (of order 1). Von Neumann analysis substitutes Fourier modes to find amplification factors: forward-time, centered-space differencing is unconditionally unstable for advection and stable for diffusion only if \nu\Delta t/\Delta x^{2} \leq \frac{1}{2}.

Linear schemes that do not create new extrema (monotone) are at most first-order accurate. Sharp, oscillation-free shock capturing at higher order therefore requires nonlinear schemes, whose coefficients adapt to the solution through limiters.

Treat the cell averages as piecewise-constant states. At each interface, solve the Riemann problem (shock, contact and rarefaction structure; Chapter 36) and use its flux. Approximate Riemann solvers:

Solver Idea Notes
Roe Exact solution of a locally linearized problem Sharp shocks and contacts; needs an entropy fix; prone to the carbuncle instability
HLL / HLLE Two-wave approximation Very robust; smears contacts and shear layers
HLLC Restores the contact wave Robust and accurate; widely used
AUSM family (AUSM⁺, AUSM⁺-up) Splits convective and pressure fluxes Good at all speeds; low dissipation
Flux-vector splitting (Steger–Warming, van Leer) Splits fluxes by the signs of the eigenvalues Robust; diffusive
Central with artificial dissipation (JST) Central flux plus tuned dissipation Simple; needs careful tuning

MUSCL reconstructs a piecewise-linear profile in each cell, with slopes limited (minmod, van Leer, van Albada, superbee) so that the scheme is total-variation diminishing (TVD). ENO/WENO schemes build high-order reconstructions from the smoothest of several stencils (fifth-order WENO is standard for shock–turbulence problems). For DNS and LES with shocks, low-dissipation central schemes are blended with shock-capturing near discontinuities using shock sensors (for example Ducros’).

Explicit strong-stability-preserving Runge–Kutta methods (SSP-RK3) suit unsteady problems with small time steps. Implicit methods (backward Euler with linearized fluxes; LU-SGS; Newton–Krylov with GMRES and preconditioning) suit steady and stiff problems. Dual time stepping solves implicit unsteady problems. Local time stepping and multigrid accelerate convergence to steady state. Declare convergence only when residuals have dropped several orders of magnitude and integrated quantities (forces, heat flux) have stopped changing.

Structured grids give the best quality and can align with shocks; unstructured grids handle complex geometry, with prismatic layers near walls; adaptive refinement (including adjoint-based adaptation) concentrates resolution where it matters. Characteristic boundary conditions specify as many quantities as there are incoming characteristics. Wall conditions include no-slip, isothermal or radiative-equilibrium temperature, catalysis and slip (Chapter 40).

Heating-quality grids. Surface heat flux is far more grid-sensitive than pressure. Use wall spacing with Re_{cell} \approx 1, align the grid with the bow shock, avoid abrupt cell-size changes, and check that heating converges under refinement. The carbuncle (a spurious protrusion of the bow shock near the stagnation line with low-dissipation solvers) corrupts stagnation heating; cure it with HLLE- or AUSM-type fluxes, entropy fixes, rotated Riemann solvers or added dissipation at shocks.

Viscous fluxes use central differences. Low-Reynolds-number turbulence models need y^{+} \approx 1 at the first cell (Chapter 37). Compressible LES and DNS need high-order, low-dissipation numerics plus shock capturing, and careful inflow turbulence generation.

Add species continuity and vibrational-energy equations (Chapter 40), mixture thermodynamics (NASA polynomials), transport models and catalytic wall conditions. The chemical source terms are stiff, so they are treated point-implicitly or fully implicitly while keeping species mass fractions positive. Radiation is usually loosely coupled. Publicly documented production codes include NASA’s LAURA, DPLR and FUN3D, the University of Minnesota’s US3D, SU2-NEMO, the University of Queensland’s Eilmer, and OpenFOAM-based solvers. NASA’s VULCAN-CFD is widely used for scramjets.

• Code verification shows the equations are solved correctly. The method of manufactured solutions chooses an analytic solution, derives the source terms that make it exact, and confirms the theoretical order of accuracy under grid refinement.
  • Solution verification estimates numerical error in a specific result. With three grids refined by ratio r, the observed order is p = ln\left\lbrack \left( f_{3} - f_{2} \right)/\left( f_{2} - f_{1} \right) \right\rbrack/lnr, the Richardson estimate is f_{exact} \approx f_{1} + \left( f_{1} - f_{2} \right)/\left( r^{p} - 1 \right), and Roache’s Grid Convergence Index is GCI = F_{s}|\varepsilon|/\left( r^{p} - 1 \right), with F_{s} = 1.25 and \varepsilon the relative difference between the two finest grids.
  • Validation shows that the right equations were solved, by comparison with experiments of quantified uncertainty along a hierarchy from unit problems to complete systems (Chapters 49 and 52). Credibility frameworks such as NASA-STD-7009 formalize this.

Domain decomposition with MPI distributes the grid; load balance and communication set the scaling. Strong scaling holds the problem fixed while adding processors; weak scaling grows the problem with them. GPUs accelerate memory-bandwidth-bound CFD kernels. I/O, data management and reproducibility (fixed seeds, recorded versions) become first-class concerns at scale.

quiz.q: Find the maximum explicit time step for \Delta x = 1 mm, |u| + a = 2000 m/s and CFL = 0.8.
quiz.a: \Delta t = 0.8\left( 10^{- 3} \right)/2000 = 4 \times 10^{- 7} s.

quiz.q: Three grids (r = 2) give f_{1} = 1.000 (finest), f_{2} = 1.010 and f_{3} = 1.050. Find p, the Richardson estimate and the fine-grid GCI.
quiz.a: p = ln(0.04/0.01)/ln2 = 2. f_{exact} \approx 1.000 - 0.010/3 = 0.9967. GCI = 1.25(0.01)/3 = 0.42\%.

quiz.q: Find the numerical viscosity of first-order upwinding for a = 1, \Delta x = 0.01 and CFL = 0.5.
Find the wall spacing for Re_{cell} = 1 with \rho_{w} = 0.01 kg/m³, a_{w} = 300 m/s and \mu_{w} = 1.8 \times 10^{- 5} Pa·s.
quiz.a: \Delta y = \mu/(\rho a) = 1.8 \times 10^{- 5}/(0.01 \times 300) = 6 μm.

quiz.q: State Godunov’s order-barrier theorem and its consequence for scheme design.
quiz.a: Linear monotonicity-preserving schemes are at most first-order accurate. High resolution without oscillations therefore needs nonlinear, solution-dependent schemes (limiters, WENO).

quiz.q: What is the carbuncle phenomenon, and how is it cured?
quiz.a: A spurious bulge or “pimple” on a captured bow shock near the stagnation line, from insufficient cross-flow dissipation in low-dissipation solvers on shock-aligned grids. Cures: HLLE- or AUSM-type fluxes near shocks, entropy fixes, rotated Riemann solvers or targeted added dissipation.

quiz.q: Use von Neumann analysis to show that forward-time, centered-space differencing is unstable for linear advection.
quiz.a: With u_{j}^{n} = G^{n}e^{ikj\Delta x}, G = 1 - i\, CFL\sin(k\Delta x), so |G|^{2} = 1 + {CFL}^{2}\sin^{2}(k\Delta x) > 1 for every nonzero mode and time step.

quiz.q: Which waves form in the Riemann problem of a shock tube, and which does each solver family resolve?
quiz.a: A shock into the driven gas, a contact discontinuity and an expansion fan into the driver. Roe and HLLC resolve all three; HLL smears the contact; flux-vector splitting is diffusive for contacts and shear layers.

chapters.goalsHtml: understand consistency, stability, convergence and numerical dissipation; apply the CFL condition; use Godunov-type methods, Riemann solvers and limiters; choose time integration; build grids and boundary conditions suited to shocks and heating; implement nonequilibrium chemistry; verify codes and solutions and validate models; use parallel computers.

chapters.title: Advanced Guidance, Navigation and Control: Estimation and Trajectory Optimization

secs.html:
For the linear model \mathbf{x}_{k} = \mathbf{F}\mathbf{x}_{k - 1} + \mathbf{G}\mathbf{u}_{k} + \mathbf{w}_{k} and \mathbf{z}_{k} = \mathbf{H}\mathbf{x}_{k} + \mathbf{v}_{k}, with white Gaussian noises of covariance \mathbf{Q} and \mathbf{R}:

Predict: {\widehat{\mathbf{x}}}^{-} = \mathbf{F}\widehat{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{Gu}, \quad\mathbf{P}^{-} = \mathbf{FP}\mathbf{F}^{T} + \mathbf{Q}. Update: \mathbf{K} = \mathbf{P}^{-}\mathbf{H}^{T}\left( \mathbf{H}\mathbf{P}^{-}\mathbf{H}^{T} + \mathbf{R} \right)^{- 1}, \quad\widehat{\mathbf{x}} = {\widehat{\mathbf{x}}}^{-} + \mathbf{K}\left( \mathbf{z} - \mathbf{H}{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}}^{-} \right), \quad\mathbf{P} = \left( \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{KH} \right)\mathbf{P}^{-}\left( \mathbf{I} - \mathbf{KH} \right)^{T} + \mathbf{KRK}^{T} (Joseph form, numerically robust).

For linear-Gaussian systems the filter is the minimum-mean-square-error estimator, and its innovations \mathbf{z} - \mathbf{H}{\widehat{\mathbf{x}}}^{-} form a white sequence. Tuning \mathbf{Q} and \mathbf{R} sets how much the filter trusts the model versus the measurements. Check consistency with the normalized estimation-error squared (in simulation, where truth is known) and the normalized innovation squared (in operation); both should follow their χ² distributions. States that are not observable cannot be estimated. Square-root and UD-factorized forms preserve positive-definite covariances in finite precision.

The extended Kalman filter linearizes the dynamics and measurements about the current estimate using Jacobians. It is efficient but can diverge under strong nonlinearity or poor initialization. The unscented Kalman filter propagates deterministically chosen sigma points through the nonlinear functions, capturing the mean and covariance to second order without Jacobians. Particle filters represent arbitrary (including multimodal) distributions by weighted samples, at higher cost. Attitude uses the multiplicative EKF on an error quaternion (Chapter 32). Smoothers (Rauch–Tung–Striebel) use all data, past and future, for post-flight trajectory reconstruction.

Inertial/GNSS integration is usually an error-state filter that estimates the INS errors and sensor biases (Chapter 34). Planetary landers add terrain-relative navigation, matching camera images to onboard maps (used by Mars 2020). Optical navigation uses stars, limbs and landmarks. Rendezvous uses lidar and cameras. During entry blackout, navigation is inertial only, so IMU quality and pre-blackout state accuracy set the error at exit.

Minimize J = \phi\left( \mathbf{x}\left( t_{f} \right),t_{f} \right) + \int_{t_{0}}^{t_{f}}L\left( \mathbf{x},\mathbf{u},t \right)\, dt subject to \dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{f}\left( \mathbf{x},\mathbf{u},t \right) and constraints. Form the Hamiltonian \mathcal{H} = L + \mathbf{\lambda}^{T}\mathbf{f}.

Necessary conditions: \dot{\mathbf{x}} = \partial\mathcal{H/}\partial\mathbf{\lambda}; \dot{\mathbf{\lambda}} = - \partial\mathcal{H/}\partial\mathbf{x}; \mathbf{u}^{*} = arg\min_{\mathbf{u} \in U}\mathcal{H} (so \partial\mathcal{H/}\partial\mathbf{u} = 0 where unconstrained); transversality \mathbf{\lambda}\left( t_{f} \right) = \partial\phi/\partial\mathbf{x} (plus multipliers for terminal constraints); \mathcal{H}\left( t_{f} \right) = - \partial\phi/\partial t_{f} for free final time.

When \mathcal{H} is linear in a bounded control, the optimum is bang-bang, switching where the switching function changes sign, unless that function vanishes over an interval (a singular arc). Goddard’s maximum-altitude sounding-rocket problem has such an arc, on which thrust is throttled to balance drag. For powered flight over a flat Earth in vacuum with constant gravity, minimizing time gives costates that make the thrust direction obey the linear tangent law \tan\theta = (a - bt)/(c - dt), which reduces to \tan\theta = a - bt for many problems (Chapter 31).

For \dot{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{Ax} + \mathbf{Bu} and J = \int\left( \mathbf{x}^{T}\mathbf{Qx} + \mathbf{u}^{T}\mathbf{Ru} \right)\, dt, the optimal control is \mathbf{u} = - \mathbf{Kx} with \mathbf{K} = \mathbf{R}^{- 1}\mathbf{B}^{T}\mathbf{P}, where \mathbf{P} solves the algebraic Riccati equation

\mathbf{A}^{T}\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{PA} - \mathbf{PBR}^{- 1}\mathbf{B}^{T}\mathbf{P} + \mathbf{Q} = 0.

Single-input LQR loops have guaranteed margins: gain margin from 1/2 to infinity and phase margin of at least 60°. LQG combines LQR with a Kalman filter (separation principle), but the combination has no guaranteed margins (Doyle, 1978). Robustness must be checked, and can be recovered by loop-transfer recovery.

Indirect methods solve the boundary-value problem defined by the necessary conditions, by single or multiple shooting. They are accurate but need good costate guesses. Direct methods transcribe the problem into a nonlinear program: collocation (trapezoidal, Hermite–Simpson) or pseudospectral methods (Legendre–Gauss–Radau, spectrally accurate for smooth problems), solved by SQP or interior-point codes with mesh refinement. Careful scaling of variables and constraints is essential.

Convex optimization for onboard guidance. Second-order cone programs are solved to global optimality in predictable time. Lossless convexification (Açıkmeşe and Ploen, 2007) relaxes the non-convex lower bound on thrust magnitude in powered descent and proves the relaxation exact, so fuel-optimal landing trajectories can be computed in real time. Successive convexification extends this to nonconvex problems such as aerodynamic descent.

In the atmosphere, open-loop pitch programs respect load limits (Chapter 31). In vacuum, closed-loop guidance re-solves the steering problem repeatedly. The Saturn V’s Iterative Guidance Mode and the Shuttle’s Powered Explicit Guidance (PEG) were built on linear-tangent steering with predictor–corrector updates of burn time and steering parameters toward the target orbit, and could re-target after an engine failure.

Entry vehicles steer by modulating bank angle: its magnitude controls the vertical lift (and hence downrange), and reversals of its sign control crossrange.

  • Apollo tracked a reference trajectory with a range predictor and decided whether to skip.
  • Shuttle built a drag-acceleration-versus-velocity reference that respected heating, load and equilibrium-glide limits. It tracked the profile through the linearized drag dynamics and reversed bank when the heading error exceeded a velocity-dependent deadband.
  • Numerical predictor–correctors integrate the remaining trajectory onboard for a candidate bank profile and correct it to reach the target. They are robust to large dispersions.

Guided entry let Mars Science Laboratory land within an ellipse of about 20 km by 7 km, far smaller than earlier unguided Mars landings.

Apollo’s lunar module used polynomial (quadratic-in-time acceleration) guidance to meet terminal position, velocity and acceleration targets. Zero-effort-miss/zero-effort-velocity feedback guidance commands, in uniform gravity,

\mathbf{a}_{cmd} = \frac{6}{t_{go}^{2}}\mathbf{ZEM} - \frac{2}{t_{go}}\mathbf{ZEV},

where ZEM and ZEV are the terminal position and velocity errors predicted if no further control were applied. This is energy-optimal for that model. Convex-optimization guidance with large diverts (G-FOLD) was flight-tested on terrestrial testbeds in 2012–2013. Reusable booster landing guidance has been publicly described as convex-optimization-based.

Safety and scope flag · Dual-use (scope note)

Concern. Guidance, navigation and control theory is shared by spacecraft and weapons.

Why it is flagged. Weapon-guidance functions give direct targeting uplift and are controlled. This chapter covers the guidance problems of civil spaceflight (ascent, entry, landing, rendezvous) and the estimation and control theory common to all fields.

Omitted here. Intercept and homing guidance laws, target tracking and engagement, terminal guidance for strike, and accuracy optimization for weapons.

Learn it safely. Graduate courses in optimal control, estimation and robust control, and the textbooks in Appendix K; the open sessions and archival papers of the AIAA Guidance, Navigation, and Control Conference. Weapon-specific guidance is studied only within authorized programs.

secs.t: Robust, scheduled, inversion-based and adaptive control
secs.html:
Uncertainty may be parametric or unstructured. H∞ synthesis minimizes worst-case gain from disturbances to errors, and μ-analysis certifies robustness to structured uncertainty. Across a flight envelope, controllers are gain-scheduled (or designed as linear parameter-varying systems). Nonlinear dynamic inversion cancels known dynamics; its incremental form (INDI) uses measured accelerations and is robust to model error. Adaptive control (model-reference, L1) adjusts gains online but complicates certification.

Air-breathing hypersonic vehicles are especially demanding. Their short-period mode is often unstable. The elevator-to-flight-path response is non-minimum-phase (the vehicle initially moves the wrong way). Thrust depends on angle of attack through the inlet. Low-frequency fuselage bending changes inlet conditions. Actuators are rate-limited, and unstart must be avoided as a hard constraint. Validation combines linear margin analysis, nonlinear Monte Carlo simulation and, increasingly, formal methods.

Onboard planning, fault-tolerant re-planning and learned policies (reinforcement learning, neural-network controllers) are research frontiers. Their safe use relies on runtime assurance: a verified simple controller that takes over when a monitor detects unsafe behavior (simplex architecture), and on formal verification of neural networks (Chapter 53).

quiz.q: A scalar filter has prior {\widehat{x}}^{-} = 10, P^{-} = 4 and measurement z = 12 with R = 1. Find K, \widehat{x} and P.
quiz.a: K = 4/(4 + 1) = 0.8; \widehat{x} = 10 + 0.8(2) = 11.6; P = (1 - 0.8)4 = 0.8.

quiz.q: With \mathbf{F} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}, \mathbf{P} = \mathbf{I} and \mathbf{Q} = 0, find \mathbf{P}^{-}.
quiz.a: \mathbf{P}^{-} = \mathbf{FF}^{T} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}: position uncertainty grows and becomes correlated with velocity.

quiz.q: Solve the scalar LQR problem for \dot{x} = x + u with q = r = 1: find P, K and the closed-loop pole.
quiz.a: 2P - P^{2} + 1 = 0 gives P = 1 + \sqrt{2} = 2.414. K = 2.414, and the closed-loop pole is 1 - 2.414 = - 1.414.

quiz.q: A double integrator \ddot{x} = u, |u| \leq 1, starts at x = 1, \dot{x} = 0. Find the minimum-time control to the origin, the switching point and the total time.
quiz.a: Bang-bang: u = - 1 for 1 s (reaching x = 0.5, \dot{x} = - 1), then u = + 1 for 1 s. The switch occurs at x = 0.5; total time 2 s.

quiz.q: Why does lossless convexification matter for flight implementation?
quiz.a: It turns a non-convex problem into a convex one with the same solution. Convex solvers converge to the global optimum in bounded, predictable time without an initial guess, which is what flight software certification and real-time operation require.

quiz.q: Why does entry guidance reverse the bank angle instead of commanding a lateral force directly?
quiz.a: A capsule or glider has one main control, the orientation of its lift vector about the velocity. The bank magnitude sets the vertical lift for downrange; the lateral component inevitably accumulates crossrange, so the sign is reversed periodically to keep the heading error within a deadband.

quiz.q: State the separation principle and Doyle’s caution about LQG robustness.
quiz.a: For linear-Gaussian systems, the optimal estimator and the optimal state-feedback controller can be designed independently and combined. The combined LQG loop can nevertheless have arbitrarily small stability margins, so robustness must be checked separately.

quiz.q: With t_{go} = 10 s, ZEM = 50 m and ZEV = −5 m/s along one axis, find the ZEM/ZEV acceleration command.
quiz.a: a = 6(50)/100 - 2( - 5)/10 = 3 + 1 = 4 m/s² (beyond gravity compensation).

chapters.goalsHtml: design and validate Kalman filters (linear, extended, unscented); integrate navigation sensors; apply Pontryagin’s principle and LQR/LQG; transcribe trajectory problems for numerical and convex optimization; understand ascent, entry and powered-descent guidance; apply robust, gain-scheduled, inversion-based and adaptive control to hypersonic vehicles.

chapters.title: Advanced Combustion: Turbulence, High Pressure, Instability and Detonation

secs.html: Non-premixed systems are organized by the mixture fraction Z, a conserved scalar; premixed systems by a progress variable c. Two dimensionless groups locate a flame’s regime: the Damköhler number Da = \tau_{flow}/\tau_{chem}, and the Karlovitz number Ka = \left( \delta_{L}/\eta \right)^{2}, which compares the laminar flame thickness with the Kolmogorov scale.

On the Borghi–Peters diagram, premixed flames are wrinkled or corrugated flamelets (Ka < 1), thin reaction zones (1 < Ka < 100, where small eddies enter the preheat zone) or broken reaction zones (Ka > 100). Models include eddy-dissipation concepts (mixing-limited), flamelet and flamelet/progress-variable methods (chemistry tabulated against Z, scalar dissipation and c), transported probability-density-function methods (exact chemistry closure, modeled mixing), conditional moment closure, and thickened-flame LES. Supersonic combustion adds compressibility, shock–flame interaction and autoignition-dominated stabilization, where flamelet assumptions often fail.

Compressibility suppresses mixing. For a shear layer between streams of speeds U_{1} and U_{2} (equal γ), the convective Mach number is M_{c} = \left( U_{1} - U_{2} \right)/\left( a_{1} + a_{2} \right). The growth rate, normalized by its incompressible value, falls to about 0.2–0.3 for M_{c} \gtrsim 1 (Papamoschou and Roshko). Scramjets therefore need mixing enhancement: streamwise vortices from ramps and struts, shock-induced (baroclinic) mixing and pulsed or angled jets.

secs.t: Ignition and flame holding in supersonic flow
secs.html: The ignition delay \tau_{ign} depends exponentially on temperature (and on pressure through chain-branching kinetics, Chapter 17). For hydrogen–air near 1000 K it is a fraction of a millisecond, much longer at lower temperatures, and longer still for hydrocarbons. The induction length u\tau_{ign} must fit inside the combustor. Cavity flame holders lengthen residence time; radicals generated in hot regions (“radical farming”) can trigger ignition downstream; plasma assistance shortens delays.

Above the critical pressure, surface tension vanishes and cryogenic propellants enter as dense, gas-like jets with steep density gradients rather than as droplets. Properties change sharply across a pseudo-boiling line. Real-gas equations of state (Peng–Robinson, Soave–Redlich–Kwong) and real-fluid transport are required. Staged-combustion engines at 20–30 MPa exceed the critical pressures of oxygen (5.04 MPa) and methane (4.60 MPa), so this regime is the norm in modern main chambers.

Liquid breakup is governed by the Weber number We = \rho_{g}u_{rel}^{2}d/\sigma (aerodynamic force over surface tension) and the Ohnesorge number Oh = \mu_{l}/\sqrt{\rho_{l}\sigma d} (viscous damping). Rising We moves breakup from bag to stripping to catastrophic regimes. Primary atomization of jets and sheets is followed by secondary droplet breakup. Spray quality is summarized by the Sauter mean diameter d_{32}; vaporization follows the d^{2} law (Chapter 17).

With unsteady heat release \dot{q}', the acoustic pressure obeys

\frac{1}{a^{2}}\frac{\partial^{2}p'}{\partial t^{2}} - \nabla^{2}p' = \frac{\gamma - 1}{a^{2}}\frac{\partial\dot{q}'}{\partial t}.

Rayleigh index R = \oint\int_{V}^{}p'\dot{q}'\, dV\, dt: oscillations grow if R > 0 exceeds acoustic losses (nozzle, walls, viscosity, radiation). Crocco’s n–τ model: \dot{q}'/\bar{\dot{q}} = n\, p'(t - \tau)/\bar{p}. A mode of frequency f is driven when the phase lag 2\pi f\tau lies within ±90° of a multiple of 360°.

Linear stability is analyzed with Helmholtz solvers or acoustic network models using measured or computed flame transfer functions. Instabilities may be linearly unstable (growing from noise) or triggered (stable to small but unstable to large perturbations, a subcritical bifurcation to a limit cycle). This is why bomb tests are used (Chapter 27). Mitigation: baffles, acoustic cavities, injector impedance tuning and added damping. Quantitative prediction remains a frontier, increasingly pursued with LES.

The Hugoniot curve of burned states (shifted by the heat release q) and the Rayleigh line from the initial state intersect where mass, momentum and energy are all conserved. The minimum-speed self-sustaining solution is the Chapman–Jouguet (CJ) detonation, where the Rayleigh line is tangent to the Hugoniot and the products leave at their local sound speed, the reacting analog of thermal choking (Chapter 24). For strong detonations, D_{CJ} \approx \sqrt{2\left( \gamma^{2} - 1 \right)q}. The ZND structure is a leading shock (the von Neumann spike, at about twice the CJ pressure), an induction zone, then a reaction zone. Real detonations are cellular, with transverse waves and triple points. Cell width \lambda measures detonability: about 1–2 mm for stoichiometric H₂–O₂ at 1 atm, about 1 cm for H₂–air, and tens of centimeters for methane–air. Detonations cannot pass through tubes narrower than a critical diameter of about 13\lambda. Deflagration-to-detonation transition (DDT) needs a run-up distance, which is a central safety concern.

Constant-volume and detonative heat addition (Humphrey or ZND cycles) are more efficient than constant-pressure (Brayton) heat addition (Chapter 16). A pulse-detonation engine fills, detonates and blows down cyclically, which limits its frequency. A rotating detonation engine (RDE) sustains one or more detonation waves running continuously around an annulus fed with propellant. Waves typically run somewhat below CJ speed, and the number of waves depends on injection and geometry. The difficulties are injector recovery and coupling, parasitic deflagration, high heat flux, and actually realizing net pressure gain. Rocket RDEs have been demonstrated in ground tests in the early 2020s. Oblique detonation wave engines stabilize a standing detonation on a wedge in hypersonic flow, promising very short combustors if the wave can be stabilized.

Safety and scope flag · Physical hazard

Concern. Detonation experiments produce extreme pressures, intense noise and fragment hazards. Test cells need blast protection, remote operation and strict procedures. Some experiments use regulated explosive initiators.

Why it is flagged. Rotating detonation engines and detonation research are legitimate propulsion science, but their hardware fails violently.

Omitted here. Initiator and explosive details.

Learn it safely. University and government combustion laboratories with formal safety programs; graduate research positions; the Combustion Institute and AIAA propulsion conferences.

quiz.q: Estimate D_{CJ} for q = 3 MJ/kg and \gamma = 1.25.
quiz.a: \sqrt{2(1.5625 - 1)\left( 3 \times 10^{6} \right)} = 1837 m/s.

quiz.q: Find the first longitudinal acoustic frequency of a 0.5 m chamber with a = 1100 m/s (closed–closed approximation).
quiz.a: f = a/(2L) = 1100 Hz.

quiz.q: For that mode, is an n–τ flame with \tau = 0.3 ms driving or damping? With \tau = 0.1 ms?
quiz.a: Phase lag = 360(1100)\left( 0.3 \times 10^{- 3} \right) = 119^{\circ}, beyond ±90°, so cos < 0: damping. With 0.1 ms, {39.6}^{\circ}: driving.

quiz.q: Streams at 1500 m/s (a = 600 m/s) and 500 m/s (a = 400 m/s) form a shear layer. Find M_{c} and the expected growth reduction.
quiz.a: M_{c} = 1000/1000 = 1.0, so growth is reduced to about 20–30% of the incompressible value.

quiz.q: Explain why compressibility reduces shear-layer growth and what that means for scramjet design.
quiz.a: At high convective Mach number, pressure fluctuations no longer communicate easily across the layer, which weakens the large-eddy entrainment that drives mixing. Scramjets therefore need active enhancement and longer combustors than incompressible scaling suggests.

quiz.q: Interpret the CJ condition as thermal choking.
quiz.a: As in Rayleigh flow, heat release drives the products toward M = 1 relative to the wave. The CJ wave releases exactly enough heat to bring the products to sonic speed, so downstream disturbances cannot overtake and weaken it: it is self-sustaining.

quiz.q: Why do injected cryogenic propellants form no droplets above their critical pressure?
quiz.a: Above the critical pressure, liquid and gas are no longer distinct phases. Surface tension, and with it the restoring force that forms droplets, vanishes, so the jet mixes as a dense fluid by diffusion and turbulence.

quiz.q: A flame has \delta_{L} = 0.5 mm in turbulence with \eta = 50 μm. Find Ka and the regime.
quiz.a: Ka = (0.5/0.05)^{2} = 100: the boundary between thin and broken reaction zones.

chapters.goalsHtml: classify turbulent combustion regimes and models; quantify compressible mixing and supersonic ignition; understand transcritical injection and atomization; analyze thermoacoustic instability (Rayleigh, n–τ, triggering); master detonation structure and CJ theory; evaluate pressure-gain combustion, including rotating detonation engines.

chapters.title: Plasma, Magnetohydrodynamics and Electric Propulsion

secs.html: A plasma is an ionized gas that is quasi-neutral over scales larger than the Debye length \lambda_{D} = \sqrt{\varepsilon_{0}kT_{e}/\left( n_{e}e^{2} \right)}. Electrons oscillate collectively at the plasma frequency \omega_{pe} = \sqrt{n_{e}e^{2}/\left( \varepsilon_{0}m_{e} \right)}, i.e. f_{pe} \approx 8.98\sqrt{n_{e}} Hz with n_{e} in m⁻³. In a magnetic field, electrons gyrate at \omega_{ce} = eB/m_{e} with Larmor radius r_{L} = m_{e}v_{\bot}/(eB). The Hall parameter \beta_{e} = \omega_{ce}/\nu_{e} (gyrofrequency over collision frequency) tells whether electrons are magnetized (\beta_{e} > 1). The electrical conductivity is \sigma = n_{e}e^{2}/\left( m_{e}\nu_{e} \right); in hypersonic shock layers it is typically tens to thousands of S/m.

Orbital entry produces shock-layer electron densities of 10^{17}–10^{20} m⁻³.

Blackout criterion: radio waves with f < f_{pe} are reflected or strongly attenuated. The critical density is n_{e,crit} = (f/8.98)^{2} m⁻³: about 6 \times 10^{16} m⁻³ at S-band (2.2 GHz) and 9 \times 10^{17} m⁻³ at X-band (8.4 GHz). Collisions add attenuation even below critical density.

Mitigation: higher frequencies (Ka-band and above); antennas in the base or wake, where densities are lower; relay geometry (the Shuttle communicated upward through its wake to relay satellites); slender, sharp shapes, which produce fewer electrons; injection of electrophilic quenchants; and applied magnetic fields that open “magnetic windows”. Navigation through blackout is inertial (Chapter 46).

The magnetic field evolves by the induction equation \partial\mathbf{B}/\partial t = \nabla \times \left( \mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{B} \right) + \frac{1}{\mu_{0}\sigma}\nabla^{2}\mathbf{B}. Two dimensionless groups govern MHD flow. The magnetic Reynolds number Rm = \mu_{0}\sigma UL (advection versus diffusion of the field) is small in most aerospace plasmas, so applied fields are barely distorted. The interaction (Stuart) parameter Q = \sigma B^{2}L/(\rho U) compares the Lorentz force \mathbf{j} \times \mathbf{B} with inertia. Hall currents and ion slip complicate real devices. Hypersonic applications include magnetoaerodynamic heat-flux and drag control during entry, MHD “energy bypass” for scramjets (extracting flow energy upstream of the combustor with an MHD generator and returning it downstream with an accelerator), and onboard power generation. The obstacles are air’s low conductivity (requiring seeding or nonequilibrium ionization) and magnet mass.

Electric propulsion separates the energy source (electric power P) from the propellant.

Jet power \frac{1}{2}\dot{m}v_{e}^{2} = \frac{1}{2}Fv_{e} = \eta P. Hence the thrust-to-power ratio is F/P = 2\eta/v_{e}: at fixed power, raising exhaust velocity lowers thrust proportionally.
